questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend, not one number. Mentation, urine output, and temperature moving toward baseline count as response, and persistent signs of poor perfusion still call for escalation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The temperature drop is the eye catcher, and it pulls toward calling the whole picture a success. Judge each finding on its own trend: two perfusion signs have not moved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare each finding with last evening
steps.detail: Mentation, urine output, and temperature have moved toward baseline.
Capillary refill and skin findings are unchanged.
Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

elimination.verdict: C, E.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with an infected leg wound. Which new finding indicates that the infection has become systemic?

options.text: Thick yellow drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: New pus shows the wound infection is worsening and is reported, but pus is a local sign.

options.text: Pain at the wound rising to 6 of 10
options.rationale: Pain at the site is a local sign. Rising pain is a change from baseline, but it does not show spread to the whole body.

options.text: Warmth at the wound edges, unchanged since morning
options.rationale: Warmth at the site is a local sign, and it has not changed. Nothing here shows a systemic response.

options.text: New chills, malaise, and a fever
options.rationale: Fever, chills, and malaise are primary indicators of systemic infection. Spreading redness from the wound would also suggest systemic spread.

questions.takeaway: Pain, swelling, heat, redness, and pus at the site describe local infection. Fever with chills and malaise means the infection now involves the whole body.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A is the tempting answer because the wound now drains pus. The stem asks about systemic spread, so look for the option whose findings are outside the wound.

steps.detail: Systemic, not simply worse.
Pus, warmth, and pain at the site are local signs.
Warmth that has not changed is still local.
New fever, chills, and malaise.

elimination.verdict: New chills, malaise, and fever.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with an infected foot wound with thick yellow drainage. Oral temperature is 38.6 °C and heart rate is 108/min. At 1000 the provider prescribed a wound culture, two sets of blood cultures, and an IV antimicrobial to start as soon as possible. Laboratory staff drew both sets of blood cultures at 1015. At 1030 the antimicrobial arrives on the unit, and the wound culture has not been obtained. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain the wound culture, then start the antimicrobial
options.rationale: Antimicrobial therapy should not begin until after the culture specimen is obtained. The wound culture is still outstanding, and collecting it takes minutes, so it comes first and the antimicrobial follows without delay.

options.text: Start the antimicrobial now that the blood cultures are drawn
options.rationale: Drawing the blood cultures first is correct, but the wound culture has not been obtained. Giving the antimicrobial now can keep the wound organism from growing and leave it unidentified.

options.text: Start the antimicrobial and obtain the wound culture at the next dressing change
options.rationale: This delays the wound culture until after the antimicrobial is running, so the specimen may not grow the organism.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial until culture results identify the organism
options.rationale: Culture results take time. The specimen must be collected first, but the antimicrobial is started once it is obtained, not after results return.

questions.takeaway: Culture is the best way to identify the organism, and every prescribed specimen is collected before the first antimicrobial dose. Collecting it promptly lets the dose start without delay.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and B both protect the cultures and both start treatment quickly. The cue that decides is "the wound culture has not been obtained": blood cultures drawn first do not cover the wound specimen.

steps.detail: Wound culture and two sets of blood cultures.
Blood cultures drawn at 1015; wound culture not obtained.

steps.action: Apply the rule to each specimen
steps.detail: Antimicrobial therapy begins after the culture specimen is obtained.
Waiting for a dressing change or for results postpones treatment or loses the specimen.

elimination.verdict: Obtain the wound culture now, then start the antimicrobial.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a wound on the shin who walks with a limp because of pain in that leg. At 0800 the nurse assesses the leg for signs of inflammation. Which documentation entry best supports comparing the client's findings over time?

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm from wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Walks 10 m with a limp."
options.rationale: The entry names the side and time, measures and marks the redness, rates pain, and measures function. Each cardinal sign that is affected can be compared at the next assessment.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm from wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Dressing clean, dry, and intact."
options.rationale: This entry is well built, but the client's walking is limited and the entry leaves out function, a cardinal sign the next nurse needs to compare. A dressing note is not a sign of inflammation to trend.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness past the wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Walks 10 m in the hallway with a limp."
options.rationale: Function is included, but the redness is described only as past the wound edge, not measured, so a change in its size cannot be measured at the next check.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm, wound appears infected. Provider made aware. Walks with a limp."
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The entry labels a cause and leaves out pain and a measured distance.

questions.takeaway: A baseline entry names the side and time and measures each affected cardinal sign, including function, so later findings can be compared.
questions.strategy: A and B are both well built. The cue that decides is "walks with a limp because of pain in that leg": function is affected, so the entry must measure it.

steps.action: Read what the stem says is affected
steps.detail: Redness, pain, and walking.

steps.action: Check each entry for all three
steps.detail: Only A and C include walking.
C lacks a measured redness.
Redness alone does not establish infection.

elimination.verdict: The entry with time, measured and marked redness, pain rating, and walking distance.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: An 87 year old client with dementia who lives in a group home was admitted at 0900 today with an indwelling urinary catheter. Group home staff report that the client is usually confused about the day and year. The nurse compares findings at 1400 with findings at 1000.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing an older adult client with dementia and an indwelling urinary catheter. For each finding at 1400, indicate whether it requires follow up or no follow up is needed.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.3 °C, was 36.1 °C at 1000
rows.rationale: Older adults often have a lower baseline temperature and may have a fever at about 37.2 °C. A rise of 1.2 °C from this client's baseline can be a fever.

rows.text: Hard of hearing in both ears, as at 1000
rows.rationale: This finding is unchanged from 1000 and does not point to infection or dehydration.

rows.text: Heart rate 104 beats per minute, was 76 beats per minute at 1000
rows.rationale: A new rise in heart rate can accompany systemic infection and is a sign of dehydration in an older adult.

rows.text: Confused about the day and year, as at 1000
rows.rationale: Group home staff report this confusion as the client's usual baseline, and it is unchanged since 1000.

rows.text: Pulling at the catheter and trying to climb out of bed, was resting quietly at 1000
rows.rationale: Restlessness is a sign to assess for in an older adult with possible infection or dehydration, and it is new since 1000.

rows.text: Dark amber urine in the catheter bag, was pale yellow at 1000
rows.rationale: Darker urine is new and points to dehydration, which the nurse assesses for in an older adult with possible infection.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, compare each finding with the client's own baseline. A small temperature rise from a low baseline, a faster heart rate, new restlessness, and darker urine need follow up; long standing confusion that matches the reported baseline does not.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two rows are traps. 37.3 °C looks close to normal, but the client's baseline was 36.1 °C. Confusion looks alarming, but group home staff describe it as usual and it has not changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Anchor each row to its baseline
steps.detail: 1000 readings and the group home report.
Fever may appear near 37.2 °C; tachycardia, restlessness, and dark urine can signal infection or dehydration.
Hearing and the usual confusion.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 3, 5, and 6 require follow up. Rows 2 and 4 need no follow up.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is taking an exposure history from a client with an oral temperature of 38.6 °C, chills, and 6 loose stools in the past 24 hours. The loose stools began yesterday. Which findings help the nurse identify a possible source of the infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Returned from travel abroad 3 days before the loose stools began
options.rationale: Recent travel is part of the infection history because it can expose the client to organisms.

options.text: Returned from travel abroad 8 months ago, with no illness since then
options.rationale: Travel 8 months before an illness that began yesterday, with no illness in between, is too distant to point to this source.

options.text: A household member has had loose stools for 4 days
options.rationale: Exposure to ill contacts is a possible source, and the household member's illness began before the client's.

options.text: Ate grilled chicken at a picnic 2 days ago, cooked through and eaten right after grilling
options.rationale: Food is part of the exposure history, but food that was cooked through and eaten right away is not described as contaminated.

options.text: Drank untreated water from a stream while camping 4 days ago
options.rationale: Contaminated water is a possible source of infection, and the timing fits.

options.text: Cleans a pet turtle's tank each week without gloves
options.rationale: Animal contact is part of the exposure history.

questions.takeaway: The exposure history looks for where an organism came from: travel, ill contacts, contaminated food or water, and animal contact. The timing and the details decide whether a given exposure fits this illness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each category appears with a twin that fails on one detail: travel 8 months ago, and food that was cooked through and eaten right away. Ask of each whether it could have brought an organism to the client in the days before the illness began.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loose stools began yesterday.
Travel 3 days before onset, ill household member, stream water, turtle tank.
8 months ago with no illness since.
Cooked through and eaten right away.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 3 week old infant who is breastfed. The parent had a contagious viral illness as a child and recovered, and an older sibling at home developed the same illness yesterday. The parent says, "My breast milk passes my antibodies to the baby, so the baby is protected the way I am." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your milk gives the baby lasting immunity with memory, the same immunity you have."
options.rationale: Antibodies through breast milk are natural passive immunity. They are temporary and build no memory in the infant.

options.text: "Your antibodies protect the baby for now, so call only if the baby develops a fever."
options.rationale: The protection is real but temporary, and an infant's first sign of illness may be a subtle change such as poor feeding. Waiting for fever alone can miss it in an immature immune system.

options.text: "Your antibodies protect the baby for now, so the baby needs no extra watching at home."
options.rationale: The protection is real but temporary, and the infant's own immune system is immature. The infant's risk is higher than the parent's, so close watching is needed.

options.text: "This protection is temporary, and the baby's defenses are immature. Call with changes."
options.rationale: Natural passive immunity from breast milk is temporary, and infants have immature immune systems. With an ill sibling at home, the parent watches closely and calls early.

questions.takeaway: Antibodies in breast milk give an infant natural passive protection that is temporary. The infant's own immune system is immature, so an exposed infant still needs close watching.
questions.strategy: B, C, and D all agree that the milk antibodies protect the baby for now. The deciding cues are the age and the ill sibling: at 3 weeks the immune system is immature, so the infant needs close watching for any change, not only fever.

steps.detail: Antibodies in breast milk are natural passive: temporary, no memory.
A gives passive immunity memory.
A 3 week old has an immature immune system, so the risk is higher than the parent's.
No watching (C) and fever only (B) both miss early subtle changes.

elimination.verdict: D. Passive protection is temporary and the infant's immune system is immature, so watch closely and call early.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with a warm, red, swollen knee and pain of 6 of 10. The skin over the knee is intact, and oral temperature is 36.8 °C. The client first noticed the swelling on waking this morning, and no one has examined the knee before today. Which question should the nurse ask first?

options.text: "Have you taken anything for the pain today, and did it help at all?"
options.rationale: A medication history is part of the assessment, but it does not help tell whether the knee findings came from an injury or an infection.

options.text: "Is the knee more swollen now than it was when you first noticed it?"
options.rationale: Comparing findings over time matters, and this sounds like the baseline rule. But the swelling was first noticed only this morning, no one has examined the knee, and nothing was measured then, so a comparison gives little to act on. What caused the inflammation is still unknown, and that is the gap to fill first.

options.text: "Did you injure, twist, or strain the knee before the swelling started?"
options.rationale: Onset is already known, so the next history item is recent injury. Inflammation can occur after an injury without infection, so the answer helps separate inflammation from injury from inflammation with infection.

options.text: "Has anyone you live with been sick with an infection in the past week?"
options.rationale: Exposure history is reviewed, but it comes after recent injury. Warmth, redness, and swelling alone do not establish infection, so the nurse first asks about what could have caused the inflammation.

questions.takeaway: When a joint is warm, red, and swollen, the nurse asks about symptom onset and recent injury; when onset is already known, recent injury comes next. Inflammation can occur without infection, so injury history helps separate the two before later findings are compared with a baseline.
questions.strategy: B and C are both sound assessment questions. The cue that decides is "first noticed the swelling this morning, and no one has examined the knee before today": no earlier exam exists to compare with and the cause is still unknown, so asking about recent injury comes first.

steps.detail: The swelling was first noticed this morning and no earlier exam exists.
With no earlier exam, B adds little until the cause is explored.
Onset is known; recent injury comes before medication and exposure history.
Injury history helps tell inflammation without infection from infection.

elimination.verdict: Ask about recent injury first.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client, 84 years old, who has had irritation on both forearms for 2 days after using a new cleaning product without gloves. Yesterday the client scratched open a small area on one forearm. The nurse compares findings at 0800 today with findings at 0800 yesterday. Which findings today suggest that an infection has developed? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redness on both forearms, the same size as yesterday
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection, as with contact with an irritant. Redness on both forearms that has not changed fits the reaction to the cleaning product.

options.text: Oral temperature 37.3 °C, was 36.2 °C yesterday
options.rationale: Older adults often run a lower baseline temperature and may have a fever at about 37.2 °C. A rise of 1.1 °C from this client's own baseline is a sign of infection even though the number looks close to the usual range.

options.text: Itching on both forearms, the same as yesterday
options.rationale: Itching on both forearms, unchanged, fits the irritant reaction. It does not point to microorganisms invading the tissue.

options.text: Thick yellow drainage from the scratched area, was dry yesterday
options.rationale: The scratch broke the skin, the best barrier against infection. New pus at that site suggests that microorganisms have invaded and are multiplying.

options.text: Redness around the scratched area spreading past the line marked yesterday
options.rationale: Redness that spreads past a marked edge around a break in the skin is a change from baseline that suggests infection at that site.

options.text: Swelling on both forearms, the same as yesterday
options.rationale: Swelling on both forearms that has not changed is part of the inflammation from the irritant. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation can occur without infection, as with an irritant reaction on intact skin. Infection is suggested by changes from the client's baseline: new pus or spreading redness where the skin is broken, and in an older adult a temperature rise that may stay below the usual fever level.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate what is the same on both arms, which fits the irritant, from what changed at the one site where the skin is open. For an older adult, compare the temperature with the client's own baseline, not with the usual fever level.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unchanged redness, itching, and swelling on both arms fit the irritant reaction.
New pus and spreading redness at the scratch suggest invasion where the barrier broke.
A rise from 36.2 °C to 37.3 °C in an 84 year old can be a fever.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.scenario: A client was admitted 3 days ago with dehydration and has a peripheral IV catheter in the forearm that was placed on admission. At 0800 the IV site had no redness, and oral temperature was 36.8 °C. At 1400 the skin is red and warm along the vein for 6 cm above the insertion site, and the site is tender, with pain of 4 of 10. The client reports chills that began at 1300 and says, "I feel awful all over." Oral temperature is 38.5 °C, heart rate 112/min, and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. The client is alert and oriented, as at 0800.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing a client with a peripheral IV catheter who has new findings at 1400. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider now
options.rationale: Chills, malaise, and a new fever with a rising heart rate are primary signs that the infection has become systemic. These changes since 0800 are reported now.

options.text: Apply a warm compress and recheck the site in 4 hours
options.rationale: This treats the site as a local problem only. Fever, chills, and malaise show spread beyond the site, so waiting 4 hours delays care.

options.text: Obtain the prescribed cultures before the first antimicrobial dose
options.rationale: Culture identifies the organism, and the specimen is obtained before antimicrobial therapy begins so the result is accurate.

options.text: Flush the catheter to check that it is still patent
options.rationale: Patency is not the problem. Flushing an infected line does nothing for the infection and may push organisms into the bloodstream.

options.text: Document the site as inflamed and continue the infusion
options.rationale: Redness along the vein with fever and chills is more than inflammation, so documenting it as inflammation alone misses the infection.

options.text: Inflammation at the IV site without infection
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection, but it does not explain the fever, chills, and malaise that began today.

options.text: Infection at the IV site that has become systemic
options.rationale: Redness extending along the vein, with new fever, chills, malaise, and a fast heart rate, shows a local infection that has spread and become systemic.

options.text: Colonization of the IV catheter
options.rationale: Colonization means microorganisms are present without causing disease. This client has local and systemic signs of disease.

options.text: Worsening of the dehydration from admission
options.rationale: Dehydration can raise the heart rate, but it does not explain redness along the vein or chills.

options.text: Oral temperature and heart rate
options.rationale: These track the systemic response and show whether treatment is working.

options.text: Extent of redness along the vein, compared with 1400
options.rationale: Comparing the red area with this baseline shows whether the local infection is spreading.

options.text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate once a week
options.rationale: The sedimentation rate shows inflammation or infection somewhere in the body, but weekly checks are far too slow for a client who is changing within hours.

options.text: Skin turgor on the forearm only
options.rationale: Turgor relates to fluid status, and a single site check does not track the infection.

questions.takeaway: Fever, chills, and malaise are the primary signs that an infection has become systemic, and redness extending from a site supports spread. Report the change and obtain cultures before the first antimicrobial dose.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate the findings at the site from the findings in the whole body. The chills, malaise, and fever since 0800 are what move this past a local problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness extends 6 cm along the vein with tenderness.
New chills, malaise, a temperature of 38.5 °C, and heart rate 112/min point to systemic infection.
Report now and culture before antimicrobials; follow temperature, heart rate, and the red area.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and C; condition B; parameters A and B.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client, 83 years old, admitted with an infection that causes loose stools. The nurse compares findings at 1200 with findings at 0800. Which finding at 1200 requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Oral temperature 37.6 °C, was 37.4 °C at 0800
options.rationale: Older adults can have a fever at a lower reading than younger adults, so this is tempting. The client is already known to have an infection, and the change since 0800 is small.

options.text: Abdominal cramping 4 of 10, was 3 of 10 at 0800
options.rationale: Cramping is expected with an infection that causes loose stools, and the rise is small.

options.text: Restless and pulling at the gown, was calm at 0800
options.rationale: In an older adult, new restlessness or acute confusion can be the first sign of dehydration or a worsening infection. A change in behavior from 0800 is the priority to assess now.

options.text: Two loose stools since 0800, was three overnight
options.rationale: Loose stools are expected with this infection, and the frequency has not risen.

questions.takeaway: Older adults often show infection and dehydration through behavior before vital signs change much. New restlessness or acute confusion requires immediate follow up, even when the temperature barely moves.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask which change is new in kind, not just a little higher. Expected symptoms of a known infection that change slightly lose to a new change in behavior.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loose stools, cramping, and a slightly raised temperature fit the known infection.
A rise of 0.2 °C in a client already treated for infection is not the most urgent change.
New restlessness in an older adult can signal dehydration or a worsening infection.

elimination.verdict: C. New restlessness is the priority change.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching an older adult client about signs of infection. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will tell my family to watch for new confusion."
options.rationale: In older adults, new confusion or restlessness can be the first sign of infection. This statement is correct.

options.text: "A high fever will be my first sign of infection."
options.rationale: With aging, the immune response weakens and fever is often lower or absent. Waiting for a high fever can delay care, so this statement needs more teaching.

options.text: "I will keep up with my recommended vaccines."
options.rationale: Vaccines build active immunity, which helps protect an older adult whose immune response is weaker. This statement is correct.

options.text: "I will eat protein at every meal to help healing."
options.rationale: Adequate protein supports immune cell function and wound healing. This statement is correct.

questions.takeaway: Older adults face a weakening immune response with age, so infection may appear as new confusion or a change in behavior with little or no fever. Teach clients and families not to wait for a high fever.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that relies on a sign older adults often do not show.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three statements are correct, and one is not.
A weaker immune response with aging often blunts fever.
Expecting a high fever first can delay care.

elimination.verdict: B. Fever is often low or absent in older adults.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client with a slow healing pressure injury has a low prealbumin level. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Dietitian referral for added protein
options.rationale: A low prealbumin level points to poor protein status. Protein supports immune cell function and wound healing, so a dietitian referral to raise protein intake fits.

options.text: Daily vitamin C supplement by itself
options.rationale: Vitamins support healing, but a vitamin alone does not replace the missing protein that the low prealbumin shows.

options.text: Extra fruit juice between meals
options.rationale: Juice adds fluid and sugar but little protein, so it does not address the deficit.

options.text: Strict bed rest until the wound closes
options.rationale: Bed rest does not correct the nutrition problem and adds pressure risk.

questions.takeaway: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function and slows wound healing. A low prealbumin level points to poor protein status, so expect a plan to raise protein intake.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Match the intervention to the deficit the lab result shows. Option B is the right idea with one thing off: it supports healing but leaves the protein deficit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low prealbumin means poor protein status.
Protein supports immune cells and wound repair.
A dietitian referral adds protein; the others do not.

elimination.verdict: A. The deficit is protein.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with diabetes mellitus and reduced feeling in both feet. A cut on the sole of one foot was found 2 days ago. Today the redness is 1 cm around the cut, the same as yesterday, but warmth and swelling now reach the ankle, and the client cannot bear full weight on that foot. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C. The nurse has reported the findings to the provider. The client says, "If it were getting worse, it would hurt." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The redness has not spread, so the cut is not getting worse."
options.rationale: Redness is the sign most people watch, and it has not changed, which makes this tempting. Warmth and swelling now reach the ankle and the client cannot bear full weight, so the foot is worsening.

options.text: "Pain often returns as an infection worsens, so tell me if it starts."
options.rationale: This invites reporting, but reduced feeling in the feet can keep pain from ever appearing. Waiting for pain repeats the client's mistaken belief.

options.text: "High blood sugar raises infection risk, so watch for a fever."
options.rationale: The risk is real, but the client's temperature is 36.9 °C while the foot is already worse. This relies on another sign that may not appear and does not correct the belief about pain.

options.text: "Reduced feeling can hide pain, so swelling and warmth tell us more."
options.rationale: Reduced feeling in the feet can mask pain, one of the cardinal signs. The other signs, warmth, swelling, and decreased function, are worsening and are what the nurse and client must compare over time.

questions.takeaway: Assess all five cardinal signs and compare them with the client's baseline. When reduced feeling masks pain, warmth, swelling, and decreased function carry the decision, and no pain or fever does not mean the foot is healing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Several options rely on one sign: redness, pain, or fever. The deciding cue is the reduced feeling in the feet, which explains why pain is absent while warmth, swelling, and function are worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reduced feeling in both feet means pain may never appear.
Redness is unchanged, but warmth and swelling reach the ankle and weight bearing is lost.
Options A, B, and C each wait on redness, pain, or fever.

elimination.verdict: D. Reduced feeling hides pain, so the other signs decide.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client admitted after 2 days of vomiting has a blood pressure of 78/42 mm Hg. Which interpretation of the mean arterial pressure (MAP) is accurate?

options.text: 54 mm Hg, too low to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: Mean arterial pressure is the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3: (78 + 84) divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg, which is under 60 mm Hg, so perfusion of the major organs is at risk.

options.text: 60 mm Hg, at the lower limit for organ perfusion
options.rationale: This is the simple average of 78 and 42. The diastolic pressure is counted twice because the cycle spends more time in diastole, so the true value is lower.

options.text: 66 mm Hg, adequate to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: This doubles the systolic pressure instead of the diastolic pressure: (156 + 42) divided by 3. The diastolic pressure is the one counted twice.

options.text: 36 mm Hg, far too low to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: The interpretation that perfusion is at risk is right, but 36 mm Hg is the systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure, which is the pulse pressure, not the mean arterial pressure.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure equals the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3. A value of 60 to 70 mm Hg is necessary to maintain perfusion of the major body organs, so anything under 60 mm Hg puts them at risk.
questions.strategy: Write the formula before you look at the choices. The wrong numbers come from the common slips: averaging the two pressures, doubling the wrong one, or subtracting them. Then check the interpretation against 60 to 70 mm Hg.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 42 times 2 is 84.

steps.action: Add the systolic and divide by 3
steps.detail: 78 plus 84 is 162; 162 divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg.
54 mm Hg is below 60 to 70 mm Hg, so perfusion is at risk.
60 is the simple average, 66 doubles the systolic, and 36 is the pulse pressure.

elimination.verdict: A. 54 mm Hg, below the level needed to perfuse the major organs.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.scenario: The nurse is completing admission assessments for several older adult clients. None of the clients has known heart disease.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the age related change in the cardiovascular system that best explains it.

rows.text: A soft murmur at the apex in a client who reports no shortness of breath
rows.rationale: With age the mitral and aortic valves calcify. A murmur may be detected before any other symptom appears.

rows.text: Resting heart rate 56 beats per minute, with occasional premature ventricular contractions on the monitor
rows.rationale: Pacemaker cells decrease in number and conduction time increases. A rate below 60 beats per minute and premature ventricular contractions are common in older adults.

rows.text: Heart rate rises only to 96 beats per minute during a walk in the hallway, and the client stops to rest after 20 meters
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume and cardiac output during exercise, and the maximum heart rate with exercise is lower. The result is activity intolerance.

rows.text: Dizziness each time the client moves from lying to standing
rows.rationale: Less sensitive baroreceptors do not adjust the pressure quickly when position changes, which causes orthostatic dizziness.

rows.text: Lightheadedness 30 minutes after lunch, with a seated blood pressure of 98/60 mm Hg compared with 132/78 mm Hg before lunch
rows.rationale: A drop in pressure after eating is a postprandial change. It comes from the same less sensitive baroreceptors as the orthostatic change, not from the valves or the ventricle.

rows.text: During an exercise test, ejection fraction falls to 48%, although it was 62% at rest
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume, ejection fraction, and cardiac output during exercise, so the heart is less able to meet increased oxygen demands.

questions.takeaway: Five areas change with age: the valves calcify, pacemaker cells decrease, the left ventricle grows larger and stiffer, the large arteries stiffen, and the baroreceptors lose sensitivity. Each change has its own finding to assess.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Link each finding to the structure that produces it. Pressure drops with position or meals belong to the baroreceptors; a limited response to activity belongs to the left ventricle; rate and premature beats belong to the conduction system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A murmur with no symptoms points to calcified valves.
Below 60 with premature beats points to fewer pacemaker cells.
A limited rise in rate with early fatigue points to the left ventricle.
Both the positional and the after meal drops come from the baroreceptors.
A fall in ejection fraction with activity points to the stiff, enlarged left ventricle.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac valves; conduction system; left ventricle; baroreceptors; baroreceptors; left ventricle.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has been on bed rest for 3 days and takes a diuretic. Before the client first walks to the bathroom, the nurse checks orthostatic vital signs. Supine: blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg, heart rate 70/min. After 1 minute standing: blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, heart rate 80/min. The client denies dizziness. Which conclusion by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: The 16 mm Hg systolic fall rules out orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: The systolic fall is under 20 mm Hg, which makes this tempting, but either pressure can meet the definition. The diastolic pressure fell 12 mm Hg, which is enough on its own.

options.text: The absence of dizziness rules out orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: Dizziness is observed and recorded, but the definition rests on the measured changes. The absence of symptoms does not cancel a diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg with a rising heart rate.

options.text: The 16 mm Hg systolic fall confirms orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: The label is right but the reason is wrong. A systolic fall must be more than 20 mm Hg to count, so 16 mm Hg does not meet the definition by itself; the diastolic fall is what meets it.

options.text: The 12 mm Hg diastolic fall confirms orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: The diastolic pressure fell from 82 to 70 mm Hg, more than 10 mm Hg, while the heart rate rose from 70 to 80/min, about 14%. This meets the definition even though the systolic fall is under 20 mm Hg and the client feels well.

questions.takeaway: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall of more than 20 mm Hg systolic or more than 10 mm Hg diastolic, with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate. Either pressure can meet it, and the client does not have to feel dizzy.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options rest on a single number, and two of them are the same number read in opposite ways. Test each pressure against its own threshold: more than 20 mm Hg systolic or more than 10 mm Hg diastolic, with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate. Either pressure is enough, and symptoms are not required.

steps.detail: Systolic 134 to 118 is 16 mm Hg; diastolic 82 to 70 is 12 mm Hg; heart rate 70 to 80 is about 14%.
16 mm Hg is not more than 20 mm Hg, so the systolic fall alone confirms nothing. C has the right label for the wrong reason.
12 mm Hg is more than 10 mm Hg with a 14% rise in heart rate, so the definition is met. A is wrong because the systolic is not the only test.
No dizziness does not cancel a measured change. Eliminate B.

elimination.verdict: D. The diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg, with a 14% rise in heart rate, meets the definition.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client with a family history of heart disease smokes, is obese, rarely exercises, and does not drink alcohol. Which topics should the nurse teach? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stopping smoking, with resources to quit
options.rationale: Cigarette smoking is a modifiable risk factor, and this client smokes. It is one of the most useful changes the client can make.

options.text: Losing weight through diet changes
options.rationale: Obesity is a modifiable risk factor, and this client is obese. Diet change is a standard way to lower this risk.

options.text: Limiting alcohol to one drink a day
options.rationale: This client drinks no alcohol, so the topic does not fit this client. Teaching should target the risk factors the client actually has.

options.text: Increasing physical activity
options.rationale: Physical inactivity is a modifiable risk factor, and this client rarely exercises, so building up activity lowers risk.

options.text: Genetic testing to remove the family risk
options.rationale: Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor. No test removes it, so teaching targets the factors the client can change.

options.text: Waiting to change until symptoms appear
options.rationale: Risk reduction works before disease shows itself. Waiting for symptoms throws away the benefit of changing the modifiable factors now.

questions.takeaway: Age, sex assigned at birth, ethnic origin and family history cannot be changed. Smoking, physical inactivity, obesity and psychological factors can. Teach the modifiable factors this client actually has.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Test each option twice: can the factor be changed, and does this client have it? Only options that pass both belong in the teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Family history cannot be changed, and waiting for symptoms is not risk reduction. Eliminate E and F.
The client smokes, is obese and rarely exercises, so A, B and D fit. The client drinks no alcohol, so C does not.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D. Smoking, weight and activity are the modifiable factors this client has.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is performing a cardiovascular assessment on a client who is 72 years old. Which findings require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Point of maximal impulse at fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
options.rationale: This is the expected location of the point of maximal impulse.

options.text: An extra sound just after S2
options.rationale: This is an S3, heard during rapid ventricular filling. It may be normal under 35 years of age, but at 72 it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.

options.text: S1 and S2 heard clearly
options.rationale: S1 and S2 are the normal heart sounds.

options.text: Warm, pink skin on both hands
options.rationale: Warm, pink skin is an expected finding of skin color and temperature.

options.text: A new whooshing sound between S1 and S2
options.rationale: A whooshing sound between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur from turbulent flow, and it was not recorded at the last visit.

options.text: Equal radial pulses on both sides
options.rationale: Pulses that are equal on both sides are expected.

questions.takeaway: An S3 may be normal before 35 years of age but in an older adult may mean decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure. A murmur is a whooshing sound from turbulent flow, and a systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2.
questions.strategy: The S3 is the trap: it can be normal, so students leave it unselected. Read the client's age. At 72 the same sound points to the ventricle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Point of maximal impulse location, S1 and S2, skin, and pulses are all expected.

steps.action: Read the age with the S3
steps.detail: At 72 years an S3 is not expected.
The systolic murmur was not present at the last visit.

elimination.verdict: B, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client with long standing hypertension has a short, low pitched extra sound just before S1 at the apex. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: An S3 gallop from decreased ventricular compliance
options.rationale: An S3 can also reflect decreased compliance, but it is heard during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. A sound just before S1 is timed to atrial contraction.

options.text: An S4 gallop from a stiff, noncompliant ventricle
options.rationale: An S4 is heard during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. It may occur with hypertension.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub from an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: A friction rub comes from an inflamed pericardium. It is not tied to atrial contraction, and nothing in the stem suggests pericarditis.

options.text: A diastolic murmur from turbulent flow through a valve
options.rationale: A murmur is a whooshing or swishing sound from turbulent flow, not a short, low pitched extra sound.

questions.takeaway: S3 comes during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. S4 comes during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle, as seen with hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial infarction, or advancing age.
questions.strategy: A and B name nearly the same cause, so the cause cannot decide. Time the sound: just before S1 is atrial contraction, which is an S4.

steps.detail: Just before S1, which is atrial contraction.
A is an S3 after S2; B is an S4 before S1.
A rub comes from the pericardium, and a murmur is whooshing.

elimination.verdict: B. A sound just before S1 is an S4, which fits a stiff ventricle from long standing hypertension.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: Four clients each have a blood clot seen on imaging. Which client should the nurse monitor most closely for a stroke if the clot breaks loose?

options.text: A clot in the left atrium
options.rationale: A clot here moves with the blood across the mitral valve into the left ventricle and out through the aortic valve, which can carry it to the arteries of the head.

options.text: A clot in a deep calf vein
options.rationale: Venous blood returns to the right atrium, right ventricle and pulmonary arteries. A clot from the calf lodges in the lungs, not the brain.

options.text: A clot in the right atrium
options.rationale: From the right atrium the clot crosses the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonic valve to the lungs.

options.text: A clot in a pulmonary artery
options.rationale: The pulmonary artery carries blood into the lungs, so a clot here moves farther into the lung vessels. It cannot reach the left heart without passing through the lungs.

questions.takeaway: Blood leaves the left atrium through the mitral valve to the left ventricle, then through the aortic valve to the arteries of the head and body. A clot on the left side can reach the brain; a clot on the right side or in a vein goes to the lungs.
questions.strategy: Trace each clot forward along the path of blood flow. Only a clot that starts after the lungs, in the pulmonary veins or the left heart, can reach the arteries of the head.

steps.detail: The calf vein, right atrium and pulmonary artery all send blood to the lungs. Eliminate B, C and D.
Left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, arteries of the head. A remains.

elimination.verdict: A. A clot in the left atrium can travel through the aorta to the brain.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: The nurse hears a whooshing sound at the apex between S1 and S2. Which statements about this sound are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: A systolic murmur, heard during ventricular ejection
options.rationale: A murmur between S1 and S2 is systolic. That is the ejection phase, when ventricular pressure peaks and blood leaves the ventricles.

options.text: The aortic and pulmonic valves are open
options.rationale: S1 is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing; the aortic and pulmonic valves then open for ejection and stay open until S2.

options.text: Recorded by location, timing, radiation, and quality
options.rationale: Murmurs are described by location, timing, radiation and quality, so the record lets the next nurse tell whether it changes.

options.text: A diastolic murmur, heard during ventricular filling
options.rationale: Diastolic murmurs fall between S2 and S1, when the mitral and tricuspid valves are open and the ventricles fill. This sound falls between S1 and S2.

options.text: Caused by an inflamed pericardium rubbing the heart
options.rationale: That describes a pericardial friction rub. A murmur is turbulent blood flow in or near the heart.

options.text: Occurs during atrial contraction, just before S1
options.rationale: Atrial contraction comes at the end of diastole, with the P wave, before S1. This sound falls after S1.

questions.takeaway: Between S1 and S2 the ventricles eject: the mitral and tricuspid valves are closed and the aortic and pulmonic valves are open. A murmur there is systolic, and every murmur is described by location, timing, radiation and quality.
questions.strategy: Place the sound on the cardiac cycle first. Once you know it sits between S1 and S2, the valve positions and the phase follow, and the murmur is recorded the standard way.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After S1 and before S2 is systole and ejection. A and B fit; D and F describe diastole. Eliminate D and F.
Whooshing is turbulent flow, a murmur, not a rub. Eliminate E.
Murmurs are described by location, timing, radiation and quality. Keep C.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C. A systolic murmur, heard during ejection, recorded in full.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client has a blood clot in a deep vein of one calf. Which finding in that leg requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Cool, pale foot without a pedal pulse
options.rationale: Delivering oxygen and nutrients is the job of the arteries. A cool, pale foot with no pulse points to blocked arterial flow, which a vein clot does not explain.

options.text: Calf swollen and larger than the other calf
options.rationale: The veins return blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart. A clot blocks that return, so blood and fluid collect in the calf.

options.text: Warm, pink foot with brisk capillary refill
options.rationale: The arteries are not blocked, so oxygen rich blood still reaches the foot. This is expected with a vein clot.

options.text: Dorsalis pedis pulse equal to the other foot
options.rationale: Pulses come from arterial flow, which the vein clot does not block. An equal pulse is expected.

questions.takeaway: Veins return blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart; arteries deliver oxygen and nutrients. A vein clot causes swelling, while the foot stays warm and pink with a pulse. Signs of lost arterial flow need follow up.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by system: venous return or arterial delivery. A vein clot explains the venous findings only, so the arterial finding is the one that needs follow up.

steps.detail: Ask whether each finding reflects venous return or arterial delivery.
Swelling fits blocked return, and a warm pink foot with a pulse shows the arteries work. Eliminate B, C and D.

elimination.verdict: A. A cool, pale, pulseless foot signals an arterial problem, not a vein clot.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client who lost blood in a fall has a heart rate of 125/min and a stroke volume of 32 mL. Which statement about cardiac output is accurate?

options.text: It is 4.0 L/min, showing the heart is unaffected by the bleeding
options.rationale: The number is correct, but the low stroke volume shows the blood loss has affected the heart. The output is held up only by the fast rate.

options.text: It is below the expected range for an adult
options.rationale: Output depends on both factors. 125 times 32 mL is 4.0 L/min, which is within the expected range, because a fast rate can offset a low stroke volume.

options.text: It is 4.0 L/min, kept in range by the fast rate
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume: 125 times 32 mL is 4,000 mL, or 4.0 L/min. The fast rate is offsetting the low stroke volume.

options.text: It cannot be judged while the heart rate is above 100/min
options.rationale: Cardiac output can be calculated at any heart rate with the formula.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped from the left ventricle per minute, equal to heart rate times stroke volume. When stroke volume falls, a faster heart rate can keep output within range.
questions.strategy: Two options give the right number; only one gives the right meaning. A normal output with a low stroke volume and a fast rate means the heart is offsetting, not unaffected.

steps.detail: 125 times 32 mL is 4,000 mL per minute, or 4.0 L/min.
B calls the output low, and D says it cannot be judged; the formula gives 4.0 L/min.
Both say 4.0 L/min; only C explains why it is within range.

elimination.verdict: C. The fast heart rate is offsetting the low stroke volume.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: A client with long standing hypertension has a blood pressure of 188/110 mm Hg. Which new finding best indicates the left ventricle is ejecting less blood?

options.text: Blood pressure 192/112 mm Hg on recheck
options.rationale: A higher pressure raises afterload further, but by itself it does not show that stroke volume has fallen. It describes the load, not the heart's output.

options.text: Bounding radial pulses on both sides
options.rationale: A bounding pulse comes from an increased ejection of blood. That is the opposite of a ventricle that is ejecting less.

options.text: Heart rate regular and unchanged from last week
options.rationale: An unchanged heart rate gives no sign of falling output. It neither confirms nor rules out a change in stroke volume.

options.text: New fatigue after walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: High arterial pressure raises afterload, the resistance the ventricle must overcome. Without compensation, stroke volume and cardiac output fall, and new fatigue after mild activity is a sign of that low output.

questions.takeaway: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle pushes against, and it rises with arterial pressure and narrowed vessels. Without compensation, stroke volume falls, and fatigue after mild activity points to the low cardiac output.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask which option shows the result of high afterload, less blood ejected, rather than the high pressure itself. Look for a sign of low cardiac output.

steps.detail: A measures the pressure, the cause, not the ejection. Eliminate A.
Bounding pulses mean more blood ejected, the opposite. Eliminate B.
An unchanged heart rate shows nothing new. Eliminate C.

elimination.verdict: D. New fatigue with mild activity reflects a falling stroke volume against high afterload.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.scenario: The nurse is caring for a client in the emergency department who has pressure in the chest that began 5 hours ago and is now 6 of 10. Blood pressure 146/90 mm Hg, heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min. The point of care troponin I is 0.48 ng/mL.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Wait for the repeat troponin before reporting the first result
options.rationale: Repeat testing is planned, but a value this far above the reference is reported now, not after the next result.

options.text: Notify the provider of the troponin result now
options.rationale: A troponin I above 0.03 ng/mL indicates myocardial injury or infarction and is reported at once.

options.text: Prepare the client for an exercise ECG to look for silent disease
options.rationale: An exercise ECG stops when chest pain appears. This client has chest pressure now and a troponin showing injury.

options.text: Walk the client to the restroom before testing begins
options.rationale: Activity raises the heart's oxygen demand in a client with ongoing chest pressure and evidence of injury.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: Troponin is evaluated together with the symptoms and ECG changes, and a 12 lead ECG is obtained for chest pain.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension
options.rationale: No positional blood pressure change is described, and the pressure is above normal.

options.text: Pericarditis from an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: Pericarditis may produce a friction rub, but the troponin result points to injury of the heart muscle.

options.text: Elevated serum lipids
options.rationale: Lipids estimate long term risk. No lipid result is given, and they do not explain an acute rise in troponin.

options.text: Myocardial injury
options.rationale: Troponin is a heart muscle protein released into the blood when heart muscle is injured. A value above the reference with ongoing chest pressure points to myocardial injury.

options.text: Troponin repeated in 3 to 6 hours
options.rationale: After the first troponin, levels are assessed again in 3 to 6 hours.

options.text: Location of the point of maximal impulse
options.rationale: The point of maximal impulse is part of the physical assessment but does not track acute injury.

options.text: Chest pressure rating
options.rationale: The pain rating tracks whether the ischemic pain continues or eases.

options.text: Total cholesterol level
options.rationale: Cholesterol guides long term risk reduction, not the course of acute injury.

questions.takeaway: A troponin T or I above its reference indicates myocardial injury or infarction. Report it, obtain an ECG, and repeat troponin in 3 to 6 hours while tracking the pain.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the condition from the troponin result with the ongoing pressure, then choose actions that treat it as injury now and parameters that follow its course over hours.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.48 ng/mL is far above the reference of below 0.03 ng/mL.
Myocardial injury.
Report now and obtain a 12 lead ECG.
Repeat troponin in 3 to 6 hours and the chest pressure rating.

elimination.verdict: Myocardial injury; notify the provider and obtain a 12 lead ECG; monitor the repeat troponin and the chest pressure rating.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client in the emergency department whose chest pressure began 40 minutes ago while shoveling snow. The pressure is now 5 of 10. The point of care troponin I is 0.01 ng/mL. The client says, "The blood test is normal, so I want to go home." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "A normal troponin is a good sign, so an exercise ECG is next."
options.rationale: An exercise ECG does detect hidden coronary disease, but it stops when chest pain appears, and this client still has pressure rated 5 of 10. It also accepts the early normal troponin as reassuring.

options.text: "Troponin can take hours to rise, so the test will be repeated."
options.rationale: The pressure began only 40 minutes ago. Troponin is repeated in 3 to 6 hours, so one early normal value does not rule out heart muscle injury. This answers the belief behind the request to leave.

options.text: "Your provider will review the ECG and troponin before discharge."
options.rationale: Review by the provider is part of the plan, which makes this sound safe, but it lets the client believe one normal troponin can clear the way for discharge. Only 40 minutes have passed, so injury cannot be excluded yet.

options.text: "You have the right to leave, but you will need to sign a form."
options.rationale: A client may refuse care, which makes this tempting, but the decision is informed only after the false belief is corrected. The client thinks the test proved the heart is fine, and that belief is the problem.

questions.takeaway: Troponin is the preferred marker of heart muscle injury and is repeated 3 to 6 hours after the first result. A single normal value soon after symptoms begin does not rule out injury.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every option is something a nurse might say. The deciding cue is time: 40 minutes after onset, one normal troponin cannot exclude injury, so the best response corrects the belief that the test cleared the client.

steps.detail: 40 minutes since onset, with pressure still at 5 of 10.
An exercise ECG is not done while chest pressure continues. Eliminate A.
The client may leave, but only after the false belief is corrected. D skips that. Eliminate D.
C lets one early value look reassuring; B explains why the marker is repeated.

elimination.verdict: B. One early normal troponin does not rule out injury, so it is repeated in 3 to 6 hours.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client returned 2 hours ago from a heart catheterization through the femoral artery. Which findings require immediate follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: New chest pressure rated 4 of 10
options.rationale: Chest pain after catheterization is a critical rescue finding. The nurse stays with the client and obtains a 12 lead ECG.

options.text: Urine output 240 mL over the past hour
options.rationale: The contrast acts as an osmotic diuretic, so a high urine output is expected. The nurse keeps oral and intravenous fluids going so the contrast is excreted.

options.text: Lost pedal pulse with a cool, pale foot
options.rationale: A dramatic change in the pulses of the affected limb is a critical rescue finding. The rapid response team or provider is contacted at once.

options.text: Vital signs matching the preprocedure values
options.rationale: The values match the client's own baseline, so they do not signal bleeding or another complication.

options.text: Warm, pink foot with a pulse equal to baseline
options.rationale: Pulses, temperature, and color in the affected limb match the baseline, which shows circulation below the site is intact.

options.text: Firm swelling growing under the groin dressing
options.rationale: A forming hematoma calls for steady, firm pressure on the site and the rapid response team or provider at once.

questions.takeaway: After catheterization, check the site and the limb below it with every vital sign check. Chest pain, dysrhythmias, bleeding, hematoma, or a dramatic change in the limb pulses call for the rapid response team or provider at once. High urine output from the contrast is expected.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with the baseline from before the procedure. Anything that matches the baseline or follows from the contrast is expected; anything new at the site, in the limb, or in the chest is acted on now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New chest pressure is a critical rescue finding.
Osmotic diuresis from contrast is expected.
A lost pulse with a cool, pale foot is a dramatic change; a pulse matching baseline is expected.
Growing firm swelling is a hematoma.

elimination.verdict: A, C, F.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the checklist at 1100 for a client scheduled for a left heart catheterization through the femoral artery at 1300. The client ate toast at 0600, drank clear apple juice at 0930, and took the usual doses of warfarin and furosemide at 0800. The consent is signed, and the client reports no allergies. Which finding is the priority for the nurse to report to the provider?

options.text: Clear apple juice at 0930
options.rationale: Clear liquids are allowed up to 2 hours before the procedure. The juice at 0930 was 3.5 hours before 1300, so it meets the rule.

options.text: Toast at 0600
options.rationale: Solids are held for 6 hours before the procedure. The toast at 0600 was 7 hours before 1300, so it meets the rule.

options.text: Warfarin at 0800
options.rationale: Warfarin and other oral anticoagulants are held when the femoral artery will be used for access, because of the bleeding risk at the arterial site. A dose this morning is the finding that puts the client at risk.

options.text: Furosemide at 0800
options.rationale: Diuretics may be held before catheterization, so this dose is worth mentioning, which makes it tempting. It is not the priority: a diuretic may be held, while an anticoagulant is held whenever the femoral artery will be used, and bleeding at an arterial site is the greater harm.

questions.takeaway: Before catheterization, clear liquids are allowed up to 2 hours before and solids are held for 6 hours. Diuretics may be held, but warfarin and other oral anticoagulants are held whenever the femoral artery will be used, so a dose taken that morning is the priority to report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three findings look like rule breaks. Count the hours against the intake rules, then separate a drug that may be held from a drug that is held whenever the femoral artery is used.

steps.detail: Juice 3.5 hours before and toast 7 hours before both meet the rules. Eliminate A and B.
Diuretics may be held; warfarin and other oral anticoagulants are held when femoral access is planned.
Bleeding at an arterial access site outranks the extra diuresis from one diuretic dose.

elimination.verdict: C. Warfarin is held when femoral access is planned, so the morning dose is the priority to report.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client has a tricuspid valve that does not open fully. Which finding is not explained by this valve problem and requires follow up?

options.text: Distended neck veins at 45 degrees
options.rationale: Blood that cannot move through the tricuspid valve backs up into the right atrium and venae cavae, raising venous pressure. Neck vein distention is expected.

options.text: Pitting edema in both ankles
options.rationale: Backup into the venae cavae raises pressure in the body's veins, and fluid collects in the lower legs. This is expected.

options.text: Crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: Crackles come from blood backing up from the left atrium into the pulmonary veins and lungs. A tricuspid problem backs blood up before it reaches the lungs, so this finding needs another cause found.

options.text: Legs feel heavy and swollen by evening
options.rationale: Raised venous pressure from backup into the inferior vena cava makes the legs swell and feel heavy. This is expected.

questions.takeaway: Blood backs up behind a valve that does not open. Behind the tricuspid valve are the right atrium and the venae cavae, so expect neck vein distention and leg edema. Lung crackles point to the left side of the heart.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Trace backward from the problem valve. Findings in the body's veins fit a tricuspid problem; findings in the lungs belong to the left side and need follow up.

steps.detail: Behind the tricuspid valve: right atrium, then the venae cavae and the body's veins.
Neck veins, ankle edema and heavy legs are all venous backup. Eliminate A, B and D.

elimination.verdict: C. Lung crackles come from the left side and are not explained by a tricuspid problem.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client has a cool, pale, hairless left leg with a weak pulse and a warm, swollen right leg with a strong pulse. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: Left leg: poor venous return; right leg: poor arterial delivery
options.rationale: This reverses the two legs. A cool, pale, hairless leg with a weak pulse is not getting enough arterial blood; a warm, swollen leg with a strong pulse is getting arterial blood but not returning it.

options.text: Both legs: poor venous return from blood pooling
options.rationale: Only the right leg shows pooling. The left leg has a weak pulse, coolness, pallor, and hair loss, which point to low arterial delivery.

options.text: Left leg: poor arterial delivery; right leg: excess arterial inflow
options.rationale: The left leg is read correctly. The right leg has a strong pulse and warm skin because arterial flow is intact, but the edema comes from blood not leaving the leg, not from extra blood entering it.

options.text: Left leg: poor arterial delivery; right leg: poor venous return
options.rationale: The arterial system delivers oxygen and nutrients, so its failure shows as coolness, pallor, hair loss, and a weak pulse. The venous system returns blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart, so its failure shows as edema in a leg that stays warm with a strong pulse.

questions.takeaway: Arteries deliver oxygen and nutrients; veins return blood to the right heart. Low arterial delivery looks cool, pale, hairless, and painful with a weak pulse. Poor venous return looks swollen and heavy in a leg that stays warm with a strong pulse.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each leg separately by asking whether blood is failing to arrive or failing to leave. The pulse and skin temperature answer the first; edema answers the second.

steps.detail: Cool, pale, hairless, weak pulse: blood is not arriving.
Warm, swollen, strong pulse: blood arrives but does not leave.
Arrival is the arterial system; return is the venous system.

steps.action: Reject the swap and the extras
steps.detail: A swapped pair, a single cause for both legs, and excess inflow each misread one leg.

elimination.verdict: Left leg arterial, right leg venous.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews a client's fasting lipid panel. Which interpretations are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Low density lipoprotein (LDL) of 164 mg/dL raises coronary risk
options.rationale: LDL is mainly cholesterol and is the bad cholesterol. A level above the desired value of less than 130 mg/dL is positively linked with coronary artery disease.

options.text: High density lipoprotein (HDL) of 36 mg/dL raises coronary risk
options.rationale: HDL is the good cholesterol, and higher levels are protective. A level of 36 mg/dL is below the desired value for any adult, so the client loses that protection.

options.text: Triglycerides of 128 mg/dL raise coronary risk
options.rationale: A triglyceride level of 128 mg/dL falls within the desired range, so this value does not add risk. Elevated triglycerides would.

options.text: Total cholesterol of 242 mg/dL raises coronary risk
options.rationale: Total cholesterol above the desired value of less than 200 mg/dL indicates increased risk for coronary artery disease.

options.text: The low HDL level offsets the risk from the high LDL
options.rationale: The two values do not cancel. High LDL raises risk and low HDL removes protection, so both push the risk in the same direction.

options.text: A higher HDL on the next panel would add risk
options.rationale: This reverses the role of HDL. A rise in HDL would lower the risk, because elevated HDL is negatively correlated with coronary artery disease.

questions.takeaway: High LDL, high total cholesterol, and high triglycerides raise the risk for coronary artery disease. HDL works the other way: a high level protects, and a low level removes that protection.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each lipid by direction first. For LDL, total cholesterol, and triglycerides, higher is worse; for HDL, lower is worse. Then compare each value with the level you know is desired.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: LDL, total cholesterol, and triglycerides: high is risk. HDL: low is risk.
LDL 164 mg/dL, total cholesterol 242 mg/dL, and HDL 36 mg/dL.
Triglycerides 128 mg/dL do not add risk.
Low HDL does not offset high LDL, and a higher HDL lowers risk.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.nursesNote: Client, 77 years old, 3 days after a myocardial infarction. Reports sharp chest pain, 5 of 10, that eases when sitting upright. Oral temperature 38.2 °C. Blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg in the right arm and 122/76 mm Hg in the left arm. Radial pulses strong and equal on the right and left. Skin on both hands warm and dry, with pink nail beds. Point of maximal impulse palpated over the left fifth and sixth intercostal spaces, lateral to the midclavicular line. S1 and S2 heard clearly. A high pitched, scratchy sound heard over the precordium with each heartbeat.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the assessment of a client 3 days after a myocardial infarction. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Reports sharp chest pain, 5 of 10, that eases when sitting upright
segments.rationale: New chest pain after a myocardial infarction always needs follow up. Sharp pain that eases when sitting upright fits pericarditis rather than ischemia, but it still must be reported and assessed.

segments.text: Oral temperature 38.2 °C
segments.rationale: A fever points to inflammation. Together with the sharp chest pain and the scratchy sound, it supports an inflamed pericardium.

segments.text: Blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg in the right arm and 122/76 mm Hg in the left arm
segments.rationale: The two arms differ by only 2 mm Hg, and neither value calls for action.

segments.text: Radial pulses strong and equal on the right and left
segments.rationale: Strong, equal pulses show intact arterial flow to both arms. This is an expected finding.

segments.text: Skin on both hands warm and dry, with pink nail beds
segments.rationale: Warm, pink skin and nail beds show adequate perfusion. Decreased perfusion would appear cool, pale, and moist.

segments.text: Point of maximal impulse palpated over the left fifth and sixth intercostal spaces, lateral to the midclavicular line
segments.rationale: The point of maximal impulse belongs at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. An impulse felt over more than one space and shifted lateral to that line can mean left ventricular hypertrophy.

segments.text: S1 and S2 heard clearly
segments.rationale: Clear first and second heart sounds are the normal finding.

segments.text: A high pitched, scratchy sound heard over the precordium with each heartbeat
segments.rationale: A scratchy sound with each beat suggests a pericardial friction rub, which comes from movement of an inflamed pericardium and may occur with pericarditis after a myocardial infarction. Rubs are often transient, so document it and report it now.

questions.takeaway: After a myocardial infarction, sharp chest pain that eases sitting upright, a fever, and a scratchy sound with each beat together point to an inflamed pericardium. A point of maximal impulse that is spread over two spaces and lateral to the midclavicular line suggests an enlarged left ventricle.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with the normal you expect: the point of maximal impulse at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, only S1 and S2, warm pink skin, and equal pulses. Anything that departs from those normals, or any chest pain, needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sharp pain 5 of 10 easing upright and a temperature of 38.2 °C.
A scratchy sound with each beat suggests a friction rub.
Felt over two spaces and lateral to the midclavicular line.
Equal arm pressures, strong equal pulses, warm pink skin, clear S1 and S2.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who is 86 years old and was admitted for observation after tripping on a rug and falling. The cardiac monitor shows a regular rhythm at 54/min with no premature beats. Blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg lying and 122/72 mm Hg standing. The client is alert, denies dizziness, and walked 50 meters in the hallway without stopping. Clinic records show resting heart rates of 52 to 56/min at every visit for the past 4 years. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Report the slow heart rate to the provider now
options.rationale: A slow rate can limit output, but this client walked 50 meters without stopping and has no dizziness. There is no sign of low output and nothing new to report urgently.

options.text: Document the rate as the client's usual baseline
options.rationale: With age, pacemaker cells decrease and conduction time increases, so a rate below 60/min is common. The deciding cue is that this rate matches 4 years of clinic readings, the rhythm is regular, and the client has no symptoms. It is the client's baseline, not a new change.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG before the client walks again
