options.rationale: Assessing the rhythm when the rate is slow is the right instinct, and it would be the choice for a new slow rate. Here the monitor already shows a regular rhythm without premature beats, and 4 years of matching readings show the rate is not new.

options.text: Keep the client on bed rest until the provider is notified
options.rationale: Restricting activity after a fall feels safe, but the fall came from tripping on a rug, the standing pressure fell only 4 mm Hg, and the client walked 50 meters without symptoms. Bed rest adds deconditioning without a reason.

questions.takeaway: A heart rate below 60 is common in older adults because pacemaker cells decrease with age. The question is whether it is new. A rate that matches years of readings, with a regular rhythm and no symptoms, is the baseline.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options act on a slow rate after a fall, and each is sound in general. Look for the cues that tell you whether the rate is new and whether it caused the fall: 4 years of matching readings, a trip on a rug, and no orthostatic change.

steps.detail: A slow rate in an older adult comes from fewer pacemaker cells and longer conduction time.
Alert, no dizziness, walked 50 meters, and only a 4 mm Hg drop on standing.
The rate matches clinic readings of 52 to 56/min for 4 years.
A 12 lead ECG fits a new slow rate; the monitor already shows a regular rhythm. Reporting or bed rest treats a baseline as a new problem.
The client tripped on a rug; nothing points to a cardiac cause.

elimination.verdict: B. Document the rate as the client's usual baseline and continue routine monitoring.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: After heart surgery, a client's blood pressure is falling and heart rate is rising. Which finding best suggests fluid in the pericardial space compressing the heart?

options.text: Bounding radial pulses on both sides
options.rationale: A bounding pulse comes from a large ejection of blood. A squeezed heart fills poorly and ejects less, so the pulse would be weak.

options.text: Distended neck veins, 16 mm Hg systolic drop on inspiration
options.rationale: Fluid between the parietal and visceral pericardium compresses the chambers. Blood backs up in the veins, and a systolic drop of more than 10 mm Hg on inspiration, a paradoxical blood pressure, occurs with pericardial tamponade.

options.text: Flat neck veins, 6 mm Hg systolic drop on inspiration
options.rationale: A fall of 3 to 10 mm Hg on inspiration is normal, and flat neck veins do not show blood backing up. This does not support compression.

options.text: A new S3 with crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: An S3 with crackles suggests an overfilled ventricle, as in heart failure. Pericardial fluid does the opposite: it keeps the ventricles from filling.

questions.takeaway: The pericardial space lies between the parietal and visceral pericardium. Fluid there squeezes the heart so the chambers cannot fill: pressure falls, the pulse pressure narrows, neck veins distend, and systolic pressure drops more than 10 mm Hg on inspiration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Ask what a heart that cannot fill would show: blood backing up in the veins and output that drops further with each breath in. Reject findings of high output or overfilling.

steps.detail: Both describe neck veins and an inspiratory drop; only B shows backup and a drop above 10 mm Hg. Eliminate C.
Bounding pulses mean high output, and an S3 with crackles means overfilling. Eliminate A and D.

elimination.verdict: B. Distended neck veins and a paradoxical blood pressure support a heart squeezed by pericardial fluid.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension for 20 years has an apical impulse at the sixth intercostal space, lateral to the midclavicular line, spread over two spaces. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: An expected point of maximal impulse at the apex
options.rationale: Pulsation in the mitral area is normal, but the expected point is the left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line, in one space. This impulse is lower, lateral, and spread over two spaces.

options.text: A displaced impulse suggesting right ventricular enlargement
options.rationale: The impulse is displaced, but the apex is formed by the left ventricle. Movement in the tricuspid area, not a shifted apical impulse, would point toward the right side.

options.text: A displaced impulse suggesting left ventricular hypertrophy
options.rationale: The point of maximal impulse belongs at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line. An impulse shifted lateral to that line and felt in more than one space suggests left ventricular hypertrophy, which fits years of pumping against high afterload.

options.text: An impulse that cannot be interpreted without imaging
options.rationale: Inspection and palpation of the precordium are interpreted at the bedside. A displaced impulse is a finding the nurse recognizes and reports now.

questions.takeaway: The point of maximal impulse is at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line. A PMI shifted lateral and spread over more than one space suggests left ventricular hypertrophy; movement over the aortic, pulmonic, or tricuspid areas is abnormal.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare the finding with the normal landmark first, then ask which chamber forms the apex. Long standing hypertension raises the work of the left ventricle.

steps.detail: Normal is left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line, one space. This impulse is displaced, so it is not expected.
Inspection and palpation of the precordium can be interpreted now, so the finding stands.
The apex is left ventricle, and 20 years of hypertension makes left ventricular hypertrophy the fit.

elimination.verdict: The impulse is displaced lateral and over more than one space, suggesting left ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client who works as a roofer has new palpitations and a new murmur between S1 and S2. Which history questions should the nurse ask? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Did you have rheumatic fever or strep throat as a child?"
options.rationale: Recurrent tonsillitis, streptococcal infections, and rheumatic fever can lead to valve abnormalities, and a new murmur raises that question.

options.text: "Have you used cocaine or other street drugs?"
options.rationale: Cocaine and illicit drugs are often associated with heart disease, including rhythm problems that cause palpitations. The drug history includes them.

options.text: "Which over the counter or herbal products do you take?"
options.rationale: The drug history covers prescription, over the counter, and herbal or natural products, along with any drug sensitivities.

options.text: "Can you do the same roofing work as a year ago?"
options.rationale: The functional history compares current activity with past activity. Patients often limit activity gradually and do not notice until asked.

options.text: "Your palpitations are from the stress of roofing in heat, aren't they?"
options.rationale: Stress and heat are worth asking about, but this is a leading question that supplies the cause. The current problem is explored openly: onset, duration, frequency, and precipitating, aggravating, and relieving factors.

options.text: "Did your grandparents have heart disease after age 80?"
options.rationale: Family history belongs in the history, but it focuses on immediate family: the age, health status, and cause of death of parents, siblings, and children. A first degree relative with coronary artery disease is the major risk factor.

questions.takeaway: A cardiovascular history goes beyond risk factors: medical history (including rheumatic fever and strep infections), drug history (prescription, over the counter, herbal, illicit), social history (work, support, ability to pay), nutrition, family and genetic history, current problems, and function.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each question to a part of the history and ask whether this client's symptoms or situation make it relevant. A leading question, or one aimed at the wrong people, is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new murmur links to childhood strep infections and rheumatic fever: true.
Illicit drugs and over the counter or herbal products both belong: true, true.
Comparing work tolerance with a year ago: true.
A leading question and a family question aimed at the wrong relatives do not collect an accurate history: false, false.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: After axillary lymph node removal, a client's arm on that side slowly swells. Pulses are strong and ultrasound shows no clot. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: Blood is not returning through the arm veins
options.rationale: Returning blood to the heart is a vascular function, and a venous clot can cause swelling in one arm. The ultrasound found no clot, so venous return is not the impaired function here.

options.text: Tissue fluid is not draining into the circulation
options.rationale: The vascular system allows lymphatic flow to drain tissue fluid back into the circulation. After lymph nodes are removed, that drainage can fail, and fluid collects in one extremity (lymphedema) while arterial and venous flow are intact.

options.text: Arteries are not delivering oxygen and nutrients to the arm
options.rationale: Reduced arterial flow causes a cool, pale limb with weak pulses. This arm has a strong pulse.

options.text: The heart is not pumping enough to clear tissue fluid
options.rationale: Fluid from heart failure usually collects on both sides and in dependent areas, such as both legs. Swelling limited to one arm points to a local cause.

questions.takeaway: The vascular system carries blood out to nourish tissues, carries wastes to excretory organs, lets lymphatic flow drain tissue fluid back into the circulation, and returns blood to the heart. Edema in one limb with intact arterial and venous flow points to lymphatic blockage.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use the findings to rule out each function in turn: pulses and color test arterial delivery, the ultrasound tests venous return, and the pattern of edema tests a whole body cause.

steps.detail: Strong pulses: arterial delivery is intact.
No clot on ultrasound: venous return is not blocked.

steps.action: Test for a whole body cause
steps.detail: Only one arm swells, so heart failure does not fit.
Lymph nodes removed on the same side: lymphatic drainage is the function impaired.

elimination.verdict: B. Tissue fluid in the arm is not draining back into the circulation through lymphatic flow.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client with a wrist fracture, in severe pain and shouting angrily, has a blood pressure and heart rate well above a recent baseline. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: Vagal stimulation from the pain
options.rationale: Pain does change autonomic activity, but vagus (parasympathetic) stimulation slows the heart rate. It does not explain a rise.

options.text: Stretched baroreceptors driving the pressure up
options.rationale: Baroreceptors are stretched by a higher pressure, but their impulses inhibit the vasomotor center, which lowers blood pressure. They work against this rise.

options.text: Fluid retention through the renin angiotensin aldosterone system
options.rationale: This mechanism raises blood pressure when renal blood flow or pressure falls. Nothing here lowered renal flow, and fluid retention does not explain a rise over minutes after an injury.

options.text: Sympathetic stimulation from pain and anger
options.rationale: Emotional behaviors such as pain and anger stimulate the sympathetic nervous system to raise blood pressure and heart rate. With a normal recent baseline, the nurse treats the pain and rechecks before labeling this hypertension.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure is regulated by the autonomic nervous system, the kidneys, and the endocrine system. Pain, anger, and excitement stimulate the sympathetic nervous system and raise blood pressure and heart rate; baroreceptors respond to a rise by lowering the pressure.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check the direction of each mechanism. Only one of them pushes the pressure up in response to what is happening to this client right now.

steps.detail: Parasympathetic stimulation slows the heart: wrong direction.
Stretch inhibits the vasomotor center and lowers pressure: wrong direction.
This responds to falling renal flow and acts through fluid retention: wrong trigger and wrong timing.
A normal recent baseline fits a sympathetic response to pain and anger, so treat the pain and recheck.

elimination.verdict: Pain and anger stimulate the sympathetic nervous system; recheck the blood pressure once the pain is treated.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client with dark brown skin has heart failure and a low oxygen saturation. How should the nurse assess for decreased perfusion and cyanosis?

options.text: Check mucosa and nail beds for gray; compare temperature bilaterally
options.rationale: Small vessels lie near the surface in the nail beds, mucous membranes, and conjunctivae, so these areas show perfusion best. In dark skin, decreased perfusion and cyanosis appear as an ash gray color, and skin temperature is compared side to side with the back of the hand.

options.text: Check face and lips for blue; compare temperature bilaterally
options.rationale: The temperature technique is right, but a bluish color is how cyanosis shows in light skin. In dark brown skin it appears as graying, best seen in the mucous membranes, conjunctivae, and nail beds.

options.text: Check mucosa and nail beds for gray; feel temperature on one side
options.rationale: The sites and color are right, but skin temperature is checked for symmetry by touching different areas with the back of the hand or fingers, comparing both sides.

options.text: Check palms for yellow brown; follow the saturation trend
options.rationale: A yellow brown color can signal decreased perfusion in brown skin, but the oxygen saturation measures oxygenation, not skin perfusion. The skin, mucous membranes, and temperature still need direct assessment.

questions.takeaway: Assess perfusion where small vessels are near the surface: nail beds, mucous membranes, and conjunctivae. In dark skin, decreased perfusion and cyanosis show as ash gray; check skin temperature for symmetry with the back of the hand.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options name the right sites. Decide on technique: temperature is compared on both sides with the back of the hand.

steps.detail: Nail beds, mucous membranes, and conjunctivae show perfusion in any skin tone. The face and arms are not the best sites in dark skin.
Ash gray in dark brown skin; bluish is the light skin presentation.
Back of the hand, both sides. One side with the fingertips misses symmetry.
Oxygen saturation does not replace a skin and perfusion assessment.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the conjunctivae, oral mucous membranes, and nail beds for ash gray color, and compare skin temperature on both sides with the back of the hand.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.scenario: The nurse on a cardiac unit is reviewing the laboratory plan for several clients.
questions.stem: For each client, indicate the laboratory test the nurse uses to monitor the problem described.

rows.text: Takes warfarin each evening for atrial fibrillation; the dose was changed 3 days ago
rows.rationale: PT and INR are used when starting and maintaining oral anticoagulants such as warfarin. The INR is the most reliable way to monitor warfarin.

rows.text: Receives a continuous intravenous heparin infusion for a clot in a leg vein
rows.rationale: The PTT is assessed in clients receiving heparin. It shows whether the infusion is reaching the prescribed level of anticoagulation.

rows.text: Takes a loop diuretic for heart failure and now has new premature ventricular beats on the monitor
rows.rationale: Diuretics can lower potassium, and hypokalemia increases electrical instability and ventricular dysrhythmias. The basic metabolic panel includes potassium.

rows.text: Has pulmonary edema, a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute, and new confusion
rows.rationale: Arterial blood gases show tissue oxygenation, carbon dioxide removal, and acid base status. Severe breathlessness with new confusion calls for that information.

rows.text: Has heart failure, the loop diuretic dose was doubled 2 days ago, and the provider wants kidney function checked
rows.rationale: Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine show kidney function, and a larger diuretic dose can also shift sodium and potassium. All of these are on the basic metabolic panel.

rows.text: Had a mechanical heart valve placed last year and takes warfarin to prevent clots on the valve
rows.rationale: Clients with prosthetic valves tend to form thrombi and often take warfarin. PT and INR monitor that therapy, whatever the reason for the anticoagulant.

questions.takeaway: Match the lab to what it monitors: PT and INR for warfarin, PTT for heparin, arterial blood gases for oxygenation, carbon dioxide, and acid base status, and the basic metabolic panel for electrolytes such as potassium and sodium.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the drug or the problem first, then the test that tracks it. Heparin and warfarin are monitored by different tests, and rhythm changes on a diuretic point to an electrolyte.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warfarin: PT and INR, for any reason it is taken. Heparin: PTT.
Pulmonary edema with confusion needs arterial blood gases.
A diuretic with new ventricular beats points to potassium; a diuretic dose increase calls for kidney function, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine. Both are on the basic metabolic panel.

elimination.verdict: PT and INR; PTT; basic metabolic panel; arterial blood gases; basic metabolic panel; PT and INR.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client scheduled for a treadmill stress test tomorrow has a prescription to hold the morning beta blocker. Which instruction by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Take your beta blocker at the usual time."
options.rationale: Keeping the usual routine sounds safe, but beta blockers are usually withheld on the day of the test so the heart rate can rise during exercise. The cardiologist ordered it held.

options.text: "Fast after midnight and plan bed rest afterward."
options.rationale: Fasting and bed rest describe preparation and follow up for cardiac catheterization. A stress test allows a light meal 2 hours before and has no bed rest.

options.text: "Eat a light meal, skip coffee, and take a hot shower after."
options.rationale: The meal, caffeine, and smoking instructions are right, but a hot shower is avoided for 1 to 2 hours after the test because it may cause hypotension.

options.text: "Eat a light meal, skip coffee, and skip your beta blocker."
options.rationale: Before a stress test the client may have a light meal 2 hours before, avoids smoking, alcohol, and caffeine on the day of the test, and follows the cardiologist's direction on cardiac drugs, here holding the beta blocker so the heart rate can rise.

questions.takeaway: Before an exercise stress test: rest the night before, a light meal up to 2 hours before, no smoking, alcohol, or caffeine that day, and cardiac drugs such as beta blockers held only as the cardiologist directs. Avoid a hot shower for 1 to 2 hours afterward.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options share the meal and caffeine instructions. Decide on the second half: holding the beta blocker follows the order, while a hot shower after the test risks hypotension.

steps.detail: The order says hold the beta blocker, so taking it is wrong.
Fasting after midnight and bed rest belong to catheterization.
Both give the right meal and caffeine teaching. Only one keeps the drug order; the other adds a hot shower, which is avoided.

elimination.verdict: Light meal up to 2 hours before, no coffee or smoking, and skip the beta blocker that morning.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is examining a client who is 24 years old and wants to join a running club. The client runs 5 km three times each week and denies shortness of breath, chest pain, or swelling. Heart rate 58/min and regular, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg, lungs clear. With the bell at the apex, the nurse hears a soft, low pitched extra sound just after S2. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document an S3 as possibly normal
options.rationale: A sound just after S2 falls in rapid ventricular filling, so it is an S3. An S3 may be normal in clients younger than 35 years, and this client is 24, has no symptoms, and has clear lungs, so the nurse documents it and finishes the assessment.

options.text: Report an S3 to the provider now
options.rationale: This is what an S3 means in an older adult, and a new extra sound often prompts a report. The client's age of 24 years, with no symptoms and clear lungs, is the cue that changes the meaning: under 35 years an S3 may be normal.

options.text: Document an S4 from athletic heart changes
options.rationale: A trained heart and a slow rate make this tempting, but an S4 is heard during atrial contraction, just before S1. This sound falls just after S2, during rapid ventricular filling, so it is an S3.

options.text: Report a possible pericardial friction rub
options.rationale: A friction rub is a high pitched, scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. This is a soft, low pitched sound just after S2, and the client has no chest pain.

questions.takeaway: An S3 occurs during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. It may be normal in clients younger than 35 years; in older adults it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.
questions.strategy: Two cues must be combined. The timing names the sound: just after S2 is an S3, just before S1 is an S4. Then the age decides what the S3 means. The slow rate of a runner is a distraction.

steps.detail: Just after S2 is rapid ventricular filling, an S3. The S4 and rub options are out.
One documents it, one reports it as a sign of decreased compliance.
At 24 years, with no symptoms and clear lungs, an S3 may be normal, so the nurse documents it.

elimination.verdict: A. Document an S3 as possibly normal at this age and complete the assessment.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is auscultating the heart of a client who had rheumatic fever as a child. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 68 years old, had rheumatic fever as a child. With the client turned toward the left side, the nurse hears a low pitched rumbling sound at the apex that begins after S2 and continues until just before the next S1. The sound is not heard in the neck or the left axilla. The nurse identifies this as [[1]].

The sound is produced by [[2]].

In the record, the nurse describes the sound by [[3]].

options.text: An S3 gallop from rapid ventricular filling
options.rationale: An S3 is a single short sound just after S2. This sound lasts through the interval from S2 to the next S1, which makes it a murmur.

options.text: A diastolic murmur
options.rationale: A murmur heard between S2 and S1 is diastolic. The sound continues across that whole interval, so it is a murmur rather than a single extra sound.

options.text: A systolic murmur
options.rationale: A systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2. This sound begins after S2 and ends before S1.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub
options.rationale: A rub is a scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. This sound is a low pitched rumble at the apex.

options.text: Movement of an inflamed pericardium against the heart
options.rationale: That produces a pericardial friction rub, which is scratchy and often transient.

options.text: Blood filling a stiff ventricle during atrial contraction
options.rationale: That produces an S4, a brief sound just before S1, not a sound lasting across diastole.

options.text: Turbulent blood flow in or near the heart
options.rationale: Murmurs are whooshing or swishing sounds from turbulent flow in or near the heart.

options.text: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
options.rationale: Closure of the semilunar valves produces S2. The murmur starts after S2.

options.text: Location, timing, radiation, and quality
options.rationale: Murmurs are described by location, timing, radiation, and quality. Here: apex, diastolic, no radiation to the neck or axilla, low pitched rumble.

options.text: Location, timing, and a grade from I to VI
options.rationale: Grading is done by the provider; the nurse is not expected to grade murmurs. Radiation and quality are also left out.

options.text: Rate, rhythm, location, and pulse deficit
options.rationale: These describe the heart rate and rhythm, not a murmur. Timing, radiation, and quality are missing.

options.text: Timing and radiation only, since location is always the apex
options.rationale: Murmurs can be loudest at any valve area, so location is always part of the description.

questions.takeaway: A murmur between S2 and S1 is diastolic; between S1 and S2 it is systolic. Murmurs come from turbulent flow and are described by location, timing, radiation, and quality.
questions.strategy: A single extra sound and a murmur can sit in the same part of the cycle. Duration decides: a murmur fills the interval, a gallop is one brief sound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After S2 until the next S1 is diastole.
The sound continues across the interval, so it is a murmur, not an S3.
Turbulent flow produces murmurs.
Location, timing, radiation, and quality.

elimination.verdict: 1: a diastolic murmur. 2: turbulent blood flow in or near the heart. 3: location, timing, radiation, and quality.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure who received 2 L of IV fluid between 0800 and 1200 for dehydration. At 0800 blood pressure was 118/72 mm Hg and the lungs were clear. At 1200 blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg, heart rate is 114/min, an S3 is heard at the apex, and crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which explanation of the change in blood pressure is accurate?

options.text: Higher preload strengthened contraction, and the vessels then dilated
options.rationale: Within limits, more filling does make the muscle contract more forcefully, which makes this tempting. The cue is the failing heart that now has crackles and an S3: the filling has gone past that limit, and the pressure fell because output fell, not because vessels dilated.

options.text: Fluid shifted into the lungs and lowered the preload
options.rationale: Crackles show fluid backing up behind the left ventricle, which means the ventricle is overfilled, not underfilled.

options.text: Excess preload overstretched the ventricle and lowered output
options.rationale: Preload is the fiber stretch at the end of diastole. Within limits, more stretch raises stroke volume, but excessive filling in a failing heart lowers cardiac output, so blood pressure falls and the heart rate rises.

options.text: The added volume narrowed the arteries and raised afterload
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle pumps against. Added fluid volume acts on filling, which is preload, and the blood pressure fell rather than rose.

questions.takeaway: Preload is the stretch of the ventricular fibers at the end of diastole. Within limits, more filling strengthens contraction; excessive filling, especially in a failing heart, lowers cardiac output.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options agree that preload rose. Decide whether the stretch still helps: a falling blood pressure with new crackles and an S3 in heart failure says the ventricle is overfilled.

steps.detail: Added fluid volume changes filling, which is preload. The afterload option is out.
Crackles mean blood is backing up, so preload rose. The falling preload option is out.
In a failing heart with crackles and an S3, the extra stretch no longer helps; output and pressure fell.

elimination.verdict: C. Preload rose past the point where stretch helps, so the overfilled ventricle ejected less blood.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who returned to the unit 30 minutes ago after a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) with sedation. The throat was sprayed with a local anesthetic before the probe was passed. The client is alert and oriented, vital signs match the values before the test, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The client says, "My mouth is so dry. Can I have some water now?" Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the gag and swallow reflexes
options.rationale: The anesthetic spray numbs the throat, so the gag and swallow reflexes may not have returned even though the client is alert. Fluids before they return can be aspirated, so the nurse checks them first.

options.text: Offer small sips of water
options.rationale: Alertness and baseline vital signs show the sedation has worn off, which makes this tempting. The throat spray is the cue: the gag reflex can still be absent in an alert client, and water could be aspirated.

options.text: Offer ice chips to suck on slowly instead
options.rationale: Ice chips feel like a safe compromise, but they melt into water and carry the same aspiration risk while the throat is numb.

options.text: Ask the provider for a diet order
options.rationale: Return of the gag reflex, not a new prescription, determines when oral intake can resume after this procedure. Waiting for an order skips the assessment the nurse can do now.

questions.takeaway: After a transesophageal echocardiogram, care is like that after an upper endoscopy. The throat is numbed, so the nurse confirms the gag and swallow reflexes have returned before any oral intake.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: An alert client with baseline vital signs looks ready to drink, and three options give or plan fluid. Ask what the procedure did to the throat: the local anesthetic is the cue that sedation recovery does not cover.

steps.detail: The anesthetic spray suppresses the gag reflex, which creates an aspiration risk.
Alertness rules out sedation as a barrier, but not a numb throat. Eliminate B and C.
The reflex check is within the nurse's role and decides intake; an order does not. Eliminate D.

elimination.verdict: A. Check the gag and swallow reflexes before giving any water.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a client for a cardiac MRI to evaluate ventricular function. The client had a permanent pacemaker placed 6 years ago, reports feeling anxious in small spaces, and is wearing a wedding ring and a wristwatch. Which action is the nurse's priority before the scan?

options.text: Request a prescription for an antianxiety drug
options.rationale: Anxiety in small spaces is a real concern during a 15 to 60 minute scan, and the nurse can address it. It does not threaten the client's heart rhythm.

options.text: Remove the ring, the watch, and any metal on clothing
options.rationale: All metal objects are removed before an MRI, so this is part of the preparation. It is not the most important step for this client.

options.text: Report the pacemaker to the provider and MRI team
options.rationale: The magnetic field can deactivate a pacemaker. Some newer machines allow scanning, but the team must confirm this before the client enters the scanner.

options.text: Explain the need to lie still during the scan
options.rationale: Teaching about the scan is appropriate, but it does not address the pacemaker.

questions.takeaway: Before an MRI the nurse removes all metal objects and screens for implanted devices. A pacemaker or implanted defibrillator can be deactivated by the magnetic field, so the team must confirm the device is compatible.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Several options are correct preparation. Rank them by harm: a device that keeps the heart beating outranks jewelry and anxiety.

steps.detail: Pacemaker, anxiety in small spaces, ring and watch.
A deactivated pacemaker can stop effective heart rhythm; jewelry and anxiety cannot.
Report the pacemaker so compatibility is confirmed before the scan.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the pacemaker to confirm the device is compatible with the MRI.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a clot in a forearm vein at an old IV site. At 1400 the client suddenly reports sharp chest pain, the respiratory rate is 30/min, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Speech, vision, and strength in all four limbs are unchanged from 0800. The family asks why a clot from the arm went to the lungs and not to the brain. Place the structures in the order the clot passed through from the arm to the lungs.

options.text: Right ventricle
options.rationale: Fourth. The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve and pumps it toward the lungs.

options.text: Superior vena cava
options.rationale: First. Venous blood from the upper body, including the arm, returns to the heart through the superior vena cava. The inferior vena cava drains the lower body.

options.text: Pulmonic valve
options.rationale: Fifth. The pulmonic valve is the semilunar valve that lets blood leave the right ventricle for the pulmonary arteries.

options.text: Right atrium
options.rationale: Second. The venae cavae empty into the right atrium.

options.text: Pulmonary artery
options.rationale: Sixth. The right and left pulmonary arteries carry unoxygenated blood to the lungs, where the clot lodges. Blood reaches the arteries of the head only after it returns from the lungs to the left side of the heart and leaves through the aortic valve.

options.text: Tricuspid valve
options.rationale: Third. The tricuspid valve is the atrioventricular valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle.

questions.takeaway: Venous blood from the upper body enters the superior vena cava and blood from the lower body enters the inferior vena cava. Both empty into the right atrium, cross the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and leave through the pulmonic valve into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. A clot in a vein meets the lungs before it could reach the left side of the heart and the arteries of the head.
questions.strategy: Start where the clot starts. An arm vein drains to the superior vena cava, and the right side of the heart always sends venous blood to the lungs before any of it reaches the brain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The clot is in the arm, so it enters through the superior vena cava, not the inferior vena cava.
Right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonic valve.
The pulmonary artery carries the clot to the lungs; the brain is reached only after the left side of the heart.

elimination.verdict: Superior vena cava, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonic valve, pulmonary artery.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: During a heart catheterization, oxygen saturations are: superior vena cava 70%, right ventricle 71%, pulmonary artery 97%, left atrium 72%. Which results require follow up?

options.text: The superior vena cava and right ventricle values
options.rationale: Both sites carry oxygen poor venous blood before it reaches the lungs, so low values of 70% and 71% are expected.

options.text: The right ventricle and pulmonary artery values
options.rationale: The pulmonary artery value is wrong for its site, but the right ventricle value of 71% is expected for oxygen poor venous blood. This pair also misses the left atrium value, which is too low.

options.text: The pulmonary artery and left atrium values
options.rationale: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, and the left atrium receives oxygen rich blood from the pulmonary veins. A high pulmonary artery value with a low left atrium value suggests the samples were switched, so the labels are checked.

options.text: None of the values; each fits its site
options.rationale: The pulmonary artery should carry oxygen poor blood like the right ventricle, and the left atrium should carry oxygen rich blood from the pulmonary veins. Two values do not fit their sites.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen poor blood flows from the venae cavae through the right atrium, right ventricle and pulmonary arteries. Oxygen rich blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Results that break this pattern need follow up.
questions.strategy: Label each site as before or after the lungs, then predict low or high oxygen. Any value that does not match its prediction needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Superior vena cava, right ventricle and pulmonary artery are before the lungs: low. Left atrium is after the lungs: high.
The superior vena cava and right ventricle match; the pulmonary artery and left atrium do not. A pairs two matching values, B pairs one of each, and D accepts all.

elimination.verdict: C. The pulmonary artery and left atrium values are reversed from what blood flow predicts.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client whose mitral valve does not close completely has a known murmur. Which finding today is not explained by the leak and requires follow up?

options.text: A whooshing sound between S1 and S2, unchanged from before
options.rationale: A mitral valve that does not close leaks while the left ventricle contracts, from the QRS and S1 onward. A murmur between S1 and S2 fits, and it is unchanged.

options.text: S1 and S2 heard with each beat
options.rationale: Both normal heart sounds are present and unchanged. This adds nothing new.

options.text: New whooshing between S2 and the next S1
options.rationale: The mitral leak happens during ventricular contraction, so its murmur is systolic. A sound between S2 and S1 is diastolic, during ventricular filling, so it is a new finding the leak does not explain and needs reporting.

options.text: Point of maximal impulse at the fifth intercostal space
options.rationale: This is the expected location of the apical impulse.

questions.takeaway: A mitral valve that does not close leaks from the left ventricle back into the left atrium when the ventricle contracts, beginning with the QRS. Its murmur falls between S1 and S2; a new murmur between S2 and S1 has another cause.
questions.strategy: Place the leak in the cardiac cycle: it happens when the valve should be shut, during ventricular contraction. Any murmur outside that phase, or anything new, needs follow up.

steps.detail: The question asks for the finding the leak does not explain.
The mitral valve should be closed during contraction, so the leak murmur is between S1 and S2. A fits; B and D are unchanged and expected. Eliminate A, B and D.

elimination.verdict: C. A new murmur between S2 and S1 falls in filling, not contraction, and needs follow up.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client with low cardiac output after a myocardial infarction has rising kidney tests and no edema. The family asks why. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Less blood reaches the kidneys to remove wastes
options.rationale: The vascular system carries cellular wastes to the excretory organs, such as the kidneys. With low output, less blood reaches the kidneys, so creatinine and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) build up and urine output falls.

options.text: Tissue fluid is not draining through the lymph vessels
options.rationale: Poor lymphatic drainage causes swelling in the tissues. The client has no edema, and lymph flow does not explain rising creatinine and BUN.

options.text: Blood is not returning to the right side of the heart
options.rationale: Poor venous return shows as swelling and pooling in the limbs. There is no edema, and this does not explain why kidney wastes are rising.

options.text: Injured heart muscle is releasing wastes the kidneys cannot clear
options.rationale: Injured heart muscle releases the cardiac enzymes troponin T and I, not creatinine or BUN. The kidney values rise because too little blood reaches the kidneys to remove the wastes.

questions.takeaway: One job of the vascular system is to carry cellular wastes to the excretory organs. When cardiac output and blood pressure fall, less blood reaches the kidneys, so wastes such as creatinine and BUN accumulate and urine output drops.
questions.strategy: Link the finding to a function. Rising kidney wastes with low output points to wastes not being delivered for removal, not to lymph or venous problems the stem rules out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client has no edema.

steps.action: Rule out the heart releasing it
steps.detail: Heart injury releases troponin, not creatinine.
Low output means less blood carries wastes to the kidneys.

elimination.verdict: A. Less blood reaches the kidneys.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client with heavy bleeding from a deep cut has a blood pressure below baseline. Which findings show compensation to raise the pressure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate 52/min
options.rationale: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation slows the heart and lowers output. With blood loss the sympathetic system is stimulated, so the rate rises.

options.text: Heart rate 118/min
options.rationale: Stretch receptors and baroreceptors sense the lower volume and pressure, and the sympathetic nervous system and circulating catecholamines raise the heart rate.

options.text: Skin on both hands cool and pale
options.rationale: Sympathetic stimulation constricts the peripheral blood vessels, shifting blood away from the skin toward the vital organs.

options.text: Skin on both hands flushed and warm
options.rationale: Dilated vessels would lower the pressure further. The compensating response is vasoconstriction, which makes the skin cool and pale.

options.text: Urine output 300 mL over the past hour
options.rationale: Releasing fluid would lower the blood volume further. The kidneys respond to low flow by holding sodium and water.

options.text: Urine output 15 mL over the past hour
options.rationale: The kidneys sense less blood flow and activate the renin angiotensin aldosterone mechanism, and antidiuretic hormone is released. Sodium and water are retained, so urine output falls.

questions.takeaway: Three systems regulate blood pressure. The autonomic nervous system responds to baroreceptors and stretch receptors by raising heart rate and constricting vessels, the endocrine system releases catecholamines, and the kidneys activate the renin angiotensin aldosterone mechanism to retain sodium and water.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding whether it would raise the pressure or lower it. Compensation always pushes the pressure up: faster rate, tighter vessels, and less fluid lost in the urine.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A faster rate raises output; vagal slowing lowers it.
Vasoconstriction makes cool, pale skin; dilation would drop the pressure.
Retaining sodium and water lowers urine output.

elimination.verdict: B, C, F.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: An 81 year old client has a blood pressure of 172/70 mm Hg on repeat readings and says, "Stiff vessels are normal at my age." Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: "Stiff arteries are expected at your age; we can recheck next year."
options.rationale: The stiffening is an expected change, but the higher systolic pressure it causes is still hypertension. Waiting a year leaves the organs exposed to the high pressure.

options.text: "Your bottom number is low, which means your heart is not strained."
options.rationale: With stiff arteries the left ventricle pumps against more resistance, which leads to thickening of the ventricle. A diastolic pressure of 70 mm Hg does not remove that strain.

options.text: "The pressure is likely high from the stress of the visit today."
options.rationale: Repeat readings that stay high point to a real change, not a passing stress response.

options.text: "Stiff arteries raise the top number, and that still needs treatment."
options.rationale: With age the aorta and large arteries stiffen, so systolic pressure rises and the pulse pressure widens. The resulting hypertension must still be treated to avoid damage to the heart, brain, and kidneys.

questions.takeaway: With aging, the aorta and other large arteries thicken and stiffen. Systolic pressure and pulse pressure rise, the left ventricle pumps against greater resistance and can hypertrophy, and the resulting hypertension must be treated to avoid target organ damage.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: An expected aging change is not the same as a finding that needs no action. Ask what the change does to the body, then choose the response that protects against it.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stiff large arteries raise systolic pressure and widen the pulse pressure.
The left ventricle pumps against more resistance.
Hypertension from stiff arteries still needs treatment.

elimination.verdict: D. It still needs treatment.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is readmitted with weight gain and says, "My adult child does all the shopping and cooking." Which plan for the nutrition history is best?

options.text: Give the client a printed list of high sodium foods
options.rationale: Teaching before the history skips assessment. The nurse does not yet know what the client eats or who chooses it.

options.text: Do a 24 hour recall including the adult child
options.rationale: A nutrition history includes a 24 hour recall of food and fluid intake, diet restrictions, and alcohol use. The person who shops and cooks should be part of it.

options.text: Ask the client about favorite foods to guide the teaching
options.rationale: Preferences matter, but the client does not choose or prepare the food. A list of favorites leaves out what is actually served and the fluid and alcohol intake.

options.text: Refer the client to the dietitian for the nutrition history
options.rationale: The dietitian may review the sodium, sugar, fat, and fiber content of the foods chosen, but the nurse obtains the nutrition history as part of the cardiovascular assessment.

questions.takeaway: A cardiovascular nutrition history covers a 24 hour recall of food and fluid, self imposed or prescribed restrictions and supplements, and the amount and type of alcohol. Include the family member who shops and cooks, and consider culture, cost, and access to food.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Assess before you teach, and assess the person who controls the food. The cue is who does the shopping and cooking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A printed list comes before anyone knows the intake.
The dietitian reviews the foods; the nurse takes the history.
The adult child shops and cooks, so the recall includes the adult child.

elimination.verdict: B. A 24 hour recall with the client and the adult child.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client who reports fatigue. Which client statements suggest a cardiac cause? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I get heartburn after spicy meals."
options.rationale: Burning pain after spicy food points to an esophageal or gastric source.

options.text: "I wake up gasping a few hours after falling asleep."
options.rationale: This is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Lying down shifts blood from the legs back to the heart, and a failing heart cannot pump the extra volume, so the lungs congest.

options.text: "My chest hurts where I bumped it last week."
options.rationale: Pain at the site of a recent injury points to the chest wall, not the heart.

options.text: "I need three pillows to sleep now instead of one."
options.rationale: This is orthopnea, dyspnea when lying flat. The number of pillows needed is a measure of its severity, and the increase shows it is worsening.

options.text: "I get short of breath climbing one flight of stairs."
options.rationale: Dyspnea on exertion is often an early symptom of heart failure. Breathlessness after a single flight of stairs is less exertion than should cause it.

options.text: "I feel tired after a long walk."
options.rationale: Tiredness after a long walk is an expected response to exertion.

questions.takeaway: Ask what brings dyspnea on, what relieves it, and the body position when it occurs. Dyspnea on exertion is often an early heart failure symptom, orthopnea is graded by the number of pillows, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea wakes the client hours after lying down.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each statement, ask what brings the symptom on and what relieves it. Breathlessness tied to lying flat, sleep, or less exertion than before points to the heart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Waking gasping, more pillows, and fewer stairs all point to the heart.
Heartburn after spicy meals is gastric; pain where the chest was bumped is the chest wall.
Tiredness after a long walk is expected.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: Before coronary CT angiography with IV contrast, a client mentions having a coronary stent placed 3 years ago. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold all oral fluids until after the scan
options.rationale: Contrast can damage the kidneys, so hydration is encouraged, not withheld. Oral fluids are encouraged after the test.

options.text: Report the stent to the provider now
options.rationale: Previous treatment for cardiovascular disease is part of the history. A coronary stent can make coronary CT angiography less reliable, so the provider needs to know before the scan.

options.text: Give a beta blocker to slow the heart rate
options.rationale: A beta blocker may be prescribed to slow the heart rate for the scan, but the nurse does not give a drug that has not been prescribed.

options.text: Record the stent in the past medical history
options.rationale: Past procedures are recorded, but this one bears directly on the test being done today. Recording it without telling the provider leaves the problem in place.

questions.takeaway: Ask about previous treatment for cardiovascular disease, including diagnostic procedures and invasive treatment. For coronary CT angiography, a stent makes the scan less reliable, the heart rate must be slow, and the contrast calls for checking kidney function and keeping the client hydrated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Connect the history to the test. The cue is a stent in the same arteries the scan is meant to show.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contrast calls for hydration, not restriction.
There is no prescription for it.
A stent can make the scan less reliable, so report it before the scan.

elimination.verdict: B. Report the stent before the scan.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.scenario: The nurse on a cardiac unit is preparing several clients for diagnostic tests ordered for today: a chest x ray, a resting 12 lead ECG, an echocardiogram, and a coronary CT angiography with intravenous contrast.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate the test it belongs to.

rows.text: Check kidney function before the test and encourage oral fluids afterward
rows.rationale: Intravenous iodinated contrast can damage the kidneys, so renal function is checked before and after and hydration is encouraged.

rows.text: Position the client on the left side with the head raised 15 to 20 degrees
rows.rationale: For echocardiography the client lies quietly on the left side with the head raised 15 to 20 degrees.

rows.text: Ask the client to lie still and breathe normally while electrodes are placed on the chest, arms, and legs
rows.rationale: A resting ECG records electrical activity through electrodes on the chest and limbs. It shows dysrhythmias, ischemia, infarction, hypertrophy, and electrolyte effects.

rows.text: Explain that the test uses sound waves, takes 30 to 60 minutes, and needs no special preparation
rows.rationale: Echocardiography uses ultrasound, is painless and risk free, and needs no special preparation.

rows.text: Ask the client to stand, take a deep breath, and hold it while a picture of the heart and lungs is taken
rows.rationale: A chest x ray is taken with a held deep breath and shows heart size and fluid in the lungs, with no needle or dye.

rows.text: Expect a prescribed drug to slow the heart rate before the images are taken
rows.rationale: Cardiac CT images are timed to the cycle and need a low resting heart rate, so a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker may be given.

questions.takeaway: Match the preparation to how the test works: contrast means kidney checks and fluids, ultrasound means left side positioning and no preparation, electrodes mean lying still for the ECG, and a chest x ray needs only a held breath.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what each test puts into or onto the body: dye, sound waves, electrodes, or radiation alone. The preparation follows from that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Kidney checks, fluids, and a slow heart rate go with coronary CT angiography.
Left side positioning and no special preparation go with echocardiography.
Electrodes on chest and limbs are the ECG; a held breath for a picture is the chest x ray.

elimination.verdict: Coronary CT angiography, echocardiography, resting 12 lead ECG, echocardiography, chest x ray, coronary CT angiography.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client with chronic heart failure has a blood pressure that has dropped to 78/46 mm Hg. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: New confusion about the date
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is now about 57 mm Hg. A mean arterial pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg is necessary to perfuse the major organs, so the brain is likely underperfused, which explains the new confusion.

options.text: Thin build, unchanged over 2 years
options.rationale: Chronic heart failure can leave a client thin and cachectic, but the build has not changed in 2 years. It needs a plan, not urgent follow up.

options.text: Sits upright on 2 pillows, as usual
options.rationale: Breathing trouble when flat is common in heart failure, but this position is usual for the client.

options.text: Warm, pink skin on both hands
options.rationale: Skin color and temperature are part of the assessment, and warm, pink skin on both hands is an expected finding. It is not the finding that changed today.

questions.takeaway: Physical assessment begins with general appearance: build, skin color, distress level, level of consciousness, shortness of breath, position, and verbal responses. Mean arterial pressure equals the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic, divided by 3, and 60 to 70 mm Hg is needed to perfuse the major organs. A new change in level of consciousness with a mean arterial pressure below that level signals poor perfusion of the brain.
questions.strategy: Separate chronic from new, then link the new finding to the numbers. Build, position, and skin match baseline; the mental status is new.

steps.detail: Build, position, and skin match prior visits.
Confusion about the date is new.
A mean arterial pressure of about 57 mm Hg is below the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the brain.

elimination.verdict: A. The new confusion.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse sees distended neck veins and hears a swishing sound over one carotid artery. Which interpretations are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Distended neck veins suggest high right heart pressure
options.rationale: Neck vein pulsations reflect blood volume and central venous pressure. Distention means the filling volume and pressure on the right side of the heart are increased.

options.text: The swishing suggests turbulent flow through a narrowed artery
options.rationale: A bruit is a swishing sound from turbulent flow in a narrowed or atherosclerotic artery. An artery with uninterrupted flow makes no sound.

options.text: A loud swishing sound means near total blockage
options.rationale: A bruit may appear when the vessel is narrowed by half or more, but its loudness does not show how severe the disease is.

options.text: A swishing sound that disappears later means the narrowing resolved
options.rationale: Once a vessel is blocked 90% or more, the bruit often cannot be heard. A bruit that disappears can mean the narrowing has worsened.

options.text: Fluid volume overload may cause the distended neck veins
options.rationale: Jugular venous distention is usually caused by fluid volume overload or right ventricular failure.

options.text: Distended neck veins reflect increased carotid artery flow
options.rationale: The neck veins show venous pressure returning to the right heart, not arterial flow in the carotids.

questions.takeaway: Neck vein distention reflects increased volume and pressure on the right side of the heart, most often from fluid overload or right ventricular failure. A carotid bruit reflects turbulent flow in a narrowed artery, but its loudness does not show severity, and it can vanish when the artery is nearly closed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Keep the veins and the arteries apart. The neck veins tell about volume returning to the right heart; the carotid sound tells about flow through a narrowed artery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distention means more volume and pressure on the right side, often from fluid overload.
A bruit means turbulent flow through narrowing.
Loudness does not show severity, and a lost bruit can mean near blockage.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A systolic murmur recorded as faint at the last visit is now loud, and the nurse feels a vibration over the area. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document the murmur as unchanged, with the same timing and location
options.rationale: Timing and location match, but loudness has changed and a thrill is now present. Murmurs are categorized by loudness as well as timing.

options.text: Assign the murmur a grade III in the record
options.rationale: A loud murmur with a palpable thrill is grade IV or higher; grade III is loud without a thrill. Assigning a grade also does not communicate that the murmur has changed since the last visit.

options.text: Document a pericardial friction rub over the area
options.rationale: A friction rub is a scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. A vibration felt over the area of a loud murmur is a thrill.

options.text: Document the louder murmur and thrill; report the change
options.rationale: The murmur has become louder and is now accompanied by a thrill, which reflects more turbulent flow. The nurse describes location, timing, radiation, and quality, notes the thrill, and reports the change.

questions.takeaway: Murmurs are categorized by timing, clinical nature, and loudness, and they are described by location, timing, radiation, and quality. Same timing and location does not mean unchanged: a murmur that has grown louder has changed, so the nurse describes it and reports the change.
questions.strategy: Compare today with the last visit on every category, not just timing and location. The cue is the change in loudness, and the trap is an option that labels the sound without reporting that it changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Faint before, loud with a thrill now.
A grade in the record does not tell anyone the murmur changed.
Describe the murmur and thrill and report it.

elimination.verdict: D. Describe the change and report it.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients on a medical unit. Which client should the nurse assess first for poor perfusion of the major organs?

options.text: A client with blood pressure 84/60 mm Hg
options.rationale: This is the lowest systolic pressure, but the mean arterial pressure is (84 + 120) / 3 = 68 mm Hg, within the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the major organs.

options.text: A client with blood pressure 102/36 mm Hg
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is (102 + 72) / 3 = 58 mm Hg, below the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the major organs. The low diastolic pressure pulls the average down, because the heart spends about two thirds of each cycle in diastole.

options.text: A client with blood pressure 90/56 mm Hg
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is (90 + 112) / 3 = 67 mm Hg, within the level needed to perfuse the major organs.

options.text: A client with blood pressure 178/104 mm Hg
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is about 129 mm Hg. This pressure is high and needs follow up, but it is not a pressure too low to perfuse the organs.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure is the average pressure in the arteries during one cardiac cycle, calculated as [systolic + (2 x diastolic)] / 3. A mean arterial pressure between 60 and 70 mm Hg is necessary to perfuse the major organs, and because diastole is counted twice, a very low diastolic pressure can drop the mean below that level even when the systolic pressure looks acceptable.
questions.strategy: Do not rank by the systolic number alone. Calculate the mean arterial pressure for each client; the diastolic value counts twice.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 68, 58, 67, and about 129 mm Hg.
The client at 84/60 mm Hg has the lowest systolic pressure but a mean of 68 mm Hg.

steps.action: Choose the one below the level
steps.detail: Only 102/36 mm Hg gives a mean below 60 mm Hg.

elimination.verdict: B. Mean arterial pressure 58 mm Hg.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with bleeding from a stomach ulcer. At 0800 blood pressure was 116/72 mm Hg and heart rate was 86/min. At 1000 blood pressure is 108/92 mm Hg and heart rate is 118/min. A new nurse says, "The mean arterial pressure went up, so perfusion is holding." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The higher mean shows that each beat is ejecting more blood."
options.rationale: The mean rose because the diastolic pressure rose from vessel constriction. A pulse pressure that shrinks from 44 to 16 mm Hg points to less blood ejected with each beat, not more.

options.text: "The mean is adequate, so routine checks can continue."
options.rationale: The mean of about 97 mm Hg is adequate for now, which makes this tempting. It ignores the narrowing pulse pressure and the rising heart rate, which show that compensation is working hard during active bleeding.

options.text: "The faster heart rate has made up for the blood loss."
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate x stroke volume. A faster rate can offset a falling stroke volume only for a time, and it does not replace lost blood.

options.text: "The narrow pulse pressure suggests a falling stroke volume."
options.rationale: Pulse pressure is the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures and is an indirect measure of cardiac output. It narrowed from 44 to 16 mm Hg as the heart rate rose, which suggests falling stroke volume from blood loss, while vessel constriction keeps the mean up.

questions.takeaway: Pulse pressure, the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures, is an indirect measure of cardiac output. With blood loss, stretch receptors trigger a faster heart rate and constriction of the vessels, so the diastolic and mean pressures can hold or rise while the stroke volume falls; a narrowing pulse pressure is the early warning.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: When the mean looks reassuring, check the pulse pressure and the heart rate. A shrinking gap between systolic and diastolic pressure with a rising rate means compensation, not recovery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mean rose from about 87 to 97 mm Hg; pulse pressure fell from 44 to 16 mm Hg.
Vessel constriction raised the diastolic pressure, which lifts the mean.
A narrow pulse pressure with a rate of 118 beats per minute suggests less blood ejected per beat.

elimination.verdict: D. The pulse pressure has narrowed.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client on day 3 after a myocardial infarction. The client jokes with staff and says, "It was just a bad case of indigestion, and I am over it now." The client has taken every prescribed medication, walked the hallway three times today as planned, and asked when the cardiac rehabilitation class meets. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Restate the troponin results until the client accepts the diagnosis
options.rationale: Pushing the client to drop a defense mechanism removes a way of coping with a threatening event. Nothing in the client's behavior shows that the denial is harming the care plan.

options.text: Accept the denial and continue teaching and monitoring adherence
options.rationale: Denial is a common and normal response that helps a client cope with threatening circumstances, and it may show as excessive cheerfulness. It becomes maladaptive only when the client does not follow the plan of care, and this client takes every medicine, walks as planned, and asks about rehabilitation.

options.text: Request a mental health referral for maladaptive denial
options.rationale: Excessive cheerfulness can be a sign of denial, so concern is reasonable. Denial is maladaptive when the client is not adherent, and this client follows every part of the plan.

options.text: Delay discharge teaching until the client accepts the diagnosis
options.rationale: Delaying teaching leaves the client without the information needed at home. The client is already taking part in the plan, so teaching continues.

questions.takeaway: Denial is a common and normal defense mechanism after a cardiac event, and the client may deny the condition, say it is gone, or be excessively cheerful. It becomes maladaptive when the client does not follow the interprofessional plan of care, so the nurse watches adherence rather than confronting the denial.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge denial by what the client does, not only by what the client says. Adherence to the plan is the cue that separates normal coping from a problem.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calling the infarction indigestion and joking fits denial.
The client takes every medicine, walks as planned, and asks about rehabilitation.
Normal coping with full adherence calls for continued teaching and watching.

elimination.verdict: B. Accept the denial as normal coping and watch adherence.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.scenario: The nurse is completing the preoperative cardiovascular assessment of a client who is 84 years old, has no known heart disease, walks 1 km each day, and is scheduled for hip surgery tomorrow.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected for this client or requires follow up.

rows.text: A low pitched extra sound at the apex just after S2, during rapid ventricular filling
rows.rationale: This is an S3. It may be normal in clients under 35 years of age, but in an older adult it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.

rows.text: A low pitched extra sound at the apex just before S1, during atrial contraction
rows.rationale: This is an S4, heard during atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle. It may occur with advancing age, and the left ventricle becomes stiffer and less distensible with aging.

rows.text: Point of maximal impulse at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
rows.rationale: This is the expected location of the point of maximal impulse.

rows.text: Blood pressure 138/80 mm Hg lying and 112/72 mm Hg after 1 minute standing, with dizziness
rows.rationale: Baroreceptors become less sensitive with age, which explains the change, but a systolic drop of 26 mm Hg with dizziness is orthostatic hypotension and a fall risk that needs follow up before the client gets up.

rows.text: Left dorsalis pedis pulse weak, right dorsalis pedis pulse strong
rows.rationale: Pulses are compared side to side. A pulse that is weaker on one side suggests reduced arterial flow to that limb, which aging alone does not explain.

rows.text: Heart rate 66 beats per minute at rest, 94 during a hallway walk, and 68 after 5 minutes of rest
rows.rationale: With aging the maximum heart rate during activity decreases. A rise with walking and a return to the resting rate within minutes is an expected response.

questions.takeaway: With aging, the left ventricle stiffens, so an S4 may occur, and the maximum heart rate with activity decreases. An S3 in an older adult may signal heart failure, and orthostatic drops from less sensitive baroreceptors or unequal pulses still require follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether aging explains it and whether it is safe. An S3 and an S4 sound alike; the timing, after S2 or before S1, decides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After S2 is an S3, which needs follow up at 84 years; before S1 is an S4, which may occur with advancing age.
Dizziness with a 26 mm Hg drop on standing is a fall risk.
A weak left pulse with a strong right pulse is not an aging change.

elimination.verdict: S3, orthostatic drop with dizziness, and the weak left pulse require follow up; the S4, the point of maximal impulse, and the heart rate response are expected.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who returned 1 hour ago from a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery. A firm swelling at the right groin site is now 5 cm across and was 2 cm across 15 minutes ago, and there is fresh blood on the dressing. The client denies chest pain, the monitor shows a regular rhythm at 92/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold steady, firm pressure over the right groin site
options.rationale: For bleeding or hematoma formation after catheterization, the nurse holds steady, firm pressure on the access site until help arrives.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG before calling for help
options.rationale: A 12 lead ECG is obtained for chest pain or dysrhythmias. This client has no chest pain and a regular rhythm, and the problem is bleeding at the site.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees so the client can sit up
options.rationale: Sitting upright bends the right hip and puts strain on the femoral artery site, which can increase bleeding.

options.text: Call the rapid response team or provider while staying with the client
options.rationale: A growing hematoma is a complication that needs prompt intervention. The nurse calls for help and remains with the client, keeping pressure on the site.

options.text: Check the right dorsalis pedis pulse, skin color, and temperature
options.rationale: Peripheral pulses, skin temperature, and color in the affected limb are assessed with every check. A hematoma can compress the artery and reduce flow to the right foot.

options.text: Leave the bedside to get a pressure dressing, then reapply pressure
options.rationale: Leaving removes pressure from an actively bleeding arterial site. The nurse keeps pressure on and calls for help instead.

questions.takeaway: For bleeding or a growing hematoma after a femoral catheterization, hold steady, firm pressure on the site, call the rapid response team or provider, stay with the client, and assess the pulses, color, and temperature of the affected limb. A 12 lead ECG is for chest pain or dysrhythmias.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each action to the problem in the stem. The problem is bleeding at the site, not ischemia, so pressure and help come first, and the ECG is not indicated without chest pain or a rhythm change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Firm pressure stays on; leaving or sitting the client up works against it.
Call the rapid response team or provider from the bedside.

steps.action: Check the limb, not the rhythm
steps.detail: No chest pain and a regular rhythm, so assess the right foot instead of obtaining an ECG.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client, 81 years old, who has fainted twice this month. Both times the client was seated in a car and turned the head quickly to look behind while backing out of the driveway. In the clinic, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg lying and 130/76 mm Hg standing, with no dizziness. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: Rise slowly from lying to sitting to standing
options.rationale: Less sensitive baroreceptors cause orthostatic changes in older adults, so this is a common and tempting instruction. This client's lying and standing pressures barely differ, and both faints happened while seated.

options.text: Eat smaller meals and rest after eating
options.rationale: Postprandial hypotension also comes from less sensitive baroreceptors in older adults. Nothing in the stem links the faints to meals.

options.text: Turn your head slowly and avoid tight collars
options.rationale: In older adults, the carotid sinus in the neck can become oversensitive. Pressure on it from turning the head quickly or from a tight collar can trigger a vagal response that drops the heart rate and blood pressure, causing syncope. Both faints followed a quick head turn.

options.text: Drink a full glass of water before driving
options.rationale: Fluid intake helps when low volume causes dizziness, but nothing in the stem points to low volume, and it does not address what triggered the faints.

questions.takeaway: Syncope in an older adult can come from an oversensitive carotid sinus, from orthostatic changes, or from postprandial changes. Match the teaching to the circumstances of the episodes: faints after quick head turning point to the carotid sinus.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Explore the circumstances of each faint before choosing the teaching. Two causes from aging are tempting here, and the head turn while seated decides between them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both faints followed a quick head turn while seated.
Lying and standing pressures differ by only 2 mm Hg, with no dizziness.
Nothing in the stem links the faints to eating or low volume.

elimination.verdict: C. A quick head turn points to an oversensitive carotid sinus.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.
