questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has smoked for 30 years and stands all day at work. The client reports an aching, heavy feeling in both lower legs by evening. Both feet are warm and pink, dorsalis pedis pulses are strong and equal, and there is 2+ pitting edema at both ankles. Which instruction should the nurse give to relieve the aching?

options.text: Let your legs hang over the side of the bed
options.rationale: Lowering the legs helps arterial flow and relieves claudication. This client's warm pink feet and strong pulses show good arterial delivery, and lowering the legs would add to the pooling.

options.text: Walk until the ache starts, then stop to rest
options.rationale: This pattern fits claudication from poor arterial flow, which the long smoking history makes tempting. The ache here comes after standing, not walking, and the pulses are strong.

options.text: Apply a heating pad to your lower legs
options.rationale: Heat does not move pooled blood back toward the heart and can injure the skin.

options.text: Raise your legs above heart level to rest
options.rationale: Aching after long standing, with ankle edema, warm feet, and strong pulses, points to poor venous return. Raising the legs helps the veins return blood to the right side of the heart.

questions.takeaway: The venous system returns blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart. Leg pain after prolonged standing, with edema and intact pulses, fits venous insufficiency and is relieved by elevation; claudication from poor arterial flow is relieved by rest or by lowering the legs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide arterial or venous from the findings, not from the risk factors. Smoking points toward arterial disease, but warm feet, strong pulses, and edema after standing point to the veins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm pink feet with strong pulses show arterial delivery is intact.
The ache comes after standing all day, and both ankles have edema.
Elevation helps venous return; lowering the legs helps arterial flow.

elimination.verdict: D. Elevation relieves aching from poor venous return.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client whose heart rate rose suddenly from 84/min to 172/min, with a regular rhythm, 20 minutes ago. Blood pressure is 88/60 mm Hg, was 124/78 mm Hg before the change, and the client reports lightheadedness. A new nurse says, "Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, so this faster rate should be raising the output." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The ventricles have too little time to fill, so stroke volume falls."
options.rationale: The ventricles fill during diastole, and a very fast rate shortens diastole. Less filling means less blood ejected with each beat, so stroke volume falls far enough that cardiac output drops. The falling blood pressure and lightheadedness fit low output.

options.text: "The output is rising, so the low pressure points to dilated arteries."
options.rationale: This accepts the formula without asking what the rate does to stroke volume. Nothing in the stem suggests dilated arteries.

options.text: "The fast rate raises afterload, so less blood leaves the ventricle."
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle pumps against, which depends on arterial pressure and vessel diameter. The pressure here is falling, so afterload is not the cause.

options.text: "The output is rising, so the lightheadedness points to anxiety."
options.rationale: Lightheadedness with a blood pressure that fell from 124/78 to 88/60 mm Hg points to poor perfusion of the brain, not anxiety.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume, but the two are linked. A very fast rate shortens diastolic filling time, so stroke volume and cardiac output can fall even as the rate climbs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: When a formula seems to give an easy answer, check whether one term changes the other. The falling blood pressure and lightheadedness show what actually happened to output.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Options B and D both claim output is rising, which the falling pressure contradicts.
Afterload rises with arterial pressure, which is falling here.
A rate of 172/min shortens diastole, so less blood fills and leaves the ventricle.

elimination.verdict: A. Short filling time lowers stroke volume and output.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure whose dose of furosemide was doubled 3 days ago. Today the client reports palpitations, and the cardiac monitor shows frequent premature ventricular contractions that were not present yesterday. The client denies chest pain, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Which laboratory result should the nurse review first?

options.text: Troponin I
options.rationale: Troponin detects injury to heart muscle, which can cause new premature beats. The client denies chest pain, and the stem points to a more likely cause: the doubled diuretic.

options.text: Arterial blood gases
options.rationale: Low oxygen can cause premature beats, but oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.

options.text: Hematocrit
options.rationale: Excessive diuresis can raise the hematocrit through hemoconcentration, so this is tempting. A high hematocrit does not explain new premature ventricular contractions.

options.text: Basic metabolic panel
options.rationale: The basic metabolic panel includes potassium. A doubled diuretic dose can lower potassium, and low potassium increases electrical instability and ventricular dysrhythmias.

questions.takeaway: Electrolyte balance is essential for normal heart rhythm. In a client whose diuretic was increased, new premature ventricular contractions call for a check of potassium on the basic metabolic panel first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Link the new finding to the most recent change in care. The diuretic was doubled 3 days ago, and the oxygen saturation and absence of chest pain make the other causes less likely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The furosemide dose was doubled 3 days ago.
Saturation of 96% and no chest pain lower the pull of the blood gases and troponin.
A diuretic can lower potassium, and low potassium causes ventricular dysrhythmias.

elimination.verdict: D. Check potassium on the basic metabolic panel first.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing an older adult client whose aortic valve has stiffened with age. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 84 years old, has an aortic valve that has stiffened with age and no longer opens fully. A systolic murmur is heard at the right second intercostal space, unchanged from past visits. At rest, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, heart rate is 72/min, and the client has no symptoms. This week the client became lightheaded and had to sit down halfway up a flight of stairs.

The narrowed valve increases the [[1]] that the left ventricle must overcome.

Because of this, [[2]] is less able to rise when the client is active.

The finding that requires follow up is [[3]].

options.text: preload
options.rationale: Preload is the stretch of the ventricle at the end of diastole, before it contracts. A narrowed aortic valve affects ejection, not filling.

options.text: afterload
options.rationale: Afterload is the pressure or resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood through the semilunar valves. The pressure needed to open a stiff aortic valve adds to it.

options.text: venous return
options.rationale: Venous return brings blood back to the right side of the heart. The aortic valve sits on the outflow of the left ventricle.

options.text: heart rate
options.rationale: The valve does not set the heart rate, which is 72/min at rest.

options.text: venous return to the right atrium
options.rationale: Venous return is not what the aortic valve limits.

options.text: lymph return to the circulation
options.rationale: Lymph flow drains tissue fluid and is not limited by the aortic valve.

options.text: cardiac output
options.rationale: Higher afterload lowers stroke volume, and with aging the heart already has less reserve. Output cannot rise to meet the demand of activity, so the brain is briefly underperfused.

options.text: blood flow through the leg veins
options.rationale: Leg vein flow returns blood to the heart and is not limited by the aortic valve.

options.text: the murmur at the right second intercostal space
options.rationale: The murmur is tempting because it is abnormal, but it is unchanged from past visits.

options.text: the resting blood pressure of 128/76 mm Hg
options.rationale: This resting pressure does not show the problem, which appears only with exertion.

options.text: the absence of symptoms at rest
options.rationale: Changes from aging often stay hidden at rest and appear only under stress, so this is not reassuring by itself.

options.text: the lightheadedness on the stairs
options.rationale: Lightheadedness with exertion is new and shows that output cannot meet demand. Valve disorders such as a narrowed aortic valve can cause syncope, so this is reported.

questions.takeaway: A stiff aortic valve raises afterload, which lowers stroke volume and limits how much cardiac output can rise. Aging changes often appear only under physical stress, so new symptoms with exertion require follow up even when resting findings look unremarkable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Follow the valve forward: outflow from the left ventricle means afterload, afterload limits output, and limited output shows up with exertion. Then pick the finding that is new, not the one that is merely abnormal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The aortic valve sits on the left ventricle's outflow, so it affects afterload.
Higher afterload lowers stroke volume, so output cannot rise with activity.
The murmur is unchanged; the lightheadedness on the stairs is new.

elimination.verdict: 1 afterload, 2 cardiac output, 3 the lightheadedness on the stairs.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: A client whose mitral valve does not open fully now sleeps in a recliner to breathe. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Blood is backing up from the right atrium
options.rationale: Backup behind the right atrium goes into the neck veins and the body, not the lungs. The tricuspid valve, not the mitral valve, guards the right atrium.

options.text: Less blood is returning from the body
options.rationale: Venous return to the right side of the heart is not limited by the mitral valve, and it does not explain trouble breathing when lying down.

options.text: Blood is backing up from the left atrium
options.rationale: The mitral valve lets blood move from the left atrium into the left ventricle. When it does not open fully, blood backs up into the left atrium and the pulmonary veins, congesting the lungs. Lying flat worsens the congestion, so the client sits up to breathe.

options.text: The left ventricle is overfilling each beat
options.rationale: A narrowed mitral valve lets less blood into the left ventricle, not more.

questions.takeaway: Blood flows from the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, through the mitral valve, and into the left ventricle. A narrowed mitral valve backs blood up into the lungs, causing shortness of breath that worsens when lying flat.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Trace the blood backward from the narrowed valve. Whatever sits upstream of the valve is where the congestion shows.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
Options A and C differ only by side; the mitral valve is on the left.
Behind the left atrium are the pulmonary veins and the lungs.

elimination.verdict: C. A narrowed mitral valve backs blood into the left atrium and lungs.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure who started a drug that relaxes the walls of the arteries. Before the first dose, blood pressure was 168/98 mm Hg, heart rate 78/min, and the client stopped to rest after walking 10 meters. Today blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg, heart rate is 78/min, the client walks 40 meters before resting, and urine output has doubled. The lungs are clear both days. A student nurse says, "The lower pressure means the heart is pumping less blood." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The drug lowered the preload, so the ventricle holds less blood."
options.rationale: Preload is the stretch of the ventricle at the end of diastole. The drug acts on the arteries, not the veins, and the clear lungs give no sign the ventricle was overstretched. Less filling would also lower output, which the findings do not show.

options.text: "The drug lowered the afterload, so more blood is ejected."
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Relaxed arteries lower that resistance, so each beat empties more blood. Better walking tolerance and more urine show more blood reaching the muscles and kidneys.

options.text: "The lower mean pressure means less blood is reaching the organs."
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure today is about 99 mm Hg, well able to perfuse the organs. More urine and longer walks show perfusion got better, not worse.

options.text: "The drug raised the heart rate, so the output rose each minute."
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, but the heart rate is 78/min on both days. Any rise in output came from stroke volume.

questions.takeaway: Afterload is the pressure or resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Relaxing the arteries lowers afterload, so stroke volume and cardiac output rise even though blood pressure falls. Judge output by perfusion findings such as activity tolerance and urine output, not by the pressure alone.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use the data to test each claim. The unchanged heart rate rules out a rate effect, the clear lungs and the drug's action on the arteries point away from preload, and the better walking and urine show output rose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate is 78/min on both days, so option D fails.
Longer walks and more urine show more output, so option C fails.

steps.action: Match the drug to the term
steps.detail: A drug that relaxes the arteries lowers resistance to ejection, which is afterload, not preload.

elimination.verdict: B. Lower afterload lets the ventricle eject more blood.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a client during a treadmill stress test. Which findings require the test to be stopped? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate rising as the speed increases
options.rationale: The test is meant to raise the heart rate toward a planned target. A rising rate is the expected response to more work.

options.text: New chest pressure while walking
options.rationale: Chest pain during the test suggests the heart muscle is not getting enough oxygen for the workload. It is a reason to end the test.

options.text: Systolic pressure falling below the resting value
options.rationale: Systolic pressure should rise with exercise. A fall below the resting value means the heart cannot keep up with the demand and ends the test.

options.text: Sweating and faster breathing
options.rationale: Sweating and a faster respiratory rate are expected during exercise. Extreme shortness of breath, not ordinary faster breathing, would end the test.

options.text: Runs of premature ventricular contractions
options.rationale: Ventricular dysrhythmias during the test signal an unsafe response to the workload and end the test.

options.text: Systolic pressure rising as the speed increases
options.rationale: A rise in systolic pressure with more work is the expected response of a healthy heart.

questions.takeaway: A stress test continues until the target heart rate is reached or the protocol is done, unless chest pain, extreme shortness of breath, dizziness, hypotension, ventricular dysrhythmias, or significant ECG changes appear.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into expected response to exercise or sign that the heart cannot meet the demand. A rise in rate and pressure is the point of the test; a fall in pressure is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rising heart rate, rising systolic pressure, sweating, and faster breathing are normal with exercise.
New chest pressure suggests the heart muscle lacks oxygen.

steps.action: Stop for failure to keep up
steps.detail: Falling pressure and ventricular dysrhythmias mean the heart cannot handle the workload.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a cardiovascular history. Which client statement reveals a risk factor that requires follow up?

options.text: "I walk my dog for 30 minutes every day."
options.rationale: Daily activity lowers risk. Physical inactivity, not this, is the modifiable risk factor.

options.text: "I quit smoking 10 years ago."
options.rationale: Smoking is a major risk factor, so this is tempting. The client quit a decade ago, so the habit is no longer an active risk to change.

options.text: "I stay angry for hours over deadlines."
options.rationale: Hostility, anger, and stress over deadlines are psychological factors closely linked to heart disease. They are modifiable, so the nurse explores them and offers ways to manage stress.

options.text: "I eat fish for dinner twice a week."
options.rationale: Fish twice a week fits a heart healthy diet and is not a risk factor.

questions.takeaway: Psychological factors are part of the cardiovascular history. People who are highly competitive, worried about deadlines, and often hostile or angry are at higher risk for heart disease, and stress, anger, and depression can be changed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that describes a current, changeable habit or trait that raises risk. A past habit that has stopped and healthy habits do not need follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily walking and fish twice a week lower risk.
Smoking stopped 10 years ago, so it is not a current habit.
Lasting anger over deadlines is a psychological risk factor.

elimination.verdict: C. Anger and stress over deadlines are a modifiable risk factor.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse hears a new soft murmur in an older adult client with no known heart disease. Which question should the nurse ask next?

options.text: "Do you get heartburn after large meals?"
options.rationale: Heartburn points to the stomach, not to a valve. It does not help judge whether the murmur is affecting the heart's function.

options.text: "Are you more short of breath lately?"
options.rationale: With aging, the mitral and aortic valves calcify and stiffen, and a murmur may be heard before other symptoms appear. Asking about shortness of breath checks whether the valve change is starting to limit the heart.

options.text: "Do your legs ache after standing all day?"
options.rationale: Aching legs after standing point to poor venous return. Leg veins are not where a heart murmur comes from.

options.text: "Do you feel lightheaded after you eat?"
options.rationale: Lightheadedness after meals comes from less sensitive baroreceptors, a different age related change. It does not follow up a valve finding.

questions.takeaway: Valves calcify with age, especially the mitral and aortic valves. When a murmur is found in an older adult, assess heart rhythm and sounds and ask about shortness of breath, because the murmur may appear before other symptoms.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match the follow up question to the structure that made the finding. A murmur comes from a valve, and valve problems show up as shortness of breath.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A murmur in an older adult points to a stiff, calcified valve.
Heartburn, leg aching, and lightheadedness after meals come from the stomach, the veins, and the baroreceptors.
Shortness of breath shows whether the valve is limiting the heart.

elimination.verdict: B. Ask about shortness of breath after a new murmur.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with hypertension who started amlodipine 2 weeks ago and returned from a 9 hour car trip yesterday. Blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg, was 158/94 mm Hg before the drug. The client reports brief lightheadedness when standing quickly that passes within seconds. Both ankles have 1+ pitting edema that began after the drug was started. One calf is 3 cm larger around than the other and tender. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: The larger, tender calf
options.rationale: Edema in one extremity points to venous obstruction such as a clot. After a long period of sitting, a swollen, tender calf suggests a deep vein clot that could break loose and travel to the lungs.

options.text: The edema at both ankles
options.rationale: Edema is abnormal, so this is tempting. Dependent ankle edema on both sides is a common side effect of amlodipine and began when the drug was started; it is reported at the next contact, not ahead of a possible clot.

options.text: The brief lightheadedness when standing
options.rationale: Cardiovascular drugs can cause postural hypotension, so this is tempting. Symptoms that pass within seconds are usually transient; the nurse teaches slow position changes and checks orthostatic vital signs after the more urgent finding.

options.text: The blood pressure of 136/84 mm Hg
options.rationale: The fall from 158/94 mm Hg is the drug's intended effect. It is still slightly high and is followed over time, not urgently.

questions.takeaway: The location of edema helps find its cause: edema in both legs can come from heart failure, venous insufficiency, or drugs such as amlodipine, while edema in one extremity points to venous obstruction or lymph blockage. A new, tender, swollen calf after prolonged sitting needs immediate follow up for a clot.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Several findings are new here. Ask which one has an explanation already in the stem and which one could become dangerous quickly; the one sided swelling after a long trip is both unexplained and dangerous.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The pressure drop and ankle edema match the new drug.
Lightheadedness that passes in seconds is followed up, but it is not the most urgent.
A calf 3 cm larger and tender after a long car trip suggests a clot.

elimination.verdict: A. One sided calf swelling after prolonged sitting suggests a clot.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with heart failure. Which findings indicate right sided heart failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Neck veins distended at 45 degrees
options.rationale: Jugular venous distention reflects systemic venous congestion. When the right ventricle fails, blood backs up into the systemic veins.

options.text: Short of breath within minutes of lying flat
options.rationale: Orthopnea comes from pulmonary congestion. Blood backs up into the lungs when the left ventricle fails, so this is a left sided finding.

options.text: New confusion with cool hands and feet
options.rationale: Confusion and cool extremities reflect decreased cardiac output and decreased perfusion, a left sided pattern.

options.text: Poor appetite, nausea, and an enlarged liver
options.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, and hepatomegaly come from systemic venous congestion of the liver and gut, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Abdominal girth up 4 cm in 3 days
options.rationale: Ascites and abdominal distention reflect systemic venous congestion, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Low urine output for 3 hours
options.rationale: Lower urine output is a decreased cardiac output finding. The failing left ventricle sends less blood to the kidneys.

questions.takeaway: Left sided failure backs blood into the lungs and lowers output: dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, cough, fatigue, tachycardia, confusion, cool extremities, lower urine output. Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins: dependent edema, JVD, weight gain, ascites, hepatomegaly, anorexia and nausea.
questions.strategy: Ask where the blood is backing up. Lungs or low output points left. Neck veins, belly, liver, and legs point right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distended neck veins, ascites, and the liver and gut findings are systemic congestion: right. Orthopnea is lung congestion: left.
Low urine output, confusion, and cool extremities come from decreased cardiac output: left.
Nausea and poor appetite sound like low perfusion of the gut, but they come from venous congestion: right.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.nursesNote: Client admitted with heart failure. Reports shortness of breath walking to the bathroom and waking at night gasping for air. Coughing frequently. Heart rate 112 beats per minute. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg. SpO2 91% on room air. Crackles in both lung bases. Abdomen soft, not distended. No edema in either ankle. Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note of a client with heart failure. Highlight the findings that indicate left sided heart failure.

segments.text: waking at night gasping for air
segments.rationale: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Coughing frequently
segments.rationale: Cough is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Above 120/80 mm Hg, but elevated blood pressure is a cause of heart failure, not one of the pulmonary congestion or decreased cardiac output findings of left sided failure.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 beats per minute
segments.rationale: Tachycardia above 100 beats per minute is a decreased cardiac output finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: SpO2 91% on room air
segments.rationale: Below 95 to 100%. Fluid in the lungs impairs gas exchange.

segments.text: Crackles in both lung bases
segments.rationale: Crackles are a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Abdomen soft, not distended
segments.rationale: No ascites or abdominal distention, so no sign of systemic venous congestion here.

segments.text: Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees
segments.rationale: No jugular venous distention. This is an expected finding.

questions.takeaway: This client shows left sided failure: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, crackles, and low SpO2 from pulmonary congestion, plus tachycardia from decreased cardiac output. The absence of edema, ascites, and JVD argues against right sided involvement.
questions.strategy: An abnormal value is not automatically a left sided finding. For each abnormal finding, ask whether it shows blood backing into the lungs or low output, or whether it is a cause of heart failure instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Night gasping, cough, crackles, and SpO2 91% all point to fluid in the lungs.
Heart rate 112 beats per minute.

steps.action: Abnormal but not a finding of left sided failure
steps.detail: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg is a cause of heart failure.
Soft abdomen, flat neck veins.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure who is newly confused at 1000 after being oriented at 0700. An intravenous diuretic was given at 0700, and urine output since then is 60 mL. Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg, heart rate 108/min, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air. Hands and feet are cool, and fine crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which explanation best accounts for the confusion?

options.text: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output
options.rationale: Correct. Low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, and only 60 mL of urine in 3 hours despite an intravenous diuretic all show low cardiac output. The brain is underperfused the same way the kidneys are.

options.text: Hypoxemia from fluid in the lungs
options.rationale: Crackles make hypoxemia tempting, but the SpO2 is 97% on room air, so the blood reaching the brain is well oxygenated. The problem is that too little of it is arriving.

options.text: Systemic venous congestion from right sided failure
options.rationale: Systemic venous congestion produces edema, neck vein distention, ascites, and liver findings, none of which are described, and it does not explain new confusion.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit from excess diuretic fluid removal
options.rationale: Low blood pressure and tachycardia after a diuretic make a deficit tempting. But excess fluid removal needs a large urine output, and the diuretic produced only 60 mL in 3 hours. The crackles also show fluid still in the lungs.

questions.takeaway: Confusion in heart failure can come from decreased cardiac output or from hypoxemia. Check the SpO2: when it is in range and the output findings (low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, low urine output) cluster, the cause is perfusion, not oxygenation.
questions.strategy: Low output, hypoxemia, and a deficit after the diuretic can each cause confusion, and each has a cue that makes it look right. Two cues decide: SpO2 97% on room air rules out hypoxemia, and 60 mL of urine in the 3 hours after a diuretic rules out excess fluid removal.

steps.detail: Low output, hypoxemia, and a deficit after the diuretic can all explain confusion.
SpO2 97% on room air rules out hypoxemia, even with crackles.
Only 60 mL of urine in 3 hours after an intravenous diuretic, with crackles still present: the fluid was not removed, so no deficit.
Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg, heart rate 108/min, cool hands and feet, low urine output: low cardiac output.

elimination.verdict: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client admitted with worsening heart failure. Which actions belong in the ongoing assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Auscultate lungs and note how high crackles are heard
options.rationale: Lung sounds are a core heart failure assessment and show whether pulmonary congestion is spreading or clearing.

options.text: Weigh daily on the same scale at the same time
options.rationale: Daily weight with a consistent technique tracks fluid gained or lost.

options.text: Record intake and output each shift
options.rationale: Intake and output show whether fluid is being retained or removed.

options.text: Assess the apical heart rate and rhythm
options.rationale: Heart rate and rhythm are part of the nursing assessment; tachycardia is a low output finding.

options.text: Delegate lung sound checks to assistive personnel
options.rationale: Assistive personnel can measure vital signs, but auscultating and interpreting lung sounds is a nursing assessment and is not delegated.

options.text: Weigh once a week on the same scale
options.rationale: Same scale is right, but heart failure weights are daily. A weekly weight misses a gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure assessment: respiratory status and SpO2, lung sounds, heart rate and rhythm, JVD and edema, activity tolerance, intake and output, and daily weight at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option keeps one correct detail (lung sounds, same scale) and breaks another (who assesses, how often).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Belongs, and the level of crackles matters.

steps.action: Weight, intake and output, heart rate and rhythm
steps.detail: All belong.
Auscultating and interpreting lung sounds stays with the nurse.
Heart failure weights are daily; weekly misses a 24 hour gain.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has received an IV diuretic for 3 days. Which result best indicates that the fluid overload is resolving?

options.text: Ejection fraction unchanged at 35%
options.rationale: Ejection fraction measures how well the ventricle contracts. Removing fluid does not change it, so it cannot show the overload resolving.

options.text: Chest x ray still showing an enlarged heart
options.rationale: An enlarged heart on the film reflects hypertrophy or dilation, a change in structure. It is unchanged, so it shows nothing about fluid leaving the body.

options.text: B type natriuretic peptide down by half
options.rationale: The ventricles release B type natriuretic peptide when they are stretched by fluid overload. A level that has fallen by half means less stretch, so the fluid overload is resolving.

options.text: Troponin unchanged at a low level
options.rationale: Troponin reflects damage to the heart muscle, not stretch or fluid volume. An unchanged low level says nothing about the overload.

questions.takeaway: B type natriuretic peptide rises when the ventricles stretch with fluid overload, so a falling level tracks fluid removal. Ejection fraction measures contraction, the chest x ray shows heart size and congestion, and troponin shows muscle damage.
questions.strategy: Name what each test measures, then pick the one that should change as fluid leaves the body.

steps.detail: The question asks which result tracks fluid overload.
Ejection fraction is contraction, an enlarged heart is structure, and troponin is muscle damage. None of these measures stretch from fluid.
Only the B type natriuretic peptide reflects ventricular stretch, and it fell by half.

elimination.verdict: C. A falling B type natriuretic peptide means the ventricles are less stretched by fluid.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: After 2 days of a diuretic, a client with heart failure shows several improved findings. Which finding best indicates that the diuretic is effective?

options.text: Oxygen saturation of 95% on 2 L nasal oxygen
options.rationale: SpO2 is in range, but it is measured on supplemental oxygen, so it reflects the oxygen as much as the fluid removal.

options.text: A resting heart rate of 88 beats per minute
options.rationale: A rate in range is welcome, but many things affect heart rate. It does not directly show fluid removal.

options.text: Crackles now at one lung base instead of both
options.rationale: Fewer crackles do suggest less lung fluid, but crackles are one location on one exam. The weight and output measure the fluid removed.

options.text: Weight down 2 lb with output above intake
options.rationale: A diuretic removes excess fluid. Weight down on the same scale and output exceeding intake measure that removal directly.

questions.takeaway: Diuretics remove excess fluid. The most direct evidence is a falling daily weight and output exceeding intake; fewer crackles, less dyspnea, and better SpO2 support it.
questions.strategy: Several options are good news. The key word is best: pick the finding that measures what the drug does.

steps.detail: Remove excess fluid.
Weight and the output to intake balance.
Fewer crackles is supportive, not a measure of volume.
SpO2 on oxygen and heart rate are influenced by other factors.

elimination.verdict: A 2 lb weight loss with output above intake.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: Four clients with heart failure: 1, chest pain at rest; 2, a diet question; 3, severe hypoxemia; 4, a 3 lb gain since yesterday. Which assessment order is correct?

options.text: Client 1, client 3, client 2, client 4
options.rationale: Two errors. Severe hypoxemia is a breathing problem and comes before chest pain, and a weight gain comes before a teaching question.

options.text: Client 3, client 1, client 4, client 2
options.rationale: Severe hypoxemia is a breathing problem and comes first. Chest pain at rest may be ischemia and comes next. A gain of 3 lb in 24 hours must be addressed today but is not an emergency. The diet question is last.

options.text: Client 3, client 4, client 1, client 2
options.rationale: Client 3 is first, but chest pain at rest outranks a weight gain, which shows worsening heart failure without a breathing or circulation emergency.

options.text: Client 3, client 1, client 2, client 4
options.rationale: The first two are right, but a gain of 3 lb in 24 hours with more edema is a physiologic change and comes before a teaching question.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize by ABCs: severe hypoxemia first, chest pain at rest next, a reportable weight gain next, and a teaching question last.
questions.strategy: Apply the ABCs, then separate an emergency from a finding that is reportable but not immediately dangerous. A physiologic change always outranks a teaching need.

steps.detail: Severe hypoxemia: first. Eliminate A.
Chest pain at rest: second. Eliminate C.
A 3 lb gain in 24 hours before the diet question. Eliminate D.

elimination.verdict: B. Client 3, client 1, client 4, client 2.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.scenario: A client with heart failure is sitting in a chair at 1400. At 0800, crackles were heard only in both lung bases, SpO2 was 94% on room air, and respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute. Over the past 20 minutes the client has become more short of breath. Now: respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 158/94 mm Hg, SpO2 86% on room air, oral temperature 37.8 °C. Crackles are heard halfway up both lungs, and the client is coughing frothy, pink tinged sputum. A prescription reads oxygen by nasal cannula or mask, titrated to keep the SpO2 at 92% or higher. The nurse will monitor the response over the next 30 minutes.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure whose breathing has worsened over the past 20 minutes. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Obtain a sputum specimen for culture before oxygen is started
options.rationale: The temperature of 37.8 °C makes a culture tempting, but collecting it first delays oxygen for an SpO2 of 86% and the sputum points to fluid, not infection.

options.text: Recline the chair and raise the legs
options.rationale: Reclining and raising the legs return more blood to the congested lungs, and the blood pressure of 158/94 mm Hg gives no reason to raise them.

options.text: Place the client in high Fowler's position
options.rationale: High Fowler's eases dyspnea and lets the lungs expand.

options.text: Apply oxygen and titrate the flow to the prescribed SpO2 target
options.rationale: Oxygen treats the hypoxemia, and titrating to the prescription keeps the SpO2 at 92% or higher.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L per minute by nasal cannula and recheck the SpO2 at the next vital sign check
options.rationale: Oxygen is right, but a fixed low flow with a recheck hours later does not titrate to the prescribed target of 92% while the SpO2 is 86%.

options.text: Worsening right sided heart failure
options.rationale: Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins, causing edema, JVD, and ascites. These findings are in the lungs.

options.text: Acute pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, SpO2 86%, crackles that rose from the bases to halfway up both lungs since 0800, and frothy, pink tinged sputum indicate pulmonary edema from left sided failure.

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: The low grade temperature and cough make this tempting, but pneumonia does not develop in 20 minutes, and frothy, pink tinged sputum with crackles rising evenly in both lungs fits fluid, not infection.

options.text: Gradual worsening of chronic left sided heart failure over several days
options.rationale: The findings are left sided, but the change came over 20 minutes, not several days. That speed, with crackles rising from the bases to halfway up both lungs and frothy, pink tinged sputum, marks acute pulmonary edema, an emergency.

options.text: Oral temperature
options.rationale: The temperature is worth rechecking later, but it does not show whether oxygen and positioning are relieving the fluid in the lungs over the next 30 minutes.

options.text: SpO2
options.rationale: Shows whether oxygen therapy is bringing the SpO2 up to the prescribed target.

options.text: Abdominal girth
options.rationale: Measures ascites from systemic congestion, which is not the current problem.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid over days. It cannot show a change within 30 minutes.

options.text: Lung sounds, including how far up the crackles are heard
options.rationale: The level of the crackles shows whether pulmonary congestion is spreading or clearing.

questions.takeaway: Rapid onset, crackles rising from the bases, and frothy, pink tinged sputum mean acute pulmonary edema, even with a low grade temperature. Sit the client up, titrate oxygen to the prescription, and watch the SpO2 and the level of the crackles.
questions.strategy: Name the problem from the time course first: a change over 20 minutes is not pneumonia. Then pick actions that relieve breathing now at the prescribed target, and parameters that change within the 30 minutes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A change over 20 minutes, crackles from the bases to halfway up, and frothy, pink tinged sputum: acute pulmonary edema.
37.8 °C does not explain a 20 minute change or the sputum.
High Fowler's, and oxygen titrated to the prescribed target.
A fixed low flow with a late recheck, a culture before oxygen, and reclining with the legs up.
SpO2 and the level of the crackles change within 30 minutes; weight and temperature do not track the response.

elimination.verdict: High Fowler's and titrated oxygen; acute pulmonary edema; SpO2 and lung sounds.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure taking digoxin and a diuretic has poor appetite, blurred vision, a slow irregular pulse, and low potassium. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: An expected effect of digoxin on heart rate
options.rationale: Digoxin does slow the rate, but a new irregular rhythm with appetite and vision changes is not an expected effect.

options.text: Right sided failure with congestion of the gut
options.rationale: Congestion can cause anorexia, but it does not explain blurred vision, a new irregular rhythm, or bradycardia.

options.text: Digoxin toxicity made more likely by low potassium
options.rationale: Anorexia, blurred vision, bradycardia, and a change from a regular to an irregular rhythm are signs of digoxin toxicity, and hypokalemia increases the risk.

options.text: Low potassium from the diuretic, offset by the digoxin
options.rationale: The potassium is low, but digoxin does not protect against hypokalemia. Hypokalemia makes digoxin toxicity more likely.

questions.takeaway: Digoxin toxicity: anorexia, fatigue, blurred vision, mental status changes, bradycardia, and new rhythm changes. Low potassium makes toxicity more likely, so check potassium along with the digoxin level.
questions.strategy: Read the cluster together. One option explains the appetite, one explains the slow rate, and one explains the potassium; only one explains all of them.

steps.detail: Anorexia, blurred vision, a slow and irregular pulse.
Potassium is low.

steps.action: Choose the explanation that covers all of them
steps.detail: Digoxin toxicity potentiated by hypokalemia.
Each other option explains one cue.

elimination.verdict: Possible digoxin toxicity, made more likely by the low potassium.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure receives a first dose of an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check blood pressure hourly for several hours
options.rationale: The first dose may cause a rapid drop in blood pressure, so blood pressure is checked hourly for several hours.

options.text: Teach slow position changes, especially on rising
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors can cause orthostatic hypotension.

options.text: Teach the client to report cough or dizziness
options.rationale: A nagging dry cough and dizziness are reportable effects of ACE inhibitors.

options.text: Suggest a salt substitute for the low sodium diet
options.rationale: Salt substitutes usually contain potassium, and ACE inhibitors can cause potassium retention. Potassium and renal status must be checked before using them.

options.text: Teach the client to stop the drug if cough develops
options.rationale: Reporting a cough is correct, but the client does not stop the drug alone. The provider decides whether to switch, for example to an angiotensin receptor blocker.

options.text: Report a slight drop to 104 mm Hg systolic
options.rationale: A slight drop to a systolic pressure of 104 mm Hg in a client without symptoms is not the report threshold. Report a systolic pressure below 90 mm Hg, or the protocol level.

questions.takeaway: After the first dose of an ACE inhibitor, check blood pressure hourly for several hours and report a systolic pressure below 90 mm Hg. Teach slow position changes, report cough and dizziness, and avoid salt substitutes without a potassium and renal check.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option starts from a correct idea: flavor the low sodium diet, report the cough, watch the blood pressure. Check each for the one detail that makes it unsafe or premature.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hourly blood pressure for several hours: yes.
Slow position changes, report cough and dizziness: yes.
Contains potassium; ACE inhibitors retain potassium.
Report, do not stop.
Above 90 mm Hg with no symptoms: not the report threshold.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A stable client with heart failure has a sodium restriction but no fluid restriction and asks for more water. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "I'll check with your provider first."
options.rationale: Sounds cautious, but there is no restriction to clarify and the client is stable. Holding the water to make a call imposes a restriction nobody ordered.

options.text: "I'll bring it and add it to your intake record."
options.rationale: No fluid restriction is prescribed and the client is stable, so the client may drink. Recording it supports intake and output monitoring.

options.text: "I'll bring it, but let's keep you to 1 liter a day."
options.rationale: The nurse does not set a fluid limit without a prescription.

options.text: "Let's try some ice chips instead."
options.rationale: Ice chips are recorded as fluid intake too, and nothing here calls for limiting fluid.

questions.takeaway: Sodium restriction is part of heart failure treatment. Fluid restriction is used when prescribed, not automatically. Record intake for every client on intake and output monitoring.
questions.strategy: Two options sound protective. The deciding cue is the order: sodium restricted, no fluid restriction, in a stable client.

steps.detail: Sodium restricted; no fluid restriction.
The client is stable: no worsening congestion to report.
A call to hold the water, a 1 liter limit, and ice chips in place of water all restrict fluid without an order.
Provide the water and record it.

elimination.verdict: Bring the water and record it on the intake record.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with heart failure who weighs 176 lb at discharge. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll weigh every morning on the same scale."
options.rationale: Correct technique: same time, same scale, similar clothing.

options.text: "I'll call if I can't walk as far as usual."
options.rationale: Reduced activity tolerance is reportable on its own.

options.text: "I'll call if I reach 181 pounds by week's end."
options.rationale: 181 lb is 5 lb above 176 lb within a week, which is reportable.

options.text: "At 179 pounds tomorrow, I'll wait for 181."
options.rationale: 179 lb is a 3 lb gain in 24 hours, which is reported that day. Waiting for 5 lb applies the weekly threshold to a one day gain.

questions.takeaway: Teach daily weights at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing. Report a gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours or 5 lb in 1 week, more edema, worsening dyspnea, reduced activity tolerance, and new dyspnea or chest pain at rest.
questions.strategy: Two statements use numbers. Subtract each from 176 lb and match the gain to its time frame: 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours, 5 lb in 1 week.

steps.detail: Need for further teaching: find the incorrect statement.
Same scale, same time, similar clothing: correct.
Reduced activity tolerance reported on its own: correct.
181 lb by the end of the week is 5 lb in a week: correct. 179 lb tomorrow is 3 lb in 24 hours: report that day, so waiting is wrong.

elimination.verdict: Waiting for 181 pounds after a 3 pound gain in one day.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse at a clinic receives a call from a client with heart failure. The client weighed 176 lb yesterday morning on the home scale in nightclothes. This morning the client weighed 179 lb on a pharmacy scale while wearing street clothes, shoes, and a winter jacket. Breathing, sleeping position, and ankle size are unchanged. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Call your provider this morning to report a 3 pound gain in 1 day."
options.rationale: A gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours is reportable, so this sounds right. But the two weights were taken on different scales in different clothing, so the gain has not actually been measured.

options.text: "Keep weighing each morning, and call if you reach 181 pounds."
options.rationale: This applies the 5 lb weekly limit to a 1 day change. If the gain were real, 3 lb in 24 hours would already be reportable, so waiting for 181 lb is wrong either way.

options.text: "Reweigh now at home in nightclothes, and call if it is 178 or more."
options.rationale: Daily weights are compared on the same scale in similar clothing. A repeat home weight shows whether the gain is real, and 178 lb would be a 2 lb gain over 176 lb in 24 hours, which is reportable. No symptoms have changed, so there is time to get a valid number.

options.text: "Watch for swelling or shortness of breath, and call if either starts."
options.rationale: Symptoms are worth watching, and none have changed, which makes this tempting. But it drops the weight entirely, and a valid weight can show fluid gain before symptoms appear.

questions.takeaway: A weight is only meaningful when taken at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing. When two weights cannot be compared and no symptoms have changed, get a valid weight before acting on the number.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the 3 lb number and one sets the weight aside for symptoms. The deciding cue is the different scale and clothing: the gain has not been measured yet, and a valid weight on the home scale settles it.

steps.action: Check how the weights were taken
steps.detail: Home scale in nightclothes versus pharmacy scale in shoes and a jacket.
Breathing, pillows, and ankles unchanged.
Get a valid weight with the same technique, with a clear threshold to call back.
Reporting an unconfirmed number, applying the weekly limit to a 1 day change, and dropping the weight for symptoms alone.

elimination.verdict: Reweigh on the home scale in nightclothes and call back if 178 lb or more.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse at a clinic receives a call from a client with heart failure who was discharged 1 week ago. For the past 3 days, the client has had to stop and rest halfway through the usual walk to the mailbox, a walk the client finished without stopping on each of the first 4 days at home. Weight is 2 lb above the discharge weight, a gradual gain over 5 days. Breathing at rest, sleeping position, and ankle size are unchanged. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Report the drop in how far you can walk to your provider today."
options.rationale: Reduced activity tolerance is a reportable finding by itself. It has lasted 3 days and is a decline from what the client did after discharge, so it is reported even though the weight is under the limits.

options.text: "Keep weighing daily, and call if you gain 5 pounds this week."
options.rationale: The weight is correctly read as under both limits, but weight is only one reportable finding. This answer lets a separate reportable change go unreported.

options.text: "Split the walk into two shorter trips, with a rest in between."
options.rationale: Balancing activity with rest is part of the teaching, but it treats a 3 day decline as a pacing problem. A new drop in activity tolerance is reported, not just managed at home.

options.text: "Rest more during the day, and call if your breathing at rest worsens."
options.rationale: Dyspnea at rest is a reportable change, which makes this sound safe. But the decline in activity tolerance is reportable now, and waiting for a second finding delays the report.

questions.takeaway: Any one reportable finding is enough: weight gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours or 5 lb in 1 week, more edema, worsening dyspnea, reduced activity tolerance, or new dyspnea or chest pain at rest. A weight under the limits does not cancel a decline in activity tolerance.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options sound like good teaching: one checks the weight against the limits, one balances activity with rest, and one watches breathing at rest. The deciding cue is a decline lasting 3 days from what the client could do after discharge, which is reportable on its own.

steps.detail: 2 lb over 5 days: under both limits, so weight is not the trigger.
Needing to rest halfway for 3 days, after 4 days of finishing: reduced activity tolerance.
Reduced activity tolerance is reportable on its own.
Pacing the walk, waiting for a weight trigger, or waiting for dyspnea at rest leaves a reportable change unreported.

elimination.verdict: Report the drop in activity tolerance to the provider today.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure whose dyspnea has increased over the last hour. Respiratory rate 26/min, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, SpO2 91% on 2 L nasal cannula, oral temperature 37.8 °C. Crackles are heard in both lung bases, and the client is now coughing up pink, frothy sputum. Oxygen is prescribed to keep the SpO2 at 92% or higher. The next diuretic dose is due in 3 hours. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the provider to give the diuretic now and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Fluid removal is the right direction, and without the sputum this could be the best choice. Pink, frothy sputum signals pulmonary edema, and a request for an early dose leaves the hypoxemia untreated and no help at the bedside.

options.text: Sit the client upright, raise the oxygen, and call rapid response
options.rationale: Pink, frothy sputum may indicate pulmonary edema, an emergency. Upright positioning and oxygen treat the dyspnea and hypoxemia now, and the rapid response team brings help.

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow and recheck the SpO2 in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Raising the oxygen is part of the answer, which makes this tempting. But pink, frothy sputum may mean pulmonary edema, and oxygen alone with a 15 minute wait leaves out positioning and help.

options.text: Collect a sputum specimen for culture and recheck the temperature
options.rationale: The temperature of 37.8 °C makes infection tempting, but a low grade temperature does not explain an hour of worsening dyspnea, and pink, frothy sputum points to fluid, not infection.

questions.takeaway: Worsening dyspnea and crackles in heart failure can be managed with the plan of care, but pink, frothy sputum may indicate pulmonary edema. That turns the situation into an emergency: position upright, give oxygen, and get help.
questions.strategy: Three options each treat one part of the picture: fluid, oxygen, or a possible infection. The deciding cue is pink, frothy sputum, which turns worsening heart failure into a likely emergency that needs positioning, oxygen, and help at once.

steps.detail: Pink, frothy sputum.
Possible pulmonary edema, a breathing emergency.
An early diuretic and oxygen alone each treat one part and delay help.
37.8 °C does not explain an hour of worsening or pink, frothy sputum.

elimination.verdict: Sit the client upright, raise the oxygen, and call the rapid response team.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with chronic heart failure has a fast heart rate, high blood pressure, and a 3 lb weight gain since yesterday. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Compensation that adds to cardiac workload; report it
options.rationale: The sympathetic system raises the heart rate and tightens vessels, and the renin angiotensin aldosterone system holds sodium and water. These compensations help for a while but raise the workload and worsen failure. A gain of 3 lb in 24 hours is reportable.

options.text: Stronger pumping that shows the failure is recovering
options.rationale: A fast rate and a high pressure in heart failure are compensations, not signs of recovery. They raise the heart's workload, and the weight gain shows fluid is building up.

options.text: Expected compensation in heart failure that needs no report
options.rationale: The mechanism is right, but the conclusion is wrong. These compensations worsen failure over time, and a gain of 3 lb in 24 hours is a finding to report.

options.text: Anxiety raising the rate and extra salt raising weight
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings points to anxiety or a diet change. The rate, pressure and weight together fit the compensations of heart failure.

questions.takeaway: In heart failure, the body speeds the heart, tightens vessels, and holds salt and water to keep blood moving. That helps at first but raises the heart's work and worsens failure. Report a gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours.
questions.strategy: Two options share the right mechanism. Decide between them with the weight: a 3 lb gain since yesterday is a reportable change.

steps.detail: A fast rate, high pressure and fluid gain are the compensations of a failing heart, so B and D are out.
A and C share the mechanism. They differ only on whether to report.
A gain of 3 lb in 24 hours is a reportable sign of worsening failure, so A is right.

elimination.verdict: A. These compensations add to the heart's work, and the weight gain must be reported.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.scenario: The nurse reviews findings documented for several clients admitted with heart failure.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the mechanism of heart failure that best explains it.

rows.text: Sleeps sitting up in a recliner because lying flat causes shortness of breath
rows.rationale: Orthopnea comes from blood backing into the lungs in left sided failure. Lying flat shifts more fluid into the lungs.

rows.text: Urine output 90 mL over the past 4 hours
rows.rationale: Low output reduces blood flow to the kidneys, so urine output falls. This is a left sided finding of decreased cardiac output.

rows.text: Coughing up pink, frothy sputum
rows.rationale: Pink, frothy sputum may indicate pulmonary edema, the most severe form of fluid backing into the lungs.

rows.text: At 1400, oriented to person only; at 0800, was oriented to person, place, and time
rows.rationale: New confusion reflects reduced blood flow to the brain from low cardiac output.

rows.text: 2+ pitting edema over the sacrum after 2 days on bed rest
rows.rationale: Dependent edema forms where gravity pulls fluid. In a client in bed, the sacrum is the dependent area, and the backup is in the systemic veins.

rows.text: Ate 2 bites of each meal for 2 days because of nausea
rows.rationale: Anorexia and nausea come from congestion of the liver and gut as blood backs up into the systemic circulation in right sided failure.

questions.takeaway: Left sided failure shows two patterns: fluid in the lungs (orthopnea, frothy sputum, crackles) and low output (low urine output, confusion, cool extremities). Right sided failure shows systemic venous congestion (dependent edema, anorexia, nausea, ascites, JVD).
questions.strategy: Ask where each finding comes from: fluid in the lungs, too little blood reaching an organ, or blood pooling in the body's veins. Watch the kidney and gut findings, which are easy to misplace.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Orthopnea and pink, frothy sputum come from pulmonary congestion.
Low urine output and new confusion come from decreased cardiac output.
Sacral edema in a client in bed comes from systemic venous congestion.
Nausea and poor intake come from congestion of the liver and gut.

elimination.verdict: Pulmonary congestion; decreased cardiac output; pulmonary congestion; decreased cardiac output; systemic venous congestion; systemic venous congestion.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has had severe chronic lung disease for 15 years and has slept on 3 pillows for the past 5 years because of it, with no change. Today the neck veins are distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees, there is 3+ pitting edema in both ankles, weight is up 4 lb in 1 week, the abdomen is distended, and the client has nausea at meals. Breath sounds are diminished in both bases with no crackles. SpO2 is 89% on 2 L nasal cannula, the same as at the last 3 clinic visits. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Left sided failure with blood backing up into the lungs
options.rationale: Orthopnea and a low SpO2 can come from pulmonary congestion, but both have been unchanged for years and fit the lung disease. Backup into the lungs would add crackles, and there are none.

options.text: Failure of both ventricles, with lung and systemic venous backup
options.rationale: This is the tempting choice, since orthopnea is a left sided finding. The 3 pillows have been unchanged for 5 years, before any of the new findings, and the lungs have no crackles, so nothing new points to the left side.

options.text: Right sided failure with blood backing up into the lungs
options.rationale: Right sided failure is correct, but the direction is wrong. Blood that the right ventricle cannot move backs up into the systemic veins, not the lungs.

options.text: Right sided failure from lung disease, with systemic backup
options.rationale: Severe lung disease is a listed cause of heart failure and strains the right ventricle. Neck vein distention, ankle edema, weight gain, a distended abdomen, and nausea are systemic venous congestion findings, and they are the only new findings.

questions.takeaway: Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic circulation: JVD, dependent edema, weight gain, ascites, and anorexia or nausea. In a client with lung disease, judge left sided failure by what is new in the lungs, such as crackles, not by an orthopnea or SpO2 that has been the same for years.
questions.strategy: Two options agree on the systemic findings and differ only on whether the left side has failed too. Ask which lung findings are new. The 3 pillows and the SpO2 have not changed for years.

steps.detail: Neck veins, both ankles, abdomen, weight, and nausea: the systemic circulation.
3 pillows for 5 years and the same SpO2 at 3 visits: the lung disease, not new congestion.
None, so nothing new points to the left side.
Right sided backup goes to the systemic veins, not the lungs.

elimination.verdict: Right sided failure from the lung disease, with systemic backup.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, crackles in both lung bases, and 1+ pitting edema in both ankles. B type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is 640 pg/mL. An echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 60% with a thick, stiff left ventricle that fills slowly. The client's adult child says, "The heart is pumping out a normal amount, so this can't be heart failure." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "It is heart failure, but symptoms will be milder than with a weak squeeze."
options.rationale: The first half is right: heart failure can occur with a preserved ejection fraction. The second half is not. Both types produce similar symptoms, and this client already has orthopnea and crackles.

options.text: "The thick wall means the heart is squeezing harder to make up for weakness."
options.rationale: A thick wall can be a compensation, which makes this tempting. But an ejection fraction of 60% shows the squeeze is normal, so there is no weakness to make up for. The stiff wall is the problem: it cannot relax and fill.

options.text: "A normal squeeze rules out heart failure, so the lungs are the likely cause."
options.rationale: This agrees with the misconception. A preserved ejection fraction does not rule out heart failure, and the high BNP points to ventricular stretch.

options.text: "It squeezes normally but is too stiff to fill, and that is heart failure."
options.rationale: The deciding cue is the stiff left ventricle that fills slowly with an ejection fraction of 60%. This is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, a problem with relaxation and filling, and it produces symptoms similar to reduced ejection fraction.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is a contraction problem, typically below 40%. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is a filling problem from a stiff ventricle, with the ejection fraction relatively preserved. Both produce similar symptoms.
questions.strategy: Three options each hold a piece of the truth: it is heart failure, the wall is thick, and the squeeze is normal. The echocardiogram cue, a stiff ventricle that fills slowly with an ejection fraction of 60%, and the fact that both types share symptoms decide it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ejection fraction 60% with a thick, stiff left ventricle that fills slowly.
Preserved ejection fraction: a relaxation and filling problem.
It is heart failure, but symptoms are similar to reduced ejection fraction, not milder.
A thick wall here is not compensation for weakness, since the squeeze is normal; a normal ejection fraction does not rule out failure.

elimination.verdict: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a stiff ventricle with similar symptoms.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: Before discharge, a client with heart failure is taught about a diuretic, a beta blocker, and low sodium. Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I'll read labels and buy fewer canned foods."
options.rationale: A low sodium diet means checking labels for sodium content and using few canned or prepared foods.

options.text: "I'll stop the beta blocker if my pulse feels slow."
options.rationale: Checking the pulse is right, but a beta blocker should not be stopped abruptly, because this raises the risk of worsening heart failure. A slow pulse is reported to the provider.

options.text: "I'll rest after making the bed, before I shower."
options.rationale: Balancing activity with rest reduces the heart's workload and keeps the client able to finish daily tasks.

options.text: "I'll skip the water pill when my ankles look normal."
options.rationale: Medications are taken as prescribed. Normal looking ankles do not mean the excess fluid is gone, and skipped doses lead to fluid buildup.

options.text: "I'll call if I wake up gasping or need more pillows."
options.rationale: New paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea or worsening orthopnea is a worsening symptom to report.

options.text: "I'll weigh each morning on the same scale before breakfast."
options.rationale: Daily weight at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing detects fluid gain early. A gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours or 5 lb in 1 week is reported.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure teaching: limit sodium by reading labels and avoiding canned foods and added salt, including salt added at the table, weigh daily on the same scale, take every medication as prescribed without stopping or skipping, balance activity with rest, and report worsening symptoms such as new night dyspnea or more pillows to breathe.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each statement on its own, without counting how many you have picked. Watch for the half right one: checking a pulse is a good idea paired with an unsafe action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Labels and fewer canned foods meet the limit.
Every morning, same scale, before eating.
Do not stop the beta blocker or skip the diuretic on your own.
Rest between tasks.
New night gasping or more pillows means worsening failure.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with heart failure has poorly controlled hypertension and often skips lisinopril. Which teaching by the nurse targets a cause of the heart failure?

options.text: "Rest in bed for most of each day to protect your heart."
options.rationale: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump enough to meet the body's needs, not that it is about to stop. Teaching is to balance activity with rest, not to stay in bed.

options.text: "Take your lisinopril every day to keep your pressure down."
options.rationale: Hypertension is a cause of heart failure. The heart pumps against the pressure, and uncontrolled readings keep adding to its work. Taking the drug every day targets that cause.

options.text: "Take your lisinopril only on days your pressure reads high."
options.rationale: Antihypertensives are taken every day as prescribed. Taking it only on high days leaves the pressure that strains the heart uncontrolled.

options.text: "Keep your fluid intake under 1 liter each day."
options.rationale: Fluid intake did not cause the failure, and a fluid limit is used only when it is prescribed. The stem names no fluid restriction.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump enough for the body's needs. Hypertension and myocardial infarction are leading causes, so controlling the pressure with daily drugs targets a cause the client can change.
questions.strategy: Find the cause in the history that the client can still change, then pick the teaching aimed at it.

steps.detail: The history names poorly controlled hypertension, and the client skips doses.

steps.action: Remove the teaching aimed at no cause
steps.detail: Bed rest and a 1 liter limit do not target the cause, so A and D are out.
C leaves the pressure uncontrolled on most days. B targets the cause with daily use.

elimination.verdict: B. Daily blood pressure control targets a cause of this client's heart failure.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: Two weeks after starting carvedilol for heart failure, a client says, "I don't feel better, so I'm stopping it." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Stop it for now; your provider can restart it later."
options.rationale: Stopping a beta blocker abruptly raises the risk of decompensation, and only the prescriber changes the regimen.

options.text: "Take it only on days your heart rate is above 70."
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a reason to hold it, and skipping doses by a self chosen rule breaks adherence and the steady blockade the drug depends on.

options.text: "Keep taking it; its benefit builds over months."
options.rationale: In heart failure, beta blockers reverse the harm of long sympathetic stimulation, and the benefit appears over months rather than immediately. Stopping suddenly can worsen the failure.

options.text: "Keep taking it, and ask about doubling the dose."
options.rationale: Continuing is right, but the dose is raised slowly by the provider, starting from a very low dose. Doubling it to speed the benefit risks bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers for heart failure start at a very low dose, are raised slowly, take months to show benefit, and are never stopped abruptly. Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, and dizziness on standing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the drug going. The difference is who changes the dose and how fast; not feeling better yet is not a reason to change it.

steps.detail: Feeling no better at 2 weeks is expected; it is not an adverse effect to act on.
Abrupt stopping or self chosen skipping risks decompensation.
Both continue the drug; doubling the dose is not how beta blockers are titrated.
The benefit builds over months.

elimination.verdict: Keep taking it as prescribed; the benefit takes time, and it is not stopped suddenly.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is short of breath at 30 degrees, with oxygen saturation above the prescribed oxygen threshold. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler's
options.rationale: High Fowler's is the intervention for dyspnea in heart failure. Sitting upright lets the diaphragm descend, eases breathing, and reduces the blood returning to the congested lungs.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L per minute by nasal cannula
options.rationale: Oxygen in heart failure is for hypoxemia. The saturation is above the prescribed threshold, so the prescription does not apply now.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to flat
options.rationale: Lying flat shifts more blood into the lungs and worsens the dyspnea; this is why clients with heart failure have orthopnea.

options.text: Elevate both legs on pillows
options.rationale: Raising the legs returns more blood to the heart and lungs, which adds to the congestion, and it does nothing for the dyspnea.

questions.takeaway: In heart failure, high Fowler's position is for dyspnea and oxygen is for hypoxemia. A short of breath client with SpO2 above the prescribed threshold needs positioning, not oxygen.
questions.strategy: Match each treatment to the finding it treats. The oxygen saturation decides whether the oxygen prescription applies; the dyspnea decides the position.

steps.detail: Above the prescribed threshold: the oxygen prescription does not apply.
High Fowler's position.
Lying flat worsens pulmonary congestion.
More venous return adds to the congestion.

elimination.verdict: Raise the client to high Fowler's position.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure who reports nausea and has eaten half of each meal for 1 week. The client says, "This low salt food has no taste." Neck veins are distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees, and there is 2+ pitting edema in both ankles.
