questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has had systemic lupus erythematosus for 12 years, has never smoked, and has no diabetes. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg, and low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is 94 mg/dL. For 2 weeks the client has had chest pressure when climbing stairs that goes away within 3 minutes of rest, and pressing on the chest does not bring it on. The client says, "It can't be my heart arteries, because I have none of the usual causes. It must be my lupus." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Track whether the pressure changes when you move or press on your chest."
options.rationale: Chest wall pain is a fair thought in lupus, but the stem already says pressing on the chest does not bring it on. Pressure that comes with stairs and goes with rest fits ischemia, so tracking it delays care.

options.text: "Lupus raises plaque risk, and this pattern needs a provider visit today."
options.rationale: Autoimmune disease is a risk factor for atherosclerosis. New angina is a reason for urgent evaluation, and the exertion and rest pattern points to the heart arteries.

options.text: "Lupus can inflame the lining around the heart; mention it at your next visit."
options.rationale: Lupus can cause pericarditis, which makes this sound informed. But that pain is usually sharp and changes with position or breathing. Pressure with stairs that ends with rest fits ischemia, and waiting for the next visit delays evaluation.

options.text: "Your normal cholesterol and pressure make a heart artery cause unlikely."
options.rationale: The numbers are in range, which makes this sound reassuring. But lupus is itself a risk factor for plaque, and new exertional chest pressure needs evaluation whatever the other risks are.

questions.takeaway: Autoimmune disease is a risk factor for atherosclerosis, so a client with lupus and none of the usual risks can still have coronary plaque. New chest pressure that comes with exertion and eases with rest needs urgent evaluation.
questions.strategy: Three options fit the client's belief: chest wall pain, pericarditis from lupus, or a low risk profile. Let the stated cue decide: the pressure comes with stairs, eases with rest, and is not brought on by pressing. Then remember that lupus is a plaque risk on its own.

steps.detail: Pressure with stairs that ends with rest and is not reproduced by pressing: ischemia until proven otherwise.
Chest wall pain is ruled out by the pressing cue, and pericarditis pain is sharp and positional; both delay care.
Normal LDL and pressure do not cancel the lupus risk.
Name lupus as a plaque risk and send the client for evaluation today.

elimination.verdict: B. Lupus is a risk factor for plaque, and new exertional chest pressure needs evaluation today.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has had chest pressure with climbing stairs, and at times with emotional upset, for 2 years from a coronary artery narrowed by plaque. Today, while seated during a heated argument, the client felt pressure, 4 of 10. Heart rate was 70/min before the argument and 114/min during it. The pressure ended within 3 minutes after the argument stopped, and the frequency, intensity, and length match the past 2 years. Which findings support that this episode fits the client's predictable angina rather than an acute coronary syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: The heart rate rose to 114/min during the argument
options.rationale: The argument raised the heart rate and the heart's need for oxygen, much as stairs do. A clear trigger for demand fits the client's known pattern.

options.text: The pressure began while the client was seated
options.rationale: Being seated looks like pressure at rest, but the heart rate of 114 beats per minute shows demand was high. Sitting alone does not support the chronic pattern.

options.text: The pressure ended within 3 minutes after the argument stopped
options.rationale: When the trigger ended, demand fell back within what the narrowed artery can supply, and the pressure stopped quickly.

options.text: The frequency, intensity and length match the past 2 years
options.rationale: An acute coronary syndrome is new, worsening, or at rest. Episodes that match a 2 year pattern are predictable.

options.text: The coronary artery has been narrowed by plaque for 2 years
options.rationale: Plaque is present in both chronic angina and an acute coronary syndrome, so it does not tell them apart.

options.text: The pressure was rated 4 of 10
options.rationale: A pain rating alone does not separate the two. The match to the past pattern is what matters, and that is a separate finding.

questions.takeaway: Emotional stress, like exertion, raises heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand. Pressure with a clear demand trigger that ends when the trigger ends, in a pattern unchanged over time, is predictable angina. New, worsening or true rest pressure points to an acute coronary syndrome.
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding: does it show a demand trigger, quick relief, or an unchanged pattern? Findings present in both conditions do not support either one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate 70 rising to 114 beats per minute shows raised demand, so A is in.
Ending within 3 minutes of the argument stopping and matching the past pattern fit the chronic form, so C and D are in.
Sitting is offset by the high rate, and plaque and a pain number appear in both conditions, so B, E and F are out.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D. A demand trigger, quick relief and an unchanged pattern fit predictable angina.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with hypertension in a clinic exam room. At 0950, blood pressure was 170/100 mm Hg, and the client was speaking clearly with equal hand grips. At 1010, blood pressure is 174/104 mm Hg. The client's speech is now slurred, and one hand grip is weaker than the other; both changes began 10 minutes ago. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Activate the emergency response and record 1000 as the onset
options.rationale: The deciding cue is the new slurred speech and one sided weakness that began at 1000. Stroke is a major complication of hypertension, and new neurologic changes need emergency evaluation whatever the exact measurement. The time of onset guides treatment.

options.text: Have the client rest 5 minutes and repeat the blood pressure
options.rationale: Without the neurologic change, a measurement below the crisis level would allow a calm recheck, which makes this tempting. A new deficit is an emergency, and waiting to recheck delays care.

options.text: Give the scheduled oral antihypertensive dose early
options.rationale: Lowering the pressure without evaluation and a prescription is not the first action, and rapid lowering can reduce perfusion to the brain.

options.text: Measure lying and standing blood pressures
options.rationale: Orthostatic readings would delay care and are unsafe with new weakness. The findings point to the brain, not to a drop on standing.

questions.takeaway: Persistent hypertension damages the brain, and stroke is a major complication. New neurologic changes in a client with hypertension are an emergency even when the reading is below the crisis level.
questions.strategy: Two options look reasonable when only the number is read. The new slurred speech and one sided weakness decide it: neurologic change outranks the threshold.

steps.detail: Speech clear and grips equal at 0950; slurred speech and a weaker grip on one side now.
New neurologic deficit in hypertension: possible stroke.
A number below the crisis level does not outweigh a new deficit.

steps.action: Reject the drug and the orthostatics
steps.detail: Both delay emergency care and may lower brain perfusion.

elimination.verdict: New slurred speech and one sided weakness: emergency response for a possible stroke.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.scenario: The nurse at a clinic reviews the average blood pressure of six adult clients. Each average comes from 3 visits, measured in the same arm with a cuff sized to the arm after 5 minutes of seated rest. The two arms read within 2 mm Hg of each other at the first visit for every client. None of the clients takes a blood pressure drug.
questions.stem: For each client, indicate the blood pressure category.

rows.text: Client 1: average 124/76 mm Hg
rows.rationale: A systolic of 120 to 129 mm Hg with a diastolic below 80 mm Hg is elevated blood pressure. It is not yet hypertension, but lifestyle change is taught now.

rows.text: Client 2: average 136/78 mm Hg
rows.rationale: A systolic of 130 to 139 mm Hg is stage 1 even though the diastolic is below 80 mm Hg.

rows.text: Client 3: average 118/84 mm Hg
rows.rationale: The systolic alone would be normal, but a diastolic of 80 to 89 mm Hg places the client in stage 1. The higher category of the two numbers sets the category.

rows.text: Client 4: average 142/88 mm Hg
rows.rationale: A systolic of 140 mm Hg or higher is stage 2. The diastolic of 88 mm Hg would be stage 1, and the higher of the two categories is used.

rows.text: Client 5: average 116/76 mm Hg
rows.rationale: Both a systolic below 120 mm Hg and a diastolic below 80 mm Hg are needed for normal blood pressure, and this client meets both.

rows.text: Client 6: average 128/92 mm Hg
rows.rationale: A systolic of 128 mm Hg alone would be elevated, but a diastolic of 90 mm Hg or higher is stage 2. Reading only the top number would wrongly call this elevated.

questions.takeaway: Normal is below 120 and below 80 mm Hg. Elevated is 120 to 129 with a diastolic below 80. Stage 1 is 130 to 139 or 80 to 89. Stage 2 is 140 or higher or 90 or higher. When the two numbers fall in different categories, the higher category applies.
questions.strategy: Classify the systolic and the diastolic separately, then take the higher of the two categories. Watch the clients whose top number looks harmless.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Place the systolic and the diastolic in their own category first.
Clients 3 and 6 move up because of the diastolic.
Stage 1 and stage 2 use or, so one number is enough; elevated requires a diastolic below 80 mm Hg.

elimination.verdict: Client 1 elevated; clients 2 and 3 stage 1; clients 4 and 6 stage 2; client 5 normal.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client with new hypertension takes no prescribed or over the counter drugs. Which findings in the record point to a secondary cause? Select all that apply.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea on a recent sleep study
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea is a condition that causes secondary hypertension. Treating the apnea is part of treating the pressure.

options.text: Hypertension in a parent and a grandparent
options.rationale: Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor for primary hypertension. It does not point to another condition causing the pressure.

options.text: Overweight and walks less than one day a week
options.rationale: Overweight and physical inactivity are modifiable risk factors for primary hypertension, not a separate condition raising the pressure.

options.text: Chronic kidney disease that came before the hypertension
options.rationale: Kidney disease is a cause of secondary hypertension. Because the kidney disease came first, it is the likely source rather than a result of the pressure.

options.text: Untreated Cushing syndrome diagnosed 4 months ago
options.rationale: Cushing syndrome is a cause of secondary hypertension. The client takes no drugs, so the pressure fits the untreated condition.

options.text: Eats takeout meals 5 nights a week
options.rationale: High sodium intake is a modifiable risk factor for primary hypertension. Diet raises the pressure without being a separate condition.

questions.takeaway: Secondary hypertension is caused by another condition or a medication: kidney disease, primary aldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, obstructive sleep apnea, pregnancy, or certain drugs. Family history, weight, inactivity and sodium are risk factors for primary hypertension.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into one of two piles: a risk factor that adds to primary hypertension, or another condition that could be driving the pressure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A condition or a risk factor.
Sleep apnea, kidney disease and Cushing syndrome each cause secondary hypertension.
Family history, weight, inactivity and takeout food fit primary hypertension.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate primary and secondary hypertension and identify major risk factors.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the record of a client with long standing, poorly controlled hypertension. Which findings suggest target organ damage? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serum creatinine unchanged from 3 years ago
options.rationale: An unchanged creatinine shows no sign of kidney damage so far. A rising creatinine would point to chronic kidney disease.

options.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiogram
options.rationale: Left ventricular hypertrophy is damage to the heart from years of high pressure. The heart is a target organ.

options.text: Peripheral vascular disease diagnosed last year
options.rationale: Persistent hypertension damages vessels, and peripheral vascular disease is the vessel form of target organ damage.

options.text: Clear speech and equal grip strength
options.rationale: Clear speech and equal grips show no sign of stroke at present.

options.text: A regular heart rate at rest
options.rationale: A regular resting rate does not by itself show damage to the heart.

options.text: Needs 3 pillows and has crackles
options.rationale: Needing more pillows to breathe at night (orthopnea) and crackles are findings of heart failure, a target organ complication of long standing hypertension.

questions.takeaway: Persistent hypertension damages vessels and decreases organ perfusion. Brain: stroke. Heart: left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary artery disease, heart failure. Kidneys: chronic kidney disease. Vessels: peripheral vascular disease.
questions.strategy: Walk through the target organs one at a time: brain, heart, kidneys and vessels. Mark a finding only when it shows damage, not when it shows the organ is still working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear speech and equal grips show no stroke.
Left ventricular hypertrophy and orthopnea with crackles show damage.
Creatinine is unchanged; peripheral vascular disease shows vessel damage.

elimination.verdict: B, C, F.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client switched from lisinopril to an angiotensin receptor blocker because of a cough. The cough is gone and readings are at goal. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reinforce daily use and the home log
options.rationale: Angiotensin receptor blockers are a first line class and a good choice when an ACE inhibitor causes a cough. The readings are at goal, so the plan is working and daily use with home checks continues.

options.text: Suggest restarting the lisinopril
options.rationale: The cough stopped because lisinopril was stopped. Restarting it would likely bring the cough back.

options.text: Teach the client to take it only on high days
options.rationale: Antihypertensives are taken every day as prescribed. The readings are at goal because the drug is taken daily.

options.text: Ask the provider to add a diuretic
options.rationale: Angiotensin receptor blockers are first line, and this client's readings are already at goal. No drug needs to be added.

questions.takeaway: Thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and calcium channel blockers are the first line classes. Drugs are matched to the client's response and side effects, so an angiotensin receptor blocker is a common switch for an ACE inhibitor cough. The client keeps taking it daily and keeps checking.
questions.strategy: Judge the outcome first: is the pressure at goal and is the side effect gone? If both are yes, keep the plan.

steps.detail: The readings are at goal, and the cough is gone.
B brings back the cough, and D adds a drug the client does not need.
C limits the drug to high days, but it works because it is taken daily, so A is right.

elimination.verdict: A. The switch kept a first line class without the cough, so the nurse reinforces the plan.

questions.objective: Describe lifestyle changes and common medication classes used to manage hypertension.

questions.stem: A client in hypertensive crisis becomes dizzy and slow to answer 30 minutes after an IV drug lowers the pressure to a normal level. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: Bleeding in the brain from the crisis pressure
options.rationale: Stroke is a complication of very high pressure, but the change began after the pressure fell sharply. The timing points to the fall in pressure, not to the high pressure.

options.text: Low blood glucose caused by the drug
options.rationale: IV antihypertensives do not lower blood glucose. The timing ties the change to the fall in pressure.

options.text: Pressure lowered too rapidly for brain perfusion
options.rationale: Vascular autoregulation maintains tissue perfusion, and pressure in a crisis is lowered gradually. Bringing a crisis pressure to normal within 30 minutes is too rapid and can decrease perfusion and cause cerebral ischemia.

options.text: Anxiety now that the pressure is normal
options.rationale: A normal number does not mean normal perfusion for this client. Assuming anxiety would miss a sign of cerebral ischemia.

questions.takeaway: Vascular autoregulation maintains tissue perfusion. In hypertensive crisis, pressure is lowered gradually, because lowering it too rapidly can decrease perfusion and cause cerebral ischemia, myocardial infarction or kidney injury. In long standing hypertension the vessels are adjusted to the higher pressure.
questions.strategy: Use the timing. The new signs began as the pressure fell, so look for the option that links them to the fall, not to the crisis itself.

steps.detail: Dizziness and slowed answers began 30 minutes after the pressure fell from crisis level to normal.
IV antihypertensives do not lower blood glucose.
A normal number is not normal perfusion for this client.

elimination.verdict: C. The pressure was lowered too rapidly.

questions.objective: Explain the basic mechanisms that regulate blood pressure and contribute to hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse is measuring blood pressure for a client at a first clinic visit. The client's upper arm measures 42 cm around. The large adult cuff is in use in another room, so after 5 minutes of seated rest the nurse uses the standard adult cuff, whose bladder does not reach around the arm. Readings are 158/98 mm Hg in one arm and 156/96 mm Hg in the other. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Record the readings as stage 2 hypertension and begin teaching
options.rationale: Two arms that agree look like a confirmed measurement, which makes this tempting. Both were taken with the same cuff that is too small, so both carry the same error.

options.text: Repeat the measurement with the standard cuff after 5 more minutes
options.rationale: Repeating readings is part of accurate measurement, but repeating with a cuff that is too small repeats the error.

options.text: Record the higher of the two arm readings for this visit
options.rationale: Using the higher arm is the right rule at a first visit, which makes this tempting. But both readings came from a cuff too small for the arm, so the higher one is still falsely high.

options.text: Obtain the large adult cuff and remeasure before recording
options.rationale: A cuff that is too small for the arm gives a falsely high measurement. Accurate measurement starts with the correct cuff size.

questions.takeaway: Accurate blood pressure measurement uses the correct cuff size, repeat readings and both arms at the first visit. A cuff that is too small reads falsely high, and agreement between arms does not fix it.
questions.strategy: Three options follow a real measurement rule: arms that agree, repeat readings, and the higher arm. Before acting on a number, check how it was measured. A cuff that is too small affects every measurement taken with it.

steps.detail: The bladder does not reach around a 42 cm arm.
A small cuff reads falsely high in both arms.
Remeasure with the large cuff before recording, choosing an arm, or teaching.

elimination.verdict: D. Remeasure with the correct cuff size.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse is measuring blood pressure at a client's first clinic visit with a cuff sized to the arm after 5 minutes of seated rest. Two readings in each arm average 144/90 mm Hg in one arm and 136/84 mm Hg in the other. The client says, "Use the lower one. My other arm always reads high at the pharmacy." Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Record the average of the two arms as today's value
options.rationale: Averaging sounds balanced, but it understates the higher arm and mixes two different measurements.

options.text: Record the lower arm, as the client asks
options.rationale: Honoring the request seems client centered, but the lower arm underestimates the pressure and would change the category from stage 2 to stage 1.

options.text: Repeat both arms after 5 more minutes of rest
options.rationale: Repeat readings are part of accurate measurement, and they were done: two readings in each arm after rest with the correct cuff. Repeating adds nothing.

options.text: Record the higher arm and use it at later visits
options.rationale: Comparing both arms at the first visit finds the arm that reads higher. That arm better reflects the true pressure and is used for later readings.

questions.takeaway: Compare both arms at the first visit, then record and use the arm with the higher reading for later measurements. The lower arm underestimates the pressure.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: When every option is a real measurement practice, ask which one keeps the reading accurate. A lower number is not a more accurate number.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Correct cuff, rest, and two readings in each arm are already done.
The lower arm underestimates the pressure.
The higher arm is recorded and used at later visits.

elimination.verdict: D. Use the arm with the higher reading.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a client who started lisinopril for hypertension 1 month ago. Home readings now average 126/78 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 5.8 mEq/L, was 4.3 mEq/L before the drug. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, unchanged. The client says, "I threw out the salt shaker, and now I use a salt substitute on everything." Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The kidneys are failing and can no longer clear potassium
options.rationale: Kidney failure can raise potassium, which makes this tempting. The creatinine is unchanged at 0.9 mg/dL, so kidney function has not changed.

options.text: Lisinopril alone explains the rise, and the diet change is helping
options.rationale: Lisinopril does reduce potassium excretion, and cutting sodium is a good change. This misses that the salt substitute is a large added source of potassium.

options.text: The rise is expected as blood pressure falls and needs no change
options.rationale: Potassium does not rise because blood pressure falls. A level of 5.8 mEq/L is a medication specific adverse effect that needs attention.

options.text: The salt substitute and lisinopril are both raising potassium
options.rationale: Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride. An ACE inhibitor reduces potassium excretion, so the two together drive the level up.

questions.takeaway: Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors such as lisinopril reduce potassium excretion. Salt substitutes are mostly potassium chloride, so a client cutting sodium on an ACE inhibitor needs to avoid them and have potassium checked.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A good change can carry a hidden risk. Look at what the client added, not only at what the client removed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Creatinine is unchanged.
Lisinopril reduces potassium excretion.
A salt substitute is potassium chloride.

elimination.verdict: D. The salt substitute and lisinopril together raise the potassium.

questions.objective: Describe lifestyle changes and common medication classes used to manage hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the 2 week home log of a client taking an antihypertensive. Which average shows that the treatment goal has been met?

options.text: 134/76 mm Hg
options.rationale: The diastolic number is below 80, but the systolic number is 130 or higher, so the goal is not met.

options.text: 128/78 mm Hg
options.rationale: Both numbers are below the goal of 130/80 mm Hg recommended for all people.

options.text: 124/82 mm Hg
options.rationale: The systolic number is below 130, which makes this tempting. The diastolic number is 80 or higher, so the goal is not met.

options.text: 136/72 mm Hg
options.rationale: A low diastolic number does not offset a systolic number of 130 or higher. The goal is not met.

questions.takeaway: The blood pressure goal is below 130/80 mm Hg, and both the systolic and the diastolic numbers must be below it.
questions.strategy: Check each number on its own. One number at goal does not make the reading at goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Below 130/80 mm Hg.
134 and 136 are too high.
82 is too high.

steps.action: Find the reading with both below

elimination.verdict: B. 128/78 mm Hg is below 130/80 mm Hg in both numbers.

questions.objective: Describe lifestyle changes and common medication classes used to manage hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the home log of a client with hypertension who started a calcium channel blocker that acts mainly by dilating arterioles 5 days ago. Blood pressure now averages 132/82 mm Hg, was 152/94 mm Hg. Resting heart rate averages 88/min, was 72/min. Weight is unchanged, and the client reports no thirst, dizziness or chest pain. Which explanation for the faster heart rate is most accurate?

options.text: Fluid loss lowering blood volume and stroke volume
options.rationale: A lower blood volume would speed the heart, which makes this tempting. The weight is unchanged and the client has no thirst, and this drug works by dilating arterioles, not by removing fluid.

options.text: Renin angiotensin aldosterone activation speeding the heart
options.rationale: This system does respond to lower pressure, which makes it tempting. It raises pressure through vasoconstriction and sodium and water retention, not by speeding the heart, and retention would show as a weight gain.

options.text: A baroreceptor reflex speeding the heart as pressure falls
options.rationale: Baroreceptors sense the drop in arterial pressure as the arterioles dilate and raise the heart rate to hold the pressure up. A modest rise in rate after a vasodilator is this reflex.

options.text: Myocardial ischemia from reduced coronary perfusion
options.rationale: A faster heart rate can come with ischemia, which makes this tempting. The client has no chest pain, and an average of 132/82 mm Hg is not low enough to reduce coronary perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure equals cardiac output times peripheral vascular resistance. When a vasodilator lowers resistance, baroreceptors sense the lower pressure and raise the heart rate to hold the pressure up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each mechanism to the cue that would prove it. Fluid loss and retention both change the weight, and ischemia needs chest pain or a low pressure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight is unchanged and there is no thirst.

steps.action: Check the renin angiotensin aldosterone system
steps.detail: It acts through vasoconstriction and retention, not heart rate.
No chest pain, and the pressure is not low.
Baroreceptors speed the heart when pressure falls.

elimination.verdict: C. A baroreceptor reflex responds to the lower pressure.

questions.objective: Explain the basic mechanisms that regulate blood pressure and contribute to hypertension.

questions.stem: A client on neutropenic precautions has new liquid stools, and Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is suspected but not confirmed. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Add contact precautions once the result is confirmed
options.rationale: Contact precautions are right, but the timing is wrong. They are started for suspected as well as confirmed C. difficile.

options.text: Replace neutropenic with contact precautions
options.rationale: Gown and gloves are right, but precautions are added, not swapped. The client still needs protective precautions.

options.text: Add contact precautions now, with gown and gloves
options.rationale: Contact precautions are initiated for suspected or confirmed C. difficile, with gown and gloves during all client contact. The client's protective precautions continue.

options.text: Add droplet precautions with a mask until the result returns
options.rationale: A mask is for droplet spread. C. difficile calls for contact precautions with gown and gloves, added now.

questions.takeaway: Start contact precautions for suspected or confirmed C. difficile, with gown and gloves for all contact. Precautions are added to what the client already needs, never swapped.
questions.strategy: Two decisions are packed into each option: what happens to the precautions the client already has, and when and how the new ones start.

steps.detail: Neutropenic precautions in place. C. difficile suspected, not yet confirmed.
Suspected or confirmed, so start now.
Contact: gown and gloves, not a mask.

steps.action: Check what happens to the first set
steps.detail: It continues.

elimination.verdict: Continue neutropenic precautions and start contact precautions now.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse finishes care for a client on contact precautions for Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile). The hands are not visibly soiled. How should the nurse perform hand hygiene?

options.text: Remove gloves, then wash with soap and water
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after gloves are removed, and for C. difficile soap and water is used when facility policy indicates it.

options.text: Remove gloves, then use alcohol based sanitizer
options.rationale: Sanitizer is preferred in most routine situations when hands are not visibly soiled. For C. difficile, facility policy directs soap and water.

options.text: Wash gloved hands with soap, then remove gloves
options.rationale: Soap and water is right, but the order is wrong. Hands are cleaned after the gloves come off.

options.text: Use sanitizer now, then wash before eating
options.rationale: Washing before eating is correct in general, but it does not replace the hand hygiene the policy requires now.

questions.takeaway: Clean hands after removing gloves. Sanitizer is preferred for routine care when hands are not visibly soiled, but for C. difficile use soap and water when facility policy indicates it.
questions.strategy: "Not visibly soiled" points toward sanitizer. C. difficile overrides the routine choice, and the order of glove removal settles the rest.

steps.detail: Not visibly soiled: sanitizer is usually preferred.

steps.action: Find the exception in the stem
steps.detail: C. difficile: soap and water, per facility policy.
Gloves come off first, then hands are cleaned.

elimination.verdict: Remove gloves, then wash with soap and water.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client on neutropenic precautions and on contact precautions for suspected Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile). The client is tearful and asks to see a family member. The family member arrives and says, "My allergies are acting up, so I have had a runny nose and a little cough since yesterday. I brought a mask, and I will stay only a few minutes." Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Have the family member wear a mask, gown, and gloves for a short visit
options.rationale: The gown and gloves match the contact precautions, which makes this tempting, but equipment does not make an ill visitor safe for a client on neutropenic precautions. The visitor reports new symptoms, and a short visit still exposes the client.

options.text: Explain the illness screening, and offer a phone call instead
options.rationale: Neutropenic precautions include screening visitors and staff for illness. The nurse explains this in plain language and still meets the client's wish for contact in a way that carries no exposure.

options.text: Ask the provider whether a short visit with a mask is safe for this client
options.rationale: Checking with the provider sounds like advocacy, but screening visitors for illness is already part of the precautions the nurse carries out. No new decision is needed, and a mask does not remove the exposure.

options.text: Allow a short visit from the doorway, with the family member in a mask
options.rationale: Distance and a mask feel like a fair compromise, but they do not make an ill visitor safe for a client on neutropenic precautions.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenic precautions protect the client: protective precautions as indicated, meticulous hand hygiene, and screening visitors and staff for illness.
questions.strategy: Every option is something a nurse might do: suit the visitor up, ask the provider, or offer a masked visit from the doorway. The visitor's own explanation, allergies, makes the symptoms sound harmless. The deciding cue is that screening is for symptoms, and this visitor has a runny nose and a cough that began yesterday.

steps.detail: The client, by the neutropenic precautions.
Runny nose and cough since yesterday, whatever the visitor thinks the cause is.
Equipment, distance, and a call to the provider do not remove the exposure, and screening is already the nurse's job.

steps.action: Meet the client's need another way
steps.detail: Explain plainly and offer contact that carries no exposure.

elimination.verdict: B. Explain the illness screening, and offer a phone call instead.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.nursesNote: 1400, day 2 of admission for pneumonia: Restless and pulling at bed linen, was calm and alert at 1000. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 at 1000. Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, same as at 1000. Oral temperature 37.1 °C. Urine output 25 mL per hour, was 60 mL per hour at 1000. Productive cough, unchanged since admission.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 1400 note of a client on day 2 of admission for pneumonia. Highlight the findings that suggest possible sepsis.

segments.text: Restless and pulling at bed linen, was calm and alert at 1000
segments.rationale: A new change in mental status in a client with an infection is an early cue of sepsis.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 at 1000
segments.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute is concerning, and this is a rise from baseline.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, same as at 1000
segments.rationale: The value matches baseline.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
segments.rationale: This reading is not a cue by itself, and it does not rule sepsis out. The nurse does not rely on fever alone.

segments.text: Urine output 25 mL per hour, was 60 mL per hour at 1000
segments.rationale: Decreased urine output signals deterioration.

segments.text: Productive cough, unchanged since admission
segments.rationale: The cough is an expected finding of pneumonia and has not changed.

questions.takeaway: Early cues of sepsis in a client with an infection: new confusion or restlessness, a respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute, temperature changes, and decreased urine output. Fever is not required.
questions.strategy: Look for change from the 1000 baseline in mentation, breathing, and urine output. An unchanged finding of the pneumonia itself is not a new cue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pneumonia.
Mentation, respiratory rate, urine output.
Oxygen saturation and cough.

steps.action: Do not lean on the temperature
steps.detail: 37.1 °C neither adds a cue nor removes the others.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse has just completed an assessment of a client with pneumonia and suspects sepsis. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Obtain the ordered specimens and check the intravenous access
options.rationale: Specimens and working access matter, but they come after help and orders are on the way. Doing them first delays escalation.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process
options.rationale: The assessment is already done and the cues are in hand. When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately so that help and orders are on the way.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs
options.rationale: Reassessment is right while help is on the way, but the stem says the assessment is complete. Repeating it before calling delays escalation.

options.text: Give the prescribed treatment and reassess the response
options.rationale: Treatment is given once it is prescribed, after specimens are obtained and access is checked. It cannot be the first step.

questions.takeaway: When sepsis is suspected and the assessment is done: escalate immediately, reassess while help is on the way, obtain ordered specimens and check intravenous access, then give prescribed treatment promptly and reassess.
questions.strategy: The stem says the assessment has been done and the cues are in hand, so the first move is to escalate. Reassessment follows while help is on the way, and treatment comes after the specimens.

steps.detail: The stem says the nurse just completed the assessment.
Suspected sepsis with the cues in hand calls for the provider or rapid response.

steps.action: Place the rest after the call
steps.detail: Reassess while help comes, then specimens and access, then treatment and reassessment.

elimination.verdict: B. Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.scenario: A client is on day 2 of admission for pneumonia. At 1000 the client was calm and alert with a heart rate of 88 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 95% on room air, and urine output of 60 mL per hour. At 1400 the client is restless and pulling at the bed linen, the heart rate is 112 beats per minute, the respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 95% on room air, urine output is 25 mL per hour, and the oral temperature is 37.1 °C. The cough is unchanged since admission. No new orders have been written.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 1400 assessment of a client with pneumonia. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse should take, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs
options.rationale: The nurse reassesses these while help is on the way.

options.text: Recheck the oral temperature in 1 hour and escalate if a fever develops
options.rationale: The nurse does not wait for fever. Several cues are already present.

options.text: Apply oxygen and recheck the respiratory rate in 30 minutes before calling
options.rationale: Oxygen would fit worsening oxygenation, but the saturation is 95% on room air, the same as at 1000. Waiting 30 minutes delays escalation of a client with new organ dysfunction.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process now
options.rationale: When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately.

options.text: Expected course of pneumonia
options.rationale: New restlessness and a fall in urine output are changes from baseline, not expected findings. The cough, the expected finding, is unchanged.

options.text: Anxiety about the hospital stay
options.rationale: Restlessness with faster breathing and less urine in a client with an infection is not treated as anxiety.

options.text: Possible sepsis
options.rationale: A client with an infection has new restlessness, a faster heart rate, a respiratory rate above 20, and decreased urine output. The changes reach beyond the lungs to mentation and kidney perfusion.

options.text: Worsening pneumonia causing hypoxemia
options.rationale: Restlessness and a faster respiratory rate can come from low oxygen, but the saturation is 95% on room air, unchanged from 1000. Hypoxemia does not explain the change, and the fall in urine output points to a whole body response.

options.text: Amount and color of sputum
options.rationale: Sputum describes the pneumonia. It does not show whether perfusion is getting better.

options.text: Mental status compared with the 1000 baseline
options.rationale: Mental status moving toward baseline is a marker of response to treatment.

options.text: Urine output each hour
options.rationale: Urine output is a key marker of adequate perfusion.

options.text: Oxygen saturation as the single measure of response
options.rationale: Oxygenation is watched, but the nurse judges the whole trend rather than one number, and the saturation never changed here.

questions.takeaway: New changes in mentation, breathing, heart rate, and urine output in a client with an infection are possible sepsis, even with no fever and an unchanged oxygen saturation. Escalate and reassess, then follow the whole trend, especially mental status and urine output.
questions.strategy: Worsening pneumonia is the defensible rival. Use the oxygen saturation: 95% on room air at both times means low oxygen does not explain the restlessness, and the falling urine output shows a response beyond the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saturation 95% at 1000 and 1400 rules out hypoxemia as the cause.
Known infection plus new changes in mentation, heart rate, breathing, and urine output: possible sepsis.
Escalate now and reassess. Options that wait for oxygen effect or for fever are out.
Choose perfusion and mentation markers, not one number or a description of the pneumonia.

elimination.verdict: Possible sepsis; escalate and reassess; monitor hourly urine output and mental status against 1000.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with pneumonia who received the prescribed antimicrobial and intravenous fluids for suspected sepsis 2 hours ago. Before treatment: restless and confused, blood pressure 96/58 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min, both feet cool and mottled, urine output 20 mL per hour. Now: blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg and respiratory rate 22/min; the client is still confused, both feet are still cool and mottled, and urine output is still 20 mL per hour. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Continue the current plan and reassess in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Two key numbers are better, which makes this the most tempting choice, but the nurse judges the whole trend. Mentation, skin, and urine output have not moved in 2 hours, and that is persistent poor perfusion.

options.text: Report the improved blood pressure at the next scheduled update
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but this report waits and leaves out the findings that have not changed. It hides the reason for concern.

options.text: Warm the feet with blankets and recheck the skin in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Warmth is a comfort measure, but mottled feet here are a sign of poor perfusion, not a cold room. Warming treats one finding and delays action.

options.text: Notify the provider that signs of poor perfusion persist
options.rationale: Mentation, skin findings, and urine output are considered together with blood pressure and breathing. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation, now.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend rather than one number: mentation, blood pressure, skin findings, breathing, and urine output together. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.
questions.strategy: A better blood pressure is the most reassuring number there is, and breathing is better too, so continuing the plan feels safe. The deciding cue is that the three findings that show perfusion at the tissues, mentation, skin, and urine output, have not moved in 2 hours.

steps.detail: Better: blood pressure, respiratory rate. Unchanged: mentation, skin, urine output.
Mentation, skin color and temperature, urine output.
Reassessing in 15 minutes fits a client improving across the board. Two hours after treatment, this client is not.
A delayed report and warm blankets each address one piece.
Persistent poor perfusion: escalate further.

elimination.verdict: D. Notify the provider that signs of poor perfusion persist.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a client with pneumonia 6 hours after treatment for sepsis began. Which findings indicate that the client is improving?

options.text: Temperature now normal, still confused, urine output unchanged
options.rationale: One normal value does not show improvement when mentation and urine output have not changed.

options.text: Alert and oriented, breathing slower, urine output increased
options.rationale: Mental status has moved toward baseline, breathing has slowed, and urine output has risen. Every finding given points the same way.

options.text: Alert and oriented, breathing slower, feet still mottled
options.rationale: Mentation and breathing are better, but cool, mottled skin is a sign of poor perfusion. The whole trend has to improve.

options.text: Breathing slower, now responds only when shaken
options.rationale: A slower rate with a drop in responsiveness is not improvement. Mental status has moved away from baseline.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend: mental status toward baseline, blood pressure and perfusion improving, urine output improving, breathing and oxygenation stabilizing.
questions.strategy: Two options start with the same good findings. Read to the end of each: one finishes with a sign of poor perfusion and one with a better urine output.

steps.detail: Sepsis cues: confusion, fast breathing, mottled skin, low urine output.

steps.action: Check each option to the end
steps.detail: Only one has every finding moving the right way.
A normal temperature, a slower rate, or two good findings with mottled skin is not improvement.

elimination.verdict: Alert and oriented, breathing slower, urine output increased.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A postoperative client who walks to the bathroom has an indwelling urinary catheter and an order for strict intake and output. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the catheter in place for strict intake and output
options.rationale: The order is for measurement, not for a catheter. A client who walks to the bathroom can have output measured another way.

options.text: Keep the catheter and increase catheter care
options.rationale: Catheter care helps prevent exposure, but it does not answer whether the device is still needed.

options.text: Ask the provider if the catheter is still needed
options.rationale: The nurse reassesses whether urinary catheters are still needed and raises it with the provider. This client walks to the bathroom, so output can be measured without the catheter.

options.text: Remove the catheter without an order
options.rationale: Measuring output another way is right, but removing the catheter without an order or protocol goes beyond the nurse's role.

questions.takeaway: Invasive devices bypass natural barriers. Reassess whether urinary catheters and vascular access devices are still needed, and raise it when the reason for the device can be met another way.
questions.strategy: The order for strict intake and output makes keeping the catheter look required. Separate what was ordered, which is measurement, from the device, and then stay within the nurse's role.

steps.detail: Postoperative, walks to the bathroom.

steps.action: Separate the order from the device
steps.detail: Output can be measured without a catheter.

steps.action: Compare the two options that question the device
steps.detail: One raises it with the provider. One removes it without an order.

elimination.verdict: C. Ask the provider if the catheter is still needed.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: A stable client with a draining surgical wound has a wound culture and a first antimicrobial dose due now. Which plan should the nurse follow?

options.text: Obtain the culture, then give the antimicrobial
options.rationale: The culture identifies the organism and guides treatment. It is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

options.text: Give the antimicrobial, then obtain the culture
options.rationale: Both actions are right, but the order is reversed. The specimen is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

options.text: Obtain the culture and hold the antimicrobial for results
options.rationale: The culture comes first, but treatment is not held for the result. Treatment of the suspected cause is given as ordered.

options.text: Give the antimicrobial and culture only if the wound worsens
options.rationale: The culture was ordered to guide treatment from the start. It is not kept in reserve.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides treatment. Collect the specimen before the antimicrobial is started when that causes no meaningful delay, and do not hold treatment for the result. In probable sepsis the antimicrobial is not delayed for cultures.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Both orders are due, which can pull toward giving the dose first. The client is stable, so collecting the specimen first causes no harmful delay.

steps.detail: Options that hold or skip an order are out.

steps.action: Compare the two that do both
steps.detail: Culture first, or antimicrobial first.
The specimen is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

elimination.verdict: Culture first, then the antimicrobial.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: Assistive personnel (AP) care for a client with a methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) wound, then an immunosuppressed client with a central line. Which AP actions require intervention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Carries the blood pressure cuff into the second room
options.rationale: Shared equipment is a vehicle that carries organisms from one client to the next. This opens the method of transmission link, so the nurse intervenes and the cuff stays in the first client's room.

options.text: Goes from glove removal to the second client without hand hygiene
options.rationale: Hands are the most common route between clients, and gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Skipping it leaves the method of transmission open, so the nurse intervenes.

options.text: Keeps an intact dressing over the draining wound
options.rationale: This is correct care. The covered dressing contains drainage at the portal of exit, so no correction is needed.

options.text: Wears the same gown into the hall to answer a call light
options.rationale: A gown worn out of the room carries organisms on its surface to the next client. The gown is removed before leaving the room, so the nurse intervenes.

options.text: Reports that the central line dressing is loose
options.rationale: This is correct. A loose dressing over a central line threatens the portal of entry, and reporting it lets the nurse act. No correction is needed.

options.text: Wipes the shared thermometer with a disinfectant wipe before reusing it
options.rationale: This is correct. Cleaning shared equipment between clients removes organisms from the vehicle, so it breaks transmission rather than opening it.

questions.takeaway: The chain runs agent and reservoir, portal of exit, method of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Hands, equipment and clothing that move between clients are the method of transmission, so any slip with them is where you step in.
questions.strategy: Follow the organism from the first client's wound toward the second client. Ask which actions let something touched in the first room reach the second room. Those are the ones to correct; the rest are correct care at other links.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for actions that are wrong and need correction.
The cuff, the unwashed hands and the gown all travel from the first room to the second: correct them.
The intact dressing protects the portal of exit, reporting the loose central line dressing protects the portal of entry, and the wiped thermometer is cleaned between clients: no correction.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client on day 2 of antimicrobial treatment for cellulitis. Which findings should the nurse report promptly? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redness spreading past the admission skin marking
options.rationale: The infection is spreading past the border marked at admission while the client receives the antimicrobial. A worsening site is reported.

options.text: Warmth and swelling at the site, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling are expected with cellulitis, and they match admission.

options.text: Heart rate up from 84 to 108/min
options.rationale: The heart rate has risen from its admission value to above the reference range, a change in circulation in a client with an infection.

options.text: Small yellow drainage, same as yesterday
options.rationale: The drainage has not changed from yesterday.

options.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
options.rationale: The temperature is within the reference range. It is not a cue by itself, and it does not cancel the other changes, because the nurse does not rely on fever alone.

options.text: New confusion, asking the same question repeatedly
options.rationale: This is a new change in mental status from baseline, a change that matters in a client with an infection.

questions.takeaway: Compare each finding with the client's baseline. A spreading site, a rising heart rate, and new confusion are reported even when the temperature is within range.
questions.strategy: Sort every finding into changed or unchanged since admission. Expected findings of cellulitis that have not changed are not new cues, and a normal temperature does not cancel the findings that have changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness past the marking, heart rate up from 84 to 108, new confusion.
Warmth and swelling, and drainage the same as yesterday.

steps.action: Do not lean on the temperature
steps.detail: 37.1 °C neither adds a cue nor removes the others.

elimination.verdict: A, C, F.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client going home with a methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) wound infection and an oral antibiotic. Which statements indicate effective teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "It spreads by touch, from the wound or things it touched."
options.rationale: MRSA is spread by contact: touching the person, the wound, or contaminated items.

options.text: "My family only cleans their hands if they touch the wound."
options.rationale: Contact is the right route, but it is too narrow. Items the drainage has touched also spread MRSA, so hands are cleaned after touching those too.

options.text: "I will clean my hands after removing gloves."
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after gloves are removed, because gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

options.text: "If my hands look dirty, hand sanitizer is enough."
options.rationale: Cleaning the hands is right, but the method is wrong. Visibly soiled hands are washed with soap and water.

options.text: "I will take every dose, even once it looks better."
options.rationale: The whole course is completed. Stopping early when the wound looks better leaves organisms behind.

options.text: "I will save leftover pills in case my child gets a cold."
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections such as a cold, unnecessary use adds to resistance, and leftover pills mean the course was not finished.

questions.takeaway: Teach MRSA as a contact organism: clean hands after touching the wound or dressing and after removing gloves, soap and water when hands are visibly soiled, finish the whole antibiotic course, and never use antibiotics for a viral illness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two wrong statements have the right idea with one fact off: contact limited to the wound in one, the hand hygiene method in the other. Check the reach of contact, the method, and the antibiotic use in each statement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contact includes items the drainage touched, not only the wound.
Visibly dirty hands need soap and water.
Finish the course; a cold is viral.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the history of a client admitted to a medical unit. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client who is 84 years old has chronic kidney disease, receives immunosuppressive treatment, and has a central venous catheter in the right chest and an abdominal surgical incision from 3 months ago that is closed with no redness or drainage. The nurse identifies [[1]] as the factors that increase this client's risk for infection by lowering the body's defenses.

The nurse identifies [[2]] as the factor that bypasses the body's natural barriers.

If this client develops an infection, the nurse expects that [[3]].

options.text: the client's age, the immunosuppressive treatment, and the central venous catheter
options.rationale: Age and the treatment lower immune status, but the catheter does not lower defenses. It bypasses the barriers, and chronic kidney disease is left out.

options.text: the chronic kidney disease, the immunosuppressive treatment, and the abdominal incision
options.rationale: Chronic illness and the treatment lower immune status, but the incision is closed with no redness or drainage, so the skin barrier is intact, and age is left out.

options.text: the client's age, the chronic kidney disease, and the immunosuppressive treatment
options.rationale: Age extremes, chronic illness, and immunosuppressive treatment all lower immune status.

options.text: the abdominal incision
options.rationale: Broken skin gives direct access to pathogens, but this incision is closed with no redness or drainage.

options.text: the central venous catheter
options.rationale: Invasive devices bypass natural barriers and give organisms a direct path into the bloodstream.

options.text: the immunosuppressive treatment
options.rationale: The treatment raises risk by lowering immune status, not by bypassing a barrier.

options.text: a fever will be the first sign, so the temperature is checked every 2 hours
options.rationale: Checking temperature is part of assessment, but fever is not relied on as the first or only sign.

options.text: a fever may not appear, so changes in behavior and function from baseline matter
options.rationale: Immune status shapes the response. The nurse does not rely on fever alone and watches for changes from baseline.

options.text: the white blood cell count will rise before other findings appear
options.rationale: A count is interpreted together with the assessment, and a client with low immune status may not mount the usual rise, so no single lab result is waited on.

questions.takeaway: Immune status drives infection risk: age extremes, chronic illness, and immunosuppressive treatment. Invasive devices and broken skin open a direct path in. In a client with low immune status, do not wait for a fever.
questions.strategy: Sort the client's factors into two groups: those that weaken the defenses and those that open a path past them. A factor belongs in only one group. Then ask what weak defenses do to the signs you expect to see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 84, chronic kidney disease, and the treatment all lower immune status.
The central line bypasses them. The incision is closed with no redness or drainage, so the skin is intact.
Fever may be absent, so compare with baseline. No single lab result replaces the assessment.

elimination.verdict: Age, chronic kidney disease, and the treatment; the central venous catheter; fever may not appear.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 1200 findings of four clients. Which client's findings indicate sepsis rather than an infection alone or an inflammatory response alone?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis, no source of infection found: temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 22/min, alert, urine output 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: Temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate are all outside the reference ranges, which is an inflammatory response. No infection has been found, and sepsis requires infection plus organ dysfunction.

options.text: Urinary tract infection and dementia: temperature 38.1 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 18/min, confused as on admission, urine output 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: Infection with a fever is present, but the confusion matches the admission baseline, and the other findings are within range. No new organ dysfunction is shown.

options.text: Cellulitis of the leg, redness spread 2 cm since 0800: temperature 37.1 °C, heart rate 84/min, respiratory rate 16/min, alert, urine output 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: The local infection is worsening, which raises the risk for sepsis, but every finding outside the leg is within range. No organ dysfunction is shown.

options.text: Urinary tract infection: temperature 37.0 °C, heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 20/min, confused since 1000 after being alert, urine output 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Infection plus a new change in mental status is evidence of organ dysfunction. Sepsis can be present without a fever or abnormal vital signs.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is infection plus organ dysfunction, such as new confusion. An inflammatory response alone does not establish sepsis, and sepsis can occur without abnormal temperature, heart rate, or respiratory rate.
questions.strategy: The client with the most abnormal numbers looks sickest, and the client with dementia also has an infection and confusion. The deciding cue is the word new: only one client's confusion began today after being alert.

steps.detail: Pancreatitis with no infection found shows inflammation, not sepsis.
Mental status, oxygenation, urine output.
One is confused as on admission. One became confused since 1000.
Infection with a fever and fast heart rate meets SIRS but is not sepsis without new organ dysfunction.
Spreading redness alone with every other finding in range is not organ dysfunction.

elimination.verdict: The client with a urinary tract infection and new confusion since 1000.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client with a respiratory infection coughs into the hands and presses the call light. The nurse touches it without gloves and later becomes ill. Which route of transmission occurred?

options.text: Droplet, from the cough
options.rationale: The organism started in a cough, but the route is named by how it reaches the next person. No droplets reached the nurse's mucous membranes.

options.text: Indirect contact, through the call light
options.rationale: The organism reached the nurse on a contaminated item. Touching a person or a contaminated item is the contact route, and spread through an item is indirect contact.

options.text: Direct contact, through touching the client
options.rationale: Contact is the right route, but direct contact is touch between people, and none happened here. The organism traveled on the call light.

options.text: Airborne, through particles in the room air
options.rationale: Airborne spread explains illness without touch or close range. Here the nurse touched a contaminated item, which accounts for the spread.

questions.takeaway: Contact spreads by touching a person or a contaminated item, droplet by respiratory droplets reaching nearby mucous membranes, and airborne by particles that stay suspended in the air. Name the route by how the organism reaches the next person, not by where it came from.
questions.strategy: A cough does not make the route droplet. Ask how the organism reached the next person: by touch, by droplets at close range, or by particles still in the air.

steps.detail: The cough is where the organism came from, not how it reached the nurse.
The call light carried the organism from the client's hands to the nurse's hands.
The stem shows touch of an item, not touch between people.

elimination.verdict: B. Indirect contact, through the call light.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting an older adult with a cough and suspected pneumonia. Which actions belong in the admission infection assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask when the cough started and how it has changed
options.rationale: Symptoms and their onset are part of the history in an infection assessment.

options.text: Ask whether anyone at home or work has been ill
options.rationale: Exposures are part of the history and can point to the source.

options.text: Ask whether any devices, such as a urinary catheter, are used
options.rationale: Devices are part of the history. They bypass natural barriers and can be a source of infection.

options.text: Ask the family how alertness compares with usual
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the client's baseline. Changes in behavior and function matter, and the family member knows what is usual.

options.text: Collect a sputum culture before finishing the history
options.rationale: The nurse obtains ordered specimens. No culture has been ordered, and the history is part of the assessment, not a step to cut short.

options.text: Document an oxygen saturation of 93% as normal for the client's age
options.rationale: 93% is below the reference range of 95 to 100%. Decreased oxygen saturation is a concerning cue, and age does not make it expected.

questions.takeaway: The infection assessment gathers symptoms, onset, exposures, recent treatment, and devices; assesses overall appearance, the likely site, and respiratory status; and compares every finding with baseline. Do not rely on fever alone.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options each sound like good practice: one rushes to identify the organism, and one explains a low value by age. Ask whether the specimen was ordered and whether the value is inside its reference range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Onset, exposures, and devices all belong.
Comparing with usual alertness and activity belongs.
No culture was ordered, and the history is not cut short.
93% is below 95 to 100%, whatever the age.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: The susceptibility report shows that a client's wound organism is resistant to the IV antimicrobial being given. The next dose is due soon. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the next dose on time, then report
options.rationale: On time dosing matters, but this drug may not treat the organism. The provider needs the report before the dose so the order can change.

options.text: Hold the next dose until provider rounds
options.rationale: Questioning the dose is right, but holding it without reporting leaves the client with no treatment and no new plan.

options.text: Report the result before the next dose
options.rationale: The culture and susceptibility test identifies the organism and guides the drug choice. The nurse supports appropriate antimicrobial use by following culture results, and the provider needs this result to change the treatment.

options.text: Check the blood count to judge the drug's effect
options.rationale: The blood count adds information about the immune response, read together with the assessment. It does not answer which drug the organism responds to.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides the antimicrobial choice. The complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response. Read every result together with the assessment, and act on a susceptibility report that does not match the drug being given.
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers: which organism and which drug, or how the body is responding. Then look for the choice that both protects the client from an ineffective drug and gets a new plan.

steps.detail: Susceptibility answers which drug works. The blood count answers how the body is responding.
Giving the dose first and holding it silently both leave the client without an effective plan.

steps.action: Choose the action that changes the plan
steps.detail: Report before the dose is due.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the result to the provider before the next dose.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a urinary tract infection who was alert at 0700 and is confused at 0900. Temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. At 0915 the provider documents probable sepsis without shock and orders blood cultures and an intravenous antimicrobial. Facility policy states that laboratory staff draw blood cultures, and they can reach the unit at 1115. The antimicrobial arrives at 0930, and the intravenous access works. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antimicrobial at 1115, after the blood cultures are drawn
options.rationale: Specimens are obtained before the antimicrobial when that causes no delay, and 1115 is within 3 hours. The 3 hour window is for possible sepsis without shock. Probable sepsis calls for the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour, and waiting for cultures until 1115 delays it 2 hours.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial and give it if the blood pressure falls
options.rationale: Rechecking vital signs is right, but waiting for a falling blood pressure waits for shock. The provider has documented probable sepsis, which calls for the antimicrobial now.

options.text: Draw the cultures from the existing IV line, then give the antimicrobial
options.rationale: Getting the specimen first is the right idea, but facility policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff, and the existing line is not the way the specimen is obtained.

options.text: Give the antimicrobial now, and have the cultures drawn at 1115
options.rationale: For probable sepsis the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Cultures come first only when drawing them delays the antimicrobial by no more than 45 minutes; here the delay would be 2 hours.

questions.takeaway: Probable or definite sepsis, or septic shock: give the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: investigate rapidly and begin treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. Obtain cultures first only when that does not delay the antimicrobial.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: "Without shock" and the culture first habit both point toward waiting until 1115, which is still inside 3 hours. The deciding cue is the provider's word probable: the 3 hour window belongs only to possible sepsis without shock.

steps.detail: The provider documented probable sepsis, not possible sepsis.
Probable sepsis: antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour.
Cultures first is right only when it causes no delay. A 2 hour wait is a delay.
A falling blood pressure is not required to act.
Policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff.

elimination.verdict: D. Give the antimicrobial now, and have the cultures drawn at 1115.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client admitted for elective surgery has a nasal swab positive for methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and no signs of infection. Which statement to the team is accurate?

options.text: "The client is colonized, so the nose is not a reservoir."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but the organism is still present and can still leave the client and reach others. A colonized client is a reservoir.

options.text: "The client is colonized and spreads MRSA by droplets."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but MRSA spreads by contact, on hands and shared equipment, not mainly by droplets.

options.text: "The client is infected but has no fever yet."
options.rationale: The nurse does not rely on fever alone, but this client has no signs of infection at any site. Nothing shows the organism invading and growing.

options.text: "The client is colonized, and hands can carry it."
options.rationale: Colonization differs from infection: the organism is present without symptomatic disease. A reservoir is where the agent lives, so hands and shared equipment can carry it to the next client.

questions.takeaway: Colonization means the organism is present without disease. A colonized client is still a reservoir, and an infection that develops during care can come from the client's own organisms or an outside source.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate carrying an organism from being infected by it, then follow the organism: where it lives and how it leaves. Three options agree on colonization, so the decision rests on the reservoir and the route.

steps.detail: Positive screen, no signs of infection at any site: colonization. This removes the infection option.
Colonized still means a reservoir, which removes the option that says it is not one.
MRSA travels by contact on hands and equipment, which removes the droplet option.

elimination.verdict: D. The client is colonized, and hands can carry it.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A client who had a stroke coughs and has a wet voice after swallowing thin liquids. Which portal of entry is at risk?

options.text: Respiratory tract, through aspirated liquid
options.rationale: Coughing and a wet voice with thin liquids mean the liquid is going into the airway. Aspiration leads to respiratory infection such as pneumonia.

options.text: Gastrointestinal tract, through swallowed liquid
options.rationale: The liquid is swallowed, but the cough and wet voice show it is not staying in the gastrointestinal tract. Ask where the organism actually gets in.

options.text: Throat lining, through injury from coughing
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes in the throat do allow entry, but nothing shows a damaged membrane. The finding points to the airway.

options.text: Respiratory tract, through a weakened immune response
options.rationale: The portal is right, but the reason is not. The stem shows liquid entering the airway, not a change in immunity.

questions.takeaway: Infections enter through the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts, through broken skin or damaged mucous membranes, and through vascular access and other invasive devices that bypass natural barriers.
questions.strategy: Ask where the organism would actually get in, not which body part is named first. A swallow that ends in a cough enters the airway.

steps.detail: A wet cough with thin liquids is aspiration, so respiratory tract.
Swallowing names the gastrointestinal tract, but the liquid is not staying there.
Two options name the respiratory tract; only one gives the path the stem supports.

elimination.verdict: A. Respiratory tract, through aspirated liquid.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with no diagnosed infection. Which actions follow standard precautions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hand hygiene before and after client contact
options.rationale: Hand hygiene before and after client contact is part of standard precautions for every client.

options.text: Gown and gloves to empty a drain that may splash
options.rationale: Equipment is chosen for the exposure expected. Gloves protect from body fluids, and a gown is worn when drainage may reach clothing or skin.

options.text: Gloves to count a radial pulse on intact skin
options.rationale: Gloves are right for body fluids and broken skin, but counting a pulse on intact skin carries no expected exposure.

options.text: Used needle into the sharps container uncapped
