options.rationale: The ECG records electrical activity and signs of ischemia. It does not measure the amount of blood pumped.

questions.takeaway: The echocardiogram shows the heart's structure and measures ejection fraction, so it answers whether the ventricle contracts poorly. The chest x ray shows size and congestion, troponin shows damage, and the ECG shows electrical activity.
questions.strategy: Match the clinical question to the test: poor contraction means ejection fraction, and ejection fraction means echocardiogram.

steps.detail: The provider wants to know how well the left ventricle contracts.
Contraction is judged by ejection fraction, which the echocardiogram measures.
The x ray, troponin and ECG each measure something else.

elimination.verdict: B. The echocardiogram measures ejection fraction and shows the heart's structure.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with an acute myocardial infarction who had a coronary stent placed at 0500, about 5 hours after chest pain began, and has had no pain since. ST segments on the 12 lead ECG returned to baseline after the stent. Troponin I was 2.1 ng/mL at 0400, 18.0 ng/mL at 1200, and 9.5 ng/mL at 0400 the next day. A family member says, "The number shot up after the stent, so the stent must have failed." Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "A rise this large means new damage, and the stent may need to be checked."
options.rationale: A rising troponin can mean new damage, which makes this defensible. The client has had no pain, the ST segments returned to baseline, and the level is now falling.

options.text: "If the stent had worked, the level would have stayed near 2.1."
options.rationale: This sounds logical, since an open artery should limit damage. But reperfusion washes troponin out of the injured muscle, so a rise to an early, high peak after the stent is expected, not a sign of failure.

options.text: "The drop to 9.5 shows the heart muscle has fully healed."
options.rationale: The falling level is good news, which makes this tempting. But healing takes weeks, and troponin stays elevated for more than a week. The fall reflects washout and clearance, not completed healing.

options.text: "Opening the artery washes troponin out, so an early peak is expected."
options.rationale: With reperfusion, troponin peaks earlier and higher and then falls sooner. No pain, ST segments at baseline and a falling level fit an open artery.

questions.takeaway: Troponin I and T are the preferred markers for acute myocardial infarction. After reperfusion the curve peaks earlier and higher, then falls. Judge the stent by the whole picture: pain, ECG and the trend.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option reads one part of the curve: the rise, the starting value, or the fall. Read the whole trend with the other findings: no pain, ST segments at baseline, and an early peak that is already falling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2.1, then 18.0, then 9.5 ng/mL: an early peak that is now falling.
No pain and ST segments back to baseline.
An early, high peak that falls fits reperfusion; the fall is clearance, not healing.

elimination.verdict: D. The early peak and fall fit an open artery.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client 3 hours after a coronary stent was placed through the femoral artery for unstable angina. The client must keep the leg straight and lie flat. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Chest pressure, 3 of 10, like the pressure before the stent
options.rationale: Recurrent chest pressure after a stent can mean acute closure of the treated artery, which threatens the heart muscle. It needs a 12 lead ECG and immediate report.

options.text: A dime sized spot of blood on the dressing, unchanged for 1 hour
options.rationale: Bleeding at the insertion site is a real complication, which makes this tempting. A small spot that has not grown is not active bleeding; the nurse keeps checking it.

options.text: Potassium 3.5 mEq/L, was 3.9 mEq/L before the procedure
options.rationale: Potassium is monitored after the procedure, and the level fell. It is still within range and does not threaten the heart muscle now.

options.text: Low back ache, 6 of 10, from lying flat with the leg straight
options.rationale: This is the highest pain score, which draws attention. Back ache from lying flat is expected and is treated with comfort measures.

questions.takeaway: After a coronary stent, recurrent chest pain can signal acute closure of the vessel, often with ST elevation. It outranks an unchanged dressing spot, a potassium within range and expected back discomfort.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Do not let the highest pain number decide. Ask which finding threatens the heart muscle right now.

steps.action: Ask what the stent can do
steps.detail: The treated artery can close again.
Chest pressure like before the stent.
A small, unchanged spot is not active bleeding.
Back ache from lying flat is expected.

elimination.verdict: A. Recurrent chest pressure may be acute closure of the stented artery.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with a predictable pattern of angina asks why metoprolol was added when the problem is narrowed arteries. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It widens the narrowed arteries so more blood gets through."
options.rationale: Improving coronary flow is a treatment goal, which makes this tempting. Widening the coronary arteries describes a nitrate; a stent or bypass opens the narrowing.

options.text: "It keeps platelets from forming a clot on the plaque."
options.rationale: Preventing clots is the job of antiplatelet therapy, not a beta blocker.

options.text: "It lowers your cholesterol so the plaque stops growing."
options.rationale: Lowering cholesterol reduces a risk factor, but a beta blocker does not do it.

options.text: "It slows the heart rate so the heart needs less oxygen."
options.rationale: A beta blocker lowers the heart rate, which reduces myocardial oxygen demand so the narrowed artery can meet it.

questions.takeaway: Angina treatment works on both sides of the balance: improve coronary flow, or reduce myocardial oxygen demand. A beta blocker reduces demand by slowing the heart rate.
questions.strategy: Match each option to the drug or treatment it really describes. Only one describes a beta blocker.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Improve flow, reduce demand, prevent complications.
A nitrate.
Antiplatelet therapy.
Slows the heart and lowers oxygen demand.

elimination.verdict: D. A beta blocker reduces myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the history of a client admitted with an acute myocardial infarction. The client has had type 2 diabetes and hypertension for 15 years and has smoked for 30 years. For the past year, chest pressure came only when walking uphill and eased with rest. This morning, pressure began while the client was at rest. Place the events in the client's coronary artery in the order they most likely occurred.

options.text: Macrophages gather and form a fatty streak, then a fibrous plaque
options.rationale: Third. Oxidized low density lipoprotein draws macrophages, which fill with lipid and build the fatty streak and then the fibrous plaque.

options.text: Years of high glucose, high pressure and smoking injure the lining
options.rationale: First. Diabetes, hypertension and smoking injure the endothelium, which starts the process.

options.text: The plaque ruptures and a clot blocks flow to the muscle
options.rationale: Fifth. Rupture with thrombosis causes the acute coronary syndrome, which fits pressure that began at rest this morning.

options.text: Low density lipoprotein (LDL) enters the wall and is oxidized
options.rationale: Second. LDL moves through the injured lining into the artery wall, where it is oxidized.

options.text: The plaque narrows the artery and limits flow on exertion
options.rationale: Fourth. A narrowed artery cannot raise flow when demand rises, which fits a year of pressure only when walking uphill.

questions.takeaway: Atherosclerosis leads to coronary artery disease in order: endothelial injury, LDL entry and oxidation, macrophages forming a fatty streak and fibrous plaque, narrowing with ischemia on exertion, then rupture and thrombosis causing an acute coronary syndrome or myocardial infarction.
questions.strategy: Anchor the ends first: injury starts the process, and rupture with a clot is the sudden event. Then use the client's history to place the steps between.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Risk factors injure the lining.
LDL enters and is oxidized, then macrophages form the streak and plaque.

steps.action: Match the year of exertional pressure
steps.detail: A narrowed artery limits flow on exertion.
Rupture and a clot.

elimination.verdict: B, D, A, E, C.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: After hip surgery under general anesthesia, a client has not voided in 8 hours and reports lower abdominal pressure. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Insert a straight catheter to drain the bladder
options.rationale: Catheterization may be needed, but it is an invasive intervention taken before the nurse knows whether the bladder is full. A catheter is used only after the indication is confirmed and alternatives are considered.

options.text: Palpate the bladder and obtain a bladder scan
options.rationale: The client has not voided for 8 hours after anesthesia and reports lower abdominal pressure. The nurse assesses bladder fullness and obtains a bladder scan to find out how much urine the bladder holds before choosing an intervention.

options.text: Give extra oral fluid to stimulate voiding
options.rationale: Lack of fluid is not the problem. More volume adds to a bladder that may not be emptying.

options.text: Request an indwelling catheter from the provider
options.rationale: Retention has not been confirmed yet. An indwelling catheter also carries a risk of catheter associated infection, so the nurse gathers bladder data first.

questions.takeaway: When retention is suspected, the nurse assesses the last void, symptoms, and output, then obtains a bladder scan when indicated. Assessment comes before catheterization or a report.
questions.strategy: Three options act on retention as if it were confirmed. Find the option that confirms it first.

steps.detail: No void for 8 hours after anesthesia, with lower abdominal pressure.
Catheterizing, adding fluid, and reporting retention all act before the bladder volume is known.
Palpate the bladder and obtain a bladder scan.

elimination.verdict: B. Palpate the bladder and obtain a bladder scan.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: After general anesthesia, a client feels the urge but cannot void. A bladder scan shows a full bladder. Which plan best fits the cause?

options.text: Increase oral fluids until the client is able to void
options.rationale: A full bladder on the scan means the kidneys are producing urine. More fluid adds to a bladder that is not emptying.

options.text: Request imaging of the ureters to check for swelling
options.rationale: The ureters carry urine to the bladder, and the scan shows urine has already arrived there. The problem is emptying the bladder, not delivery to it.

options.text: Coach pelvic muscle tightening and rescan in 2 hours
options.rationale: The sphincter must relax, not tighten, for urine to leave. Waiting 2 hours also leaves an overdistended bladder untreated.

options.text: Drain the bladder now and expect voiding to recover
options.rationale: Voiding needs nerve signals about fullness, bladder muscle contraction and sphincter relaxation. Anesthesia is a non obstructive cause that slows those signals, so you drain the bladder as prescribed and expect function to return as the effect fades.

questions.takeaway: Urine collects in the bladder, nerve signals report fullness, the bladder muscle contracts and the sphincter relaxes. Anesthesia disrupts this coordination and causes non obstructive retention, so the plan is to drain the bladder as ordered and watch for voiding to return.
questions.strategy: Use the scan to place the problem first: is urine being made, is it reaching the bladder, or is it failing to leave? Then pick the plan that matches that cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A full bladder rules out low production (A) and a ureter problem (B).
The sphincter relaxes to let urine out, so tightening (C) is backward.
Anesthesia slows the nerve signals for emptying; drain now and expect it to recover (D).

elimination.verdict: D. Drain the bladder now and expect voiding to recover.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who had hip surgery 2 days ago and has a prescription for straight catheterization if the postvoid residual is greater than 300 mL. The assistive personnel helped the client void 150 mL at 1000 and scanned the bladder at 1045, which showed 380 mL. The client reports no abdominal pressure. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Perform the straight catheterization as prescribed
options.rationale: The 380 mL is above the 300 mL limit, which makes this look like simply following the prescription. The scan was done 45 minutes after the void, so the kidneys kept filling the bladder and the number is not a postvoid residual.

options.text: Record 380 mL as the postvoid residual
options.rationale: Recording the value treats the scan as valid. A scan done 45 minutes after voiding also measures newly made urine, so it cannot be charted as a residual.

options.text: Have the client void, then rescan within 15 minutes
options.rationale: A postvoid residual is accurate only when it is measured within 5 to 15 minutes after the client voids. The 1045 scan was too late, so the nurse obtains a valid measurement before applying the prescription.

options.text: Palpate the bladder and catheterize if it is distended
options.rationale: Palpation is a sound assessment, which makes this tempting. The prescription is based on a measured residual, not on palpation, and the client has no pressure, so the nurse first obtains a valid scan.

questions.takeaway: Measure a postvoid residual within 5 to 15 minutes after the client voids. A scan done later includes newly produced urine and overstates what the bladder failed to empty.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options act on the 380 mL as if it were a true residual. Check how the number was obtained: a scan 45 minutes after the void is not a postvoid residual.

steps.detail: Void at 1000, scan at 1045: 45 minutes apart.
A scan that late includes new urine, so 380 mL is not a valid residual.
The prescription depends on a measured residual, not palpation, and the client has no pressure.
Have the client void and rescan within 5 to 15 minutes, then apply the prescription.

elimination.verdict: C. Have the client void, then rescan within 15 minutes.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: While inflating the balloon of an indwelling urinary catheter, the nurse feels resistance and the client reports sudden pain. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Stop, withdraw the water, advance, and reinflate
options.rationale: Sudden pain and resistance mean the balloon may be inflating in the urethra. The nurse stops, lets the fluid return, advances the catheter farther into the bladder, and reinflates.

options.text: Finish injecting the full volume to seat the balloon
options.rationale: Continuing to inflate a balloon that may be in the urethra can injure the urethra. Pain and resistance are signals to stop.

options.text: Leave the balloon partly inflated and secure the catheter
options.rationale: An underinflated balloon can become distorted and damage the bladder, and the catheter may still sit in the urethra.

options.text: Remove the catheter and report the pain to the provider
options.rationale: Removal and a report are the steps if pain continues after the catheter is repositioned. The first step is to deflate, advance, and reinflate.

questions.takeaway: If the client reports sudden pain or the nurse feels resistance during balloon inflation, stop, let the fluid return, advance the catheter, and reinflate. If pain continues, remove the catheter and notify the provider.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options stop inflating. Ask which one corrects the likely cause before giving up on the catheter.

steps.detail: Sudden pain and resistance during inflation suggest the balloon is in the urethra.
Finishing the injection or leaving it partly inflated both risk injury.
Removal is for pain that continues; repositioning comes first.

elimination.verdict: A. Stop, withdraw the water, advance, and reinflate.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse observes assistive personnel caring for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which actions require the nurse to intervene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hangs the bag on the bed frame below the bladder
options.rationale: Keeping the bag below the bladder lets urine drain by gravity and prevents backflow. No correction is needed.

options.text: Sets the bag on the floor while repositioning
options.rationale: The bag must stay off the floor. Contact with the floor contaminates the bag and its emptying spout.

options.text: Disconnects the catheter from the tubing to empty the bag
options.rationale: Separating the catheter from the tubing opens the closed drainage system and lets organisms in. The bag is emptied through its spout.

options.text: Places the bag on the client's lap for a transfer
options.rationale: On the lap, the bag sits above the bladder, so urine can flow back into the bladder.

options.text: Coils extra tubing on the mattress without kinks
options.rationale: Tubing free of kinks keeps urine flowing. No correction is needed.

options.text: Leaves the tubing under the client's thigh
options.rationale: Lying on the tubing compresses it and blocks drainage. The tubing must stay free of kinks and pressure.

questions.takeaway: Routine indwelling catheter care: hand hygiene before all care, a closed drainage system, tubing free of kinks, and the bag below the bladder and off the floor.
questions.strategy: Test each action against the four routine care rules: hand hygiene, closed system, no kinks, bag below the bladder and off the floor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bed frame below the bladder is correct; the floor and the lap are not.
Disconnecting the catheter breaks the closed system.
Coiled tubing with no kinks is correct; tubing under the thigh is compressed.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: A client, 66 years old, had an indwelling urinary catheter removed at 0600 after 3 days. The nurse reviews the findings recorded between 0600 and 1400.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the findings of a client whose indwelling urinary catheter was removed this morning. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected after catheter removal or requires follow up.

rows.text: Mild burning with the first void at 0930
rows.rationale: Mild burning or discomfort with the first voids after removal comes from urethral irritation and soon subsides.

rows.text: Voided 320 mL of clear, pale yellow urine at 0930
rows.rationale: A void of 320 mL of clear urine within a few hours shows the bladder is filling and emptying after removal.

rows.text: Voids of 40 mL at 1130, 1200, and 1230, with a feeling of incomplete emptying
rows.rationale: Small, frequent voids with a sensation of incomplete emptying can mean retention. The nurse assesses for bladder distention and obtains a bladder scan.

rows.text: Oral temperature 38.5 °C at 1300, was 36.8 °C at 0600, with flank pain
rows.rationale: Any client whose catheter was recently removed is at risk for urinary tract infection. A new fever with flank pain may mean an upper urinary tract infection.

rows.text: Burning with every void through 1400, rated 6 of 10
rows.rationale: Burning with the first few voids is expected, but burning that continues with every void may mean infection.

rows.text: Drinking 240 mL of fluid every 2 hours as taught
rows.rationale: Maintaining fluid intake after removal is part of the teaching, and it supports normal urine output.

questions.takeaway: After catheter removal, expect mild burning with the first voids. Evaluate for retention (small, frequent voids, incomplete emptying) and for infection (fever, flank pain, continued painful voiding).
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Separate the first void from the pattern. A brief symptom at the first void is expected; the same symptom that persists, or a new systemic sign, needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning at the first void is expected; burning with every void through 1400 is not.
Three voids of 40 mL with incomplete emptying need a bladder assessment.
A new temperature of 38.5 °C with flank pain needs follow up.
A 320 mL clear void and intake as taught show the plan working.

elimination.verdict: Expected: rows 1, 2, 6. Requires follow up: rows 3, 4, 5.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A client at the clinic reports leaking urine before reaching the toilet, burning, frequent voiding, and cloudy, foul smelling urine. Which problem is most likely?

options.text: Urgency incontinence from involuntary bladder contractions
options.rationale: Leakage with a sudden urge fits urgency incontinence, but the burning, the cloudy foul smelling urine, and the frequency point to an infection as the cause.

options.text: Urinary tract infection causing urgency and frequency
options.rationale: Burning with urination, urgency, frequent voiding, and a change in urine appearance are the signs of a urinary tract infection. The urgency explains the leakage.

options.text: Stress incontinence from weak pelvic floor muscles
options.rationale: Stress incontinence is leakage with coughing, sneezing, or activity. The client leaks with urgency, not with effort.

options.text: Chronic retention with leakage from an overfull bladder
options.rationale: Retention can cause small voids and leakage, but it does not explain the burning or the cloudy urine.

questions.takeaway: A urinary tract infection presents with burning or pain with urination, urgency or frequency, lower abdominal discomfort, and possible changes in urine appearance.
questions.strategy: Leakage pulls toward an incontinence type. Ask which problem explains every finding, including the burning and the cloudy urine.

steps.detail: Burning, leakage before reaching the toilet, frequency, cloudy urine with odor.
Urgency incontinence explains the leakage but not the burning or the urine change; stress incontinence has the wrong trigger.
Retention does not explain burning or cloudy urine.
A urinary tract infection explains all the findings.

elimination.verdict: B. Urinary tract infection causing urgency and frequency.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client to collect a clean voided urine specimen for culture. Which client statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will start in the toilet, then catch midstream."
options.rationale: The first part of the stream flushes organisms from the urethral opening. The specimen is caught from the middle of the stream, and the cup is removed before the flow stops.

options.text: "I will catch the very first part of the stream."
options.rationale: The first urine carries organisms from the urethral opening and contaminates the culture. The first part goes into the toilet.

options.text: "I will pour urine from the toilet hat into the cup."
options.rationale: A toilet hat is not sterile. Pouring from it contaminates the specimen.

options.text: "I will hold the lid by its inside surface."
options.rationale: The inside of the lid and the cup must not be touched. The client handles only the outside surfaces.

questions.takeaway: For a clean voided specimen, cleanse the urethral opening, start the stream into the toilet, collect from the middle of the stream, and touch only the outside of the cup and lid.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Find the step each wrong statement contaminates: the first stream, a nonsterile container, or the inside of the lid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The first urine flushes the opening, so it is not collected.
A toilet hat is not sterile.
Only outside surfaces are touched.
Start in the toilet, then catch midstream.

elimination.verdict: A. "I will start in the toilet, then catch midstream."

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A client in long term care walks with help and has urine leakage. Which nursing actions support dignity and independence? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask about the client's usual voiding times at home
options.rationale: Asking about the usual routine lets the plan follow the client's own pattern.

options.text: Explain each step of perineal care before uncovering
options.rationale: Explaining care before exposing or touching the client respects the client's privacy and gives the client control.

options.text: Keep an absorbent product on the client at all times
options.rationale: This replaces toileting with containment for staff convenience. The client can walk with help and needs access to the toilet, not a product worn at all times.

options.text: Offer a bedpan at night in place of the preferred commode
options.rationale: The client's preferred toileting method is supported when it is safe. Saving staff time is not a reason to override it.

options.text: Have the client pull up the pants as able after toileting
options.rationale: Encouraging participation in self care supports independence.

questions.takeaway: Dignity in elimination care: ask about the usual routine, explain before exposing or touching, provide privacy and respectful language, support the preferred toileting method when safe, and encourage self care.
questions.strategy: Mark each action true or false by asking whose need it serves: the client's routine, privacy, and independence, or staff convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Asking about home voiding times and explaining before uncovering are correct.
Having the client pull up the pants encourages self care.
A product worn at all times and a bedpan in place of the preferred commode serve staff, not the client.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with weakness of the left arm and leg after a stroke. The client uses the call light as soon as the urge to void begins, and urine leaks while the client waits 10 to 15 minutes for help walking to the bathroom. When staff help the client onto the toilet within 5 minutes of the urge, no leakage occurs and each void is 250 to 300 mL. Which intervention best addresses the cause of the leakage?

options.text: Begin bladder training to lengthen the time between voids
options.rationale: Leakage that follows an urge looks like urgency incontinence, which bladder training treats. The cue is that no leakage occurs when the client reaches the toilet within 5 minutes and voids 250 to 300 mL: the bladder holds urine normally, and the delay is the problem.

options.text: Limit fluids in the evening to reduce the urge to void
options.rationale: Less fluid seems to lower the chance of leaking, but the leakage happens while the client waits for help, and restricting fluid concentrates urine and irritates the bladder. It does not shorten the wait.

options.text: Apply an absorbent brief to wear while waiting for help
options.rationale: A brief protects the clothing and seems caring, but it contains leakage without treating the cause and leaves urine on the skin. The client stays dry when access is quick.

options.text: Place a commode on the right side and schedule toileting
options.rationale: The client recognizes the urge but leaks while waiting for help to walk, which is functional incontinence. A commode on the stronger right side and scheduled toileting remove the delay in reaching the toilet.

questions.takeaway: Functional incontinence is leakage because the client has difficulty reaching or using the toilet. Care improves access, such as a bedside commode, and schedules regular toileting assistance.
questions.strategy: Leakage after an urge points toward urgency incontinence, and two options only manage the leakage. Decide by what happens when the toilet is reached quickly: no leakage within 5 minutes means the barrier is access, not the bladder.

steps.detail: The client feels the urge and calls, then leaks while waiting for help to walk.
No leakage when on the toilet within 5 minutes, with voids of 250 to 300 mL, rules out a bladder that cannot hold urine.
A brief and fewer evening fluids do not shorten the wait.

steps.action: Match the care to the cause
steps.detail: Functional incontinence needs better access on the stronger side and scheduled toileting.

elimination.verdict: D. Place a commode on the right side and schedule toileting.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: After abdominal surgery, a client's hourly urine output is falling while the heart rate rises and blood pressure drops. The catheter drains freely. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline at the bedside
options.rationale: The catheter drains freely. Irrigation is done only when it is indicated and prescribed, and the rising heart rate and falling blood pressure point away from a blocked catheter.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and recheck output in 2 hours
options.rationale: Waiting 2 more hours delays the report of falling output while the heart rate rises and the blood pressure falls.

options.text: Report the output and vital sign trends
options.rationale: Output is falling while the heart rate rises and the blood pressure falls. The nurse has already ruled out a drainage problem, so a significant decrease in output is reported promptly with the trends that go with it.

options.text: Document the output and continue hourly measurement
options.rationale: Documenting is required, but recording the trend without reporting it leaves a significant decrease in output untreated.

questions.takeaway: Compare output with the trend and the clinical situation. Once the drainage system is checked, a significant decrease or absent output is reported promptly, together with the vital sign changes.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you the assessment of the drainage system is already done. Pick the action that moves the problem forward without waiting.

steps.detail: Hourly output falling, heart rate up, blood pressure down.
The catheter drains freely, so drainage is not the cause.
Rechecking in 2 hours and only documenting both postpone the report.
Irrigation needs an indication and an order.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the output and vital sign trends.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client on intake and output receives IV fluid and walks to the bathroom alone. Which actions should the nurse plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place a collection device in the toilet before the next void
options.rationale: Using the correct collection device lets each void be caught and measured while the client keeps privacy in the bathroom.

options.text: Record only the client's oral fluid intake
options.rationale: Intake is recorded from every source, including intravenous fluid. Leaving it out makes the comparison with output inaccurate.

options.text: Compare the output trend with total intake each shift
options.rationale: Trends are compared with intake and the clinical situation, so a drop in output relative to intake is recognized early.

options.text: Document the amount and time of each void
options.rationale: Amount and time are both documented so trends can be compared.

options.text: Estimate each void from how full the device looks
options.rationale: An estimate is not an accurate measurement. Output is measured.

options.text: Total the shift's output from memory
options.rationale: Output is documented with the amount and time of each void, not reconstructed later from memory.

questions.takeaway: Accurate intake and output means the correct collection device, measured output, every source of intake recorded, the amount and time of each entry, and trends compared with intake.
questions.strategy: Ask of each option whether it makes the numbers more accurate or less accurate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The correct device is in place before the next void.
Measured, never estimated or remembered.
All intake sources; amount and time for each void.
Output trend against intake.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client who has vomited for 2 days has not voided in 9 hours, and a bladder scan shows a nearly empty bladder. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: The kidneys are producing very little urine
options.rationale: The kidneys filter blood and produce urine, and the bladder only stores what reaches it. A nearly empty bladder after 9 hours means little urine is being made, which fits the fluid loss from vomiting. Retention would show a full bladder.

options.text: The sphincter is not relaxing to release urine
options.rationale: Failure of the sphincter to relax would trap urine in the bladder. The scan shows the bladder is nearly empty, so it is not holding urine back.

options.text: The urethra is blocked and holding urine back
options.rationale: A blocked urethra would leave urine in the bladder, and the scan would show a full bladder.

options.text: The bladder muscle is not contracting to empty
options.rationale: Weak contraction causes retention with a full bladder. A nearly empty bladder has little to empty.

questions.takeaway: Low output and retention look alike at first because the client is not voiding. A bladder scan separates them: retention means urine is stored and not emptied, while a nearly empty bladder points to the kidneys making little urine.
questions.strategy: Three options describe a bladder that holds urine. The scan says the bladder holds very little.

steps.detail: A nearly empty bladder after 9 hours without voiding.
Sphincter, urethra, and bladder muscle problems all leave a full bladder.
Little urine is being produced by the kidneys.

elimination.verdict: A. The kidneys are producing very little urine.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with urinary problems. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Chronic incomplete emptying, residual unchanged from yesterday
options.rationale: This is ongoing incomplete emptying that has not changed. It needs follow up but is not a sudden change.

options.text: Leaks small amounts with coughing for 3 years
options.rationale: Leakage with coughing is a long standing pattern of stress incontinence. It affects quality of life but is not urgent.

options.text: Mild burning on day 2 of antibiotics for cystitis
options.rationale: Mild burning on the second day of treatment is expected to ease as the antibiotic works. The client is being treated.

options.text: No void for 8 hours, palpable bladder, severe pain
options.rationale: Sudden inability to void with severe pain and a palpable bladder is acute retention. A sudden inability to void needs urgent attention.

questions.takeaway: Acute retention is a sudden inability to urinate and needs urgent attention. Chronic retention and long standing incontinence patterns are ongoing problems that can wait for the acute one.
questions.strategy: Sort acute from chronic. A new, sudden problem with severe pain outranks problems that are unchanged or already treated.

steps.detail: No void for 8 hours with severe pain and a palpable bladder.
Residual the same as yesterday; leakage for 3 years.
Cystitis on day 2 of an antibiotic.
The client with acute retention.

elimination.verdict: D. No void for 8 hours, palpable bladder, severe pain.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: After knee surgery, a client allowed up with help cannot void on a bedpan with the curtain open. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Insert a straight catheter to empty the bladder
options.rationale: Catheterization is considered only after measures that promote normal voiding are tried. The client has not yet tried a usual position with privacy.

options.text: Close the curtain and assist to a commode
options.rationale: The client cannot void lying on a bedpan with no privacy. A usual sitting position, privacy, and adequate time help the bladder empty, and the nurse then reassesses with the void amount or a bladder scan.

options.text: Leave the client on the bedpan and check back later
options.rationale: Staying in the same position without privacy does not change what is keeping the client from voiding, and the bladder keeps filling.

options.text: Give extra oral fluid to strengthen the urge
options.rationale: The problem is emptying, not the urge. More fluid adds volume without helping the bladder empty.

questions.takeaway: For suspected retention, provide safe positioning, privacy, and time before an invasive step, and reassess after each intervention.
questions.strategy: The stem names the barriers: lying on a bedpan and an open curtain. Pick the option that removes them safely.

steps.detail: Lying on a bedpan with no privacy.
The client is allowed up with help.
A catheter comes after normal voiding measures.
Neither removes a barrier.

elimination.verdict: B. Close the curtain and assist to a commode.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the histories of six clients who each have urinary retention.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the histories of clients who have urinary retention. For each history, indicate whether it points to obstructive or non obstructive retention.

rows.text: Spinal anesthesia for surgery 5 hours ago
rows.rationale: Anesthesia interferes with the nerve signals and muscle function that empty the bladder. Nothing blocks the outflow.

rows.text: A stone lodged at the outlet of the bladder
rows.rationale: A bladder stone at the outlet physically blocks urine from leaving the bladder.

rows.text: Nerve damage from diabetes for 20 years
rows.rationale: Nerve damage weakens the signals that tell the bladder it is full and trigger contraction.

rows.text: A new medication that slows bladder muscle contraction
rows.rationale: Medications can cause retention by reducing bladder contraction. The outflow path is open.

rows.text: A tumor that narrows the urethra
rows.rationale: A tumor narrowing the urethra blocks the path urine takes out of the body.

rows.text: A spinal cord injury at the level of the waist
rows.rationale: Spinal cord injury interrupts the nerve pathways that coordinate bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation.

questions.takeaway: Obstructive retention comes from something blocking the outflow, such as stones, tumors, an enlarged prostate, or pelvic organ prolapse. Non obstructive retention comes from nerve damage, spinal cord injury, medications, or anesthesia that interfere with the signals and muscles of emptying.
questions.strategy: Ask one question for each row: is something in the way, or are the nerves and muscle not working?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stone at the bladder outlet and the tumor narrowing the urethra.

steps.action: Find the signal and muscle problems
steps.detail: Anesthesia, diabetic nerve damage, the medication, and spinal cord injury.

elimination.verdict: Obstructive: rows 2 and 5. Non obstructive: rows 1, 3, 4, and 6.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client leaks small amounts of urine when sneezing, laughing, or lifting, with no urgency. Which intervention should the nurse plan?

options.text: Teach pelvic floor muscle exercises
options.rationale: Leakage with sneezing, laughing, and lifting is stress incontinence. Pelvic floor muscle training strengthens the muscles around the urethra so that they hold urine when abdominal pressure rises.

options.text: Schedule toileting every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting addresses functional or urgency patterns. This client leaks with pressure, not with a full bladder or difficulty reaching the toilet.

options.text: Repeat a bladder scan after each void
options.rationale: Nothing suggests incomplete emptying. Repeated scans do not address leakage with pressure.

options.text: Advise the client to limit fluid intake
options.rationale: Restricting fluid concentrates the urine and irritates the bladder. It does not strengthen the muscles that fail under pressure.

questions.takeaway: Stress incontinence is leakage with coughing, sneezing, or activity. Match care to the cause: pelvic floor muscle training for stress leakage.
questions.strategy: Name the incontinence type from the trigger first, then pick the intervention that treats that cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sneezing, laughing, lifting: rises in abdominal pressure.
No urgency and no sign of incomplete emptying.
Pelvic floor muscle training.

elimination.verdict: A. Teach pelvic floor muscle exercises.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client with long standing diabetes reports constant dribbling and small voids. The bladder is still palpable after voiding. Which problem is most likely?

options.text: Urgency incontinence from sudden bladder contractions
options.rationale: Urgency incontinence follows a sudden strong urge, and the bladder empties. This bladder stays full after voiding.

options.text: Stress incontinence from weak pelvic floor muscles
options.rationale: Stress leakage follows coughing, sneezing, or activity, and the bladder empties normally between episodes.

options.text: Overflow incontinence from incomplete bladder emptying
options.rationale: Constant dribbling, small voids, and a bladder still palpable after voiding show leakage from a bladder that does not empty. Long standing diabetes can damage the nerves that signal fullness.

options.text: Functional incontinence from difficulty reaching the toilet
options.rationale: Functional incontinence happens when the client cannot get to or use the toilet in time. Nothing in the stem describes a barrier to the toilet.

questions.takeaway: Overflow incontinence is leakage with incomplete emptying. Small voids or leakage can occur with retention, so a palpable bladder and a high residual after voiding point to overflow.
questions.strategy: Look for the finding that only one type explains: urine left in the bladder after voiding.

steps.detail: Bladder still palpable after a void.
No urge or pressure trigger is described.
No barrier to the toilet is described.

elimination.verdict: C. Overflow incontinence from incomplete bladder emptying.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client who walks independently leaks urine after a sudden strong urge, before reaching the nearby bathroom. Which intervention best addresses the cause?

options.text: Place a bedside commode next to the bed
options.rationale: A commode helps when reaching the toilet is the problem. This client walks independently and the bathroom is close; the leakage starts with the urge itself.

options.text: Limit fluid intake to reduce leakage
options.rationale: Restricting fluid concentrates urine, which irritates the bladder and can worsen urgency.

options.text: Apply an absorbent product and change it often
options.rationale: An absorbent product contains leakage but does not treat its cause, and leaves the skin wet between changes.

options.text: Start bladder training to lengthen intervals
options.rationale: A sudden strong urge with leakage is urgency incontinence. Bladder training teaches the client to delay voiding and gradually lengthen the interval, which reduces urgency and leakage.

questions.takeaway: Urgency incontinence is a sudden strong urge followed by leakage. Bladder training lengthens the time between voids and treats the cause.
questions.strategy: The cue is that the client is independent and close to the bathroom, so access is not the problem. The urge is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden strong urge, then leakage: urgency incontinence.
Walks independently, bathroom nearby.
Absorbent products and fluid limits do not treat the urge.
Bladder training.

elimination.verdict: D. Start bladder training to lengthen intervals.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client with frequent urinary incontinence has red perineal skin with no open areas. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash with soap and a washcloth using firm strokes
options.rationale: Firm scrubbing and soap residue damage skin that is already red. Cleansing after incontinence is gentle.

options.text: Cleanse gently after each episode and pat dry
options.rationale: Gentle cleansing removes urine without friction, and patting dry avoids rubbing the reddened skin.

options.text: Leave each pad in place until it is fully soaked
options.rationale: A soaked pad keeps urine against the skin and worsens the moisture damage.

options.text: Apply a barrier cream after cleansing
options.rationale: A barrier cream protects the skin from urine between episodes.

options.text: Request an indwelling catheter to keep the skin dry
options.rationale: A catheter is used only when indicated and carries a risk of infection. Incontinence alone is not an indication.

options.text: Inspect the perineal skin with each episode of care
options.rationale: Inspecting the perineal skin is indicated with ongoing incontinence, so early damage is found and the plan can change.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence care includes gentle cleansing, skin protection with a barrier cream, and regular inspection of the perineal skin. A catheter is not a skin care measure.
questions.strategy: Judge each option by whether it shortens contact between urine and skin without adding friction or risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gentle cleansing, patting dry, barrier cream.
Inspect the skin with each episode of care.
Scrubbing, soaked pads, and a catheter without an indication.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.nursesNote: Clinic visit. Client is 81 years old, 2 weeks after starting a plan for functional incontinence with a bedside commode and toileting every 2 hours. Leakage 1 time this week, was 6 times in the week before the plan. Uses the commode at night without help. Perineal skin red with a 2 cm open area on the buttock. Pain with voiding 0 of 10. Says, "If my urine turns cloudy or I get a fever, I will wait for my next visit." Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid per day as planned. A family member reports that toileting at 1400 is skipped when the client naps.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the clinic note of a client 2 weeks after a plan of care for functional incontinence began. Highlight the findings that show the plan of care needs revision.

segments.text: Leakage 1 time this week, was 6 times in the week before the plan
segments.rationale: Leakage has dropped from 6 episodes to 1, which shows the plan is working on this outcome.

segments.text: Uses the commode at night without help
segments.rationale: Independent use of the commode meets the goal of greater independence.

segments.text: Perineal skin red with a 2 cm open area on the buttock
segments.rationale: The outcome is intact skin. An open area means skin protection in the plan needs revision.

segments.text: Pain with voiding 0 of 10
segments.rationale: No pain with voiding meets the comfort outcome.

segments.text: Says, "If my urine turns cloudy or I get a fever, I will wait for my next visit."
segments.rationale: Cloudy urine and fever are reportable changes. The client does not know to report them, so teaching needs revision.

segments.text: Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid per day as planned
segments.rationale: Fluid intake matches the plan.

segments.text: A family member reports that toileting at 1400 is skipped when the client naps
segments.rationale: A missed scheduled toileting time means the client cannot fully manage the plan as written. The schedule needs to be revised with the client and family.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the pattern is better, the client has comfort, the skin is intact, the client can manage the plan, and the client knows reportable changes. A no to any of these means the plan needs revision.
questions.strategy: Hold each finding against one evaluation question. Findings that meet their outcome are not the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leakage down from 6 to 1, uses the commode alone: met.
Open area on the buttock: not met.
Would wait with fever and cloudy urine; 1400 toileting skipped: not met.
Pain 0 of 10 and 1,800 mL per day: met.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse needs a urine culture from a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Drain urine from the bag spout into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has been standing and can grow bacteria, so a specimen from the bag gives an inaccurate culture. A specimen is never collected from the drainage bag.

options.text: Aspirate from the cleansed sampling port after clamping
options.rationale: Clamping below the port lets fresh urine collect. Cleansing the port and using a sterile syringe and container avoids contaminating the specimen and keeps the drainage system closed.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter and let urine drip into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Disconnecting opens the closed drainage system, which lets bacteria enter and raises the risk of infection.

options.text: Withdraw urine from the balloon inflation port
options.rationale: The balloon port leads to the balloon, not the bladder. It holds sterile water, not urine.

questions.takeaway: Avoid contaminating a specimen. With an indwelling catheter, collect urine from the sampling port with sterile technique, never from the bag, and never by opening the closed system.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options open the system or use old urine. One uses the wrong port. Choose the one that gets fresh urine with the system closed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Urine in the bag has been standing.
Disconnecting invites infection.
The balloon port holds water.
Sampling port after clamping below it.

elimination.verdict: B. Aspirate from the cleansed sampling port after clamping.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is collecting urinalysis specimens from three clients. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Label all three specimens together in the utility room
options.rationale: Labeling away from the client after collecting several specimens risks switching them. Each specimen is labeled at the bedside.

options.text: Verify each order and use two client identifiers
options.rationale: The nurse verifies the order and the client's identity before collection so that the right test is done on the right client.

options.text: Label each container at the bedside
options.rationale: Specimens are labeled according to requirements so the laboratory can match the result to the right client. Labels usually include the name, date, time, and type of collection.

options.text: Leave the specimens at the bedside until pickup
options.rationale: Specimens are transported according to requirements. Urine left standing at the bedside grows bacteria and changes the results.

options.text: Use urine that has stood in the bedpan
options.rationale: Urinalysis needs fresh urine. Urine left standing grows bacteria and changes the results.

options.text: Explain the collection method to each client first
options.rationale: The nurse explains the collection method so the client can help collect the specimen correctly and without contamination.

questions.takeaway: Specimen collection: verify the order and identity, explain the collection method, use the correct container and technique, avoid contamination, and label and transport according to requirements.
questions.strategy: Look at each step from order to laboratory and ask whether it keeps the right specimen with the right client and the result accurate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Verify the order and two identifiers; explain the method.
Fresh urine, not urine that has stood in a bedpan.
Label at the bedside; transport, do not leave it waiting.

elimination.verdict: B, C, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: A nurse observes the urine of six clients during the morning assessment and reviews each client's history.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the urine findings and histories of six clients during the morning assessment. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or requires follow up.

rows.text: Dark amber urine in a client who drank 600 mL in the past 24 hours and has a dry mouth
rows.rationale: Dark urine sits at the concentrated end of the urine color chart. With low intake and a dry mouth, the finding points to a fluid deficit that needs follow up.

rows.text: Cloudy, foul smelling urine with burning and urgency on voiding
rows.rationale: A change in urine appearance with burning and urgency fits a urinary tract infection.

rows.text: Pale yellow, clear urine in a client who drinks 2,000 mL per day
rows.rationale: Pale, clear urine fits the dilute end of the color chart and the client's intake.

rows.text: Dark yellow first morning void that lightens to pale yellow after the client drinks 720 mL
rows.rationale: Urine held overnight is more concentrated. It lightens as intake increases, and the trend matches the history.

rows.text: Urine output of 120 mL in 8 hours with an intake of 1,600 mL
rows.rationale: Output far below intake is a significant decrease that is compared with intake and reported promptly.

rows.text: Light yellow urine with a mild odor, 250 to 300 mL every 3 to 4 hours
rows.rationale: Light color, mild odor, and regular voids of this size are an expected pattern.

questions.takeaway: Observe color, clarity, and odor, measure output, and combine the findings with symptoms and history. Dark urine with low intake, cloudy foul urine with burning, and output well below intake need follow up.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether the history explains it. If the history makes it worse rather than explains it, follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use the color chart with the history
steps.detail: Dark with low intake: follow up. Dark in the morning that lightens with fluid: expected.
Cloudy and foul with burning and urgency: follow up.
120 mL out against 1,600 mL in: follow up.

elimination.verdict: Requires follow up: rows 1, 2, and 5. Expected: rows 3, 4, and 6.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client with cystitis starts an oral antibiotic today, and the urine culture is pending. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "The culture takes a few days to grow."
options.rationale: This is correct. Bacteria need time to grow, so a culture usually takes 48 to 72 hours.

options.text: "I will start the antibiotic today."
options.rationale: This is correct. Treatment starts once the culture has been collected, and the result is used to adjust it later.

options.text: "If the clinic changes my antibiotic, I will switch."
options.rationale: This is correct. The culture and sensitivity result shows which antibiotics the organism responds to, so a change is possible.

options.text: "Today's urine test showed which antibiotic works."
options.rationale: This needs teaching. The urinalysis screens for signs of infection, such as nitrites and white blood cells. Only the culture identifies the organism and the antibiotics it responds to, so the antibiotic may still change.

questions.takeaway: A urinalysis screens urine for signs of infection; a culture identifies the organism and the antibiotics it responds to, in about 48 to 72 hours. Teach the client that the antibiotic started today may change once the culture returns.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. Match each test to the question it answers, then find the statement that gives the urinalysis the culture's job.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Urinalysis screens; the culture identifies the organism and its sensitivity.
A, B and C fit a pending culture that may change the antibiotic; D credits the urinalysis with the culture's result.

elimination.verdict: D. "Today's urine test showed which antibiotic works."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: Before an imaging study of the urinary tract tomorrow, which client finding requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: Signed consent form is on the chart
options.rationale: A signed consent on the chart is expected preparation. It does not need action.

options.text: Vital signs are at the client's baseline
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs give no reason to delay or change the preparation for the study.

options.text: Says, "Nobody told me why I need this test."
options.rationale: The nurse explains the purpose of each test. The client does not know why the study is ordered or what will happen, so the nurse explains the purpose and the procedure before the test.

options.text: Plans to collect urine in the bathroom with a device
options.rationale: Using the collection device in the bathroom supports privacy and independence. It does not need correction.

questions.takeaway: For laboratory and diagnostic tests, the nurse explains the purpose so the client understands what is being done and why.
questions.strategy: Three options describe preparation that is already in place. Find the cue that shows a need the nurse can meet now.

steps.detail: Consent signed, vital signs at baseline.
Using the device in the bathroom is correct.
The client does not know the purpose of the test.

elimination.verdict: C. Says, "Nobody told me why I need this test."

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is matching three clients to the urinary catheter each one needs. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse matches three clients to the catheter each needs.

A client who needs continuous irrigation after bladder surgery to keep blood clots from forming needs a [[1]] catheter.

A client whose urethra is blocked by scar tissue and who needs long term drainage is expected to have a [[2]] catheter.

A client with a postvoid residual of 450 mL and an order to drain the bladder one time needs a [[3]] catheter.

options.text: three way
options.rationale: A three way catheter includes a separate channel for irrigation, which allows continuous irrigation through a closed system.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter is inserted briefly for drainage and removed. It cannot deliver continuous irrigation.

options.text: suprapubic
options.rationale: A suprapubic catheter drains the bladder through the abdominal wall. It is not chosen for continuous irrigation.

options.text: indwelling urethral
options.rationale: An indwelling urethral catheter passes through the urethra, which is blocked in this client.

options.text: suprapubic
options.rationale: A suprapubic catheter enters the bladder through the abdomen, so it drains urine when the urethra is blocked.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter also passes through the urethra and is removed after one drainage.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter is inserted briefly to drain the bladder and then removed, which fits a one time order.

options.text: three way
options.rationale: A three way catheter stays in place for irrigation. Nothing here calls for irrigation.

options.text: indwelling
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter remains in the bladder and adds infection risk when only one drainage is ordered.

questions.takeaway: Straight catheters drain once and are removed, indwelling catheters remain in the bladder, three way catheters add an irrigation channel, suprapubic catheters enter through the abdomen, and external devices collect urine outside the urethra.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each client: does the catheter stay or come out, and which path can it take?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Continuous irrigation needs an irrigation channel: three way.
A blocked urethra needs a path through the abdomen: suprapubic.
One drainage needs a catheter that is removed: straight.

elimination.verdict: Three way; suprapubic; straight.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: Before inserting an indwelling urinary catheter for hourly output after major surgery, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear clean gloves for the insertion
options.rationale: Catheter insertion uses aseptic technique with sterile gloves and sterile equipment to keep bacteria out of the bladder.

options.text: Ask about a latex allergy
options.rationale: Catheters and gloves can contain latex. The nurse checks for relevant allergies before insertion.

options.text: Choose a larger catheter size than usual
options.rationale: The smallest appropriate catheter is used. A larger catheter increases trauma to the urethra and the risk of infection.

options.text: Confirm the order documents the indication
options.rationale: The nurse confirms the indication before insertion. Hourly output after major surgery is the indication here.

options.text: Secure the catheter to the client's upper thigh
options.rationale: Securing the catheter prevents movement and pulling that injure the urethra and raise infection risk.

options.text: Leave the catheter unsecured after insertion
options.rationale: An unsecured catheter moves and pulls with each position change, which causes trauma.

questions.takeaway: Catheter safety: confirm the indication, consider an alternative, check allergies, use aseptic technique and sterile equipment, use the smallest appropriate catheter, and secure it after insertion.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is the opposite of a safety step. Find the pairs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sterile, not clean.
Smallest appropriate, not larger.
Secured to the thigh, not left free.
Indication and latex allergy.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: On day 3 after abdominal surgery, a client walks with help. The catheter was placed for hourly output, which has ended. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the catheter in place until discharge
options.rationale: Each day a catheter remains raises the risk of a catheter associated infection. The risk of retention is managed by monitoring voiding after removal.

options.text: Replace the catheter with a new one today
options.rationale: Routine catheter changes do not prevent infection. The question is whether the catheter is still needed.

options.text: Remove the catheter per order or protocol
options.rationale: The reason for the catheter, hourly output, no longer exists. Catheters are removed promptly when no longer indicated, per order or protocol, and voiding is monitored after removal.

options.text: Send a urine culture before removing the catheter
options.rationale: The client has no signs of infection. A culture without symptoms does not decide whether the catheter stays.

questions.takeaway: Prevent catheter associated urinary tract infection: use a catheter only when needed, review the indication regularly, and remove it promptly when no longer indicated.
questions.strategy: Ask why the catheter was placed and whether that reason still exists.

steps.detail: Hourly output, which has ended.
Walks with help, no output order.
Review the indication and remove per protocol.

elimination.verdict: C. Remove the catheter per order or protocol.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A long term urinary catheter with gritty sediment has stopped draining, and the bladder is full. There is no irrigation order. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Notify the provider of the blocked drainage
options.rationale: The catheter is likely blocked by sediment, and the bladder is filling. Irrigation is done only when indicated and ordered, and changing a blocked catheter is often safer than flushing debris into the bladder. The provider needs the findings to decide.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter through a closed system
options.rationale: Closed irrigation is the right technique, but irrigation is done only when it is prescribed, and there is no prescription.

options.text: Reposition the client and recheck in 2 hours
options.rationale: The bladder is already full. Waiting 2 more hours lets it keep filling.

options.text: Disconnect the tubing and flush the catheter
options.rationale: Disconnecting opens the closed drainage system, and flushing without a prescription risks pushing debris into the bladder.

questions.takeaway: Irrigate only when indicated and ordered, and follow the approved procedure. When a catheter is blocked and there is no order, report the findings so the provider can order irrigation or a change.
questions.strategy: One option uses the right technique without the order. The cue that decides is the missing irrigation order.

steps.detail: Sediment present, no drainage, full bladder.
No order for irrigation.

steps.action: Reject delay and opening the system
steps.detail: Waiting 2 hours; disconnecting to flush.
Report and obtain an order.

elimination.verdict: A. Notify the provider of the blocked drainage.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse evaluates discharge teaching for a client with a new continent urinary reservoir. Which client statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "My spouse will do all of my stoma care."
options.rationale: Self management support aims for the client to take part in device care. Avoiding the stoma also means the client cannot check drainage and skin.

options.text: "I will call if the skin gets sore or urine changes."
options.rationale: The client names reportable changes in skin and drainage, which shows the client knows what to watch for and can manage the plan.

options.text: "I will wait for my next visit if the skin breaks down."
options.rationale: Skin breakdown is a reportable change. Waiting for the next visit leaves it untreated.

options.text: "An internal reservoir needs no drainage checks."
options.rationale: Drainage and skin are assessed with every urinary diversion, including a continent reservoir.

questions.takeaway: With a urinary diversion, care includes assessing drainage and skin, supporting device care and self management, and individualized teaching. Evaluation checks whether the client can manage the plan and knows reportable changes.
questions.strategy: Use the evaluation questions: can the client manage the care, and does the client know what to report?

steps.detail: Handing all care to a spouse.
Waiting for the next visit with skin breakdown.
Drainage is checked with every diversion.
Reports skin and urine changes.

elimination.verdict: B. "I will call if the skin gets sore or urine changes."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: On day 3 after creation of an ileal conduit, which client finding requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: Clear, pale yellow urine, 900 mL in 8 hours
options.rationale: Clear, pale urine with this output is an expected drainage finding.

options.text: Pouch emptied and output recorded every 4 hours
options.rationale: Emptying the pouch and recording output supports device care and accurate intake and output.

options.text: Watched the pouch change and asks to do the next one
options.rationale: Asking to take part in device care shows readiness for self management.

options.text: Red, weeping skin where urine has leaked
options.rationale: Assessing drainage and skin is part of continuing care, and the outcome is intact skin. Red, weeping skin where urine leaked needs follow up.

questions.takeaway: With an ileal conduit, assess drainage and skin, support device care, and support self management. Skin damage from leaking urine needs follow up.
questions.strategy: Three options describe care and drainage that are on track. Find the one that describes harm.

steps.detail: Clear, pale urine and output recorded: on track.
Asks to try the next change: on track.
Red and weeping where urine leaked: requires follow up.

elimination.verdict: D. Red, weeping skin where urine has leaked.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse admits a client with new nighttime urine leakage. Which findings can affect the client's urinary elimination? Select all that apply.

options.text: Takes a new diuretic each evening
options.rationale: Medications affect urinary elimination. A diuretic increases urine output, and an evening dose produces more urine overnight.

options.text: Allergy to penicillin
options.rationale: A drug allergy does not change how the client stores or empties urine.

options.text: Hand arthritis and pants with small buttons
options.rationale: Clothing management is a factor. Stiff hands and small buttons slow undressing once the client reaches the toilet.

options.text: Does crossword puzzles each afternoon
options.rationale: Puzzle habits do not affect urinary elimination.

options.text: Finds it hard to void with a roommate behind the curtain
options.rationale: Privacy affects the ability to void. A shared room can make the client hold urine or not empty fully.

options.text: Drinks 4 cups of coffee each evening
options.rationale: Fluid intake and habits are factors. A large volume of a caffeinated drink in the evening adds to urine overnight.

questions.takeaway: Factors that influence urinary elimination include fluid intake and habits, growth and development, illness and medications, mobility and clothing management, privacy and culture, and toilet access.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether it changes how much urine is made, how fast the client can get to and use the toilet, or how easily the client can void.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Evening diuretic and evening coffee add overnight urine.
Small buttons with arthritis; a roommate behind the curtain.
Penicillin allergy and afternoon puzzles.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client reports hesitancy and a feeling of incomplete emptying that began 4 days ago, with no burning. Which question should the nurse ask next?

options.text: "Do you leak urine when you cough, sneeze, or lift?"
options.rationale: This question screens for stress incontinence. The client reports trouble starting and emptying, not leakage.

options.text: "How much coffee or tea do you drink?"
options.rationale: Fluid habits matter, but caffeine does not explain a new delay in starting the stream.

options.text: "Have you started any new medicines this week?"
options.rationale: Hesitancy and incomplete emptying that began suddenly 4 days ago suggest retention. Medications are a common non obstructive cause, so a recent medication history is the most useful next question.

options.text: "Do you need help getting to the bathroom?"
options.rationale: Toilet access does not explain hesitancy or incomplete emptying.

questions.takeaway: The nursing history covers pain, urgency, hesitancy, leakage, the feeling of incomplete emptying, fluid intake, and medication history. A new onset of hesitancy and incomplete emptying calls for the medication history.
questions.strategy: Ask what could have changed 4 days ago to cause a new problem with starting and emptying.

steps.detail: Leakage with coughing and toilet access do not cause hesitancy.
Caffeine does not explain a new delay in the stream.

steps.action: Find the cause of a new change
steps.detail: A recently started medication.

elimination.verdict: C. "Have you started any new medicines this week?"

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: During the night, the nurse finds an alert client incontinent of urine in bed while the roommate is awake. Which statement best supports dignity?

options.text: "Let's get your diaper changed so you won't wet the bed again."
options.rationale: "Diaper" and "wet the bed" are childlike terms that shame an adult. Respectful language uses neutral words.

options.text: "I'll close the curtain and explain each step as we change."
options.rationale: Closing the curtain gives privacy from the awake roommate, neutral words respect the client, and explaining each step before touching supports dignity.

options.text: "Next time, please call before you have an accident."
options.rationale: This places blame on the client. The client may have been unable to call in time, and blame increases embarrassment.

options.text: "Don't worry, this happens to everyone your age."
options.rationale: This minimizes the client's feelings and is not true of every older adult. It does not provide privacy or explain care.

questions.takeaway: Support dignity with privacy, respectful language, and an explanation of care before exposing or touching the client.
questions.strategy: Eliminate the options that shame, blame, or dismiss. Then confirm the remaining option includes privacy.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Diaper and wet the bed.
Calling before an accident.
Happens to everyone your age.
Curtain closed, each step explained.

elimination.verdict: B. "I'll close the curtain and explain each step as we change."

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.stem: A client who needs help to reach the commode wants to stop leaking to eat in the dining room. Which outcome is most appropriate?

options.text: Client will have 1 or fewer leaks daily by 1 week
options.rationale: This outcome is set with the client's goal in mind, is measurable by the number of episodes, includes a time frame, and is realistic for a client who still needs help to transfer.

options.text: Client will understand the importance of the toileting schedule
options.rationale: Understanding cannot be measured as written. It names no observable behavior.

options.text: Nurse will offer toileting assistance every 2 hours while awake
options.rationale: This is a nursing intervention, not a client outcome. Outcomes describe what the client will do or experience.

options.text: Client will never leak urine again once the toileting plan begins
options.rationale: Never is absolute and unrealistic for a client who still needs help to reach the commode.

questions.takeaway: Set priorities with the client and choose measurable outcomes: a client behavior, a number, and a time frame, realistic for the client's situation.
questions.strategy: Check each option for three parts: the client as the subject, something you can count or observe, and a time frame.

steps.detail: Offering toileting is an intervention.
Understand names no behavior.
Never is unrealistic.
1 or fewer leaks daily by 1 week.

elimination.verdict: A. Client will have 1 or fewer leaks daily by 1 week.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who had knee surgery under spinal anesthesia 7 hours ago and has received 1,800 mL of IV fluid since surgery. The client has not voided since before surgery and says, "I do not feel any need to go." Which interpretation should guide the nurse's next action?

options.text: The bladder is not yet full enough to cause an urge
options.rationale: An urge depends on nerve signals that report bladder fullness, and anesthesia can block them. After 7 hours and 1,800 mL with no void, the missing urge does not show an empty bladder, and waiting risks overdistention.

options.text: The client is holding urine to avoid using a bedpan
options.rationale: Privacy and position can make voiding hard, which makes this tempting. This client reports no need to go at all; a client holding urine back still feels the urge.

options.text: Anesthesia may be blocking the sense of fullness
options.rationale: Nerve signals communicate bladder fullness, and anesthesia is a non obstructive cause of retention that can interrupt them. The nurse assesses the bladder now, by palpation and a bladder scan, instead of relying on the client's urge.

options.text: The bladder will empty by leaking once it is full
