options.rationale: Urination needs coordinated bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation. Anesthesia causes retention, not free leakage, so waiting for leakage leaves a full bladder unrecognized.

questions.takeaway: Voiding depends on nerve signals of fullness, bladder contraction, and sphincter relaxation. Anesthesia can block the fullness signal, so after surgery the nurse compares intake and time since the last void with the bladder findings, not with the client's urge.
questions.strategy: Three options explain the missing urge in ways that let the nurse wait. The 7 hours and 1,800 mL of intake decide that the bladder is likely full and the sensation is what is missing.

steps.detail: 7 hours, 1,800 mL in, no void.

steps.action: Ask what the urge depends on
steps.detail: Nerve signals that spinal anesthesia can block.
A client holding urine back still feels the urge.
Waiting for an urge or for leakage leaves a full bladder unassessed.

elimination.verdict: C. Anesthesia may be blocking the sense of fullness.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with chronic urinary retention managed with double voiding, whose daily postvoid residual is about 200 mL. At 0900 the client says, "I have not been able to pass any urine since 0400, and my lower belly hurts." Pain is 7 of 10, and the bladder is palpable above the symphysis pubis. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Have the client double void as usual, then scan the bladder
options.rationale: Double voiding is the client's usual plan, which makes it tempting. The client has passed no urine for 5 hours, which is a new, sudden problem that the chronic plan does not address.

options.text: Scan the bladder and report the new inability to void
options.rationale: Chronic retention is ongoing incomplete emptying. A sudden inability to void with pain and a palpable bladder is acute retention, which needs urgent attention. The nurse obtains the bladder scan and reports the findings so they can be acted on.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess in 1 hour
options.rationale: Pain of 7 of 10 needs relief, but treating the pain alone delays care for its cause. A sudden inability to void needs urgent attention, not a 1 hour wait.

options.text: Help the client to the toilet with water running in the sink
options.rationale: Running water and privacy help a client who is able to void. This client has been unable to pass urine for 5 hours and has a painful, palpable bladder, so simple measures delay the urgent report.

questions.takeaway: Chronic retention means ongoing incomplete emptying. A client with chronic retention who suddenly cannot void at all has a new acute problem, and sudden inability to void needs urgent attention.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is something a nurse would do for chronic retention or for pain. Compare with baseline: a client who usually voids now cannot void at all, which is acute retention.

steps.detail: Usual: voids with a residual of about 200 mL. Now: no urine for 5 hours.
Sudden inability to void with pain 7 of 10 and a palpable bladder.

steps.action: Reject the usual plan and comfort measures
steps.detail: Double voiding, running water, and an analgesic all delay the report.
Bladder scan now and report.

elimination.verdict: B. Scan the bladder and report the new inability to void.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a client who walks to the bathroom independently and safely. The client says, "At home I always rinse with water after I use the toilet. Paper alone does not feel clean to me." Which action by the nurse best supports the client's dignity?

options.text: Place warm water in the bathroom for rinsing
options.rationale: Supporting the client's preferred toileting method when it is safe respects the client's culture and comfort. The client toilets independently and safely, so providing the water lets the client keep both the routine and independence.

options.text: Offer moist wipes to use in place of rinsing
options.rationale: Wipes may seem like a fair compromise, but nothing makes rinsing unsafe, and substituting wipes ignores the client's routine.

options.text: Help the client rinse with water after each void
options.rationale: This honors the preference, which makes it tempting. The client toilets independently and safely, so doing the care for the client takes away self care and privacy.

options.text: Ask the family to bring a rinse bottle from home
options.rationale: Involving family is reasonable, but the client goes without the preferred method until the bottle arrives, when the nurse can provide water now.

questions.takeaway: Dignity supporting care asks about the usual routine, supports the preferred toileting method when safe, provides privacy, and encourages participation in self care.
questions.strategy: Two options honor the rinse. The client's independence decides who does it.

steps.detail: Rinsing with water after toileting.

steps.action: Find the safety and ability cue
steps.detail: Walks to the bathroom independently and safely.

steps.action: Reject options that substitute or delay
steps.detail: Wipes instead, or waiting for a bottle from home.
Independent and safe, so the client rinses alone.

elimination.verdict: A. Place warm water in the bathroom for rinsing.

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the plan of care for a client with urgency incontinence who started bladder training 3 weeks ago. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 70 years old, with urgency incontinence started bladder training 3 weeks ago. The client now voids every 2.5 hours, was every 1 hour before training. Leakage occurred 2 times this week, was daily before training. Perineal skin is intact. The client drinks 4 cups of coffee each afternoon, and both leakage episodes this week happened between 1500 and 1700. The client says, "I can hold it now when the urge starts."

The nurse evaluates the plan as [[1]].

The finding that most supports revising the plan is [[2]].

The change the nurse discusses with the client is [[3]].

options.text: effective, needing no change
options.rationale: The interval is longer and leakage is less often, which makes this tempting. Leakage still occurs, and it follows a pattern that can be addressed, so the plan is not finished.

options.text: partly effective, needing revision
options.rationale: The voiding interval lengthened and leakage fell from daily to 2 times a week, so the training is working. Leakage that remains with a clear pattern means the plan needs revision.

options.text: ineffective, needing to stop
options.rationale: The interval lengthened and leakage fell from daily to 2 times a week. Stopping the training would discard a plan that is working.

options.text: the voiding interval of 2.5 hours
options.rationale: A longer interval is the goal of bladder training. It shows progress, not a need for change.

options.text: the client's report of holding the urge
options.rationale: The client's report shows better urge control, which is progress. It does not point to what still causes the leakage.

options.text: the timing of leakage after the afternoon coffee
options.rationale: Both episodes occurred in the hours after the coffee. Caffeine is a bladder irritant that can cause contractions, urgency, and leakage, so this pattern points to the revision.

options.text: shortening the voiding interval back to every 1 hour
options.rationale: Going back to a 1 hour interval undoes the progress of training and does not address the cause of the remaining leakage.

options.text: replacing the afternoon coffee with a drink without caffeine
options.rationale: Replacing the caffeine targets the identified contributing factor while keeping fluid intake within the plan.

options.text: limiting total fluids to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restricting all fluids is not the answer. Adequate fluids are supported within the care plan, and the problem is the irritant, not the volume.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the urinary pattern has changed toward the goal, whether the skin is intact, and whether the plan needs revision. A plan can be working and still need revision when a contributing factor, such as a bladder irritant, is found.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Judge each finding against the outcome. Improvement shows the plan works; a leakage pattern tied to one cause shows what to revise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Better interval and less leakage, but leakage remains: partly effective.
Leakage only after the afternoon coffee.
Remove the irritant, keep the fluids and the training.

elimination.verdict: Partly effective, needing revision; the timing of leakage after the afternoon coffee; replacing the afternoon coffee with a drink without caffeine.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a 24 hour urine collection that begins at 0800, and the laboratory instructions require the urine to be kept cold. At 0800 the client voids 350 mL. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Discard the 0800 void and record 0800 as the start time
options.rationale: The timed period begins after the client urinates. The first void is discarded because that urine was made before the collection period began.

options.text: Save the 0800 void as the first specimen
options.rationale: Saving every void sounds thorough, which makes this the trap. The 0800 urine was made before the period began, so adding it makes the result inaccurate.

options.text: Keep the collection container on ice
options.rationale: The laboratory instructions call for cold storage, so the container stays on ice and the urine does not change before testing.

options.text: Note any flushed void and continue the collection
options.rationale: A missed specimen makes the whole collection inaccurate. The nurse follows agency and laboratory policy, which usually means starting again.

options.text: Add the 0800 void tomorrow to the container
options.rationale: The period ends with a final void at the end of the 24 hours, and that urine is included.

options.text: Post a sign and tell the team that all urine is saved
options.rationale: Signs and verbal communication help every caregiver save all urine during the timed collection.

questions.takeaway: A 24 hour collection starts after a discarded first void and ends with a saved final void. Every void in between is saved, kept cool if required, and a missed void makes the collection inaccurate.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Picture the 24 hours as a box. Urine made before 0800 is outside the box; the final void at 0800 tomorrow is inside it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Discard the 0800 void today.
Save the 0800 void tomorrow.
Ice if required, signs posted, every void saved.
The collection is no longer accurate.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with continuous bladder irrigation through a three way catheter after bladder surgery. From 1200 to 1400, 800 mL of irrigant infused and the drainage bag collected 650 mL. The drainage is light red with small clots, and the client reports bladder spasms and lower abdominal pressure. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Increase the irrigation rate to flush the clots
options.rationale: Clots make a faster rate tempting. The drainage is 150 mL less than the irrigant, so fluid is already staying in the bladder. More inflow adds to the pressure until the outflow is open.

options.text: Give the prescribed antispasmodic medication
options.rationale: The spasms are real and need relief, but they are a sign of the problem. Fluid going in without coming out is the cause, and medicating first leaves the bladder filling.

options.text: Record 650 mL as the urine output
options.rationale: Drainage during irrigation includes the irrigant. The 650 mL is less than the 800 mL infused, so true urine output cannot be 650 mL, and recording it hides a blocked catheter.

options.text: Stop the irrigation and check for a blockage
options.rationale: Drainage 150 mL less than the irrigant, clots, spasms, and lower abdominal pressure show the outflow is blocked and the bladder is filling. Stopping the inflow and checking patency comes first, then the nurse reports and follows the irrigation order.

questions.takeaway: During irrigation, drainage must equal the irrigant plus urine. Drainage less than the irrigant, with spasms and pressure, means the outflow is blocked: stop the inflow, then check the catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Compare what went in with what came out before reading the clots or the spasms.

steps.detail: 800 mL in, 650 mL out: 150 mL is held in the bladder.
Spasms and pressure fit a filling bladder.
A faster rate worsens the distention.
The antispasmodic and the 650 mL entry leave the blockage in place.

elimination.verdict: D. Stop the irrigation and check for a blockage.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: At 1000 the nurse finds a capped urine specimen for culture, labeled with the client's identifiers, on the bedside table. The client says, "I collected it at 0630, midstream, the way you showed me." The specimen has no preservative and has stayed at room temperature. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: It is usable because the client used the right technique
options.rationale: Correct midstream technique limits contamination at collection. It does not protect urine that then stands for 3.5 hours at room temperature.

options.text: It is usable if it is placed on ice before sending
options.rationale: Cooling slows bacterial growth only from the time it starts. The urine has already stood for 3.5 hours without cooling or a preservative.

options.text: It is no longer accurate, and a new specimen is needed
options.rationale: Most urine specimens must reach the laboratory within 2 hours of collection or be preserved. Urine standing at room temperature grows bacteria, so after 3.5 hours the culture would not reflect the bladder. The nurse collects a new specimen and sends it promptly.

options.text: It is usable for urinalysis but not for culture
options.rationale: Urine that stands at room temperature changes in ways that affect the accuracy of testing, so the urinalysis is also unreliable.

questions.takeaway: A correct collection can still give a wrong result. Urine that stands at room temperature without a preservative past the time limit grows bacteria, so the nurse recollects it and sends it promptly.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Several options rescue the specimen. Ask what happened to the urine after it was collected, not only how it was collected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Collected 0630, found 1000: 3.5 hours.
No preservative, room temperature.
Ice now and a urinalysis only both use urine that has already changed.
Good technique does not undo the delay.

elimination.verdict: C. It is no longer accurate, and a new specimen is needed.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client admitted with pneumonia who is alert, walks to the bathroom with standby assistance, and voids 300 to 400 mL every 3 to 4 hours. The provider prescribes strict intake and output and an indwelling urinary catheter "for accurate output." Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Insert the smallest catheter that will drain the urine
options.rationale: Using the smallest appropriate catheter is part of catheter safety, which makes this tempting. The earlier steps are to confirm the indication and consider an alternative, and this client needs neither a catheter nor a smaller one.

options.text: Discuss measuring output with a urine hat instead
options.rationale: Catheter safety starts with confirming the indication and considering an appropriate alternative. The client is alert, walks to the bathroom, and voids normal amounts, so output can be measured accurately with a collection device in the toilet, with no infection risk from a catheter.

options.text: Insert the catheter and review the need for it daily
options.rationale: Daily review prevents catheter associated infection once a catheter is in, but it does not justify inserting one that is not needed.

options.text: Apply an absorbent pad and weigh each pad
options.rationale: The client is continent and walks to the bathroom. Pads take away independence and are less accurate than measuring each void.

questions.takeaway: Before any catheter, the nurse confirms the indication and considers an alternative. A client who is alert and voids on their own can have accurate output measured with a collection device, without the infection risk of a catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options are good catheter practice. Ask first whether this client needs a catheter at all.

steps.detail: Alert, walks, voids 300 to 400 mL: no need to drain the bladder.
Accurate output, which a urine hat provides.
Smallest size and daily review are care for a catheter that should not be placed.
Less accurate and takes away continence.

elimination.verdict: B. Discuss measuring output with a urine hat instead.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: A client is preparing for discharge 6 days after creation of an ileal conduit. The nurse asks the client to describe care at home.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating discharge teaching for a client with a new ileal conduit. For each client statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs further teaching.

rows.text: "Urine will drain all the time, so I will wear the pouch day and night."
rows.rationale: An ileal conduit gives no sensation or control over the continuous flow of urine, so a pouch collects it at all times.

rows.text: "I will wash the skin around the stoma with soap so it stays clean."
rows.rationale: Soap leaves a residue that keeps the pouch from sealing. The skin is cleansed with warm water and patted dry.

rows.text: "I will put a catheter into the stoma 4 to 6 times a day to drain it."
rows.rationale: Catheterizing the stoma 4 to 6 times a day is care for a continent reservoir. An ileal conduit drains on its own into a pouch.

rows.text: "I will measure the stoma and cut the pouch opening to fit."
rows.rationale: A pouch that fits snugly around the stoma prevents urine from leaking onto the skin.

rows.text: "A red, moist stoma is what I expect to see each day."
rows.rationale: A healthy stoma is red and moist.

rows.text: "If urine leaks under the pouch, I will wait to change it until the weekend."
rows.rationale: Urine leaking under the pouch damages the skin. A leaking pouch is changed promptly, and ongoing leaks are reported so the fit can be checked.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the client can manage the care plan. For an ileal conduit, that means a pouch at all times, a snug fit, water without soap on the skin, a red and moist stoma, and prompt changes for leaks.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask which diversion each statement describes. Catheterizing the stoma belongs to the continent reservoir, not the conduit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Continuous drainage into a pouch.
Warm water without soap; change a leaking pouch now.
Cut the opening to fit; red and moist is expected.
Catheterizing 4 to 6 times a day is the continent reservoir.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 4 and 5 show understanding; rows 2, 3 and 6 need further teaching.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who wakes 4 times each night to void and fell last week on the way to the bathroom at 0300. The client drinks 3 cups of tea between 1900 and 2200, takes a diuretic at 0800, and voids 250 to 300 mL each time with no burning or leakage. Which intervention best addresses the cause of the nocturia?

options.text: Move the evening tea to earlier in the day
options.rationale: Three cups of tea in the 3 hours before bed add both volume and caffeine, a bladder irritant, at the time the client sleeps. Avoiding fluids in the 2 hours before bedtime reduces nocturia while keeping the total intake.

options.text: Take the diuretic at bedtime instead of 0800
options.rationale: A diuretic taken in the evening causes nocturia. The 0800 dose is timed correctly, and moving it to bedtime would add more voids at night.

options.text: Place a bedside commode for use at night
options.rationale: After a fall, the commode is a sound safety measure and is tempting for that reason. It shortens the walk but does not reduce how often the client wakes to void.

options.text: Limit total fluid intake to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restricting all fluids risks dehydration and concentrated urine, which irritates the bladder. The problem is the timing of the tea, not the total amount.

questions.takeaway: Fluid intake and habits shape the voiding pattern. Nocturia from evening fluids and caffeine is managed by moving fluids earlier and avoiding them 2 hours before bed, not by cutting total fluids.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The fall makes the commode tempting. The question asks about the cause of the nocturia, so match the option to the timing of the intake.

steps.detail: 3 cups of tea from 1900 to 2200; the diuretic is in the morning.
Voids 250 to 300 mL without burning or leakage.
The commode helps the fall risk but not the waking.
A bedtime diuretic and a total fluid limit both make things worse.

elimination.verdict: A. Move the evening tea to earlier in the day.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client, 84 years old, in long term care who has always been continent and oriented. Since yesterday the client has had 3 episodes of urine leakage, is confused about the day, and is eating less. Oral temperature is 37.3 °C. The assistive personnel suggests absorbent briefs and toileting every 2 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Start a toileting schedule every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting is sound incontinence care, which makes it tempting. It treats the leakage as a lasting pattern before the nurse knows why the leakage started yesterday.

options.text: Assess the urine and voiding for infection
options.rationale: Incontinence that begins suddenly with new confusion and poor appetite in an older adult points to a reversible cause, and infection is a common one. Older adults often show infection as confusion, appetite loss, or new leakage instead of burning or a high fever, so 37.3 °C does not rule it out. The nurse assesses before choosing an incontinence plan.

options.text: Apply absorbent briefs and protect the skin
options.rationale: Skin protection matters once leakage occurs, but briefs only contain the urine. They take away continence the client had until yesterday and leave the cause unexamined.

options.text: Place a bedside commode near the bed
options.rationale: Better toilet access fits functional incontinence. Nothing states a new mobility problem, and a commode does not explain a sudden change in a client who was continent.

questions.takeaway: New incontinence is a change to investigate, not a pattern to manage. In an older adult, sudden leakage with new confusion and poor appetite suggests a reversible cause such as infection, even without a high fever, so the nurse assesses first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Every option is reasonable incontinence care. Ask what is new: a continent, oriented client changed in one day, and a sudden change calls for assessment before a plan.

steps.detail: Continent and oriented until yesterday; now leakage, confusion, and poor appetite.
37.3 °C does not rule out infection in an older adult.
A schedule, briefs, and a commode all manage leakage without finding its cause.
Assess the urine and voiding pattern before choosing a plan.

elimination.verdict: B. Assess the urine and voiding for infection.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.scenario: The nurse is caring for a client, 82 years old, on day 5 after hip surgery. An indwelling urinary catheter was placed for surgery, and the need for it has not been reviewed since day 1. Nurse's note, 0800: Oral temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. Urine in the tubing is cloudy and foul smelling. Reports tenderness above the pubic bone. Oriented to person only, was oriented to person, place, and time on day 4. Incision dry with edges closed.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the note of a client with an indwelling urinary catheter after hip surgery. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Obtain a urine specimen from the sampling port
options.rationale: A culture identifies the organism. Urine from the cleansed sampling port is fresh and keeps the drainage system closed.

options.text: Report the findings and the need for the catheter
options.rationale: Fever, cloudy foul urine, suprapubic tenderness, and new confusion need prompt reporting. The catheter has not been reviewed since day 1, and removing a catheter that is no longer needed is a key step in managing this infection.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter to clear the cloudy urine
options.rationale: Irrigation is done only when indicated and ordered. Cloudy urine is a sign of infection, not a blockage, and opening the system adds risk.

options.text: Collect urine from the drainage bag spout
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has stood at room temperature and is not fresh, so a culture from it is not accurate.

options.text: Restrict fluids to reduce the urine output
options.rationale: Adequate fluids support bladder health. Restricting them concentrates the urine and does nothing for the infection.

options.text: Catheter associated urinary tract infection
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter for 5 days, fever, cloudy foul smelling urine, suprapubic tenderness, and new confusion in an older adult fit an infection linked to the catheter.

options.text: Acute urinary retention
options.rationale: The catheter drains the bladder, and nothing suggests it is blocked. Retention does not explain the fever or cloudy urine.

options.text: Infection of the surgical incision
options.rationale: The incision is dry with closed edges. The urine findings place the infection in the urinary tract.

options.text: Functional incontinence
options.rationale: The client has a catheter in place, and functional incontinence does not cause fever or cloudy urine.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Temperature shows whether the infection is responding to treatment or progressing.

options.text: Urine color, clarity, and odor
options.rationale: Cloudy, foul smelling urine is a cue of infection, and its change shows the response to treatment.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Bowel sounds do not track a urinary tract infection.

options.text: Hip range of motion
options.rationale: Range of motion is part of recovery after hip surgery, but it does not track this problem.

options.text: Pedal pulses
options.rationale: Pedal pulses check circulation and do not reflect the urinary infection.

questions.takeaway: A catheter left in without review raises the risk of infection. In an older adult with a catheter, fever, cloudy foul urine, suprapubic tenderness, and new confusion point to a catheter associated infection: obtain a proper specimen, report, and question the need for the catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Name the problem from the cues that cluster, then choose actions that fit it and keep the system closed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Catheter for 5 days without review, fever, cloudy foul urine, suprapubic tenderness, new confusion.
Incision is intact; the catheter drains; no retention or functional problem.
Fresh specimen from the sampling port; report and review the catheter's need.
Temperature and urine appearance track the infection.

elimination.verdict: Actions: obtain a specimen from the sampling port and report the findings and the catheter's need. Condition: catheter associated urinary tract infection. Monitor: temperature and urine color, clarity, and odor.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client, 79 years old, with urgency incontinence who started an antimuscarinic medication for overactive bladder 5 days ago. The client now has constant dribbling, voids of about 50 mL every hour, and lower abdominal fullness. The bladder is palpable after voiding. The urine is clear, with no burning. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's next action?

options.text: The medication may be causing urinary retention
options.rationale: The medication relaxes the bladder muscle, and in an older adult it can keep the bladder from emptying. A bladder still palpable after voiding, small frequent voids, and constant dribbling point to retention with overflow leakage, which started after the new medication.

options.text: Urgency incontinence is worsening despite treatment
options.rationale: Small, frequent voids look like urgency, which makes this tempting. Urgency incontinence empties the bladder, so it does not leave a palpable bladder after voiding or cause constant dribbling.

options.text: A urinary tract infection is causing the frequency
options.rationale: Infection causes frequency and urgency, but the urine is clear and there is no burning. Infection also does not explain a bladder that stays full after voiding.

options.text: Stress incontinence is causing the dribbling
options.rationale: Stress incontinence leaks small amounts with coughing, sneezing, or activity, and the bladder empties. Constant dribbling with a full bladder after voiding is not this pattern.

questions.takeaway: Small voids or leakage can mean the bladder is not emptying. When a client on a medication that relaxes the bladder has a palpable bladder after voiding and constant dribbling, the nurse suspects retention, not a worsening of the condition being treated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The frequent small voids pull toward urgency. Ask what the bladder looks like after the client voids, and what changed 5 days ago.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new antimuscarinic medication 5 days ago.
Palpable after voiding, small voids, constant dribbling: incomplete emptying.
Clear urine and no burning.
Both empty the bladder; neither leaves it full after voiding.

elimination.verdict: A. The medication may be causing urinary retention.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A parent asks the nurse whether a 2 year old is ready to begin toilet training. Which finding best indicates readiness?

options.text: Wakes dry from sleep each morning
options.rationale: Control develops during the day first. Night dryness often comes later, so waiting for it would delay training a child who may be ready.

options.text: Has just reached 2 years of age
options.rationale: Age alone does not show that the nervous system can signal fullness. Readiness depends on what the child can sense, hold, and communicate.

options.text: Watches an older sibling use the toilet
options.rationale: Interest helps, but watching an older sibling does not show the child can feel the urge or hold urine.

options.text: Stays dry 2 hours and names the urge
options.rationale: A child is ready when the child recognizes bladder fullness, can hold urine for 1 to 2 hours, and can communicate the urge. This finding shows all three.

questions.takeaway: Urinary control depends on nerve signals that report bladder fullness. A child is ready for toilet training when the child senses fullness, holds urine for 1 to 2 hours, and communicates the urge.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Match readiness to what the child's body can do, not to age or interest.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sense fullness, hold urine 1 to 2 hours, and communicate the urge.
Neither shows bladder control.
Day control comes first, so it is not the sign to wait for.
Dry for 2 hours and names the urge.

elimination.verdict: D. Stays dry 2 hours and names the urge.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: A client with frequent incontinence empties the bladder fully with each void and needs accurate output. Which device should the nurse plan to use?

options.text: Indwelling catheter to a drainage bag
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter measures output exactly, which makes it tempting, but it adds infection risk when the bladder empties on its own.

options.text: Absorbent pads weighed after each leak
options.rationale: Weighing pads estimates output but is less accurate, and wet pads in place add skin risk.

options.text: External collection device to a bag
options.rationale: An external device collects urine without entering the bladder. It suits a client who is incontinent and empties the bladder fully, and it measures output with less infection risk than a catheter.

options.text: Straight catheter every 4 hours
options.rationale: Straight catheterization drains a bladder that does not empty. This client empties fully, so repeated insertions add risk without benefit.

questions.takeaway: Catheter safety starts with considering an alternative. A client who is incontinent but empties the bladder fully can have output collected and measured with an external device instead of a catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask whether the bladder empties. If it does, nothing needs to go inside it.

steps.detail: Empties the bladder fully with each void.
Accurate output with the least risk.
Both indwelling and straight catheters enter a bladder that empties.
Less accurate and harder on the skin.

elimination.verdict: C. External collection device to a bag.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client going home with a suprapubic catheter. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will clean around the tube site each day."
options.rationale: Daily inspection and cleansing of the insertion site is part of suprapubic catheter care.

options.text: "I will keep the bag below my bladder."
options.rationale: Keeping the bag below the bladder lets urine drain and prevents backflow.

options.text: "I will call if urine stops draining."
options.rationale: No drainage can mean a blocked catheter, which is a reportable change.

options.text: "I will drink less so the bag fills slowly."
options.rationale: Adequate fluids support bladder health and help prevent infection and sediment. Drinking less concentrates the urine and raises those risks.

questions.takeaway: Home teaching is effective when the client can manage the care plan: site care, a bag below the bladder, adequate fluids, and knowing what to report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that trades bladder health for convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs further teaching: find the wrong statement.
Daily site care and a bag below the bladder are correct.
No drainage is reportable, so that statement is correct.
Limiting fluids for convenience needs correction.

elimination.verdict: D. "I will drink less so the bag fills slowly."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A client who uses a cane limits fluids to avoid leaking, is constipated, and has a dim, cluttered hallway to the bathroom. Which recommendations should the nurse make? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear absorbent briefs in place of walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of toileting leave urine against the skin and do nothing to remove the contributors named. The client can still walk to the bathroom with a cane once the path is safe.

options.text: Spread fluids through the day for pale urine
options.rationale: The kidneys need enough fluid to produce dilute urine. Restricting fluid concentrates the urine, which irritates the bladder and raises the risk of infection, and it does not prevent leakage.

options.text: Wait until the urge is strong before walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Waiting for a strong urge leaves less time to reach the toilet. With a long walk and a cane, the client needs more time, not less.

options.text: Light the hallway and clear the clutter
options.rationale: Poor lighting, clutter and an inaccessible bathroom are environmental barriers to reaching the toilet in time, and they add fall risk for a client who walks with a cane.

options.text: Stop drinking fluids after the noon meal
options.rationale: Fluid is limited only in the 2 to 4 hours before bed, not for the whole afternoon. The client is already taking in too little fluid for dilute urine.

options.text: Add fiber and fluid to relieve constipation
options.rationale: Constipation places pressure on the bladder and urethra and contributes to incontinence. It is a reversible contributor.

questions.takeaway: Normal elimination depends on enough fluid for dilute urine, regular bowel movements, and a safe, short path to the toilet. Fluid restriction, constipation, limited mobility and environmental barriers all work against continence.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each option by whether it removes a contributor named in the stem: low fluid, constipation, or a long dim cluttered path.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Limited fluid, constipation, a dim cluttered hallway and a cane are each a contributor.
Fluid spread through the day, bowel regularity, and a clear lit path.
Waiting for a strong urge, briefs in place of toileting, and stopping fluid at noon add risk.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions and factors that support normal elimination

questions.stem: A resident with dementia voids about every 2 hours, does not recognize the urge, and needs help to walk. Which toileting program should the nurse plan?

options.text: Bladder training with voids every 45 minutes
options.rationale: Bladder training depends on a client who is aware of bladder fullness and able to resist the urge. This resident does not recognize the urge.

options.text: Scheduled toileting with staff assistance every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting relies on a time schedule set from the voiding pattern and does not require the resident to sense fullness or delay voiding. The 2 hour interval matches the resident's pattern, and the goal is to reach the toilet before leakage.

options.text: Absorbent briefs changed every 2 hours in place of toileting
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of timed toileting undermine the program and leave urine on the skin. They also lead residents to get up alone, a common cause of falls.

options.text: Prompted voiding alone, with the resident asking for help
options.rationale: Prompted voiding supplements scheduled toileting by prompting the resident to ask for help. Used alone, it fails for a resident who does not recognize the need to void.

questions.takeaway: Match the toileting program to cognition. Bladder training needs an alert client who can suppress the urge. Scheduled toileting works on a timed interval set from the voiding diary and suits cognitive impairment, with prompted voiding added as a supplement.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Prompted voiding is the right idea with one thing off: it depends on the resident asking. The cue that decides is that the resident does not recognize the need to void.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The resident does not sense the urge to void.
It requires suppressing the urge between intervals.
It depends on the resident asking for help.
Briefs replace toileting and harm skin and safety.

elimination.verdict: B. Scheduled toileting with staff assistance every 2 hours.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: A client, 74 years old, has urge incontinence. The provider is choosing between an antimuscarinic drug, oxybutynin, and mirabegron. The nurse prepares teaching and monitoring points for each drug.
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing teaching for a client with urge incontinence whose provider is choosing between an antimuscarinic and mirabegron. For each item, indicate the drug it applies to.

rows.text: Reduces involuntary bladder contractions
rows.rationale: Antimuscarinics block the nerve signals that trigger involuntary contractions of the bladder.

rows.text: Relaxes the detrusor muscle by stimulating beta 3 receptors
rows.rationale: Mirabegron relaxes the bladder muscle while urine is stored, which increases bladder capacity.

rows.text: Report new forgetfulness or confusion
rows.rationale: Cognitive effects are an antimuscarinic side effect and are a particular concern in older adults, so they are monitored closely.

rows.text: Report straining to void or a feeling that the bladder is not empty
rows.rationale: Antimuscarinics can cause urinary retention, which shows as straining or incomplete emptying.

rows.text: Check the blood pressure at follow up visits
rows.rationale: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so blood pressure is monitored while the client takes it.

rows.text: Use sugarless hard candy for dry mouth and add fiber for constipation
rows.rationale: Dry mouth and constipation are expected antimuscarinic side effects managed with these measures.

questions.takeaway: Antimuscarinics reduce involuntary bladder contractions and cause dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and cognitive effects. Mirabegron relaxes the bladder during storage and requires blood pressure monitoring.
questions.strategy: Learn one unique point for mirabegron, blood pressure. Antimuscarinic side effects follow the drying, slowing pattern: dry mouth, constipation, retention, confusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Beta 3 relaxation of the detrusor and blood pressure.
Fewer involuntary contractions with dry mouth, constipation, retention and cognitive effects.
Every drying or slowing side effect belongs to the antimuscarinic.

elimination.verdict: Mirabegron: beta 3 relaxation of the detrusor and blood pressure. Antimuscarinic: involuntary contractions, confusion, retention, dry mouth and constipation.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse evaluates a client's pelvic floor muscle training. Which client statement shows the exercises are done correctly?

options.text: "I hold each squeeze as long as I can without relaxing between."
options.rationale: Training is a controlled contraction followed by complete relaxation. Holding without relaxing fatigues the muscle and is not the method.

options.text: "I do the squeezes only on days when the leaking is worse."
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training needs consistent, regular practice over time. Practicing only on bad days does not build strength.

options.text: "I squeeze, then fully relax, and I practice when not voiding."
options.rationale: Correct muscle identification is essential, and stopping the stream once can help find the muscles. Each controlled contraction is followed by complete relaxation, and practice happens outside of urination.

options.text: "I practice by stopping and starting my stream every time I void."
options.rationale: Stopping the stream is a way to identify the muscles, not the exercise itself. Practice is done outside of urination.

questions.takeaway: Pelvic floor training: identify the correct muscles, contract with control, relax completely, practice outside of urination, and keep practicing regularly over time on an individualized plan.
questions.strategy: Option D is the right idea with one thing off: stopping the stream identifies the muscles, but practice happens outside of urination.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Option A skips complete relaxation.
Option B practices only on bad days.
Option D practices during urination.
Option C identifies, contracts, relaxes and practices outside of urination.

elimination.verdict: C. "I squeeze, then fully relax, and I practice when not voiding."

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with diabetic neuropathy who reports leaking small amounts of urine many times a day and night for 3 weeks, with a weak stream and a feeling of urgency. An antimuscarinic was started for urgency 4 weeks ago. The client denies burning. Intake over 24 hours was 2,000 mL, and voided output was 700 mL. The area above the pubic bone is firm, and a bladder scan right after voiding shows 450 mL. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Urge incontinence that needs a higher antimuscarinic dose
options.rationale: Urgency and frequent leakage fit urge incontinence, and that is the reason the drug was started. The postvoid volume of 450 mL shows the bladder is not emptying, and an antimuscarinic adds to retention.

options.text: Cystitis causing urgency and frequent leakage
options.rationale: Urgency with frequent small leaks fits cystitis, which makes this tempting. The client denies burning, and infection does not explain 450 mL left in the bladder after voiding.

options.text: Reduced urine production by the kidneys
options.rationale: Output far below intake suggests low production, but the urine is being made and held: the area above the pubic bone is firm and the bladder holds 450 mL right after voiding. More fluid adds to a bladder that is not emptying.

options.text: Overflow leakage from retention the drug may worsen
options.rationale: Leakage can occur with incomplete emptying. A postvoid volume of 450 mL, output far below intake, and a firm suprapubic area point to retention. Diabetic neuropathy and the antimuscarinic are both contributors.

questions.takeaway: Leakage does not always mean an overactive bladder. When output is well below intake and the bladder holds a large volume right after voiding, the leakage comes from incomplete emptying, and antimuscarinics, which cause retention, can make it worse.
questions.strategy: Urge incontinence, cystitis, and low kidney output each explain part of the picture. The 450 mL scan right after voiding, with a firm suprapubic area, decides it: the bladder is not emptying, and an antimuscarinic adds to retention.

steps.detail: 450 mL remains in the bladder right after voiding, and the suprapubic area is firm.
Involuntary contractions empty the bladder; a full bladder after voiding means it is not emptying.
Diabetic neuropathy and an antimuscarinic both promote retention.
No burning argues against cystitis, and a full bladder rules out low production.

elimination.verdict: D. Overflow leakage from retention the drug may worsen.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.nursesNote: 1015. Client is 34 years old. Oral temperature 37.0 °C. Has type 1 diabetes. Denies flank pain and denies chills. Reports burning during voiding since yesterday. Drank 1800 mL of fluid yesterday. Voids small amounts every 30 to 45 minutes and feels a sudden need to void. Reports no change in vision. Urine is pink tinged. Reports aching above the pubic bone, 4 of 10.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the clinic note of a client who reports burning with voiding. Highlight the findings that are cues for a lower urinary tract infection, including risk factors.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
segments.rationale: The temperature is within the expected range. Fever would suggest spread beyond the bladder.

segments.text: Has type 1 diabetes
segments.rationale: Diabetes and reduced immunity are risk factors for urinary infection.

segments.text: Denies flank pain and denies chills
segments.rationale: Flank pain and chills point to the kidney. Their absence fits a lower urinary infection.

segments.text: Reports burning during voiding since yesterday
segments.rationale: Dysuria, a stinging or burning pain during voiding, is a hallmark of cystitis.

segments.text: Drank 1800 mL of fluid yesterday
segments.rationale: This intake is adequate and is not a cue for infection.

segments.text: Voids small amounts every 30 to 45 minutes and feels a sudden need to void
segments.rationale: Frequency and urgency, often with small amounts, are signs of cystitis.

segments.text: Reports no change in vision
segments.rationale: Vision is unrelated to the urinary findings.

segments.text: Urine is pink tinged
segments.rationale: Hematuria, with pink, red or tea colored urine, warrants evaluation and occurs with cystitis.

segments.text: Reports aching above the pubic bone, 4 of 10
segments.rationale: Suprapubic discomfort is a sign of bladder inflammation.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis presents with dysuria, urgency and frequency in small amounts, suprapubic discomfort and hematuria. Diabetes raises infection risk. Fever, chills and flank pain suggest the infection has spread to the kidney.
questions.strategy: Read each phrase against the cystitis signs and the infection risk factors. Leave expected and absent findings unhighlighted.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Type 1 diabetes.
Burning, small frequent voids with urgency, pink urine, suprapubic aching.
Normal temperature, no flank pain or chills, adequate intake and normal vision.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A client started on an antibiotic for cystitis yesterday reports slightly less burning. The culture shows an organism resistant to that antibiotic. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Report the susceptibility result to the provider
options.rationale: Culture identifies the organism, and susceptibility testing guides the antibiotic choice. An organism resistant to the current drug will not be treated by it, so the result is reported.

options.text: Reassure the client that the antibiotic is working
options.rationale: A slight drop in pain in less than a day is not evidence that the drug works. The culture shows the organism is resistant to it.

options.text: Repeat the urinalysis before changing the antibiotic
options.rationale: The infection is already supported by symptoms, urinalysis and culture. Repeating the urinalysis delays effective treatment.

options.text: Request phenazopyridine and continue the antibiotic
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection. Continuing a drug the organism resists leaves the infection untreated.

questions.takeaway: Urinalysis suggests infection; culture identifies the organism; susceptibility testing guides antibiotic choice. Results are interpreted together with the symptoms, and a resistant organism means the antibiotic needs to change.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A small drop in pain is tempting evidence. The culture result outweighs it because it shows the drug cannot kill this organism.

steps.detail: The organism is resistant to the current antibiotic.
A slight drop in pain does not override resistance.
Repeating the urinalysis adds no new information.
Phenazopyridine treats discomfort, not infection.

elimination.verdict: A. Report the susceptibility result to the provider.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: A client with cystitis is prescribed an oral antibiotic and phenazopyridine. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm drug allergies before the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Allergies are checked before any antibiotic, because antibiotic allergies are common and change the drug choice.

options.text: Teach the client to expect orange or red urine
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns the urine orange or red. Knowing this ahead prevents alarm.

options.text: Teach the client to stop the antibiotic when burning ends
options.rationale: The full course is taken exactly as prescribed even when symptoms end early, to prevent recurrence and resistance. Adverse effects are reported rather than handled by stopping the drug.

options.text: Teach the client to report fever, flank pain, or vomiting
options.rationale: Fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms suggest the infection is spreading upward and need immediate reporting.

options.text: Explain that phenazopyridine treats the infection
options.rationale: The roles are reversed. Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection; the antibiotic treats the infection.

options.text: Encourage regular fluid intake and bladder emptying
options.rationale: Unless fluids are restricted, appropriate hydration and regular bladder emptying flush bacteria from the bladder.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis care: check allergies before antibiotics, monitor for improvement and adverse effects, encourage fluids within limits, and give ordered pain relief. Teach the full course, report adverse effects rather than stop, and report fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening at once. Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red and does not treat infection.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option has the client stopping a drug or misreading what phenazopyridine does. Keep the options that complete treatment and report danger signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Allergy check before the antibiotic.
Orange or red urine with phenazopyridine; complete the antibiotic course.
Fever, flank pain or vomiting are reported right away.
Stopping when the burning ends, and calling phenazopyridine a treatment, are errors.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A client with an indwelling urinary catheter now drinks well and walks with help. A urine culture is due, and the perineal skin is red. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review with the provider whether the catheter is needed
options.rationale: Necessity is reviewed daily and the catheter is removed promptly. A client who drinks well and walks with help may no longer need it.

options.text: Collect the culture from the sampling port using aseptic technique
options.rationale: A proper specimen comes from the sampling port without opening the closed system, so the result reflects the bladder and not the bag.

options.text: Pour the culture specimen from the bag into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has been standing and is not a proper specimen. Specimens are collected properly so they can be interpreted.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to obtain the specimen
options.rationale: The closed drainage system is maintained. Disconnecting opens a route for bacteria.

options.text: Keep the drainage bag below the bladder and off the floor
options.rationale: The bag stays below the bladder and off the floor so urine drains away from the bladder and the bag is not contaminated.

options.text: Cleanse the red skin gently, with privacy
options.rationale: Skin protection and dignity are part of catheter care: gentle cleansing keeps the irritated skin intact, and privacy preserves dignity.

questions.takeaway: CAUTI prevention: use an indwelling catheter only for an appropriate indication, keep the drainage system closed and the tubing unobstructed, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and review necessity daily and remove promptly. Collect specimens properly and protect skin and dignity.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The specimen options test the closed system. Keep the port with aseptic technique; reject the bag and the disconnection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client drinks well and walks, so review the need today.
Port with aseptic technique, not the bag or a disconnection.
Bag below the bladder and off the floor.
Gentle cleansing, dry skin and privacy.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E, F.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a resident in long term care, 88 years old, who became confused this morning and was alert and oriented at 2000 yesterday. A new sleeping medication was given at 2100. Temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate 78/min, and blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. The resident has no dysuria, urgency, frequency, or suprapubic or flank pain. A urine culture sent 2 days ago grew bacteria. A family member asks the nurse to request an antibiotic for a urinary infection. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Bacteria alone are not an infection. I will check other causes, like the new sleeping pill."
options.rationale: Bacteria in urine without attributable infection symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria, and confusion alone does not establish a urinary infection. The nurse assesses other causes; a sleeping medication started the night before is a likely one.

options.text: "Confusion is often the only sign of infection at this age. I will ask the provider for an antibiotic."
options.rationale: Confusion can be the main sign of infection in older adults, which makes this tempting. With normal vital signs, no urinary findings, and a sleeping medication started the night before, a positive culture plus confusion does not establish infection, and most asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults is not treated.

options.text: "The culture grew bacteria, which confirms an infection. I will call the provider now."
options.rationale: A positive culture alone does not establish symptomatic infection. Results are matched with clinical findings.

options.text: "I will send a new urine sample, and if it grows bacteria again, we can treat it then."
options.rationale: A second positive culture still shows only bacteria in the urine. Treatment depends on infection symptoms, not on culture results.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, bacteria in the urine without urinary or systemic findings is asymptomatic bacteriuria and usually is not treated. Confusion or falls alone do not establish a urinary infection; assess other causes and look for urinary or systemic findings.
questions.strategy: Both the antibiotic request and the search for other causes are defensible, because confusion can signal infection in older adults. The cue that decides is the absence of any urinary or systemic findings, with a sleeping medication started the night before.

steps.detail: New confusion, normal vital signs, no urinary symptoms, positive culture.
A positive culture plus confusion alone is not a urinary infection.
A new sleeping medication started at 2100 yesterday.
Treating or repeating the culture ignores the missing symptoms.

elimination.verdict: A. Bacteria alone are not an infection; check other causes, like the new sleeping pill.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: A nurse on a medical unit reviews urinary findings recorded today for several clients.
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical unit is reviewing urinary findings recorded today for several clients. For each finding, indicate the term that describes it.

rows.text: Voids 15 times while awake, 50 to 80 mL each time, with a 24 hour output of 1400 mL
rows.rationale: Urinating more often than usual is frequency. The voids are small, but the 24 hour output of 1400 mL shows the total output is not decreased, so this is not oliguria.

rows.text: Sleeps from 2200 to 0600 and is woken 3 times by the need to void
rows.rationale: Waking from sleep to urinate is nocturia. The problem is the timing during sleep, not the number of voids while awake.

rows.text: Total urine output 300 mL over 24 hours, with 3 voids
rows.rationale: Oliguria is decreased urine output. Few voids with a low 24 hour total point to less urine, not to a voiding pattern problem.

rows.text: Reports a sudden, compelling need to void while in the shower and rushes out to reach the toilet
rows.rationale: A sudden, compelling need to urinate is urgency. One episode with a rush to the toilet describes the sensation, not how often voiding occurs.

rows.text: Indwelling catheter has drained 18 mL per hour for 4 hours, was 60 mL per hour yesterday
rows.rationale: A falling hourly output through a draining catheter is decreased urine output, oliguria. Urgency, frequency and nocturia do not apply to a client whose urine drains through a catheter.

rows.text: Wakes at 0200 and 0430 each night to void 250 mL, with 6 voids while awake
rows.rationale: Six voids while awake is not more often than usual. The finding that stands out is waking from sleep to void: nocturia.

questions.takeaway: Each term names one thing: nocturia is waking from sleep to urinate, frequency is urinating more often than usual, urgency is a sudden compelling need, and oliguria is decreased urine output. Small voids are not oliguria when the 24 hour total is not decreased.
questions.strategy: Ask which part of the pattern is off for each finding: the time of night, the number of voids, the sensation, or the total amount.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 300 mL in 24 hours and 18 mL per hour are decreased output: oliguria. 1400 mL is not.
15 voids while awake: frequency.
Woken from sleep to void: nocturia. Sudden compelling need: urgency.

elimination.verdict: Frequency, nocturia, oliguria, urgency, oliguria, nocturia.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with new urine leakage. Which findings are risk factors or contributors for incontinence? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pelvic surgery 2 years ago
options.rationale: Pelvic surgery is a cause of pelvic floor weakness, a patient factor for incontinence. Aging adds to the weakness.

options.text: Levothyroxine taken each morning
options.rationale: The medications that contribute are those affecting awareness, urine production or emptying, such as diuretics, sedatives and anticholinergics. Levothyroxine is not one of them.

options.text: Stroke with arm and leg weakness
options.rationale: Neurologic conditions such as stroke impair bladder control, and the weakness limits mobility to reach the toilet.

options.text: Drinks 8 glasses of fluid spread through the day
options.rationale: Adequate fluid spread through the day supports dilute urine and normal elimination. It does not contribute to leakage.

options.text: Urethral stricture with incomplete emptying
options.rationale: Obstruction causes incomplete emptying, and leakage can occur when the bladder does not empty.

options.text: Burning, urgency, and positive nitrites
options.rationale: Urinary infection is a clinical contributor to incontinence and is reversible with treatment.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence risk factors: pelvic floor weakness from childbirth, pelvic surgery or aging; neurologic disease such as stroke, spinal cord injury or diabetic neuropathy; obstruction with incomplete emptying; urinary infection; constipation; medications affecting awareness, production or emptying; and limited mobility or environmental barriers.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into a known category of contributor. A drug counts only when it changes awareness, urine production or emptying.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pelvic surgery and stroke.
Stricture with incomplete emptying, and urinary infection.
Levothyroxine and adequate fluid spread through the day are not contributors.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A resident has woken wet for 5 nights without sensing the urge, with no burning or stress leakage. A bedtime sedative started 6 days ago. Which contributor is most likely?

options.text: The long standing morning diuretic
options.rationale: Diuretics raise urine production, but this one is taken in the morning and has been taken for years without nighttime leakage. Its effect is greatest during the day.

options.text: A urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Infection is a reversible contributor, but there is no burning or other urinary sign to support it.

options.text: The bedtime sedative
options.rationale: Sedatives affect awareness. The leakage began the night after the sedative started, occurs during sleep, and the resident does not sense the urge.

options.text: Pelvic floor weakness from aging
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness causes leakage with coughing or lifting, which the resident denies.

questions.takeaway: Medications contribute to incontinence by changing awareness (sedatives), urine production (diuretics) or emptying (anticholinergics). Timing points to the cause: the new drug whose start matches the onset is the first to consider.
questions.strategy: The diuretic is the right idea with one thing off: it raises production, but it is old and taken in the morning. The cue that decides is the sedative starting the day before the leakage began.

steps.detail: Leakage started 5 nights ago; the sedative started 6 days ago.
No sensation of the urge during sleep fits reduced awareness.
The diuretic is long standing and taken in the morning, infection has no signs, and no stress leakage is present.

elimination.verdict: C. The bedtime sedative.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: An external urine collection device keeps coming loose, the linens are wet, and the skin under its edge is red. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The device is not effective, and its fit needs reassessment
options.rationale: External devices are evaluated for fit, skin contact and effectiveness. Repeated loosening, wet linens and red skin show the device fails on all three.

options.text: The device is effective, and the plan can continue
options.rationale: Collecting some urine is not the measure. Most of the output is leaking onto the linens, and the skin is red.

options.text: The device has failed, and an indwelling catheter is needed
options.rationale: Indwelling catheters are used only for an appropriate indication. Incontinence is not one, and the skin has no open areas.

options.text: The device is loose and needs to be applied more tightly
options.rationale: A tighter fit adds pressure to skin that is already red. The fit itself needs to be reassessed, with another size or device considered.

questions.takeaway: External collection devices are evaluated on 3 points: fit, skin contact and effectiveness. Wet linens and red skin mean the device is failing, and the answer is to reassess the device, not to switch to an indwelling catheter.
questions.strategy: Options C and D both accept that the device failed but choose a fix that adds risk. The global option names all 3 evaluation points.

steps.detail: Wet linens and repeated loosening.
Red skin under the edge.
An indwelling catheter lacks an indication; a tighter fit adds pressure.

elimination.verdict: A. The device is not effective, and its fit needs reassessment.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: After an onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) bladder injection for urge incontinence, a client no longer leaks but strains to void and retains urine after voiding. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Add an antimuscarinic to the injection therapy
options.rationale: Combining approaches is reasonable in some clients, but antimuscarinics cause retention. Adding one now worsens the problem.

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter until the leaking returns
options.rationale: Indwelling catheters are used only for an appropriate indication and removed promptly, and device therapy includes intermittent catheterization for incomplete emptying.

options.text: Arrange an artificial urinary sphincter
options.rationale: An artificial sphincter controls leakage at the urethra; it does not empty the bladder. Surgical options are individualized and do not treat retention.

options.text: Teach intermittent self catheterization
options.rationale: Botox relaxes the bladder muscle, which stops the leakage, and straining with urine left after voiding shows incomplete emptying. Self catheterization is a device therapy that empties the bladder for a client able to perform it. The retention after Botox is usually temporary.

questions.takeaway: Botox relaxes the bladder muscle and relieves urge incontinence. When the bladder then does not empty, device therapy with intermittent self catheterization empties it. Treatment is individualized, and approaches are combined only when they do not add to the problem, as an antimuscarinic adds retention.
questions.strategy: The cue that decides is the urine left in the bladder after voiding. Treat the retention with the device therapy that empties the bladder.

steps.detail: Leakage stopped, but urine remains after voiding: retention.
Botox relaxes the bladder muscle.

steps.action: Choose the fix that empties the bladder
steps.detail: Intermittent self catheterization, taught to a client able to perform it.
The antimuscarinic adds retention, an indwelling catheter needs an appropriate indication and prompt removal, and a sphincter does not empty the bladder.

elimination.verdict: D. Teach intermittent self catheterization.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a client looks away and says, "Leaking is normal for my age. I just deal with it." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Leaking is often treatable. When does it happen?"
options.rationale: Urinary concerns are assessed directly and with dignity. Normalizing the topic and asking when leakage happens starts identifying the type and cause.

options.text: "Leaking is part of aging, and pads manage it well."
options.rationale: Incontinence is not a normal part of aging, and accepting pads without assessment skips identifying a cause that may be reversible.

options.text: "I will note that you have no urinary concerns."
options.rationale: Recording no concerns when there are cues of leakage denies the problem and leaves it unassessed.

options.text: "Your family may know, so I can ask them for you."
options.rationale: Asking a family member without consent breaks privacy and dignity. The client is the source of this history.

questions.takeaway: Assess urinary concerns directly, in private, and with dignity. Clients often hide leakage from embarrassment or the belief that it is normal with age. Specific questions about how often and when it happens identify the type and cause.
questions.strategy: Options B and C both close the topic. The patient centered option keeps the client talking and gathers data.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Looking away and calling leakage normal for age.
Calling it normal for age, or noting no concerns, ends the assessment.
Asking the adult child without consent.
Normalize, then ask how often and when.

elimination.verdict: A. "Leaking is often treatable. When does it happen?"

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A client receiving pelvic radiation has burning, urgency, and frequency, but the urinalysis and urine culture are negative. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: A lower urinary tract infection that needs an antibiotic
options.rationale: Symptoms alone do not establish infection. Urine tests are matched with the clinical findings, and here they show no organism.

options.text: Bladder inflammation without an infection
options.rationale: Bladder inflammation can occur without infection, from irritation by other sources. Cystitis symptoms with no nitrites and no organism on culture fit inflammation without infection. Pelvic radiation is one such irritant.

options.text: Asymptomatic bacteriuria that needs no antibiotic
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteria in the urine without symptoms. This client has symptoms and no bacteria, the opposite pattern.

options.text: A contaminated specimen that needs to be repeated
options.rationale: A contaminated specimen grows mixed organisms. No growth with a negative urinalysis does not suggest contamination.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis is inflammation of the bladder, and bladder inflammation can occur without infection. Urine tests are interpreted with the symptoms: the culture identifies organisms, and symptoms with no organism point away from infection. Radiation, drugs and chemicals are examples of irritants.
questions.strategy: Options B and C are an opposite pair. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteria without symptoms; this client has symptoms without bacteria.

steps.detail: Classic symptoms, but no nitrites and no growth.
No organism identified, so there is no infection to treat.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria needs bacteria and no symptoms.

elimination.verdict: B. Bladder inflammation without an infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A client with recurrent cystitis often holds urine for a whole work shift. Which client statement shows understanding of how the infection developed?

options.text: "Bacteria reached my bladder through my blood."
options.rationale: Spread through the blood is uncommon. Bacteria most often ascend through the urethra to the bladder.

options.text: "I will drink less during my shift so I void less."
options.rationale: Less fluid concentrates the urine and means fewer voids to flush bacteria, adding to the risk.

options.text: "Bacteria move up the urethra, so I will void often."
options.rationale: Upward migration through the urethra is the most frequent route. Regular voiding flushes bacteria out before they multiply in the bladder.

options.text: "I will scrub with antiseptic soap several times a day."
options.rationale: Perineal hygiene is gentle. Harsh, repeated scrubbing goes against that teaching.

questions.takeaway: Bacteria most commonly ascend through the urethra to the bladder. Prevention follows from the route: adequate hydration, emptying the bladder regularly, and gentle perineal hygiene.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is a prevention idea with one thing off: the wrong route, too little fluid, or harsh hygiene. Match the teaching to the ascending route.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Upward through the urethra.

steps.action: Check the habit in the stem
steps.detail: Holding urine for a whole shift.

steps.action: Keep the statement that fixes it
steps.detail: Voiding often flushes bacteria.

elimination.verdict: C. "Bacteria move up the urethra, so I will void often."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A client with a urethral stricture has had 4 bladder infections this year, each cleared by antibiotics. Fluid intake and glucose are normal. Which factor most likely explains the recurrence?

options.text: Urine stasis from the stricture
options.rationale: Obstruction and incomplete emptying cause stasis, and bacteria multiply in urine that stays in the bladder. The stricture keeps the bladder from emptying.

options.text: Low fluid intake concentrating the urine
options.rationale: Fluid intake is adequate and does not explain the repeated infections.

options.text: Antibiotic resistance from repeated courses
options.rationale: Each episode resolved with treatment, so the drugs are working. The problem is that the infections keep returning.

options.text: Reduced immunity from diabetes
options.rationale: Diabetes is a risk factor, but the glucose is normal.

questions.takeaway: Incomplete emptying and obstruction, such as strictures, tumors, stones or reflux, cause stasis that lets bacteria multiply. Recurrent infection plus a high volume after voiding points to the obstruction.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real risk factor; the stem rules out all but one. Use the data given to test each.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intake is adequate.
Glucose is normal.
Each episode resolved.
The stricture causes incomplete emptying.

elimination.verdict: A. Urine stasis from the stricture.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis
