questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy is on day 2 of an antibiotic for cystitis and calls about vomiting and worse burning. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Without a fever or side pain, waiting for your visit is fine."
options.rationale: Fever and flank pain are only two of the findings to report. Vomiting and worsening symptoms are reported immediately on their own.

options.text: "Extra water will flush your bladder. Call back if a fever starts."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged, but they do not replace evaluation, and waiting for fever ignores vomiting and worsening burning.

options.text: "Stop the antibiotic, since it may be causing the vomiting."
options.rationale: Adverse effects are reported rather than managed by stopping. Stopping also leaves the infection untreated.

options.text: "Vomiting and worse burning need to be checked today."
options.rationale: Vomiting and worsening symptoms are reported immediately. Reduced immunity from chemotherapy raises the risk of infection, so these signs need evaluation now.

questions.takeaway: Teach clients with cystitis to report fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms immediately. Any one of them is enough. Reduced immunity is a risk factor for urinary infection, which makes prompt reporting matter more.
questions.strategy: Options A and B wait for fever, which is the trap: the findings to report are fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening, and this client has two of the four.

steps.detail: Chemotherapy: reduced immunity.
Vomiting and burning worse than yesterday.
Waiting for a visit, waiting for fever, or stopping the antibiotic.
Arrange a visit today.

elimination.verdict: D. "Vomiting and worse burning need to be checked today."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse cares for several clients with indwelling urinary catheters. Which actions help prevent catheter associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Declines a catheter to keep an incontinent client dry
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter is used only for an appropriate indication. Keeping linens dry is staff convenience, not an indication.

options.text: Clamps the drainage tubing while the client walks
options.rationale: Tubing is kept unobstructed. Backflow is prevented by keeping the bag below the bladder, not by clamping.

options.text: Disconnects the tubing to flush slow drainage
options.rationale: Opening the connection breaks the closed drainage system and lets bacteria enter.

options.text: Inserts a catheter for acute retention using aseptic technique
options.rationale: Acute retention is an appropriate indication, and hand hygiene with aseptic insertion keeps bacteria out of the bladder.

options.text: Straightens tubing kinked under a client's thigh
options.rationale: A kink obstructs flow and causes urine to pool. Keeping tubing unobstructed is a prevention step.

options.text: Leaves a catheter in overnight in case of retention
options.rationale: Necessity is reviewed daily and the catheter is removed promptly. In case is not an indication.

questions.takeaway: Prevent catheter associated urinary tract infection: use an indwelling catheter only for an appropriate indication, perform hand hygiene and insert aseptically, keep the drainage system closed and the tubing unobstructed, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and review necessity daily and remove promptly.
questions.strategy: Test each action against the 6 prevention steps. Any action that breaks the system, blocks flow, or keeps a catheter without an indication is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Incontinence and in case are not indications; acute retention is.
Disconnecting the tubing breaks closed drainage.
Clamping blocks flow; straightening a kink restores it.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A client with heart failure on a 1,500 mL daily fluid limit starts an antibiotic for cystitis. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will spread my 1,500 mL over the day."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged within prescribed limits. Spreading the allowed amount through the day supports regular voiding without exceeding the limit.

options.text: "I will drink as much water as I can."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged only within prescribed limits. Drinking without limit can overload a client with heart failure.

options.text: "If I get diarrhea, I will call instead of stopping."
options.rationale: Clients report adverse effects rather than stopping the antibiotic, so the provider can adjust treatment.

options.text: "I will call for fever, side pain, or vomiting."
options.rationale: Fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms are reported immediately because they suggest the infection is spreading.

questions.takeaway: Encourage fluids within prescribed limits. For a client with a fluid restriction, the limit wins over the usual advice to drink more. Teach the client to report adverse effects instead of stopping the antibiotic.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. The fluid limit in the stem is the cue that turns usual advice into an error.

steps.detail: Find the statement that is incorrect.
Heart failure with 1500 mL a day.
A, C and D follow the plan; B ignores the limit.

elimination.verdict: B. "I will drink as much water as I can."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a client on day 3 of treatment for cystitis. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 45 years old, is on day 3 of a 5 day oral antibiotic and a 2 day course of phenazopyridine for cystitis. Today: dysuria 1 of 10, was 6 of 10 on day 1; voids every 3 hours, was every 30 minutes on day 1; urine is orange; oral temperature 36.8 °C; 4 watery stools since 0600, with none before today.

The orange urine is [[1]].

The change in dysuria and voiding shows [[2]].

The nurse [[3]].

options.text: a sign of new hematuria that needs a culture
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine explains the color, and the other findings are moving the right way.

options.text: an expected effect of phenazopyridine
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red. It is expected and not a sign of bleeding.

options.text: a sign of dehydration from the stools
options.rationale: Concentrated urine is dark yellow or amber. Orange urine on phenazopyridine is a drug effect.

options.text: an allergic reaction to the antibiotic
options.rationale: Urine color is not a sign of allergy.

options.text: a response to treatment, with the full course still to be finished
options.rationale: Symptoms are decreasing, which is the expected improvement. The full course is completed even when symptoms ease.

options.text: a cure, so the remaining antibiotic doses can be stopped
options.rationale: Stopping early leaves bacteria behind. The full course is completed.

options.text: masking by phenazopyridine, so the antibiotic is failing
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine eases pain, but the voiding interval has also returned toward normal, which is an antibiotic effect.

options.text: spread of infection toward the kidney
options.rationale: Spread brings fever, flank pain or vomiting. The temperature is 36.8 °C and symptoms are easing.

options.text: tells the client to stop the antibiotic until the stools end
options.rationale: Clients report adverse effects rather than stopping. The provider decides on a change.

options.text: tells the client that watery stools are expected and need no follow up
options.rationale: Four new watery stools in a few hours are an adverse effect to report.

options.text: asks the provider to extend the phenazopyridine course
options.rationale: Pain is 1 of 10, and phenazopyridine does not treat infection.

options.text: reports the watery stools to the provider as a possible adverse effect
options.rationale: Monitoring includes adverse effects. New watery stools after starting an antibiotic are reported rather than ignored or managed by stopping the drug.

questions.takeaway: During cystitis treatment, monitor both improvement and adverse effects. Decreasing dysuria and frequency show response, but the full course is completed. Orange urine on phenazopyridine is expected. New adverse effects are reported, not managed by stopping the drug.
questions.strategy: Evaluate each finding separately: expected drug effect, treatment response, or adverse effect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Orange urine from phenazopyridine.
Pain 6 to 1 and voids every 30 minutes to every 3 hours, with the course unfinished.
4 new watery stools today: report.

elimination.verdict: 1: expected effect of phenazopyridine. 2: response to treatment, finish the course. 3: report the watery stools.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client in an urgent care clinic who has had burning and urgency with voiding for 2 days and has taken no antibiotic. Prescriptions are a clean catch midstream urine for urinalysis and culture with susceptibility, and the first dose of an oral antibiotic now. The client says, "Please give me the antibiotic first, then I will give you the urine." Place the actions in the order the nurse should perform them.

options.text: Have the client pass the first part of the stream into the toilet
options.rationale: Third. The first urine flushes organisms from the urethral opening, so it is not collected.

options.text: Confirm drug allergies and give the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Sixth. The allergy check comes before the dose, and the dose comes after the culture specimen is collected and sent. An antibiotic given first can reduce the organisms in the specimen and make the culture and susceptibility result unreliable, so the client's request does not change the order.

options.text: Explain the method and give a sterile cup and towelettes
options.rationale: First. The client needs to understand the method before starting, or the specimen is likely to be contaminated.

options.text: Cap the cup, label it, and send it to the laboratory
options.rationale: Fifth. The specimen is capped, labeled and sent promptly once it is collected.

options.text: Have the client cleanse the urethral opening with the towelettes
options.rationale: Second. Cleansing removes organisms from the skin around the opening before any urine is passed.

options.text: Have the client catch the middle of the stream in the cup without touching the inside
options.rationale: Fourth. Midstream urine is the sample that reflects the bladder, and touching the inside of the cup contaminates it.

questions.takeaway: Collect the urine culture specimen before the first antibiotic dose, using a clean catch midstream method: teach, cleanse, pass the first stream into the toilet, catch the midstream without touching the inside of the cup, then label and send. The culture and susceptibility result guides the antibiotic choice.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: The client's request makes giving the antibiotic first look kind. The prescription for culture and susceptibility is the cue that decides: the specimen has to be collected before the antibiotic, because the result is what guides the antibiotic choice.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A culture with susceptibility is prescribed, and no antibiotic has been taken yet.
It goes last, after the specimen is collected and sent, with the allergy check right before it.
Teach, cleanse, first stream into the toilet, midstream into the cup, then cap, label and send.

elimination.verdict: Explain and give supplies; cleanse; first stream into the toilet; midstream into the cup; cap, label and send; confirm allergies and give the antibiotic.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a resident in long term care, 86 years old, who became confused at 0600 and was oriented at 2100 yesterday. Since last evening the resident has voided small amounts every 30 to 60 minutes, reports burning with voiding, and has tenderness above the pubic bone. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 30 mL. Temperature is 38.3 °C, heart rate 102/min, and blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg. No new medications were started. A urine culture 3 months ago grew bacteria without symptoms and was not treated. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Confusion alone does not indicate a urinary infection
options.rationale: This rule is correct when confusion is the only finding. Here the confusion comes with new frequency, burning, suprapubic tenderness and a temperature of 38.3 °C, so it is not alone.

options.text: The earlier culture shows harmless bladder colonization
options.rationale: The culture 3 months ago was asymptomatic bacteriuria and was rightly not treated. The resident now has symptoms, which changes the decision; an old result does not explain new findings.

options.text: Small frequent voids show retention with overflow
options.rationale: Small, frequent voids can come from a bladder that does not empty, which makes this tempting. The scan shows only 30 mL after voiding, so the bladder is emptying, and retention does not explain burning or fever.

options.text: Urinary symptoms with fever point to infection
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated, but these are infection symptoms. Urinary findings plus fever and a heart rate of 102 make a urinary infection likely, so the resident needs evaluation with urine testing.

questions.takeaway: Confusion or falls alone do not establish a urinary infection, and bacteria without symptoms are not treated. When confusion comes with urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency or suprapubic pain, or with systemic findings such as fever, infection is likely and needs evaluation.
questions.strategy: Two options rest on true rules about older adults, and one reads the small voids as retention. Combine the cues: new burning, suprapubic tenderness, and fever, with only 30 mL left after voiding, point to infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New frequency, burning, suprapubic tenderness and a temperature of 38.3 °C.
Confusion alone does not show infection, but this confusion is not alone.
30 mL after voiding shows the bladder empties.
Bacteria 3 months ago with no symptoms do not cancel today's symptoms.

elimination.verdict: D. Urinary symptoms with fever point to infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who had abdominal surgery yesterday and whose indwelling catheter was removed at 0800. At 1500 the client feels an urge but cannot void on a bedpan in bed, and a bladder scan shows 380 mL. The prescribed activity is out of bed with assistance, and the client stood at the bedside with 1 staff member at 1300. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Insert a straight catheter to drain the bladder now
options.rationale: Catheterization adds infection risk, and simple measures to help the client void have not been tried yet.

options.text: Help the client onto a bedside commode in private
options.rationale: Sitting upright on a commode is a normal voiding position, and privacy promotes the urge. The activity prescription and the client's standing at 1300 show this is safe.

options.text: Close the curtain and offer the bedpan again
options.rationale: Privacy and a raised head of bed help, so this is a defensible choice. The client already could not void on the bedpan, and the activity prescription allows a more normal position on the commode.

options.text: Wait 1 hour and repeat the bladder scan
options.rationale: Rescanning gathers more data, but the bladder already holds 380 mL and the client has an urge. Waiting lets the bladder keep filling without helping it empty.

questions.takeaway: Normal voiding is supported by a normal position (sitting or standing), privacy and cues such as running water. Try these before invasive measures such as catheterization.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options use privacy to help the client void, and one waits for more data. The activity prescription and the client standing at 1300 decide: the client can use the commode, which gives a normal voiding position.

steps.detail: Out of bed with assistance, and the client stood at 1300.
The commode gives a normal sitting position; the bedpan already failed.
Catheterization comes after simple measures.
A repeat scan in 1 hour adds data but lets the bladder keep filling.

elimination.verdict: B. Help the client onto a bedside commode in private.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions and factors that support normal elimination

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 24 hour intake and output record of a client. Intake is 2,200 mL, and output is 650 mL from 3 voids measured in a collection hat. During the night the assistive personnel changed the client's soaked bed pad 4 times and discarded the pads. The urine in the hat is light yellow, the bladder is not palpable after voiding, and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, unchanged since admission. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The client has oliguria to report to the provider
options.rationale: The recorded output is low, so this looks right. The 4 soaked pads were never measured, so the record does not show the true output.

options.text: The client is retaining urine in the bladder
options.rationale: Low recorded output with leakage can mean overflow from a full bladder, which makes this tempting. The bladder is not palpable after voiding, so urine is not being held.

options.text: The recorded output is incomplete
options.rationale: The night leakage was not counted. Weighing wet pads and subtracting the dry weight measures that urine, and the light yellow urine and unchanged creatinine fit an output that is not truly low.

options.text: The client is retaining fluid in the tissues
options.rationale: Daily weights track fluid balance, but the gap between intake and output here is explained by urine that was not measured.

questions.takeaway: Intake and output is only as accurate as what is measured. Urine lost to pads or linens is part of output; weigh wet pads (1 g equals about 1 mL) before concluding that output is low.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three conclusions accept 650 mL as the real output. The 4 soaked pads discarded without measurement decide it, supported by light yellow urine, an unchanged creatinine, and a bladder that is not palpable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four soaked pads during the night were not measured.
Light yellow urine, a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL unchanged, and no palpable bladder.

steps.action: Reject the conclusions built on a false total
steps.detail: Oliguria, urine held in the bladder, and fluid in the tissues all assume the 650 mL is the real output.
Complete the record by weighing wet pads.

elimination.verdict: C. The recorded output is incomplete.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a resident in long term care who walks slowly with a walker and wets the brief about 4 times a day when the bathroom cannot be reached in time. The resident does not leak when coughing, and a bladder scan right after voiding shows 40 mL. The perineal skin is red with no open areas. Staff have been layering 2 pads inside the brief, and an assistive personnel asks for an indwelling catheter to keep the skin dry. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Request an indwelling catheter for the resident
options.rationale: Keeping skin dry sounds protective, but incontinence is not an appropriate indication for an indwelling catheter, and the skin has no open areas. A catheter adds infection risk.

options.text: Assist the resident to the toilet every 2 hours while awake
options.rationale: The leakage happens when the bathroom is not reached in time, and the bladder empties (40 mL after voiding). Scheduled toileting gets the resident there before the urge becomes urgent.

options.text: Cleanse the skin with a no rinse cleanser after each episode
options.rationale: Gentle cleansing removes urine without adding friction to reddened skin.

options.text: Continue layering 2 pads inside the brief
options.rationale: Layered pads trap heat and sweat, which can cause dermatitis even when urine is kept off the skin.

options.text: Apply a moisture barrier to the reddened skin
options.rationale: A barrier protects the skin from urine between changes.

options.text: Scrub the skin with soap and a washcloth
options.rationale: Scrubbing adds friction and damages reddened skin. Perineal hygiene is gentle.

questions.takeaway: For incontinence with reddened skin, protect the skin with gentle cleansing and a moisture barrier, avoid layered pads, and treat the cause of leakage. Leakage from not reaching the toilet in time responds to scheduled toileting. Incontinence alone is not an indication for an indwelling catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options sound like skin protection: the catheter and the extra pad. Decide each by its risk. The intact skin and the cause of leakage (not reaching the bathroom) point to toileting and gentle skin care instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leakage only when the bathroom is not reached in time, with 40 mL left after voiding.
Toilet every 2 hours while awake.
Gentle no rinse cleanser and a moisture barrier.
No catheter for incontinence alone; no layered pads that trap heat and sweat.
Do not scrub reddened skin.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: The nurse receives a call from a client with type 1 diabetes who has had burning with voiding and frequency since yesterday. Oral temperature at home is 37.0 °C, there is no flank pain, and blood glucose this morning was 214 mg/dL, was 120 mg/dL last week. The client says, "This happened years ago and went away with water. I will drink extra and mention it at my visit next month." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Extra water is a good plan. Call back if a fever starts."
options.rationale: Fluids and reporting fever are sound teaching for cystitis, which makes this tempting. Diabetes lowers the body's defenses and raises the risk of complications, and the glucose has risen, so waiting for a fever delays care.

options.text: "With diabetes, these symptoms need a check today."
options.rationale: Burning and frequency are symptoms of cystitis, and diabetes is a risk factor for urinary infection and its complications. A client with diabetes is taught to have urinary symptoms checked right away, and the rise in glucose from 120 to 214 mg/dL suggests the body is already under stress, so the nurse arranges an evaluation today.

options.text: "Burning often eases on its own, so watch it for now."
options.rationale: This accepts the client's past experience and ignores the diabetes and the rising glucose.

options.text: "Bring a urine sample to next month's visit for testing."
options.rationale: Testing is the right idea, but a month is far too long for urinary symptoms in a client with diabetes.

questions.takeaway: Diabetes changes the threshold for action: it reduces defenses against urinary infection and raises the risk of complications, so urinary symptoms need prompt evaluation even without fever or flank pain.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The normal temperature and the client's past recovery both pull toward waiting. The diabetes and the rising glucose decide the timing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning and frequency since yesterday.
Type 1 diabetes; glucose 214 mg/dL, was 120 mg/dL.
Waiting for fever, watching the burning, and testing next month all delay evaluation.
Evaluation today.

elimination.verdict: B. "With diabetes, these symptoms need a check today."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client on day 2 of an oral antibiotic and phenazopyridine for cystitis. Oral temperature is 37.4 °C. Which finding requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: Orange urine in the collection hat
options.rationale: The color looks alarming, which is the trap. Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red, so this is an expected drug effect.

options.text: Burning with voiding, 3 of 10, was 6 of 10
options.rationale: Burning that is still present on day 2 but has halved shows the treatment is working.

options.text: A dull ache in the flank since this morning
options.rationale: Flank pain is a hallmark of pyelonephritis, an infection that has moved up from the bladder to the kidney, and it needs immediate attention. Fever may not have appeared yet, so a temperature of 37.4 °C does not rule it out.

options.text: Small voids every hour, were every 30 minutes
options.rationale: Voiding is still frequent, but the interval has doubled since yesterday, which shows improvement.

questions.takeaway: During treatment for cystitis, a new flank ache is a sign the infection may be ascending to the kidney. Orange urine with phenazopyridine and lower tract symptoms that are easing are expected.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into expected drug effect, improving, or new. The new finding is the one to follow up, even without a fever.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Phenazopyridine turns urine orange.
Burning 6 to 3 and voids every 30 to 60 minutes are improving.
A flank ache, which points above the bladder.

steps.action: Do not be reassured by the temperature
steps.detail: 37.4 °C does not rule out pyelonephritis.

elimination.verdict: C. A dull ache in the flank since this morning.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a resident in long term care who has moderate memory loss, cannot follow a plan to delay voiding, and walks to the bathroom with 1 staff member. When staff ask, the resident correctly says whether the brief is wet or dry and asks to use the toilet. The resident's goal is to ask for help without waiting to be taken. Which toileting approach should the nurse plan?

options.text: Bladder training to lengthen the voiding interval
options.rationale: Bladder training depends on the client following a plan to delay voiding, which this resident cannot do.

options.text: Scheduled toileting by staff every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting works for clients with cognitive impairment and prevents leaks, which makes it tempting. It relies completely on a time schedule, so it does not build the resident's awareness or the goal of asking for help.

options.text: Absorbent briefs checked every 2 hours
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of toileting undermine continence, and they do nothing toward the resident's goal.

options.text: Prompted voiding with regular staff check ins
options.rationale: The resident recognizes wet or dry and asks to void when prompted. Prompted voiding builds awareness of the need to void and prompts the resident to ask for toileting help, which matches the stated goal.

questions.takeaway: Match the toileting program to the client's ability and goal: bladder training needs the ability to delay voiding, scheduled toileting relies on staff timing, and prompted voiding builds awareness and asking for help in a client who responds when prompted.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Scheduled toileting is a correct answer for many residents with memory loss. The resident's response to prompts and the goal of asking decide here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cannot follow a plan to delay voiding.
They replace toileting instead of supporting it.

steps.action: Compare the two staff led programs
steps.detail: Schedule only versus prompting the resident to ask.
Responds to prompts and wants to ask for help.

elimination.verdict: D. Prompted voiding with regular staff check ins.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the history of a client with urge incontinence before giving the first dose of a newly prescribed antimuscarinic. Which findings increase this client's risk of harm from the drug? Select all that apply.

options.text: Postvoid residual of 260 mL with a weak stream
options.rationale: Antimuscarinics reduce bladder contractions and can cause urinary retention. A client who already empties incompletely is at risk for worse retention.

options.text: Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid spread through the day
options.rationale: Fluid intake spread through the day supports normal elimination and helps offset the constipation these drugs can cause.

options.text: Voids 10 times a day with sudden strong urges
options.rationale: Urgency and frequency are the reason the drug is prescribed, not a risk from it.

options.text: Glaucoma treated with eye drops
options.rationale: Antimuscarinics can raise the pressure in the eye and worsen glaucoma, so the nurse asks about it before the drug is started.

options.text: Family reports new forgetfulness this month
options.rationale: Antimuscarinics can cause cognitive effects, and new forgetfulness could worsen or be blamed on the drug later. The change needs to be reported before the first dose.

options.text: Leaks a large amount on the way to the toilet
options.rationale: Leaking on the way to the toilet is the typical pattern of urge incontinence that the drug treats.

questions.takeaway: Before an antimuscarinic, the nurse looks for conditions the drug can worsen: incomplete emptying, glaucoma, and changes in thinking. Symptoms of urge incontinence are the indication, not a risk.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Treat each finding as either the reason for the drug or something the drug could make worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 260 mL left after voiding: the drug can worsen it.
Glaucoma: the drug can raise eye pressure.
New forgetfulness: the drug can cause cognitive effects.
Urges, leaks on the way, and spread fluids are not risks.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the findings of a resident in long term care with new urine leakage. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A resident in long term care, 84 years old, has had new urine leakage with urgency for 1 week and voids small amounts every 1 to 2 hours. The last bowel movement was 6 days ago, and the lower abdomen is firm. The resident denies burning with voiding. Urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 90 mL.

The most likely contributor to the new leakage is [[1]].

The finding that most argues against cystitis is [[2]].

The nurse plans to [[3]].

options.text: cystitis
options.rationale: Urgency and small frequent voids fit cystitis, which makes this tempting. There is no burning, and the urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells.

options.text: constipation
options.rationale: Six days without a bowel movement and a firm lower abdomen point to stool pressing on the bladder and urethra, which causes urgency and leakage.

options.text: pelvic floor weakness
options.rationale: Aging can weaken the pelvic floor, but that develops slowly and causes leakage with coughing or activity, not new urgency over 1 week.

options.text: retention with overflow
options.rationale: Overflow comes from incomplete emptying. A residual of 90 mL right after voiding does not show a bladder that stays full.

options.text: the urgency with small voids
options.rationale: This pattern supports cystitis rather than arguing against it.

options.text: the negative urinalysis with no burning
options.rationale: Burning is a key symptom of cystitis, and a urinalysis without nitrites or white blood cells does not suggest infection. Together they argue against cystitis.

options.text: the firm lower abdomen
options.rationale: The firm abdomen supports constipation, but it does not by itself rule out an infection.

options.text: request an antibiotic for the urgency
options.rationale: Nothing suggests infection, and an antibiotic does not treat stool pressing on the bladder.

options.text: begin pelvic floor muscle training
options.rationale: Training does not address the new cause and takes weeks to work.

options.text: restore bowel elimination with fluid and fiber
options.rationale: Treating the constipation removes the pressure on the bladder, which is a reversible cause of the new leakage. Fluid and fiber are given within the care plan.

options.text: limit fluids to reduce the leakage
options.rationale: Limiting fluids worsens constipation and concentrates the urine.

questions.takeaway: New leakage has reversible causes. Constipation presses on the bladder and urethra and can cause urgency and leakage; treating the bowel removes the cause.
questions.strategy: Weigh each tempting diagnosis against the data that rules it out: the urinalysis and no burning for cystitis, the residual for overflow, the 1 week onset for pelvic floor weakness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6 days without a bowel movement and a firm abdomen: constipation.
No burning and a negative urinalysis argue against cystitis.
Treat the reversible cause with bowel care, fluid, and fiber.

elimination.verdict: Constipation; the negative urinalysis with no burning; restore bowel elimination with fluid and fiber.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions and factors that support normal elimination

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a urinary history from a client at a clinic visit. Which client statement requires further assessment?

options.text: "I void about every 3 to 4 hours while awake."
options.rationale: Voiding every 3 to 4 hours while awake is a usual adult pattern and needs no follow up.

options.text: "I void right before bed each night."
options.rationale: Emptying the bladder at bedtime is a healthy habit that supports normal elimination.

options.text: "My urine has looked pink for 2 days."
options.rationale: Pink, red, or tea colored urine can mean hematuria, blood in the urine, and it always warrants evaluation. The nurse asks about onset, pain, burning, foods, and medications and reports the finding.

options.text: "My first morning urine is darker yellow."
options.rationale: Urine collected after a night without fluid is more concentrated, so a darker morning color is expected.

questions.takeaway: Pink, red, or tea colored urine suggests hematuria and needs evaluation. Concentrated first morning urine and a regular voiding schedule are expected.
questions.strategy: Sort each statement into a usual pattern or a change in the urine itself. A color change toward pink or red is the one that needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every 3 to 4 hours and voiding at bedtime are usual.
Morning urine is concentrated after the night.
Pink urine for 2 days suggests blood in the urine.

elimination.verdict: C. "My urine has looked pink for 2 days."

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with recurrent cystitis about perineal hygiene. Which client statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will scrub the area with a washcloth daily."
options.rationale: Scrubbing irritates the perineal and urethral tissue, and irritated tissue lets bacteria take hold more easily. Hygiene is gentle, not vigorous.

options.text: "I will wash gently with mild soap and water."
options.rationale: Gentle perineal hygiene with mild soap and water keeps the area clean without irritating the tissue, which is the self care teaching for preventing cystitis.

options.text: "I will use a scented spray to stay fresh."
options.rationale: Scented products irritate the perineal and urethral tissue and do not lower the risk of infection.

options.text: "I will use an antibacterial wipe after each void."
options.rationale: Cleaning after voiding sounds protective, which makes this tempting. Harsh antibacterial products used many times a day irritate the tissue, and the teaching is gentle hygiene.

questions.takeaway: Perineal hygiene for cystitis prevention is gentle: mild soap and water. Scrubbing, scented products, and harsh antibacterial cleansers irritate the tissue.
questions.strategy: Every option is about cleanliness. Choose the one that cleans without irritating, and reject the options that are more aggressive than the teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vigorous cleaning irritates the tissue.
Fragrance irritates and does not prevent infection.
Harsh products many times a day irritate the tissue.
Mild soap and water, washed gently.

elimination.verdict: B. "I will wash gently with mild soap and water."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A client is started on mirabegron for urge incontinence. Which assessment should the nurse plan at follow up visits to detect an adverse effect?

options.text: Mouth and eye dryness
options.rationale: Dryness is a classic adverse effect of antimuscarinic drugs, which block bladder contractions. Mirabegron works by a different action.

options.text: Stool frequency
options.rationale: Constipation is an antimuscarinic adverse effect. It is not the effect that is monitored for mirabegron.

options.text: Memory and attention span
options.rationale: Cognitive effects are a concern with antimuscarinic drugs, especially in older adults, not the key adverse effect of mirabegron.

options.text: Blood pressure readings
options.rationale: Mirabegron relaxes the bladder during the storage phase and can raise blood pressure, so blood pressure is checked periodically and an increase is reported.

questions.takeaway: Know which monitoring goes with which drug: antimuscarinics cause dry mouth, constipation, retention, and cognitive effects; mirabegron can raise blood pressure.
questions.strategy: Three options belong to the same drug class. The odd one out matches the drug named in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mirabegron, not an antimuscarinic.
Dryness, constipation, and memory are antimuscarinic effects.
Mirabegron can raise blood pressure.

elimination.verdict: D. Blood pressure readings.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching bladder training to an alert client with urge incontinence who can resist the urge briefly. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Void as soon as any urge is felt
options.rationale: Voiding with every urge keeps the bladder small and the urgency in control. Bladder training teaches the client to control the bladder instead.

options.text: Void at set times, even without an urge
options.rationale: Bladder training uses a fixed voiding schedule based on the client's current pattern, so the client voids at the set time whether or not an urge is present.

options.text: Start with a 4 hour interval right away
options.rationale: The first interval is based on the client's current pattern, often 30 to 45 minutes. A 4 hour start would lead to leaks and discouragement.

options.text: Use slow breathing to hold off urges
options.rationale: Relaxation and distraction help the client suppress the urge between scheduled voids, which is the core skill of bladder training.

options.text: Limit fluids to keep the bladder empty
options.rationale: Limiting fluids concentrates the urine, which irritates the bladder and raises infection risk. Fluids are spread through the day.

options.text: Lengthen the interval in small steps once dry
options.rationale: When the client stays dry between voids, the interval is lengthened by about 15 to 30 minutes at a time until 3 to 4 hours is reached.

questions.takeaway: Bladder training is for an alert client who can resist the urge: void on a schedule, suppress urges between voids, and lengthen the interval gradually once continent.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem says the client is alert and can resist the urge, which is what bladder training requires. Keep the options that build control on a schedule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Void at set times, even without an urge.
Slow breathing to hold off urges between voids.
Lengthen the interval in small steps once dry.
Voiding with every urge, a 4 hour start, and limiting fluids.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure who has wet the bed on 4 of the last 5 nights and wakes 3 times a night to void large amounts. Last week the client began taking the daily furosemide at 2000 instead of 0800 to avoid leaking during morning errands. The client has had 1 cup of tea with dinner for many years and reports a weak stream. There is no burning, and the urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 35 mL. Which contributor is most likely?

options.text: The evening diuretic dose
options.rationale: Diuretics increase urine production, often in large amounts. Moving the dose to 2000 places that output during sleep, which explains the new timing, the large night voids, and the wet bed that began last week.

options.text: The cup of tea at dinner
options.rationale: Caffeine can irritate the bladder, which makes this tempting. The tea is a habit of many years and cannot explain a change that started last week.

options.text: A urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Urgency at night can come from cystitis, but there is no burning and the urinalysis has no nitrites or white blood cells.

options.text: Overflow from retention
options.rationale: The weak stream suggests incomplete emptying, which makes this tempting. A residual of 35 mL right after voiding shows the bladder empties well, so overflow is unlikely.

questions.takeaway: When new leakage appears, look for what changed. Diuretics affect urine production, and taking one in the evening moves the large output into the night.
questions.strategy: Each distractor has a cue that makes it tempting: the tea, a weak stream, nighttime urgency. Weigh each against the data that rules it out and against the timing of the change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The furosemide moved from 0800 to 2000 last week.
Large night voids fit increased urine production.
A habit of many years cannot cause a new problem.
Negative urinalysis, no burning, residual 35 mL.

elimination.verdict: A. The evening diuretic dose.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the home bladder diary of a client with a spinal cord injury who does not sense bladder fullness and performs intermittent self catheterization every 8 hours. Each catheterization drains 650 to 750 mL, and urine leaks between catheterizations. Fluid intake is 2,000 mL spread through the day, the urine is clear yellow, and oral temperature is 36.9 °C. The client asks to switch to an indwelling catheter to stop the leaking. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Limit fluid intake to 1,000 mL a day
options.rationale: Less fluid would lower the volumes, which makes this tempting. The intake of 2,000 mL is appropriate, and limiting it concentrates the urine and raises infection risk.

options.text: Change to an indwelling catheter
options.rationale: This answers the client's request, but an indwelling catheter is a major infection risk, and intermittent catheterization is the preferred method for a neurogenic bladder. The leaking has a correctable cause.

options.text: Catheterize at shorter intervals
options.rationale: Volumes of 650 to 750 mL show the bladder is overdistended between catheterizations, and the leaking is overflow. A regular schedule that empties the bladder more often prevents distention and mucosal trauma and stops the leaking.

options.text: Catheterize only when an urge is felt
options.rationale: Catheterizing by urge works only when the client can sense fullness. This client does not, so the bladder would overfill even more.

questions.takeaway: Intermittent self catheterization works only if the schedule keeps the bladder from overfilling. Large volumes with leaking between catheterizations call for a shorter interval, not a fluid limit or an indwelling catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every option would change the volume or the leaking. Weigh the cues: intake is appropriate, sensation is absent, and the infection risk of an indwelling catheter is avoidable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 650 to 750 mL means overdistention; the leak is overflow.
2,000 mL a day is appropriate intake.
The client does not sense fullness.
An indwelling catheter adds infection risk when the schedule can be fixed.

elimination.verdict: C. Catheterize at shorter intervals.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A client who has had burning on urination for 4 days now has a high fever, chills, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Cystitis confined to the bladder
options.rationale: Burning is a lower tract symptom and can be present in pyelonephritis too. Cystitis does not explain a high fever, chills, and costovertebral angle tenderness.

options.text: Pyelonephritis involving the kidney
options.rationale: Fever and chills signal that infection has spread beyond the lower tract, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of kidney involvement. Dysuria may still be present.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis from kidney injury
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis presents with cola colored urine, facial and peripheral edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output. None of those findings are described, and fever with flank tenderness points to infection.

options.text: Urinary retention from a bladder not emptying
options.rationale: Retention causes a distended bladder and incomplete emptying. It does not explain fever, chills, and costovertebral angle tenderness.

questions.takeaway: Lower tract symptoms (dysuria, urgency) can occur in both cystitis and pyelonephritis. Fever with chills and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness are what move the infection up to the kidney.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into local bladder symptoms and systemic or kidney findings. The option that accounts for every finding wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning is lower tract; high fever, chills, and flank tenderness are systemic and kidney findings.
Costovertebral angle tenderness points to the kidney.
Cystitis explains only the burning.
Glomerulonephritis needs edema, high blood pressure, and cola colored urine, which are absent.

elimination.verdict: B. Pyelonephritis involving the kidney.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client with a recent ureteral stone is admitted with fever, tachycardia, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Which diagnostic tests should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: 24 hour urine collection for total protein
options.rationale: Measuring urine protein levels belongs to the workup for glomerulonephritis, where damaged glomeruli leak protein. It does not identify the organism or the spread of a kidney infection.

options.text: Urinalysis and urine culture with susceptibility
options.rationale: Urinalysis shows findings such as white blood cells and nitrites, and the culture identifies the organism. Susceptibility testing guides the antibiotic choice.

options.text: Blood cultures
options.rationale: Blood cultures are drawn when sepsis is a risk. Fever with tachycardia raises that risk.

options.text: Imaging of the kidneys and ureters
options.rationale: Imaging is used when obstruction or complications are suspected. A recent ureteral stone makes obstruction a real concern.

options.text: Serum creatinine and electrolytes
options.rationale: Kidney function tests and electrolytes show whether the infection is affecting kidney function and give a baseline to trend.

questions.takeaway: The pyelonephritis workup has four parts: urinalysis and urine culture, blood cultures when sepsis is a risk, kidney function tests and electrolytes, and imaging when obstruction or a complication is suspected.
questions.strategy: Match each test to a question the nurse needs answered: which organism, has it reached the blood, how are the kidneys working, and is something blocking flow. A test that answers none of these is out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Urinalysis and culture with susceptibility testing.
Fever with tachycardia justifies blood cultures.
Creatinine and electrolytes.
The recent ureteral stone justifies imaging.
Urine protein measurement is a glomerulonephritis test.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: A client with pyelonephritis is going home on a 10 day oral antibiotic. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will drink the fluid amount you told me each day."
options.rationale: Taking the prescribed fluid intake is part of the plan. This statement is correct.

options.text: "I will keep my appointment for a repeat urine test."
options.rationale: Follow up testing confirms the infection has cleared. This statement is correct.

options.text: "If the pills upset my stomach, I will stop and call."
options.rationale: Adverse effects are reported to the provider rather than handled by stopping the drug, and the full course is completed even when the client feels better. Stopping early risks a return of the kidney infection.

options.text: "I will call right away if the chills or flank pain return."
options.rationale: Fever, chills, or worsening symptoms are reported promptly. This statement is correct.

questions.takeaway: Pyelonephritis teaching: complete the full antibiotic course, report adverse effects instead of stopping, report fever, chills, or worsening, take the prescribed fluids, and keep follow up testing.
questions.strategy: In a need for further teaching item, look for the statement with one wrong step hidden inside a correct one. Calling is right; stopping the drug on its own is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Fluids, follow up testing, and calling about chills or pain are all correct.
Stopping the antibiotic for stomach upset abandons the full course.
Adverse effects are reported, not treated by stopping.

elimination.verdict: C. "If the pills upset my stomach, I will stop and call."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.scenario: A client, 67 years old, weighing 70 kg, was admitted at 0800 with pyelonephritis and started on IV antibiotics. The nurse reassesses the client at 1600.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing a client with pyelonephritis 8 hours after IV antibiotics began. For each finding at 1600, indicate whether it is expected with pyelonephritis or signals progression toward sepsis.

rows.text: Confused about the date and place, was oriented at 0800
rows.rationale: New confusion is the first warning sign in the progression from urinary infection to sepsis.

rows.text: Flank pain 6 of 10 with costovertebral angle tenderness, was 7 of 10 at 0800
rows.rationale: Flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of pyelonephritis, and the pain has not grown worse since 0800.

rows.text: Blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg, was 126/78 mm Hg at 0800
rows.rationale: Hypotension with poor perfusion is the next stage of the progression to sepsis.

rows.text: Respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, was 20 at 0800, and urine output 60 mL over the past 4 hours
rows.rationale: Rapid breathing and decreased urine output are late signs of sepsis. An output of 60 mL in 4 hours in a client weighing 70 kg is about 0.2 mL/kg per hour.

rows.text: Burning and urgency with each void
rows.rationale: Dysuria and urgency may be present with pyelonephritis because the infection usually ascends from the bladder.

rows.text: Nausea with one episode of vomiting
rows.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are associated findings in pyelonephritis.

questions.takeaway: The progression from urinary infection to sepsis runs from new confusion, to hypotension and poor perfusion, to rapid breathing and decreased urine output. Flank pain, dysuria, and nausea belong to the kidney infection itself.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each finding is the kidney infection itself or a sign that the infection is now affecting the brain, circulation, lungs, or kidney output. Changes from the 0800 baseline are the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria, urgency, and nausea are pyelonephritis findings.
New confusion, a fall in blood pressure from 126/78 to 88/52 mm Hg, a respiratory rate rising to 30, and 60 mL of urine in 4 hours.
Confusion, then hypotension and poor perfusion, then rapid breathing and low urine output.

elimination.verdict: Expected: flank pain with tenderness, burning and urgency, nausea. Sepsis progression: new confusion, hypotension, rapid breathing with low urine output.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: On day 2 of IV antibiotics for pyelonephritis, a client's creatinine and blood urea nitrogen have doubled and urine output has fallen. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Kidney function is declining
options.rationale: Creatinine is excreted only by the kidneys, so a creatinine that doubles reflects about a 50% loss of filtration. When blood urea nitrogen and creatinine rise together and output falls, the kidneys themselves are failing to clear waste.

options.text: A fluid volume deficit is raising the BUN
options.rationale: Dehydration does raise the blood urea nitrogen (BUN), but it raises the BUN faster than the creatinine. Here both values doubled at the same rate, which points to kidney dysfunction rather than low blood volume.

options.text: The infection is resolving
options.rationale: Falling urine output on day 2 is a warning sign, not a sign of recovery. Response to treatment is judged by fever, pain, and kidney function trends.

options.text: Fluid overload is causing the changes
options.rationale: Low output can lead to fluid retention, but overload is a possible result of failing kidneys, not the cause of a doubling creatinine.

questions.takeaway: Rising creatinine with falling urine output means kidney dysfunction. When BUN and creatinine rise together, the cause is the kidney itself, not dehydration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use creatinine as the kidney specific value. Then check whether the BUN rose alone or alongside the creatinine.

steps.detail: The creatinine has doubled.
BUN also doubled, so the ratio is unchanged and dehydration does not fit.
Falling urine output with a rising creatinine means the kidneys are clearing less.
Overload does not raise creatinine, and falling output is not recovery.

elimination.verdict: A. Kidney function is declining.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a client with pyelonephritis who has vomited 6 times in 2 days and has dry oral mucosa. BUN is 36 mg/dL, was 15 mg/dL on admission 2 days ago. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, unchanged since admission. Urine is dark amber, 180 mL over 8 hours, and the bladder is not palpable. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: A fluid volume deficit is raising the BUN
options.rationale: Dehydration concentrates the blood and raises the BUN faster than the creatinine. Creatinine is excreted only by the kidneys, and an unchanged value of 0.9 mg/dL shows filtration has not fallen. Vomiting, dry mucosa, and dark amber urine fit fluid loss.

options.text: Infection is damaging the kidney tissue itself
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis can damage the kidney, and the output is low, which makes this tempting. Kidney damage raises creatinine along with BUN, and the creatinine is unchanged at 0.9 mg/dL.

options.text: The antibiotic is injuring the kidneys
options.rationale: Some antibiotics can injure the kidneys, which makes this tempting. Kidney injury from any cause raises creatinine along with BUN, and the creatinine has not changed.

options.text: The bladder is not emptying completely
options.rationale: Low output can come from urine held in the bladder, but the bladder is not palpable, and retention does not explain a rising BUN with a steady creatinine.

questions.takeaway: BUN rises with dehydration as well as with kidney dysfunction. Creatinine is the kidney specific value: a high BUN with an unchanged creatinine points to low blood volume, while both rising together points to the kidney.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options blame the kidneys or the bladder for the high BUN and low output. The unchanged creatinine decides it, because any kidney injury would raise creatinine too, and the vomiting points to fluid loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: BUN 15 to 36 mg/dL; creatinine 0.9 to 0.9 mg/dL.

steps.action: Use creatinine as the kidney marker
steps.detail: No change means filtration has not fallen, which rules out infection or drug injury to the kidney.
Vomiting 6 times, dry mucosa, and dark amber urine fit fluid loss.
The bladder is not palpable.

elimination.verdict: A. A fluid volume deficit is raising the BUN.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: Two weeks after a sore throat, a client has puffy eyelids, cola colored urine, and new high blood pressure, with no fever. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Pyelonephritis from an ascending infection
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis is a kidney infection with fever, chills, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness. This client has no fever.

options.text: Cystitis with bladder inflammation
options.rationale: Cystitis causes dysuria, urgency, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. It does not cause facial edema or new high blood pressure.

options.text: Urinary retention with a full bladder
options.rationale: Retention holds urine in the bladder but does not cause cola colored urine, eyelid edema, or hypertension.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis after infection
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis may follow a bacterial infection. Damaged glomeruli leak blood into the urine, giving cola or tea colored urine, and reduced filtration causes fluid retention with facial edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis cues: cola or tea colored urine, facial and peripheral edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output, often after a recent infection. Fever and flank pain point instead to pyelonephritis.
questions.strategy: Two options name the kidney. Decide between them by asking whether the picture is infection (fever, flank pain) or fluid retention with blood in the urine (edema, hypertension, low output).

steps.detail: A sore throat 2 weeks ago can precede glomerulonephritis.
Cola colored urine, eyelid edema, and new hypertension.

steps.action: Rule out infection of the kidney
steps.detail: No fever.
Cystitis and retention do not cause edema or hypertension.

elimination.verdict: D. Acute glomerulonephritis after infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the results of a client with acute glomerulonephritis. Which results indicate glomerular injury or reduced kidney filtration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Urine protein 3+
options.rationale: Damaged glomeruli leak protein into the urine, so protein on the urinalysis is a direct sign of glomerular injury.

options.text: Negative urine nitrites
options.rationale: Nitrites point to bacteria in the urine. A negative result says nothing about the glomeruli.

options.text: Serum creatinine more than doubled recently
options.rationale: Creatinine is cleared by the kidneys, so a creatinine that more than doubles shows reduced filtration.

options.text: Hemoglobin level unchanged since the last clinic visit
options.rationale: A stable hemoglobin does not reflect glomerular leakage or filtration.

options.text: Many red blood cells in the urine
options.rationale: Damaged glomeruli also leak blood, which is why the urine can look cola or tea colored.

options.text: Elevated serum potassium
options.rationale: When filtration and urine output fall, the kidneys excrete less potassium, so the serum level rises. Electrolytes are checked for this reason.

questions.takeaway: The glomerulonephritis workup is urinalysis for protein and blood, urine protein levels, creatinine, and electrolytes. Protein and blood show leaky glomeruli; creatinine and potassium show reduced filtration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each result ask two questions: is it abnormal, and does it come from the glomerulus leaking or from the kidney filtering less? Only results that answer yes to both are selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Protein 3+ and many red blood cells.
Creatinine more than doubled and potassium elevated.
Negative nitrites relate to bacteria, not the glomerulus.
Hemoglobin does not measure kidney filtration.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with acute glomerulonephritis on a prescribed fluid and sodium restriction. Findings at 1200: blood pressure 166/100 mm Hg, was 168/102 mm Hg at 0800; urine output 25 mL/hr, unchanged since 0800, when it was reported to the provider; weight 74.2 kg, was 73.9 kg yesterday; crackles in both lower lobes with a respiratory rate of 28/min, lungs were clear with a respiratory rate of 18/min at 0800. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Blood pressure 166/100 mm Hg, was 168/102 mm Hg
options.rationale: Elevated blood pressure is an expected cue in glomerulonephritis, and it has not risen since 0800.

options.text: Crackles in both lower lobes, respiratory rate 28/min
options.rationale: Reduced filtration causes fluid retention, and fluid in the lungs is the dangerous form of it. Crackles and a respiratory rate rising from 18 to 28 since 0800 are new and show respiratory distress, which is reported immediately.

options.text: Urine output 25 mL/hr, unchanged since reported at 0800
options.rationale: Decreased urine output signals kidney dysfunction and is a serious finding, but it is unchanged since 0800 and the provider already knows it.

options.text: Weight 74.2 kg, was 73.9 kg yesterday
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid retention, and the trend is documented. A gain of 0.3 kg in a day is not the most urgent change here.

questions.takeaway: Report respiratory distress or worsening kidney function immediately. A finding that is new since the last assessment outranks a serious finding that is unchanged and already reported.
questions.strategy: Both the low urine output and the crackles are reportable. The cue that decides is the 0800 comparison: output is unchanged and the provider already knows; the crackles are new and affect breathing.

steps.detail: Blood pressure and urine output are unchanged; the lungs have changed.
Urine output was reported at 0800.
New crackles with a rising respiratory rate threaten oxygenation.
A 0.3 kg gain is documented for the trend.

elimination.verdict: B. Crackles in both lower lobes, respiratory rate 28/min.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with acute glomerulonephritis who is going home on sodium and fluid restrictions. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will weigh myself once a week and call if it rises."
options.rationale: Weight is the right measure, but it is checked daily, not weekly. A weekly weight misses fluid gained over a few days.

options.text: "I will drink extra water every day to flush my kidneys."
options.rationale: Reduced filtration causes fluid retention, so the prescribed fluid limit is followed. Extra water adds to the fluid overload.

options.text: "I will call if I become short of breath."
options.rationale: Respiratory distress signals fluid in the lungs and is reported immediately.

options.text: "I can use regular salt once the puffiness is gone."
options.rationale: The sodium restriction is part of the prescribed plan and is not stopped on the client's own judgment when the edema goes down.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis home care: follow the prescribed fluid, sodium, and dietary limits, weigh daily, take medications as ordered, and report respiratory distress or worsening kidney function immediately.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against the plan. The weekly weight option is the right idea with the wrong frequency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid and sodium limits, daily weight, report breathing changes.
Weighing is correct, but weekly is not daily.
Extra water and resuming salt break the restrictions.
Shortness of breath is reported right away.

elimination.verdict: C. "I will call if I become short of breath."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the history of a client admitted with pyelonephritis. Which findings increase this client's risk for pyelonephritis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Drinks plenty of fluid each day
options.rationale: A steady fluid intake keeps urine moving through the tract. It does not cause obstruction, reflux, or stasis.

options.text: A ureteral stone seen on recent imaging
options.rationale: A ureteral stone obstructs urine flow. Obstruction lets bacteria multiply above the blockage.

options.text: A small postvoid residual on a recent bladder scan
options.rationale: This is the right idea with one thing off: incomplete emptying is a risk, but a small residual means the bladder is emptying, so urine is not pooling.

options.text: Vesicoureteral reflux since childhood
options.rationale: Reflux carries bladder urine back up the ureter toward the kidney, giving bacteria a route from the bladder to the renal pelvis.

options.text: Spinal cord injury with urinary retention
options.rationale: Urine held in the bladder is urinary stasis. Stagnant urine lets bacteria multiply and ascend to the kidney.

options.text: Hypertension controlled with one daily drug
options.rationale: Treated hypertension does not block urine flow, reverse it, or cause it to pool, so it does not raise the risk of an ascending kidney infection.

questions.takeaway: The three pyelonephritis risk factors are urinary obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, and urinary stasis. Each one lets bacteria multiply or travel upward toward the kidney.
questions.strategy: Ask of every history item: does it block urine, push it backward, or let it sit? Only those three raise the risk of an ascending kidney infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pyelonephritis usually starts as an ascending urinary infection.
The ureteral stone blocks flow.
Vesicoureteral reflux carries urine back toward the kidney.
The spinal cord injury leaves urine sitting in the bladder.
A small residual shows the bladder empties, so there is no stasis.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client with vesicoureteral reflux has had three episodes of pyelonephritis this year, and creatinine is rising. Which long term complication is the client at greatest risk for?

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis from the repeated infections
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis can follow a bacterial infection, so this option sounds connected. It presents with cola colored urine, edema, and high blood pressure, none of which are described, and repeated pyelonephritis damages the kidney through scarring instead.

options.text: Urinary incontinence from pelvic floor weakness
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness is an incontinence risk factor. Nothing in the stem describes leakage, and reflux with repeated kidney infections threatens the kidney rather than bladder control.

options.text: Kidney scarring and lost function
options.rationale: Recurrent kidney infections can scar the kidney and cause permanent impairment. A creatinine that rises over a year of repeated infections suggests that loss has already begun.

options.text: Bacteriuria needing lifelong antibiotics
options.rationale: Most asymptomatic bacteriuria does not need antibiotics, and each episode here was a symptomatic kidney infection. This is not the long term threat.

questions.takeaway: Recurrent pyelonephritis can scar the kidney and cause permanent kidney impairment. A creatinine that climbs across repeated episodes is the cue that damage is accumulating.
questions.strategy: The cues are a repeated kidney infection plus a rising creatinine. Pick the complication that explains a slow rise in creatinine; the others describe different organs or different diseases.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Creatinine is rising across 3 kidney infections.
Repeated infection of the kidney leads to scarring.
Glomerulonephritis needs edema, high blood pressure, and cola colored urine.
Incontinence and bacteriuria do not explain a rising creatinine.

elimination.verdict: C. Kidney scarring with permanent loss of function.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client with pyelonephritis is prescribed an IV antibiotic, an analgesic, and IV fluids. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check drug allergies before the first dose
options.rationale: Antibiotics are given after an allergy check. Asking before the first dose is the step that prevents an allergic reaction to a drug the client has never received in this admission.

options.text: Hold all oral fluids during treatment
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged within prescribed limits during pyelonephritis treatment. Withholding oral fluids is not part of the prescriptions and does not rest an infected kidney.

options.text: Give the analgesic for flank pain
options.rationale: Ordered analgesics are part of pyelonephritis treatment, and flank pain is expected with a kidney infection.

options.text: Measure intake and output every shift
options.rationale: Intake and output are monitored to track hydration and to catch a fall in urine output, which can signal worsening infection or kidney dysfunction.

options.text: Teach that phenazopyridine will clear the kidney infection
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves urinary discomfort and turns urine orange or red, but it does not treat infection. The antibiotic treats the kidney infection.

options.text: Recheck vital signs and report new confusion
options.rationale: Vital signs and response to treatment are monitored to watch for worsening. New confusion is the first warning sign of progression toward sepsis.

questions.takeaway: Pyelonephritis care: antibiotics after an allergy check, ordered analgesics, fluids within prescribed limits, vital signs and intake and output, and a watch for worsening or adverse effects.
questions.strategy: Sort each option by whether it treats the infection, relieves pain, supports fluid balance, or monitors for worsening. An option that misstates what a drug does or invents a restriction is out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The allergy check comes before the first antibiotic dose.
The analgesic is ordered for the flank pain of a kidney infection.
Intake and output, vital signs, and mental status catch worsening.
Fluids are encouraged within limits, not withheld.
Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort only.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.scenario: A client, 74 years old, was admitted 48 hours ago with pyelonephritis and has received IV antibiotics since admission. The nurse compares the findings now with the findings on admission.
questions.stem: The nurse is comparing current findings with admission findings for a client with pyelonephritis. For each finding, indicate whether it shows an effective response to treatment or a response that is not effective.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.2 °C, was 39.2 °C on admission
rows.rationale: The fever that signaled spread of infection to the kidney has resolved, which shows the antibiotic is working.

rows.text: Flank pain 2 of 10, was 8 of 10 on admission
rows.rationale: Flank pain is the hallmark of kidney infection. A drop from 8 of 10 to 2 of 10 shows the inflammation is settling.

rows.text: Urine output 140 mL over the past 8 hours, was 520 mL over 8 hours on admission
rows.rationale: Falling urine output is a warning sign of progression toward sepsis or of kidney dysfunction. It needs follow up even though other findings are better.

rows.text: Heart rate 84 beats per minute, was 118 beats per minute on admission
rows.rationale: Tachycardia is an associated finding of pyelonephritis. A return to 84 beats per minute shows the systemic response is easing.

rows.text: Asking repeatedly where the client is, was oriented on admission
rows.rationale: New confusion is the first warning sign in the progression from urinary infection to sepsis. It cannot be dismissed as age related because it is new since admission.

rows.text: Eating breakfast with no nausea, was vomiting on admission
rows.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are associated findings of pyelonephritis. Eating without nausea shows the systemic illness is resolving.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate each finding against its own baseline. Resolving fever, flank pain, tachycardia, and nausea show response to treatment, but new confusion or falling urine output means worsening even when the other numbers look better.
questions.strategy: Read each row as now versus admission. A finding that moved toward normal is effective; a finding that is new or moving the wrong way is not, regardless of how the rest of the picture looks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature, pain, heart rate, and nausea all moved toward normal.
Confusion is new since admission.
Urine output fell from 520 mL to 140 mL over 8 hours.
Several good findings do not cancel two warning signs.

elimination.verdict: Effective: temperature, flank pain, heart rate, nausea. Not effective: urine output and new confusion.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: A client with an immune mediated disease and new glomerulonephritis asks, "My cousin's kidney inflammation cleared after a throat infection. Will mine?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Yes, this kind almost always clears in a few weeks."
options.rationale: This is false reassurance. Recovery from glomerulonephritis varies by cause, and the client's cause is different from the cousin's.

options.text: "This cannot happen without an infection first."
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis can occur with immune mediated disease as well as after a bacterial infection, so a missing infection does not rule it out.

options.text: "No, with an immune disease it always leads to failure."
options.rationale: The absolute word always makes this inaccurate. Severity and recovery vary, so the nurse does not promise either a full recovery or a permanent loss.

options.text: "Recovery depends on the cause, and yours differs."
