Placement was confirmed by x ray 3 days ago, and the tube was documented at 58 cm at the naris. Facility policy is to obtain an x ray if the external length, securement or respiratory status changes. At 1200 the mark is at 58 cm, the tape is intact, and the aspirate looks like formula with a pH of 6.5. The client takes no acid suppressing medication. Respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, no cough. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: The tube has likely moved out of the stomach
options.rationale: A pH above 5 can raise concern, but the length, securement and breathing all match the baseline. Under this policy none of the findings that call for an x ray is present.

options.text: Formula is raising the pH, and placement is supported
options.rationale: Formula makes pH results less reliable, and aspirate pH alone cannot confirm or rule out placement. The mark matches the documented 58 cm, the tape is intact and the respiratory status has not changed, so the findings taken together support placement.

options.text: Acid suppressing medication is raising the gastric pH
options.rationale: Acid suppressing drugs can raise gastric pH, but the client takes none. The cause named here does not fit this client.

options.text: The tube tip has likely moved into the small intestine
options.rationale: This is the near miss: intestinal fluid is less acidic, so a pH of 6.5 seems to point there. But the mark is unchanged at 58 cm, and aspirate pH cannot confirm where the tip lies.

questions.takeaway: Gastric aspirate is usually acidic (pH 5 or less), but formula and acid suppressing drugs can raise it. pH alone cannot confirm placement; interpret it with the external length, securement and respiratory status, and hold tube use only when placement is uncertain.
questions.strategy: Three options read the pH alone and each names a real cause of a higher pH. Read the pH with everything else: the matching mark, intact tape, unchanged breathing and the formula in the aspirate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mark at 58 cm as documented, tape intact, no respiratory change.
Formula in the stomach during continuous feeding can raise the pH.
The client takes no acid suppressor, and the unchanged mark argues against a tip that has moved.
No trigger for an x ray is present, so placement is supported.

elimination.verdict: B. Formula is raising the pH, and placement is supported.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.scenario: A client, 79 years old, with heart failure receives continuous feeding through a gastrostomy tube at 65 mL per hour, with 60 mL water flushes every 4 hours and water flushes before, between and after medications. The intake record lists only the formula volume; the flushes have not been recorded. Weight 66.4 kg today, was 64.2 kg 2 days ago. Both ankles have 2+ edema, were without edema 2 days ago. Crackles are heard in the bases of both lungs. Respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute 2 days ago. SpO2 92% on room air. Head of the bed at 40 degrees. No vomiting, coughing or choking during the feedings.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure who receives continuous gastrostomy tube feeding. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Add all water flushes to the intake record, and compare total intake with output
options.rationale: Flushes count as fluid intake. Without them the record hides part of what the client is receiving, so the nurse totals all intake and compares it with output.

options.text: Stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and call for help
options.rationale: This is the priority action for suspected aspiration. The client has not vomited, coughed or choked, and the crackles are in both bases with edema and weight gain, which point to fluid, not formula in the airway.

options.text: Report the weight gain, edema and lung findings to the provider
options.rationale: A gain of 2.2 kg in 2 days with new edema and crackles in a client with heart failure needs the provider's review of the fluid volume in the feeding plan.

options.text: Increase the water flushes to keep the tube from clogging
options.rationale: More water adds to the fluid the client already cannot handle.

options.text: Check the gastric residual volume before the next flush
options.rationale: Residual volume addresses gastric intolerance. It does not measure the fluid problem shown by the weight, edema and lungs.

options.text: Fluid overload
options.rationale: Weight gain over 2 days, new edema in both ankles and crackles in both lung bases in a client with heart failure fit fluid overload. Unrecorded flushes add to the intake.

options.text: Aspiration of formula
options.rationale: Aspiration usually follows vomiting, coughing or choking during feeding. None is present, and aspiration does not explain the weight gain and ankle edema.

options.text: Refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is an electrolyte shift in a severely undernourished client after nutrition restarts. Nothing here describes severe undernutrition or electrolyte results.

options.text: Dehydration
options.rationale: Dehydration causes weight loss, not a gain with edema and crackles.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight on the same scale shows whether fluid is building up or being removed.

options.text: Lung sounds and SpO2
options.rationale: Crackles and oxygen saturation show whether fluid in the lungs is worsening or clearing.

options.text: Stool frequency and consistency
options.rationale: Stool pattern tracks feeding tolerance in the gut, not fluid volume.

options.text: Gastric residual volume
options.rationale: Residual volume does not measure fluid overload and does not reliably predict aspiration.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Glucose is unrelated to the fluid findings in this scenario.

questions.takeaway: Fluid imbalance is a metabolic complication of enteral nutrition. Water flushes are part of total fluid intake; monitor intake and output, daily weights and ordered labs, and report signs of overload.
questions.strategy: Two conditions share the lung findings. Weight gain, new edema in both ankles and no vomiting or coughing during feedings separate fluid overload from aspiration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Crackles in both bases and a lower SpO2 fit both aspiration and fluid.
A 2.2 kg gain, new ankle edema and no vomiting or coughing point to fluid overload.
Count every flush in the intake, compare with output, and report the findings.
Daily weight, lung sounds and SpO2.

elimination.verdict: Add the flushes to intake and compare with output, and report the findings; fluid overload; daily weight and lung sounds with SpO2.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who takes nothing by mouth and receives 4 intermittent feedings a day through a gastrostomy tube between 0800 and 2000. The feedings are tolerated. The client says, "Next month I will fast from sunrise to sunset for Ramadan, as I do every year. I would like to keep the fast if I can." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Tell me about the fast. I can ask about an overnight pump schedule."
options.rationale: The nurse supports the client's cultural and treatment preferences and explores them. A cyclic feeding by pump over a set period, such as overnight, may fit the fast, but any change in the method or timing needs a new order.

options.text: "You can skip the daytime feedings and take larger ones after sunset."
options.rationale: Moving feedings to the evening is the right idea, but the nurse cannot change the schedule without an order. Larger volumes over a short time also add to the risk of intolerance and aspiration.

options.text: "Tube feedings do not count as eating, so you can keep your schedule."
options.rationale: This answers a religious question for the client. Whether a tube feeding breaks the fast is the client's decision, and the response closes the conversation.

options.text: "People who are ill do not have to fast, so you can skip it this year."
options.rationale: This dismisses a preference the client has stated clearly. The nurse explores the wish instead of deciding for the client.

questions.takeaway: Support emotional concerns, cultural needs and treatment preferences. Feeding methods include bolus, intermittent, continuous and cyclic (pump feeding over a set period, such as overnight); a change in method or rate is made only by order.
questions.strategy: Two options move the feeding to the night. The one that keeps the change inside an order and keeps the client talking is the better response.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client wants to keep the fast and asks if it can be done.
Telling the client what the fast allows or that fasting is not needed overrides the client's choice.
Skipping daytime feedings changes the order without approval.
Explore the fast and ask the team about an overnight cyclic schedule.

elimination.verdict: A. Explore the fast and ask about an overnight pump schedule.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating discharge teaching for a client going home with a new gastrostomy tube and bolus feedings. Weakness in both hands prevents the client from handling the syringe, so the client's adult child will give every feeding. Which findings indicate that the teaching is effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: The adult child gives a bolus feeding with flushes while the nurse watches
options.rationale: Return demonstration by the person who will do the feedings shows that the skill can be performed correctly.

options.text: The client explains every step of the feeding correctly, in order
options.rationale: Teach back is useful, but the client will not be the one giving the feedings. The adult child must show the skill.

options.text: The adult child watches a feeding and says, "I understand, that looks easy."
options.rationale: Saying "I understand" is not evidence of learning. It shows neither teach back nor return demonstration.

options.text: The adult child explains when to stop the feeding and get help
options.rationale: Teach back by the caregiver shows understanding of when to stop feeding and seek help, which is part of the required teaching.

options.text: The adult child plans to clear a blocked tube with a little cola
options.rationale: Carbonated drinks and juice are avoided for clogged tubes. This plan shows a need for more teaching.

options.text: The adult child cleans the site and names findings to report
options.rationale: Performing site care and naming the findings to report shows the caregiver can carry out tube care at home.

questions.takeaway: Use teach back and return demonstration with the person who will perform the care. Teach when to stop the feeding and seek help, site care and what to report, and that cola or juice is not used to clear a blocked tube.
questions.strategy: Ask who will do the feedings at home. Effective teaching is shown by that person, through teach back or return demonstration, not by agreement alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The adult child gives every feeding because of the client's hand weakness.
Return demonstration of the feeding and site care, and teach back about when to stop.
The client's explanation and the caregiver's "I understand" do not show the caregiver's skill.
Cola is not used to unclog a tube.

elimination.verdict: A, D, F.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a confused client receiving continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube that was documented at 56 cm at the naris after x ray confirmation. The client is found pulling at the tape, and the mark is now at 44 cm. The client is coughing, and SpO2 is 89% on room air, was 96% at 0800. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the feeding and assess breathing
options.rationale: Coughing and a fall in SpO2 from 96% to 89% during feeding point to suspected aspiration. The priority action is to stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and obtain help.

options.text: Hold tube use and obtain an x ray
options.rationale: The tube has moved 12 cm, so displacement is likely and placement must be verified before the tube is used again. That is correct, but the coughing and desaturation make the airway the first concern.

options.text: Advance the tube back to the 56 cm mark
options.rationale: Pushing the tube back in does not confirm where the tip lies and delays the response to the breathing changes.

options.text: Check the aspirate pH for placement
options.rationale: Aspirate pH alone cannot confirm placement, and testing it delays the response to the coughing and desaturation.

questions.takeaway: Suspected displacement calls for stopping tube use and verifying placement, but when respiratory signs appear during feeding, treat it as suspected aspiration first: stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and obtain help.
questions.strategy: Two options stop the tube. The coughing and the fall in SpO2 decide which complication the nurse acts on first.

steps.detail: The mark moved from 56 cm to 44 cm (displacement), and the client is coughing with SpO2 89%, was 96% (aspiration).
Breathing changes outrank verifying the tube position.
Advancing the tube and checking pH do not confirm placement and delay airway care; the x ray is right but comes after breathing is assessed.
Stop the feeding and assess breathing.

elimination.verdict: A. Stop the feeding and assess breathing.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give 3 medications through the gastrostomy tube of a client with heart failure who is on a fluid restriction. The pharmacist has confirmed that each medication is appropriate for the tube. The prescription reads: flush with 15 mL of water before, between and after medications. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Flush with 30 mL each time and record the flushes as intake
options.rationale: 30 mL is the usual flush volume, but individualized orders take precedence. This client has a fluid restriction and an order for 15 mL.

options.text: Flush with 15 mL each time and record the flushes as intake
options.rationale: The nurse follows the individualized order, gives each medication separately with a flush before, between and after, and counts the flushes in total fluid intake.

options.text: Mix the medications in 15 mL of water and give one flush
options.rationale: Medications are given separately with ordered flushes. Mixing them saves fluid but risks interactions and tube clogging.

options.text: Give them separately and omit the flush between doses
options.rationale: Giving the medications separately is correct, but skipping the ordered flush between them risks clogging the tube and mixing the drugs.

questions.takeaway: Flush before, between and after medications. The usual volume is 30 mL of water, but follow individualized orders, and include every flush in total fluid intake.
questions.strategy: Two options use the correct sequence and record the intake. The ordered volume for a client on a fluid restriction decides between them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 15 mL before, between and after medications, for a client on a fluid restriction.
30 mL is the usual volume, but the individualized order says 15 mL.
Mixing the medications and skipping the flush between doses both break the rule of separate medications with flushes.
Flush with 15 mL each time and record the flushes as intake.

elimination.verdict: B. Flush with 15 mL each time and record the flushes as intake.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients receiving enteral feeding. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Gastric residual 280 mL, was 200 mL; abdomen soft; no nausea
options.rationale: The residual rose, but gastric residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration. A soft abdomen and no nausea show no intolerance.

options.text: Three loose stools in 24 hours since an antibiotic started
options.rationale: Diarrhea needs assessment of medications, infection, contamination and formula tolerance, but it is not an immediate threat to the airway.

options.text: Pump alarming for occlusion; formula not infusing
options.rationale: A clogged tube needs gentle flushing, but a paused feeding does not threaten breathing.

options.text: Nasojejunal feeding running; head of bed flat since a bath
options.rationale: Feeding into the small intestine lowers but does not eliminate aspiration risk. Feeding with the head of the bed flat is an immediate airway risk that the nurse corrects now by raising it to 30 to 45 degrees.

questions.takeaway: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding for every tube, including small intestine tubes. A risk to the airway comes before problems that are real but not dangerous right now.
questions.strategy: Every client needs something. The one whose problem threatens the airway is seen first, and a jejunal tube does not remove that risk.

steps.detail: Head of bed flat during feeding is an airway risk; the others are tolerance, diarrhea and patency problems.
A nasojejunal tube lowers aspiration risk but does not eliminate it.
A residual under the policy limit with no intolerance, loose stools, and a clogged tube can wait a few minutes.
The client with the nasojejunal feeding and the head of the bed flat.

elimination.verdict: D. The nasojejunal feeding with the head of the bed flat.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the plans of care for clients on a medical unit. For which clients should the nurse anticipate enteral nutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cancer of the tongue; cannot chew or swallow; bowel sounds active
options.rationale: The gastrointestinal tract works, but the client cannot ingest food safely. This is the classic indication for enteral nutrition.

options.text: Extensive small bowel removal; cannot absorb nutrients from the gut
options.rationale: Enteral nutrition depends on a gut that digests and absorbs. When the tract cannot be adequately used, parenteral nutrition is anticipated.

options.text: Dysphagia after a stroke; passed a repeat swallow test; eats 90% of meals
options.rationale: Dysphagia is a risk factor, but this client now swallows safely and meets needs by mouth, so a feeding tube is not indicated.

options.text: Eats 30% of meals despite supplements; weight down 6 kg in 2 months
options.rationale: The gastrointestinal tract works, but oral intake cannot meet nutritional needs. Enteral nutrition is indicated.

options.text: Unresponsive after a head injury; bowel sounds present in all quadrants
options.rationale: The client cannot swallow or protect the airway, and the gastrointestinal tract works, so enteral nutrition is indicated.

options.text: Functional gut; declined a tube after discussing risks and benefits
options.rationale: Selection considers treatment goals and patient preferences. An informed refusal means a tube is not planned.

questions.takeaway: Anticipate enteral nutrition when the gastrointestinal tract works but oral intake is unsafe or not enough to meet needs, consistent with the client's goals and preferences. When the tract cannot digest or absorb, anticipate parenteral nutrition.
questions.strategy: Check two things for each client: can the gut digest and absorb, and is eating unsafe or inadequate? Then check the client's preference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client with extensive small bowel removal cannot absorb nutrients, so parenteral nutrition fits.
The client after a stroke now swallows safely and eats 90% of meals.
An informed refusal rules out the tube.
Cancer of the tongue, intake of 30% with weight loss, and unresponsiveness with bowel sounds present.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.scenario: A client admitted 3 weeks ago with undernutrition receives continuous gastrostomy tube feeding at 60 mL per hour for 24 hours. Weight 49.0 kg on admission, 49.8 kg 2 days ago, 51.6 kg today. Both ankles have new 1+ edema today. Sacral pressure injury 2 cm, was 3 cm on admission. Phosphorus 2.0 mg/dL, was 3.4 mg/dL on admission. Pump shows 1,420 mL delivered in the past 24 hours. Grip strength is stronger, and the client naps once a day, was 3 times a day on admission.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response to enteral feeding of a client with undernutrition. For each finding, indicate whether it shows progress or requires follow up.

rows.text: Sacral pressure injury 2 cm, was 3 cm
rows.rationale: Poor wound healing is a sign of undernutrition. A wound that is shrinking shows that nutrition is supporting healing.

rows.text: Weight 49.8 kg 2 days ago, was 49.0 kg on admission
rows.rationale: A gain of 0.8 kg over about 19 days is gradual and fits the rebuilding of body tissue.

rows.text: Weight 51.6 kg today, was 49.8 kg 2 days ago, with new ankle edema
rows.rationale: A gain of 1.8 kg in 2 days with new edema is too fast to be tissue. It points to fluid imbalance, which needs intake and output review and reporting.

rows.text: 1,420 mL of formula delivered in the past 24 hours
rows.rationale: The prescribed amount is 1,440 mL. Delivery that nearly matches the prescription shows the client is receiving the planned nutrition.

rows.text: Phosphorus 2.0 mg/dL, was 3.4 mg/dL on admission
rows.rationale: A falling phosphorus during nutrition support is an electrolyte imbalance and can signal a dangerous shift. The nurse reports it.

rows.text: Stronger grip and one nap a day, was 3 naps a day
rows.rationale: Muscle weakness and fatigue are signs of undernutrition. Their improvement shows response to the feeding.

questions.takeaway: Monitor the response to feeding with weight, wound healing, strength and energy, formula delivered versus prescribed, intake and output, and ordered laboratory results. A rapid gain with edema is fluid, not nutrition, and a falling phosphorus is an electrolyte problem.
questions.strategy: Two weight rows look alike. The rate of gain and the new edema separate tissue from fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.8 kg over about 19 days is gradual; 1.8 kg in 2 days with new edema is fluid.
Phosphorus fell from 3.4 mg/dL to 2.0 mg/dL during feeding.
1,420 mL delivered of 1,440 mL prescribed.
A smaller wound, stronger grip and fewer naps show progress.

elimination.verdict: Requires follow up: the 2 day weight gain with edema and the falling phosphorus. The other four show progress.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A client receiving feedings through a small bore nasogastric tube develops a bowel obstruction, and gastric decompression is prescribed. Which tube should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A small bore nasojejunal feeding tube
options.rationale: A nasojejunal tube places formula in the small intestine. It is a feeding tube and does not drain the stomach.

options.text: The current small bore tube set to suction
options.rationale: Small bore tubes are single lumen and used only for feeding and medications. They are too narrow for decompression and collapse under suction.

options.text: A large bore double lumen nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Large bore, double lumen nasogastric tubes are used for gastric decompression and lavage, which is what this client now needs.

options.text: A small bore tube advanced into the duodenum
options.rationale: Moving a small bore tube deeper still leaves a single lumen feeding tube that cannot decompress the stomach.

questions.takeaway: Small bore tubes are for feeding and medications only. Gastric decompression needs a large bore, double lumen nasogastric tube.
questions.strategy: Three options are small bore tubes. Ask what each tube is built to do: feed or drain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gastric decompression, not feeding.
Small bore, single lumen tubes feed; large bore, double lumen tubes decompress.
The nasojejunal tube, the current tube on suction and the duodenal tube are all small bore feeding tubes.
A large bore double lumen nasogastric tube.

elimination.verdict: C. A large bore double lumen nasogastric tube.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: The nurse reads the x ray result confirming placement of a newly inserted small bore nasogastric tube. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Inject air and listen over the stomach
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation does not reliably verify placement, and the x ray has already confirmed it.

options.text: Measure nose to earlobe to xiphoid again
options.rationale: That measurement estimates insertion length before the tube is placed. It does not help once the tube is in.

options.text: Wait for a second x ray before feeding
options.rationale: One documented x ray confirmation is enough to begin use. A repeat film delays nutrition without a reason.

options.text: Mark and record the length at the naris
options.rationale: Marking and documenting the external length at the exit site sets the baseline for every later placement check.

questions.takeaway: After x ray confirmation, mark and document the tube length at the exit site. Every ongoing check compares the external length with that baseline.
questions.strategy: Placement is already confirmed. Look for the step that makes later checks possible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The x ray result is in and confirms placement.
Later checks need a documented baseline length.
Air auscultation is unreliable, remeasuring is a step done before insertion, and a second x ray is not needed.
Mark and record the length at the naris.

elimination.verdict: D. Mark and record the length at the naris.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with decreased consciousness who receives continuous nasogastric feeding. Which actions should the nurse take to reduce aspiration risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lay the client flat to turn with the pump running
options.rationale: Lowering the head of the bed while formula is running raises the risk of reflux and aspiration.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees during feeding is the core aspiration prevention measure.

options.text: Rely on residual volume alone to judge risk
options.rationale: Gastric residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration. It is interpreted with vomiting, distention and other findings.

options.text: Check the external length and securement
options.rationale: A tube that has moved can deliver formula into the esophagus. Checking the length against the baseline and keeping the tube secured reduces that risk.

options.text: Switch to bolus feeding to shorten feeding time
options.rationale: A bolus delivers a larger volume over a short period, which increases reflux. It does not lower aspiration risk.

options.text: Monitor for reflux and vomiting
options.rationale: Reflux and vomiting are warning signs that formula may reach the airway, so the nurse watches for them throughout the feeding.

questions.takeaway: Prevent aspiration by keeping the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees, verifying placement and securement, and monitoring reflux, vomiting and intolerance. Residual volume alone is not a safety check.
questions.strategy: Test each action: does it keep formula moving down and out of the airway?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees, length and securement checks, and monitoring for reflux and vomiting.
Lying flat with the pump running invites reflux.
Residual volume alone does not predict aspiration.
A larger volume in a short time increases reflux.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.stem: Before an intermittent nasogastric feeding, which finding should cause the nurse to hold the feeding?

options.text: External mark at the documented length
options.rationale: A mark that matches the baseline supports correct placement.

options.text: New cough and hoarse voice
options.rationale: New respiratory findings raise concern that the tube has moved or formula has been aspirated. Tube use is held until placement and breathing are assessed.

options.text: Aspirate pH of 4 with a gastric appearance
options.rationale: An acidic aspirate fits gastric placement and is used with the overall assessment.

options.text: Bowel sounds active in all quadrants
options.rationale: Active bowel sounds fit a working gastrointestinal tract and support feeding.

questions.takeaway: Compare respiratory status with the baseline before each feeding. A new cough or voice change makes placement uncertain, so tube use is held for further assessment.
questions.strategy: Three findings support feeding. The one that is new and involves breathing is the one that stops it.

steps.detail: Matching mark, acidic aspirate and active bowel sounds all support feeding.
A new cough and hoarse voice involve the airway.
Breathing concerns come before giving formula.
New cough and hoarse voice.

elimination.verdict: B. New cough and hoarse voice.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with delayed gastric emptying who receives continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube. The client has vomited formula twice today with the head of the bed at 45 degrees. Bowel sounds are active. The provider expects the client to resume eating in about 10 days. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Hold feedings and request parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: Vomiting is tempting as a reason to stop using the gut, but bowel sounds are active and the intestine works. Parenteral nutrition is for a gastrointestinal tract that cannot be adequately used.

options.text: Request a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy
options.rationale: A gastrostomy gives long term access, but it still delivers formula into a stomach that empties slowly, so the vomiting and aspiration risk remain.

options.text: Request a direct percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy
options.rationale: Feeding into the jejunum fits the delayed gastric emptying, but this is a long term surgical route. About 10 days of feeding calls for a less invasive nasal tube.

options.text: Request a nasojejunal feeding tube
options.rationale: Feeding past the stomach bypasses the delayed gastric emptying and may reduce aspiration risk, and a nasal route is preferred when feeding is needed for a short time.

questions.takeaway: Route selection weighs two things: where the tube should end (gastric emptying and anatomy) and how long it is needed (nasal for short term, gastrostomy or jejunostomy for long term).
questions.strategy: Each distractor answers one cue. Only one option fits both the slow stomach and the 10 day timeline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Delayed gastric emptying with vomiting means formula should go past the stomach.
About 10 days means a short term, nasal route.
Parenteral nutrition ignores a working gut; the gastrostomy still feeds the stomach; the jejunostomy is right on site but too invasive for 10 days.
A nasojejunal feeding tube.

elimination.verdict: D. Request a nasojejunal feeding tube.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to resume intermittent feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube that was confirmed by x ray 2 days ago. Overnight the client retched and vomited forcefully three times. The external mark is at the documented length, and the tape is intact. The client has no cough, and breathing is unlabored. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?

options.text: Placement is supported because the mark is unchanged
options.rationale: An unchanged mark is reassuring, but forceful vomiting can move the tip up into the esophagus without changing the length at the naris.

options.text: Placement is supported if the aspirate is acidic
options.rationale: Aspirate pH is used according to policy, but pH alone cannot guarantee correct placement, especially after an event that may have moved the tip.

options.text: Placement is uncertain and must be verified
options.rationale: Forceful vomiting is a known cause of tube displacement. When placement is uncertain, the nurse holds tube use and obtains further verification before giving formula.

options.text: The vomiting reflects intolerance, not displacement
options.rationale: Vomiting is a sign of intolerance and needs assessment, but it does not rule out displacement. Both must be considered before the feeding resumes.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing checks compare the length, securement and respiratory status with the baseline, but an event that can move the tip makes placement uncertain even when the mark has not changed. Hold tube use and verify.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options sound reassuring or explain the vomiting. The forceful vomiting overnight is the cue that outweighs the unchanged mark and the normal breathing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mark at the documented length, tape intact, no cough.

steps.action: Find the cue that outweighs them
steps.detail: Forceful vomiting three times can move the tip without changing the external length.
The mark and pH alone do not confirm placement after this event, and calling it intolerance ignores possible displacement.
Placement is uncertain and must be verified.

elimination.verdict: C. Placement is uncertain and must be verified.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

skills.title: Cardiac Assessment
skills.subtitle: Pulse and apical pulse, cardiac monitoring, recording and reading a 12 lead ECG, heart sounds, and a heart failure home visit

questions.stem: Before giving digoxin, the nurse cannot palpate the apical impulse on a client with large breasts. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Lift the breast and auscultate the apex for 1 minute
options.rationale: The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line. A client with large breasts is asked to lift the breast. The impulse cannot be felt in every client, and the count is still made by listening for 1 full minute.

options.text: Count the radial pulse for 1 full minute instead
options.rationale: A full minute is right, but the site is wrong. An impulse that cannot be felt is not a reason to change sites, and the apical pulse is heard, not only felt.

options.text: Auscultate the right 2nd intercostal space for 1 minute
options.rationale: A full minute with the diaphragm is right, but this is the aortic area. The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line.

options.text: Lift the breast and auscultate the apex for 30 seconds, doubled
options.rationale: The site and the breast are handled correctly, but the apical pulse before digoxin is counted for 1 full minute.

questions.takeaway: The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line. Listen with the diaphragm for 1 full minute. Ask a client with large breasts to lift the breast. Not feeling the impulse is not a reason to switch sites.
questions.strategy: Each option gets something right, and two options match on site and breast. Check the site first, then the length of the count.

steps.detail: 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line.
1 full minute, by listening.
The client lifts the breast.
An impulse that cannot be felt is common and expected in some clients.

elimination.verdict: Have the client lift the breast, listen at the 5th intercostal space on the left midclavicular line, and count 1 full minute.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is locating the apical pulse of a client by landmarks. Place the steps in the order the nurse performs them.

options.text: Move just to the left of the sternum into the 2nd intercostal space
options.rationale: The 2nd intercostal space lies just beside the angle of Louis, so it is the first space the nurse can name with certainty.

options.text: Find the sternal notch between the clavicles
options.rationale: The sternal notch is the starting landmark.

options.text: Place the diaphragm and count for 1 full minute
options.rationale: Listening comes after the site is found, and the count is a full minute.

options.text: Find the angle of Louis, the ridge on the sternum
options.rationale: The angle of Louis is the next landmark below the notch.

options.text: Count down to the 5th intercostal space on the left midclavicular line
options.rationale: From the 2nd space, the nurse counts down the spaces along the midclavicular line to the 5th.

questions.takeaway: To find the apical pulse: sternal notch, angle of Louis, 2nd intercostal space just to the left, then down the midclavicular line to the 5th space, then listen for 1 full minute.
questions.strategy: Start with the landmark that cannot be mistaken, the notch, and let each step name the next one. The space cannot be counted until the 2nd space has been found.

steps.detail: The sternal notch.
The angle of Louis comes next, below the notch.
2nd intercostal space, just left of the angle of Louis.
Midclavicular line to the 5th space, then listen.

elimination.verdict: Notch, angle of Louis, 2nd space, down the midclavicular line to the 5th space, listen for 1 full minute.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give digoxin to a client. The apical pulse, counted for 1 full minute, is 56/min and regular. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. The client is alert and says, "My pulse is always in the fifties. My doctor knows about it." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the digoxin and document the client's statement
options.rationale: The client's report and the lack of symptoms matter, but the rate is below the range wanted before digoxin. The nurse does not decide alone that a low rate is acceptable; the statement is reported, not acted on.

options.text: Hold the digoxin and report the rate to the provider now
options.rationale: Before digoxin the heart rate should be within 60 to 100/min. At 56/min the dose is held, and the report gives the provider both the rate and the client's statement so a decision can be made now.

options.text: Hold the digoxin and recheck the rate before the next dose
options.rationale: Holding is right, but a held dose and the reason are reported at the time. Whether a rate in the fifties is acceptable for this client is the provider's decision, and without a report the client simply misses the medication.

options.text: Recount the apical pulse and give the digoxin if it is higher
options.rationale: The first count was already a full apical minute with a regular rhythm. A recount only looks for a number that permits the dose.

questions.takeaway: Count the apical pulse for 1 full minute before digoxin. The adult range wanted is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Below 60, hold the dose and report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Two options hold the dose. The deciding cue is who may accept a rate below 60 beats per minute: the provider, today, not the nurse and not the next shift.

steps.detail: Apical 56 beats per minute for a full minute.
60 to 100 beats per minute before digoxin.
It is reported, not acted on alone.
One reports now. One leaves the decision until the next dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the digoxin and report the rate with the client's statement.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: Before cardiac monitoring, the nurse notes an alert client's chest is damp with sweat and has thick hair. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Dry the skin, then press and tape electrodes over the hair
options.rationale: Drying is right, but hair still prevents good contact, and tape does not fix that.

options.text: Obtain consent, shave, and apply electrodes to the damp skin
options.rationale: Consent and hair removal are right, but the skin must be dry.

options.text: Dry the skin and shave the sites with consent
options.rationale: Skin should be clean and dry with good contact. With the client's consent, chest hair may be shaved to allow contact.

options.text: Dry the skin, shave the sites, then explain the shaving
options.rationale: Both problems are solved, but consent comes before shaving. This client is alert.

questions.takeaway: For cardiac monitoring the skin must be clean and dry with good electrode contact. Chest hair may be shaved, with the client's consent.
questions.strategy: Check three things in each option: dry skin, hair removed, and consent given first.

steps.detail: Moisture and hair.

steps.action: Drop options that leave one unsolved
steps.detail: Tape over hair, or damp skin.

steps.action: Compare the two that solve both
steps.detail: Consent before shaving, or explanation after.

elimination.verdict: Dry the skin and, with consent, remove hair at the electrode sites.

questions.objective: Consider when cardiac monitoring may be used for a patient and how the clinician might apply this

questions.nursesNote: 1030, review of a 12 lead ECG recorded as a routine baseline: Calibration box is 2 large squares high and speed is 25 mm per second. One P wave comes before each QRS complex. PR interval is 7 small squares on every beat. QRS width is 2 small squares. R waves are evenly spaced, 4 large squares apart. ST segment is raised above the baseline in leads II, III and aVF.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a 12 lead ECG recorded as a routine baseline. Highlight the findings that are outside the expected range and must be reported.

segments.text: Calibration box is 2 large squares high and speed is 25 mm per second
segments.rationale: This is the standard calibration: 1 millivolt equals 2 large squares, and the speed is 25 mm per second.

segments.text: One P wave comes before each QRS complex
segments.rationale: One P wave per QRS is the expected finding.

segments.text: PR interval is 7 small squares on every beat
segments.rationale: The PR interval should be 3 to 5 small squares. Consistently longer could indicate first degree heart block.

segments.text: QRS width is 2 small squares
segments.rationale: The QRS should be 3 small squares or less, so 2 small squares is within range.

segments.text: R waves are evenly spaced, 4 large squares apart
segments.rationale: The rhythm is regular, so 300 divided by 4 gives 75 beats per minute, within the adult range of 60 to 100 beats per minute.

segments.text: ST segment is raised above the baseline in leads II, III and aVF
segments.rationale: ST elevation could indicate myocardial infarction. Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall of the heart.

questions.takeaway: Read an ECG in order: clean trace, calibration, rhythm, one P per QRS, measurements (PR 3 to 5 small squares, QRS 3 or less, rate by the 300 rule), then scan for ST and T wave changes.
questions.strategy: Take each line of the note as one of the six steps and test it against its normal. Two lines fail: one measurement and one finding from the scan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 large squares and 25 mm per second: correct.
PR 7 is long. QRS 2 is in range. 300 divided by 4 is 75 beats per minute.
ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF needs review now.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: While the nurse records a 12 lead ECG, the client talks and shifts, and the baseline is thick and wavy. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Send the printout with a note that the client moved
options.rationale: A note is honest, but interference should be sorted at the point of recording. A poor trace can hide or mimic changes.

options.text: Replace all electrodes and record the ECG again at once
options.rationale: Recording again is right, but the cause is movement and talking. New electrodes do not remove it, and the second trace will look the same.

options.text: Estimate the rate from the visible R waves and report it
options.rationale: Reporting is reasonable, but a rate taken from a poor trace may be wrong, and the trace can be fixed now.

options.text: Have the client lie still and quiet, and repeat it
options.rationale: The first step in interpreting an ECG is a clean trace. Interference is fixed at the time of recording, so the cause is removed by having the client lie still with the hands relaxed at the sides and not talk, and the ECG is recorded again.

questions.takeaway: Step 1 of reading a 12 lead ECG is a clean trace. Fix interference at the point of recording and record again if in doubt.
questions.strategy: Two options record again. Only one removes the cause stated in the stem, movement and talking.

steps.detail: Talking and moving during the recording.

steps.action: Ask whether it can be fixed now
steps.detail: Yes: the client lies still and the ECG is repeated.

steps.action: Drop the options that miss the cause
steps.detail: A note, an estimated rate, or new electrodes.

elimination.verdict: Have the client lie still and quiet, and record again.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who reports chest pain that began 20 minutes ago, rated 6 of 10. A 12 lead ECG recorded 5 minutes ago shows a clean trace, correct calibration, and no ST elevation in any lead. The pain is still 6 of 10. A colleague says, "There is no ST elevation. Let the client rest." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Record a second ECG now to compare with the first
options.rationale: Repeat ECGs are real practice, which makes this tempting, but the first trace is 5 minutes old, clean, and correctly calibrated. A second recording delays the report of pain that has lasted 20 minutes.

options.text: Recheck vital signs and the pain rating in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Monitoring vital signs is right, but the pain has already been reassessed and is unchanged at 6 of 10. Waiting 15 minutes delays the report.

options.text: Report the ongoing pain and get the ECG reviewed
options.rationale: A myocardial infarction can be present without ST elevation. The pain is unchanged, so the nurse reports now and has the ECG reviewed by a competent clinician.

options.text: Check lead placement and repeat the ECG
options.rationale: The trace was clean and correctly calibrated. Nothing suggests a recording error, and repeating it delays the report.

questions.takeaway: ST elevation could indicate myocardial infarction, but an infarction can be present without it. Ongoing chest pain is reported, and a competent clinician reviews the ECG.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Three options do something useful before reporting. The deciding cues are that the pain is unchanged at 6 of 10 after 20 minutes and that the ECG is already clean and 5 minutes old, so nothing needs to come before the report.

steps.action: Separate the ECG from the client
steps.detail: ECG: no ST elevation. Client: pain still 6 of 10.
An infarction can be present without ST elevation.
A repeat ECG and vital signs are useful, but not before the report.
Clean trace and correct calibration.

elimination.verdict: Report the ongoing chest pain and the ECG now for review.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.scenario: The home health nurse is visiting a client with heart failure. The client's furosemide was increased from 40 mg to 80 mg once a day last week because of weight gain and swollen ankles. The client's spouse weighs the client every morning and keeps the record. The client also takes simvastatin 80 mg at night.
questions.stem: For each finding at today's visit, indicate whether it is an expected finding or requires follow up.

rows.text: Weight is 2 kg lower than before the dose was increased
rows.rationale: The diuretic was increased to remove extra fluid. A lower weight shows it is working.

rows.text: The client reports feeling light headed when standing up from the bed
rows.rationale: A doubled diuretic can remove too much fluid. Light headedness on standing is a new symptom that needs assessment and reporting.

rows.text: Respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 97% and no increased shortness of breath
rows.rationale: These findings show no sign that fluid is affecting the breathing.

rows.text: The client says the simvastatin has been skipped for the last 3 nights
rows.rationale: Medication adherence is part of the assessment. A missed medication is explored and addressed with the client.

rows.text: Radial pulse is 62 beats per minute and regular, the hand is warm, and capillary refill is 2 seconds
rows.rationale: The rate is within 60 to 100 beats per minute, the rhythm is regular, and the limb is well perfused.

rows.text: The spouse is tearful and says, "I am not sleeping. I lie awake listening to the breathing."
rows.rationale: A holistic assessment includes the wellbeing of the family. A caregiver who is not sleeping needs attention and support.

questions.takeaway: After a diuretic increase, a lower weight with a respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, pulse and capillary refill in range is expected. New light headedness on standing, missed medication, and a caregiver who is not sleeping each need follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into what the dose was meant to achieve and what is new or going wrong. Follow up is not only for abnormal vital signs: adherence and the caregiver count too.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the goal of the change
steps.detail: Less fluid: lower weight, less swelling.
All in range.
A new symptom, a missed medication, and a tearful caregiver.

elimination.verdict: The lower weight, the breathing findings, and the right radial pulse findings are expected. Light headedness, skipped simvastatin, and the spouse's distress require follow up.

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

questions.stem: A client with heart failure had a diuretic dose increase last week. Which statement by the home health nurse best explores how the client is managing?

options.text: "You have been taking the new dose every morning, haven't you?"
options.rationale: This is a leading question. It invites the client to agree and makes a missed dose harder to admit.

options.text: "Tell me how things have been since the dose changed."
options.rationale: An open question lets the client describe what matters most, including problems the nurse did not think to ask about.

options.text: "How is your breathing today compared with last week?"
options.rationale: This is open, but it covers one symptom on one day, not how the client has been managing since the change.

options.text: "What side effects have you noticed since your water pill was increased?"
options.rationale: This is open in form, but it limits the answer to side effects and assumes there are some.

questions.takeaway: Open questions let the client tell the nurse how things are going. A leading question or a question limited to one topic narrows what the client will say.
questions.strategy: Three options are questions the client can answer at length. Match each to the stated goal: how the client has been managing since the change.

steps.detail: "Haven't you?" invites agreement.
One asks only about breathing today.
One assumes side effects.
"Tell me how things have been."

elimination.verdict: "Tell me how things have been for you at home since your water pill was increased."

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has an S2 at the pulmonic area that splits on inspiration and is single on expiration. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Report a new abnormal heart sound to the provider
options.rationale: Reporting is right for a new abnormal sound, but a second heart sound that splits only on inspiration is a normal finding.

options.text: Move to the 5th intercostal space, where S2 is loudest
options.rationale: The second heart sound is loudest at the aortic and pulmonary areas, where the nurse already is. The mitral area is where the first heart sound is best heard.

options.text: Document a murmur at the pulmonic area for routine review
options.rationale: A murmur is an extra sound. Here the second heart sound itself divides, and only on breathing in, which is a normal finding and not a murmur.

options.text: Document the split S2 and continue the assessment
options.rationale: On inspiration more blood returns to the right side of the heart, so the pulmonary valve closes slightly after the aortic valve. This physiologic splitting of the second heart sound is expected.

questions.takeaway: S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, loudest at the 2nd intercostal spaces. A split on inspiration that disappears on expiration is physiologic and expected.
questions.strategy: A client with heart failure and an unusual sound pulls toward reporting. The deciding detail is the timing: two sounds only on breathing in.

steps.detail: S2, heard at the pulmonary area.
Split on inspiration, single on expiration.
Physiologic splitting is expected.
S2 is loudest at the base, not the apex.

elimination.verdict: Document the split on inspiration and continue the assessment.

questions.objective: Identify how to undertake cardiac auscultation and what these sounds represent in relation to the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: The nurse is starting 5 lead continuous cardiac monitoring for a client with heart failure. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Select lead II for the monitor display
options.rationale: Lead II is usually selected for monitoring because it is easily interpreted.

options.text: Place the right arm electrode just below the right clavicle
options.rationale: The right arm electrode sits under the right clavicle near the shoulder, on the chest and inside the rib cage frame.

options.text: Place the leg electrode on the upper left thigh
options.rationale: The leg electrode is placed on the chest, at the lower edge of the left rib cage below the pectoral muscles, not on the limb.

options.text: Place the chest electrode at the 4th intercostal space, left sternal margin
options.rationale: The space is right but the side is wrong. On a 5 lead system this electrode sits at the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin.

options.text: Set alarm limits to this client's condition
options.rationale: Alarm limits are set based on the client's clinical condition, so they warn of change that matters for this client.

options.text: Leave the low heart rate alarm at the unit default
options.rationale: A default limit ignores the client's condition. Every alarm limit, high and low, is set based on this client's clinical condition.

questions.takeaway: For continuous monitoring: lead II on display, electrodes on the chest within the rib cage frame, the 5th electrode at the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin, and alarm limits set to the client's condition.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement on its own. For electrode positions, check two things: is it on the chest inside the rib cage frame, and is it on the correct side.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lead II, easily interpreted: correct.
Right arm under the right clavicle is correct. The leg electrode belongs on the lower left rib cage. The chest electrode belongs at the right sternal margin.
Set to the client's condition, not left at default.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Consider when cardiac monitoring may be used for a patient and how the clinician might apply this

questions.stem: A new 12 lead ECG has a clean trace, but the calibration box is only 1 large square high. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Measure the PR interval, QRS width, and heart rate
options.rationale: Measurements are step 5. With the wrong calibration the trace cannot be interpreted accurately, so this comes too early.

options.text: Scan every lead for ST and T wave changes
options.rationale: Scanning the leads is the last step. With the wrong calibration the size of ST changes would be misjudged.

options.text: Correct the calibration and record the ECG again
options.rationale: The calibration box should be 2 large squares high, equal to 1 millivolt. A box of 1 large square fails step 2, so the nurse fixes it and records again before interpreting the trace.

options.text: Check the lead II strip for sinus rhythm
options.rationale: This is step 3, the right next step only after calibration is confirmed. Here calibration has failed.

questions.takeaway: Read a 12 lead ECG in order: clean trace, calibration (2 large squares at 25 mm per second), sinus rhythm on lead II, one P wave per QRS, measurements, then scan the leads. A failed step is fixed before you move on.
questions.strategy: Check each step against the client's trace in order. The first step that fails decides the action, even when a later step sounds more useful.

steps.detail: The trace is clean, so step 1 passes.
The box is 1 large square, not 2. Step 2 fails, so later steps wait. Eliminate A, B and D.

elimination.verdict: C. Fix the calibration and record again before interpreting the trace.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client on continuous cardiac monitoring who reports palpitations. The lead II rhythm strip, recorded at 25 mm per second, shows spaces between R waves that vary from 2 to 4 large squares with no pattern. The first two R waves are 3 large squares apart. The nurse counts 12 R waves within 30 large squares. Which heart rate should the nurse document?

options.text: 120/min, from 12 R waves in 30 large squares times 10
options.rationale: With an irregular rhythm the rate is found by counting the R waves in 30 large squares, which is 6 seconds, and multiplying by 10. This gives 120 beats per minute, above the expected range.

options.text: 100/min, from 300 divided by the first R to R interval
options.rationale: The 300 rule is a correct method, but only for a regular rhythm. Here the spacing varies from 2 to 4 large squares, so one pair of R waves does not represent the rate, and the result falsely sits inside the expected range.

options.text: 75/min, from 300 divided by the widest R to R interval
options.rationale: The widest space gives the slowest beats only. With an irregular rhythm, no single R to R space gives the rate.

options.text: 110/min, from 11 R to R intervals in 30 large squares times 10
options.rationale: The 6 second method and the multiplier are right, but the method counts R waves, not the spaces between them. 12 R waves have only 11 spaces, so this undercounts by 1 beat in every 6 seconds.

questions.takeaway: Use 300 divided by the large squares between R waves only when the rhythm is regular. When it is irregular, count the R waves in 30 large squares (6 seconds) and multiply by 10.
questions.strategy: Two methods are both correct ways to calculate a rate. The deciding cue is in the stem: the R to R spacing varies with no pattern, so the rhythm is irregular and only the 6 second count applies.

steps.detail: R to R spacing varies from 2 to 4 large squares: irregular.
Any 300 rule answer uses one space that does not represent the rate.
30 large squares is 6 seconds, so multiply by 10.
12 R waves times 10 is 120 beats per minute, above 60 to 100.

elimination.verdict: 120 beats per minute, from 12 R waves in 30 large squares multiplied by 10.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: A client with ongoing chest pain has ST elevation in leads V1 through V4 only. Which actions and interpretations are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Report changes in the inferior, right coronary artery area
options.rationale: The inferior leads are II, III and aVF. V1 to V4 are the septal and anterior leads.

options.text: Report changes in the left anterior descending artery area
options.rationale: V1 and V2 are septal and V3 and V4 are anterior; both groups are supplied by the left anterior descending artery.

options.text: Conclude that changes in only four leads rule out infarction
options.rationale: ST elevation in any group of leads could indicate a myocardial infarction. The number of leads does not rule it out.

options.text: Report the ongoing pain and ST elevation now
options.rationale: ST elevation could indicate a myocardial infarction, and the pain is still present, so the report cannot wait.

options.text: Stop reassessing pain if a later ECG shows no ST elevation
options.rationale: A myocardial infarction can occur without ST elevation, so ongoing pain still needs assessment and reporting.

options.text: Ask a clinician skilled in ECG interpretation to review it
options.rationale: The nurse asks a competent clinician to help interpret the ECG and confirm the findings.

questions.takeaway: Septal V1 and V2 and anterior V3 and V4 reflect the left anterior descending artery; inferior II, III and aVF the right coronary artery; lateral I, aVL, V5 and V6 the circumflex. ST elevation with ongoing pain is reported now, and an infarction can occur without ST elevation.
questions.strategy: First match the leads to their artery, then decide what the finding means for this client: ongoing pain plus ST elevation is an urgent report, with expert help to interpret.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: V1 to V4 are septal and anterior: left anterior descending. Keep B; eliminate A.
ST elevation with pain could be an infarction, and its absence does not rule one out. Keep D; eliminate C and E.
A competent clinician reviews the trace. Keep F.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F. Name the artery, report now, and get expert interpretation.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse auscultating a client's heart cannot tell which sound is S1. Which finding identifies S1?

options.text: The sound that is louder at the right 2nd intercostal space
options.rationale: The aortic area is where the second sound, the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, is loudest.

options.text: The sound that splits on inspiration
options.rationale: Splitting on inspiration belongs to the second sound, because the pulmonary valve closes slightly later when more blood returns to the right heart.

options.text: The shorter, sharper of the two sounds
options.rationale: The second sound is short and sharp. The first sound is long and loud.

options.text: The sound louder at the left 5th intercostal space
options.rationale: The first sound is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing at the start of systole, and it is best heard at the mitral and tricuspid areas. At the mitral area, the left 5th intercostal space near the midclavicular line, it is the louder sound.

questions.takeaway: S1 is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing at the start of systole: long, loud, and loudest at the mitral and tricuspid areas. S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing: short, sharp, loudest at the 2nd intercostal spaces, and split on inspiration.
questions.strategy: Link each sound to its valves, then to the area named after those valves. Three options describe S2 features; the remaining one is the S1 cue.

steps.detail: Loudest at the aortic area, split on inspiration, short and sharp are all S2. Eliminate A, B and C.
S1 is the atrioventricular valves, so it is loudest at the mitral area. D remains.

elimination.verdict: D. The sound that is louder at the mitral area is S1.

questions.objective: Identify how to undertake cardiac auscultation and what these sounds represent in relation to the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to record a 12 lead ECG for an alert client. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm the client's name and date of birth
options.rationale: Identity is confirmed with the name and date of birth before the recording, so the trace belongs to the right client.

options.text: Ask about chest pain at this moment
options.rationale: Asking about chest pain at the moment of recording is part of preparing the client, and chest pain is one of the reasons a 12 lead ECG is recorded.

options.text: Have the client sit upright with hands in the lap
options.rationale: Relaxed hands are right, but the position is wrong. The client lies back on the bed with the hands relaxed and flat at the sides, which reduces movement interference.

options.text: Place the limb electrodes on the chest, inside the rib cage
options.rationale: Inside the rib cage frame is the placement for continuous monitoring. For a 12 lead ECG the 4 limb electrodes go on the wrists and ankles.

options.text: Palpate the chest to locate electrode landmarks
options.rationale: The chest is palpated to find the landmarks for the chest electrodes, so each one is placed accurately.

options.text: Apply electrodes first, then explain and gain consent
options.rationale: Explanation and consent are right, but they come before the client is touched. This client is alert.

questions.takeaway: Before a 12 lead ECG: confirm name and date of birth, explain and gain consent, ask about chest pain, have the client lie back with the hands relaxed flat at the sides, palpate the chest for landmarks, and place the limb electrodes on the wrists and ankles.
questions.strategy: Check each option for the one detail that is off: the position, the limb electrode site, or the point at which consent is gained.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Name and date of birth first; consent before touching the client.
Chest pain now is asked about.
Lying back, hands relaxed flat at the sides, not sitting.
Chest landmarks by palpation; limb electrodes on wrists and ankles, not the chest.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: On a lead II monitor, a client's P waves and QRS complexes suddenly point downward. The client is unchanged. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the right arm and leg electrode positions
options.rationale: In lead II the right arm electrode is negative and the leg electrode is positive. The wave normally travels toward the leg electrode and points upward, so a sudden downward trace with no change in the client suggests the electrodes were moved or swapped.

options.text: Report a new conduction problem to the provider now
options.rationale: The client is unchanged, and the most likely cause is electrode position. Check the equipment before reporting a rhythm change.

options.text: Document the downward complexes as the new baseline
options.rationale: The trace changed suddenly with no change in the client. Recording it as baseline accepts a probable equipment error.

options.text: Switch the display to a different lead
options.rationale: Lead II is usually selected because it is easily interpreted. Changing leads hides the problem instead of finding its cause.

questions.takeaway: A wave moving toward a positive electrode gives an upward deflection. In lead II the leg electrode is positive and the right arm negative, so the normal trace points up. A sudden downward trace in an unchanged client points to electrode position first.
questions.strategy: When the monitor changes but the client does not, suspect the equipment. Check the electrodes before you report or accept the new trace.

steps.detail: The client is unchanged, so the trace change is likely technical.
Reporting, recording a new baseline or switching leads all skip the check. Eliminate B, C and D.

elimination.verdict: A. Check the right arm and leg electrode positions first.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse hears a whooshing sound that begins just after S2 and ends before the next S1. Which interpretations are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The mitral and tricuspid valves are open
options.rationale: After the second sound the aortic and pulmonary valves are closed and the mitral and tricuspid valves open so the ventricles can fill.

options.text: The ventricles are relaxed and filling
options.rationale: This is diastole, when the ventricles relax and fill, with atrial contraction at the end.

options.text: The aortic and pulmonary valves are open
options.rationale: These valves are open during systole, between the first and second sounds. They close to make the second sound.

options.text: The left ventricle is pumping blood to the body
options.rationale: Pumping to the body happens in systole, after the first sound. This sound comes after the second sound.

options.text: It falls in diastole, which begins at S2
options.rationale: The second sound marks the start of diastole, and the first sound marks the start of systole. A sound between them is diastolic.

options.text: It falls in systole, which begins at S1
options.rationale: The first sound marks the start of systole, so a sound that ends as the first sound begins lies in diastole, not systole.

questions.takeaway: S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing at the start of diastole. Between S2 and the next S1 the ventricles relax and fill through open mitral and tricuspid valves, so a sound there is diastolic.
questions.strategy: Anchor the sound to the heart sound it follows. After S2 is diastole, and the valve positions and ventricle activity follow from that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It follows S2, the start of diastole. Keep E; eliminate F.
Mitral and tricuspid valves open, ventricles filling. Keep A and B; C and D describe systole. Eliminate C and D.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E. The sound falls in diastole, while the ventricles fill.

questions.objective: Identify how to undertake cardiac auscultation and what these sounds represent in relation to the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client admitted 2 days ago with pneumonia. The radial pulse has been documented at 64 to 70/min, regular, at every check since admission. Today the radial pulse is 98/min and regular, oxygen saturation is 95% on room air, capillary refill is 2 seconds, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document the findings and recheck at the next scheduled time
options.rationale: Each value sits inside its expected range, but the pulse has risen by 28 to 34 beats per minute from this client's own documented rate. Pulse assessment gives a baseline so that change can be identified, and waiting hides that change.

options.text: Reassess the client now and report the rise in pulse rate
options.rationale: The pulse has risen from 64 to 70 beats per minute at every check to 98 beats per minute. A change from the client's own baseline is acted on even when the number is still in range, so the nurse reassesses and reports it.

options.text: Recount the pulse and document it if it remains in range
options.rationale: Rechecking is reasonable, but the plan accepts any rate within the adult range. It still compares the pulse only with that range, not with this client's usual rate of 64 to 70/min.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L/min and recheck the saturation
options.rationale: The saturation of 95% is within the expected range, and starting oxygen treats one number before the client has been reassessed. The finding that has changed is the pulse.

questions.takeaway: Pulse is assessed alongside oxygen saturation, blood pressure and capillary refill, and it gives a baseline of what is usual for the client. A clear change from that baseline needs action even when every value is still within the expected range.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible because every value is in range. The deciding cue in the stem is the documented rate of 64 to 70 beats per minute at every check since admission.

steps.detail: Every value is within its expected range.
Pulse 98 against a usual 64 to 70 beats per minute: a clear change.
Documenting, or recounting against 100 beats per minute, ignores the baseline.
Oxygen for a saturation inside the range skips reassessment.

elimination.verdict: Reassess now and report the rise from the client's usual pulse rate.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

skills.title: Infusion Therapy
skills.subtitle: IV solution types, blood product safety, access devices and PICC teaching, delegation, and local and systemic complications

questions.stem: A client with a head injury and low blood pressure has a new prescription for 0.45% sodium chloride. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Start the infusion with hourly neurologic checks
options.rationale: Hourly neurologic checks are good care, but 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic. It moves water into cells, including brain cells, and it is contraindicated with head trauma and low blood pressure.

options.text: Start the infusion at a slower rate
options.rationale: A slower rate still moves water into brain cells. The problem is the type of fluid, not the speed.

options.text: Hold the infusion and question the prescription
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with head trauma, raised pressure in the skull and low blood pressure. This client has both a head injury and low blood pressure, so the order is questioned before it starts.

options.text: Hang 0.9% sodium chloride instead
options.rationale: An isotonic fluid may well be what this client needs, but the nurse cannot change the type of fluid without an order.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid (0.45% or 0.225% sodium chloride) moves water into cells. Do not give it with head trauma, raised pressure in the skull, low blood pressure or third spacing. Question the order before starting.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options give the ordered fluid and one changes it without an order. Ask what the fluid does once it is in the vein, then match that against the head injury.

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic.
Into cells, including brain cells.
Head injury and low blood pressure: both are contraindications.
Question the order. Do not swap fluids without one.

elimination.verdict: C. Hold the hypotonic fluid and question the prescription.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the IV fluid orders for six clients on a medical surgical unit.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the IV fluid prescriptions for six clients on a medical surgical unit. For each client, indicate whether the ordered fluid is appropriate or the order should be questioned.

rows.text: A client bleeding after a car crash, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, ordered 0.9% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and is used for volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation.

rows.text: A client with new confusion and serum sodium 118 mEq/L, ordered 3% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: 3% sodium chloride is the hypertonic fluid for severe hyponatremia. Sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance are watched closely.

rows.text: A client with ascites from fluid shifting into the abdomen, ordered 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Third spacing is a contraindication to hypotonic fluid. More water would leave the vessels.

rows.text: A client with blood glucose 48 mg/dL, ordered D10W
rows.rationale: D10W is a hypertonic dextrose solution used for hypoglycemia.

rows.text: A client with intracranial pressure 24 mm Hg, ordered D5W as the continuous maintenance fluid
rows.rationale: Once the body uses the dextrose, D5W leaves free water. It acts as a hypotonic fluid and moves water into brain cells.

rows.text: A client about to receive packed red blood cells, ordered Lactated Ringer's to prime the blood tubing
rows.rationale: Blood products run with 0.9% sodium chloride only.

questions.takeaway: Match the fluid to where the water goes. Isotonic stays in the vessels, hypertonic pulls water out of cells, hypotonic pushes water into cells. D5W behaves as hypotonic once the dextrose is used.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Judge each row on its own. For each fluid ask where the water goes, then ask whether that helps or harms this client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.9% isotonic. 3% and D10W hypertonic. 0.45% hypotonic. D5W acts as hypotonic once the dextrose is used.
Third spacing and raised intracranial pressure rule out hypotonic fluid.
0.9% sodium chloride only with blood.
