elimination.verdict: Appropriate: rows 1, 2 and 4. Question: rows 3, 5 and 6.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.stem: The nurse is receiving a client with diabetic ketoacidosis from the emergency department, where the blood pressure was 82/50 mm Hg and the client received 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride. Blood pressure is now 118/72 mm Hg, heart rate 92/min, and the client is alert and oriented. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L. The provider prescribes 0.45% sodium chloride at 150 mL/hour. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Question the prescription before starting the infusion
options.rationale: This is the near miss: hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with low blood pressure, and the blood pressure was 82/50 mm Hg in the emergency department. It is now 118/72 mm Hg after 2 L of isotonic fluid, so the contraindication is no longer present.

options.text: Start the infusion and monitor sodium and neurologic status
options.rationale: In diabetic ketoacidosis, hypotonic fluid follows the initial isotonic resuscitation. The blood pressure is in range, the client is alert and the sodium is high, so the order fits. Sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance are the checks.

options.text: Request a change to Lactated Ringer's solution
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid was the first step and the blood pressure has recovered. Lactated Ringer's does not give the cells the free water a sodium of 147 mEq/L calls for.

options.text: Hold the infusion until a repeat sodium level results
options.rationale: The sodium is already known to be above range. Waiting delays the ordered next step of the fluid plan.

questions.takeaway: Diabetic ketoacidosis fluid plan: isotonic fluid first to restore volume, then hypotonic fluid once the blood pressure has recovered. Hypotonic fluid is unsafe while blood pressure is low.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options seem defensible: start the hypotonic fluid, or question it because of the emergency department blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg. The deciding cue is the current blood pressure, 118/72 mm Hg.

steps.action: Find where the client is in the plan
steps.detail: 2 L of isotonic fluid already given.
Blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg: no longer low.
147 mEq/L: water is needed in the cells.
Lactated Ringer's adds no free water. Waiting for a repeat sodium delays care.

elimination.verdict: B. Start the infusion and monitor sodium and neurologic status.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.stem: The bedside check for a unit of packed red blood cells is complete. The client has a 22 gauge IV with Lactated Ringer's infusing. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Start an 18 or 20 gauge IV with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Blood needs an 18 or 20 gauge catheter and 0.9% sodium chloride only. This solves both problems with the current line.

options.text: Use the 22 gauge IV with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: The solution is now right, but a 22 gauge catheter is smaller than the 18 to 20 gauge needed for blood.

options.text: Infuse the unit through the existing line
options.rationale: Verification is complete, but the line is the wrong size and Lactated Ringer's cannot run with blood.

options.text: Keep the unit at the bedside until a new IV is placed later
options.rationale: Packed red cells must be infused within 4 hours of issue. A new line is needed now, not later in the shift.

questions.takeaway: Every blood product needs two nurse verification, an 18 to 20 gauge catheter and 0.9% sodium chloride only. Packed red cells are infused within 4 hours of issue.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: The verification is done, which makes using the current line tempting. Check two things in each option: the catheter size and the solution.

steps.detail: 22 gauge is too small. Blood needs 18 to 20.
Lactated Ringer's cannot run with blood.
4 hours from issue: do not wait until the end of the shift.

elimination.verdict: A. Start an 18 or 20 gauge IV with 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse receives a prescription to transfuse packed red blood cells. Baseline vital signs are recorded. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Pick up the unit from the blood bank
options.rationale: The unit is collected only after consent is confirmed, so this comes second.

options.text: Confirm signed consent is on file
options.rationale: Consent must be on file before the unit is picked up from the blood bank. It is the first step.

options.text: Verify the unit with a second nurse at the bedside
options.rationale: Two licensed nurses verify the unit at the bedside, which is after the unit has been collected.

options.text: Reassess vital signs at the bedside
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs are already recorded. The next reassessment is 15 minutes after the transfusion starts.

questions.takeaway: Blood order: consent on file, then pick up the unit, then two nurse bedside check, then start, then vital signs at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes and at completion.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Anchor the first step. Consent comes before the unit leaves the blood bank, and every other option needs the unit in hand or the transfusion running.

steps.detail: Baseline vital signs are recorded; the unit has not been picked up.
Consent must be on file before the unit is retrieved.
Pick up, two nurse bedside check, start, then recheck at 15 minutes.

elimination.verdict: B. Confirm signed consent is on file.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing the IV site of a client receiving 0.9% sodium chloride. Which findings indicate infiltration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cool, pale skin around the site
options.rationale: Fluid in the tissue cools the skin and makes it pale: a sign of infiltration.

options.text: Edema around the site
options.rationale: Fluid leaking into the tissue causes swelling around the site.

options.text: A slowed drip rate
options.rationale: Fluid going into the tissue meets resistance, so the drip slows.

options.text: No blood return on aspiration
options.rationale: The course lists absent blood return with infiltration because the catheter tip may have left the vein. On its own it can also mean a positional or blocked catheter, so read it together with the cool, pale, swollen site.

options.text: No redness or streak along the vein
options.rationale: Redness and a streak are signs of phlebitis. Their absence does not point to infiltration.

options.text: Capillary refill of 2 seconds beyond the site
options.rationale: Normal capillary refill shows circulation beyond the site is intact. It is not a sign of infiltration.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration: cool, pale skin, edema, a slowed drip and no blood return. Phlebitis: pain, redness, warmth, a streak and a cord along the vein.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into infiltration, phlebitis or normal. Only the infiltration findings are selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool, pale, swollen.
Slowed drip, no blood return.
No phlebitis signs and a normal capillary refill.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing the forearm IV site of a client receiving an IV antibiotic through a 20 gauge catheter. There is mild swelling at the site, redness and warmth along the vein, a red streak 3 cm above the site, and a firm cord when the vein is palpated. Pain at the site is 5 of 10. The infusion runs at the prescribed rate, and there is a blood return. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Flush the catheter and continue the infusion
options.rationale: The blood return rules out infiltration, but redness, warmth, a streak and a cord mean the vein wall is inflamed. The catheter does not stay.

options.text: Remove the catheter, elevate the arm, and apply a compress
options.rationale: This is the infiltration plan, with the compress chosen for the solution. Swelling is present, but the skin is warm and red with a streak and a cord, not cool and pale, and blood still returns. That points to phlebitis.

options.text: Remove the catheter, apply warm moist heat, and notify the provider
options.rationale: Redness, warmth, a streak and a palpable cord are phlebitis. The plan is stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade.

options.text: Stop the infusion, leave the catheter, and apply a warm moist compress
options.rationale: The compress is right, but a catheter in an inflamed vein is removed, not saved.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis: pain, redness, warmth, a streak and a palpable cord. Stop, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options stop and remove the catheter. The swelling suggests infiltration. The deciding cue is warm, red skin with a cord and a blood return, which means phlebitis, not the cool, pale skin of infiltration.

steps.detail: Red, warm, streak, cord: phlebitis.
A blood return does not make an inflamed vein safe.
Warm moist compress and notify for phlebitis. Elevate and compress by solution for infiltration.

elimination.verdict: C. Remove the catheter, apply warm moist heat, and notify the provider.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.scenario: The tubing of a client's central line separates at the hub while the client is sitting up in a chair. Within a minute the client reports sudden shortness of breath and chest pain. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg, heart rate is 124 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation is 86%. A churning sound is heard over the heart.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client whose central line tubing has separated at the hub. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Return the client to bed on the left side with the head down
options.rationale: Left lateral Trendelenburg traps the air in the right side of the heart, away from the lungs.

options.text: Lay the client flat on the back with the legs raised
options.rationale: A shock position does not trap the air in the right side of the heart. The left side with the head down does.

options.text: Clamp the catheter
options.rationale: Clamping stops more air from entering the vein.

options.text: Remove the central line
options.rationale: The line is clamped, not removed, in this emergency.

options.text: Flush the line with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Flushing pushes more of what is in the line into the vein.

options.text: Fluid overload
options.rationale: Fluid overload builds over hours of infusion. This began within a minute of the line opening.

options.text: Catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Infection brings fever and chills over time, not a sudden onset after a disconnection.

options.text: Speed shock
options.rationale: Speed shock follows a fast infusion, with flushing, headache and chest tightness. Nothing was infusing fast.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: An open line, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, low blood pressure and a churning sound over the heart.

options.text: Urine specific gravity
options.rationale: This does not guide care in the next minutes.

options.text: Blood pressure
options.rationale: 82/48 mm Hg shows the heart is struggling to pump.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Temperature does not track an air embolism.

options.text: Appearance of the insertion site
options.rationale: The problem is in the heart and lungs, not at the skin.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: 86% shows the air is blocking blood flow to the lungs.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, low blood pressure and a churning murmur after air enters a line. Clamp the tubing, turn onto the left side head down, call rapid response and give 100% oxygen.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Link the timing to the event: an open central line, then sudden breathing and chest symptoms. Then choose actions that stop more air and keep the air away from the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Central line open at the hub.
Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a churning sound.
Clamp.
Left side, head down.
Oxygen saturation and blood pressure.

elimination.verdict: Clamp the catheter and turn onto the left side head down. Air embolism. Watch oxygen saturation and blood pressure.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client going home with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will cover the site when I shower."
options.rationale: Showering is allowed with a waterproof cover over the site.

options.text: "I can swim laps once the site heals."
options.rationale: The arm is not submerged: no swimming and no baths while the PICC is in.

options.text: "No blood pressure cuffs on my PICC arm."
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuffs and no needle sticks on the PICC arm.

options.text: "If the flush is hard to push, I will push harder."
options.rationale: Resistance during a flush means stop and do not use the line. Force can break the catheter.

options.text: "I will call if my temperature reaches 38.2 °C."
options.rationale: A fever above 38 °C is a warning sign to report at once.

options.text: "I can carry my 20 lb laundry basket with that arm."
options.rationale: Heavy lifting over 10 lb with the PICC arm is avoided.

questions.takeaway: PICC teaching: keep the dressing dry, shower with a cover, no swimming, no blood pressure cuff or needle sticks on that arm, nothing over 10 lb, never force a flush, and report a fever above 38 °C.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement as true or false against the PICC rules: water, that arm, lifting, flushing and fever.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shower with a cover. No swimming.
No blood pressure cuff, no lifting over 10 lb.
Resistance means stop.
Above 38 °C: call.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The registered nurse is making assignments for a licensed practical nurse (LPN) and assistive personnel (AP). Which task is appropriate to delegate?

options.text: Ask the LPN to hang checked platelets
options.rationale: Starting any blood product stays with the registered nurse, even after the check.

options.text: Ask the AP to decide whether an IV comes out
options.rationale: The AP can report how a site looks. Deciding what the finding means is the registered nurse's judgment.

options.text: Ask the LPN to start a heparin infusion
options.rationale: Heparin is a high alert IV medication, which the registered nurse gives.

options.text: Ask the LPN to flush an established IV line
options.rationale: Flushing an established line is within the LPN's role, per the state practice act. The registered nurse stays accountable.

questions.takeaway: The registered nurse keeps insertion, site selection, starting blood, high alert IV drugs, interpreting findings and teaching. The LPN can monitor sites, flush established lines and hang non high alert fluids. AP take vital signs and report what a site looks like.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Each option hands off a real task. Ask whether the task needs judgment, starts blood or involves a high alert drug.

steps.detail: Platelets: registered nurse.
Deciding a catheter comes out: registered nurse.
Heparin: registered nurse.
Flushing an established line: LPN.

elimination.verdict: Delegate the flush of an established line to the LPN.

questions.objective: RN Responsibility & Delegation

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing vascular access plans for four clients receiving non vesicant therapy. For which client is a midline catheter the best fit?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride for 2 days after minor surgery
options.rationale: Short term isotonic fluid can run through a short peripheral IV, which is less invasive than a midline.

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Total parenteral nutrition requires central access. A midline is not used for it, however long the therapy lasts.

options.text: A continuous vasopressor for several days
options.rationale: A midline is not used for continuous vasopressors. Over several days a continuous vasopressor needs central access.

options.text: An IV antibiotic at home for 3 weeks
options.rationale: Therapy longer than 6 days warrants a midline or PICC. A midline can dwell up to 4 weeks and suits non vesicant antibiotics, so it is the less invasive choice.

questions.takeaway: Choose access by duration and solution. Short term isotonic fluid: short peripheral IV. Non vesicant therapy longer than 6 days, up to 4 weeks: midline. Total parenteral nutrition or continuous vasopressors: central line.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each client: how long, and what is going in. Total parenteral nutrition and a continuous vasopressor go straight to a central line, and 2 days of fluid does not need a midline.

steps.detail: Total parenteral nutrition and a continuous vasopressor need a central line.
2 days of isotonic fluid fits a short peripheral IV.
3 weeks of a non vesicant antibiotic is longer than 6 days and under 4 weeks: midline.

elimination.verdict: D. An IV antibiotic at home for 3 weeks.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The nurse observes a student insert a peripheral IV for an older adult with lymphedema of one arm after mastectomy. Which student actions require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Selected a 22 gauge catheter
options.rationale: A 22 to 24 gauge catheter is recommended for older adults with fragile veins and is enough for maintenance fluid.

options.text: Scrubbed with chlorhexidine back and forth for 30 seconds
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine applied with a back and forth scrub for at least 30 seconds is the correct prep.

options.text: Fanned the site to speed drying
options.rationale: The antiseptic must air dry completely. Fanning, blotting or wiping is not done.

options.text: Palpated the vein again after the prep
options.rationale: Touching the cleansed site again with unsterile fingers contaminates it and cancels the prep.

options.text: Kept advancing after the client reported shooting pain
options.rationale: Shooting pain, burning, numbness or tingling during insertion signals nerve injury. Insertion stops immediately, the catheter is removed and neurologic function is assessed.

options.text: Chose a hand vein on the lymphedema arm as backup
options.rationale: The lymphedema arm after mastectomy is avoided. Dorsal hand veins are also avoided in older adults when possible.

questions.takeaway: Air dry the chlorhexidine without fanning, never touch the site again after prep, stop at once for shooting pain or tingling during insertion, and avoid the arm on the mastectomy side and the dorsal hand in older adults.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Read each action against three checklists: the skin prep steps, the sites to avoid and the nerve injury signs. Select only what breaks a rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scrub for 30 seconds is right. Fanning and touching the site again are wrong.
The lymphedema arm and the dorsal hand are wrong for this client.
Shooting pain during advancement means stop, not finish.
A 22 gauge catheter needs no follow up.

elimination.verdict: C, D, E, F.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: A client with a central line has new fever, chills, hypotension, and confusion. The lungs, urine, and insertion site show no other source. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Fever, chills, hypotension and new confusion with no other source in a client with a central line point to a catheter related bloodstream infection. Treatment is blood cultures twice, IV antibiotics, and catheter removal if needed.

options.text: One set of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotics are right, but blood cultures are drawn twice, not once.

options.text: A warm moist compress over the insertion site
options.rationale: This is a phlebitis intervention. The site has no redness, and the findings point to the bloodstream.

options.text: An oral antipyretic and a temperature recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: An antipyretic treats the fever but not its source. Fever, chills, hypotension and new confusion with a central line call for cultures and antibiotics, not watchful waiting.

questions.takeaway: Catheter related bloodstream infection: fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status with no other source. Draw blood cultures twice, start IV antibiotics and remove the catheter if needed.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: First rule out every other source the stem hands you: lungs, urine and site. What is left with a central line is the bloodstream infection. Then match each treatment to the complication it belongs to.

steps.detail: Clear lungs, clear urine, clean site: the line is the source.
No redness for phlebitis; an antipyretic treats the fever, not the source.
A and B share antibiotics; cultures are drawn twice, not once.

elimination.verdict: A. Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client, 87 years old, receiving hospice care in a long term care facility who has had poor oral intake for 3 days. The client is alert and oriented, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 96/min, and the oral mucous membranes are dry. The provider prescribes fluid replacement. Three peripheral IV attempts with a vein illumination device have failed. Ultrasound guided insertion would require transfer to the hospital, and the hospice plan of care documents the client's wish to avoid transfer. Which route should the nurse recommend to the provider?

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion in the abdomen at about 1 mL per minute
options.rationale: Subcutaneous infusion is used for mild to moderate dehydration in older and palliative clients and is avoided only in severe dehydration or shock. The abdomen is a common site and about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate. It needs no transfer.

options.text: Hospital transfer for ultrasound guided IV insertion
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the standard for difficult access, but it requires a transfer the client has declined, and mild to moderate dehydration in a palliative client can be treated subcutaneously.

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion in the thigh at about 5 mL per minute
options.rationale: The route and site are right, but about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate for subcutaneous infusion.

options.text: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia
options.rationale: Intraosseous access does deliver all IV fluids when IV access fails, but it is for emergencies such as cardiac arrest or trauma and is limited to 24 hours. This client is alert with a blood pressure in range.

questions.takeaway: When IV access fails, match the alternative to the client's goals and urgency. Ultrasound guided insertion is the standard for difficult access. Subcutaneous infusion (hypodermoclysis) suits mild to moderate dehydration in older or palliative clients at about 1 mL per minute and is avoided in severe dehydration or shock. Intraosseous access is for emergencies and is limited to 24 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible: ultrasound guided IV insertion, the standard for difficult access, and subcutaneous infusion. The deciding cue is the documented wish to avoid hospital transfer, with findings that show neither severe dehydration nor shock.

steps.detail: Alert, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per minute: not shock, not an emergency.
Ultrasound requires a hospital transfer the client has declined.
Intraosseous access is for cardiac arrest, trauma or pediatric emergencies and lasts 24 hours at most.
Same route, but the rate limit is about 1 mL per minute, not 5.

elimination.verdict: A. Subcutaneous infusion in the abdomen at about 1 mL per minute.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment
